The antibacterial activity of the SPIONs under AMF is attributed to several effects resulting from the heat generated by the SPIONs. 33 These include direct thermal damage to bacterial cells, disruption of biofilms and enhanced immune response. 34 The thermal energy can denature bacterial proteins, disrupt membrane integrity, and induce oxidative stress, which causes cell death. 35 Heating at the site further increases the permeability of bacterial cell membranes, thus allowing the uptake of co-delivered antibiotics and enhancing their antimicrobial effects.

## Underlying Mechanisms for SPION-Mediated Hyperthermia

The efficacy of SPION-mediated hyperthermia is predicated on several key scientific mechanisms. The heat generated by SPIONs under an AMF is primarily due to hysteresis losses and the Néel and Brownian relaxation mechanisms. 36 Hysteresis losses occur as the magnetic moments of the NPs attempt to align with the oscillating magnetic field, resulting in energy dissipation as heat. 37 The Néel relaxation mechanism involves the reorientation of magnetic moments within the NPs, while Brownian relaxation pertains to the physical rotation of the entire NP in response to the magnetic field. 38 Furthermore, The selection of appropriate magnetic field parameters is crucial for optimizing the therapeutic efficacy of MHT. The frequency of the AMF typically ranges from 100 kHz to 1 MHz, and the amplitude ranges 5–15 kA/m. 30 These parameters must be carefully balanced to achieve sufficient heating without causing excessive non-specific heating of surrounding tissues. 39 Additionally, the concentration of SPIONs at the target site is a critical determinant of therapeutic outcomes, necessitating efficient targeting strategies to maximize the accumulation of NPs at the infection site. 40 , 41

The therapeutic outcome of SPIONs as a thermal ablation of bacterial pathogens is not only determined by the macroscopic temperature elevation of a nanoparticle suspension. Instead, bactericidal efficacy depends on the localised thermal dose delivered directly to the bacterial cell wall as well as in the viscoelastic microenvironment of the biofilm matrix. Specific absorption rate (SAR) and intrinsic loss power (ILP) provide complementary measures of SPION heating performance. SAR describes the heat generated per unit mass of magnetic material, whereas ILP partially normalizes SAR for differences in alternating magnetic field amplitude and frequency. ILP is most informative within the linear-response regime and should not be treated as an invariant material constant because aggregation, nonlinear magnetization reversal, and magnetic saturation can alter the expected field dependence. Accordingly, both parameters should be reported with particle concentration, normalization basis, dispersion medium, AMF conditions, and exposure duration.

Experimental studies demonstrate that heating efficiency cannot be predicted from saturation magnetization or particle size alone. Kallumadil et al reported maximum ILP values of approximately 3.1 nH m 2 kg −1 for commercial colloids containing 12 nm crystallites and 70 nm hydrodynamic particles, while nominally similar production batches exhibited different ILP values because of variations in crystallite size. 42 Ansari et al subsequently identified a nonlinear dependence of ILP on SPION size and dopant composition, with midsized Mn-substituted ferrites providing the most favorable operating region; ILP correlated more strongly with coercivity and remanence than with saturation magnetization. 43 Surface engineering is similarly important: Vassallo et al showed that coating-induced improvements in dispersion increased heating by modifying aggregation and magnetostatic interactions. Nanocubes can also produce exceptionally high SAR through enhanced anisotropy and hysteretic losses. 44

For antibacterial applications, SAR and ILP are useful only when they translate into an effective thermal dose within the biofilm. Nguyen et al demonstrated that SPION-mediated heating dispersed Pseudomonas aeruginosa biofilms and, when combined with gentamicin, produced an approximately 2-log reduction in viable biofilm and planktonic cells. 45 Future antibacterial studies should therefore correlate SAR and ILP with biofilm-localized temperature, bacterial log reduction, antibiotic sensitization, and host-cell safety rather than reporting final bulk temperature alone.

## Antibacterial Mechanism of Action of SPIONs

The mechanism of action of Fe 3 O 4 NPs as antibacterial therapeutics is multifaceted and involves several key processes ( Figure 2 ). One primary mechanism includes the generation of reactive oxygen species (ROS) 46 and Fenton-like reactions. 47 Upon interaction with biological environments, the ROS generated initiate a genotoxic mechanism that results in DNA damage. Additionally, Fe 3 O 4 mimics peroxidase-like activity through the Fenton reaction, catalyzing the decomposition of hydrogen peroxide (H 2 O 2 ) to produce highly reactive hydroxyl radicals ( • OH) and superoxide radicals (O 2 •- ). These ROS play a pivotal role in inducing oxidative stress within bacterial cells Notably, IONPs compromise the integrity of bacterial cell walls where ROS can oxidize lipids, leading to lipid peroxidation and disruption of membrane integrity. A microscopic analysis revealed the direct interaction between IONPs and cell walls of Staphylococcus aureus ( S. aureus ). 48 Through electrostatic interactions, Fe 3 O 4 NPs adhere to the bacterial cell surface, leading to disruption of membrane integrity and permeability. 46 This disruption compromises the structural integrity of the bacterial membrane, causing leakage of intracellular components and eventual cell lysis. 49 Furthermore, ROS-induced oxidative stress can cause protein denaturation and DNA damage, ultimately resulting in bacterial cell death. The diagram illustrates the antibacterial mechanisms of iron oxide nanoparticles. Superparamagnetic iron oxide nanoparticles are shown interacting with bacterial cells through adsorption and diffusion or endocytosis. Inside the cell, reactive oxygen species are generated, leading to DNA damage, enzyme protein degradation and lipid membrane oxidation. Fenton′s reaction is depicted as iron ions react with hydroxyl radicals and hydrogen peroxide, producing more reactive species. Membrane depolarization and enzyme protein inactivation are also shown. The diagram includes anti-biofilm actions, with nanoparticles disrupting bacterial biofilms through high temperature, mechanical vibrations and cell membrane vibrations. The process involves free iron ions and the generation of reactive oxygen species, contributing to the antibacterial effect. Iron oxide nanoparticles: ROS generation, Fenton′s reaction, biofilm disruption.

Fe 3 O 4 NPs also possess a high surface area and can directly interact with bacterial cell membranes. Metal ions exhibit a propensity to bind with thiol (-SH), amino (-NH), and carboxyl (-COOH) groups of proteins, including enzymes, leading to their inactivation or partial inhibition. 50 Additionally, IONPs were found to suppress expressions of antibiotic resistance genes (ARGs) in antibiotic-resistant bacteria typically encountered in clinical settings. 49 Mechanistic insights suggest that IONPs disrupt the function of F0/F1-ATPase, impeding H+ flow across membranes and altering the redox potential. 51 Such antimicrobial actions attributed to IONPs are consistent across various studies and are shared by other metal oxide NPs. 52 Moreover, NPs with smaller dimensions were implicated in inhibiting DNA replication through inactivating topoisomerases. 53 Electron microscopic studies indicated direct interaction of Fe 2 O 3 NPs with cell walls of Escherichia coli ( E. coli ). 54 IONPs can penetrate the cytoplasm, accumulate, induce vacuole formation, and disrupt cell walls.

Fe 3 O 4 IONPs exhibit distinct antimicrobial mechanisms, particularly effective against gram-negative bacteria due to their ability to concentrate between the outer and inner membranes of bacterial cell walls. 55 This concentration is facilitated by the binding of Fe 3 O 4 IONPs to the formate hydrogen lyase (FHL) complex in the inner membrane, enhancing their antimicrobial efficacy against these bacteria. 51 The bactericidal and antibiofilm activities of Fe 3 O 4 IONPs are well-documented. For instance, positively charged and neutral IONPs significantly reduce Streptococcus mutans biofilms more effectively than negatively charged IONPs, likely due to better electrostatic interactions with the bacterial cell surface. 56 Moreover, Fe 3 O 4 IONPs coated with oleic acid prevented biofilm formation by S. aureus and Pseudomonas aeruginosa , suggesting that surface modifications can enhance the antibiofilm properties of these NPs. 57 The physicochemical characteristics of IONPs, including surface charge, hydrophobicity, and a high surface area-to-volume ratio, facilitate their adsorption onto and penetration into bacterial biofilms, disrupting the biofilm matrix and impairing bacterial communication and survival. 58

Beyond the intrinsic oxidative, membrane-disruptive, and antibiofilm effects described above, recent magnetic nanoplatforms increasingly exploit the simultaneous generation of thermal, mechanical, and catalytic stresses. These mechanisms are closely interconnected because the same Fe 3 O 4 -based platform can produce heat under an alternating magnetic field, undergo field-driven displacement or rotation, and catalyze ROS formation through iron-mediated reactions. Luo et al developed hyaluronic acid-coated MnFe 2 O 4 nanoparticles that combined magnetic hyperthermia with quorum-sensing interference. 59 Downregulation of agrA, agrC , and hld weakened bacterial stress responses, improved nanoparticle penetration, and enhanced treatment in an implant-associated infection model. Mesoporous Fe 3 O 4 nanoparticles loaded with IR-820 similarly combined AMF-induced heating with photodynamic ROS generation, resulting in improved biofilm disruption and bacterial clearance in infected wound and subcutaneous abscess models. 60 These approaches illustrate how modulation of the biofilm microenvironment can enhance magnetothermal efficacy without relying exclusively on high bulk temperatures.

Compared to traditional magnetothermal damage, magnetomechanical systems exploit field-driven torque, oscillation, or rotation ( Figure 3 ). Šavli et al used anisotropic iron oxide nanochains under a rotating magnetic field to remove more than 90% of selected Gram-negative biofilms, although the principal outcome was physical detachment rather than bacterial killing. 61 By comparison, Fe 3 O 4 @polydopamine nanospears concentrated mechanical stress at the bacterial envelope, producing membrane puncture and enhanced S. aureus killing when combined with localized heating. 62 These findings demonstrate that particle geometry and field mode determine whether magnetic actuation primarily causes matrix disruption, bacterial dispersal, or irreversible membrane injury. Figure 3 Multimodal therapies deployed with SPIONS based magnetic hyperthermia. The diagram illustrates SPIONS-based multimodal antibacterial strategies. Magnetothermal Heating: AMF-induced heating elevates local temperature, weakens biofilm matrix and bacterial structures, enhancing susceptibility to antibacterial stress. Magnetomechanical Actuation: Rotation, torque, vibration, or oscillation exert mechanical stress on biofilms and bacterial membranes, causing detachment, membrane damage and enhanced killing. Nanozyme-Mediated Catalysis: SPIONs with iron active sites catalyze H subscript 2 O subscript 2 decomposition to produce ROS, degrade EPS and induce oxidative damage to bacteria. Integrated Multimodal Effects: Combines heat, mechanical stress, catalysis (ROS/EPS degradation) and ROS for efficient biofilm eradication and infection control. SPIONS antibacterial: heating, mechanical actuation, nanozyme catalysis.

Fe 3 O 4 -based platforms may also function as magnetically responsive nanozymes ( Figure 3 ). He et al showed that magnetic stimulation enhanced the peroxidase-like activity of iron oxide nanoparticles, indicating that localized magnetic energy can accelerate catalytic reactions without a pronounced increase in bulk temperature. 63 Ma et al translated this principle into a magneto-nanozyme platform in which magnetic assembly, AMF heating, and multivalent-iron catalysis promoted EPS degradation and ROS-mediated bacterial killing in a mouse skin-infection model. 64 Copper-doped magnetic vortex nanorings further integrated magnetic hyperthermia, Cu-mediated chemodynamic therapy, and photothermal activation, producing near-complete elimination of E. coli and S. aureus under low-H 2 O 2 conditions. 65 Positively charged Fe 3 O 4 @Polyethyleneimine nanoparticles likewise accumulated within S. aureus biofilms and generated combined thermal, mechanical, and oxidative stress under AMF exposure. 66

Furthermore, SPIONs have reported to establish multimodal mechanism with optical, catalytic, and immune-directed platforms and to identify the relative advantages and limitations of each approach. Koç et al combined aminolevulinic acid-loaded SPIONs with photothermal and photodynamic activation, producing 3–6-log reductions in Pseudomonas aeruginosa , 2–4-log reductions in Staphylococcus epidermidis , and up to a 13-log reduction in P. aeruginosa biofilms; however, light penetration and oxygen dependence may restrict application to deep infections. Ma et al developed an electromagnetically actuated magneto-nanozyme that integrated magnetic heating, mechanical biofilm disruption, and iron-mediated ROS generation, achieving 99.99% antibacterial efficacy in an MRSA-infected wound model while maintaining the treatment temperature at approximately 45 °C. 64 Host-directed platforms provide a complementary strategy: a STING-adjuvanted P. aeruginosa outer-membrane-vesicle nanoparticle vaccine completely protected mice from lethal pneumonia at an antigen dose of 0.01 μg and reduced pulmonary bacterial burden by approximately 2 log units, 67 whereas infection-responsive macrophage-targeted nanoparticles enhanced intracellular vancomycin delivery, ROS generation, bacterial clearance, and wound healing. 68 Compared with these platforms, SPIONs offer deep magnetic-field penetration, remote activation, potential MRI guidance, and the capacity to integrate magnetothermal, magnetomechanical, catalytic, and drug-delivery functions. Their principal advantage therefore lies in providing a localized and externally controlled multimodal platform.

## Synthesis Techniques

Fe 3 O 4 NPs, owing to their unique size-dependent properties, have been applied across diverse fields; therefore, it is pivotal to understand fabrication methods to tailor these NPs to specific uses. Generally, Fe 3 O 4 NPs are synthesized by two major routes: a top-down approach and a bottom-up approach. The top-down approach involves mechanical fractionation of bulk materials into smaller particles, achieved through techniques like milling or laser ablation. While effective, these methods may limit control over the particle size and shape. In contrast, the bottom-up approach builds NPs from molecular or atomic precursors. It encompasses both chemical and biological routes. Chemical methods utilize organic solvents as reaction media, allowing precise control over the size, composition, and surface properties. Examples include sol-gel synthesis and hydrothermal methods. Biological methods, on the other hand, leverage living organisms or their components. Green synthesis approaches minimize environmental impacts, making them attractive for sustainable NP production. Challenges include standardization, reproducibility, and optimization. Recent research focused on hybrid approaches, combining top-down and bottom-up methods. As we unravel the intricacies of these techniques, we pave the way for transformative applications in medicine, energy, and materials science.

### Physical Approaches

#### Ball Milling

Ball milling is a dominant method for the physical synthesis of Fe 3 O 4 NPs. This technique utilizes the principles of impact and attrition to achieve solid-state size reduction, transforming iron precursors into refined NPs. The process employs a rotating cylindrical chamber filled with micron-sized grinding media, which mechanically fractures the precursor materials into NPs. The incorporation of solvents or excess salts can improve the milling efficiency and prevent agglomeration of the synthesized NPs. 69 The ball mill process is described in Figure 3 . Notably, advancements in ball milling have enabled the synthesis of magnetic catalysts, such as Cu/Fe/Fe 3 O 4 , through applying an auxiliary electromagnetic field during the milling process. It was established that the ball milling process plays a critical role in determining the morphology and electromagnetic absorption properties of the resulting NPs. 70 , 71

#### Laser Ablation

Laser ablation has emerged as an alternative to ball milling for MNP synthesis. 72 This technique places the solid material below a thin sheet through which laser irradiation is applied from the top as illustrated in ( Figure 4 ). This technique offers precise control over particle properties but suffers from limitations like low production rates and polydispersity. 73 Unlike ball milling, laser ablation is simpler and requires no temperature or pressure adjustments. The laser power can be tailored to achieve the desired NP characteristics. For instance, the effects of laser power and solvent choice on Fe 3 O 4 /Au NP properties using neodymium-doped yttrium aluminum garnet (Nd:YAG) laser ablation highlight the potential for optimizing laser ablation parameters to address its limitations and facile NP synthesis. 74 Figure 4 Illustration of the underlying mechanisms of the ball mill and laser ablation methods of synthesis. Created with BioRender.com. Scientific schematic comparing ball milling and laser ablation synthesis setups with labeled parts and arrows.

#### Sonolysis

The sonolysis method, which utilizes ultrasonic waves to induce acoustic cavitation, is an efficacious technique for synthesizing Fe 3 O 4 NPs. This process entails dissolving iron salts, such as FeCl 2 or FeCl 3 , in an appropriate solvent, followed by ultrasonic irradiation. 75 The implosive collapse of cavitation bubbles generates extreme localized temperatures and pressures, facilitating the nucleation and growth of Fe 3 O 4 NPs. Critical factors influencing NP properties include the precursor concentration, pH, irradiation duration, and presence of surfactants. 76 This method allows precise control over the NP size, shape, and surface characteristics, making it highly suitable for biomedical applications. 77

### Chemical Approaches

#### Coprecipitation

First deployed in 1981 by Massart et al, coprecipitation remains a gold standard in the industry due to its simplicity, ease, and efficacy. 78 It uses the principle of the alkalization of metals, using homogeneous solutions containing the ions to be mixed and precipitated. Upon the addition of anions and a change in the pH, the desired NPs are precipitated, which are then washed and magnetically separated. The coprecipitation methos is well described in Figure 5 . conclusions: SPIONs represent a promising platform for the localized treatment of antibiotic-resistant and biofilm-associated infections because they combine remotely activated magnetic heating with catalytic, mechanical, drug-delivery, and imaging functions. The therapeutic performance is determined by the coupled effects of particle size, morphology, crystallinity, magnetic anisotropy, oxidation state, surface chemistry, aggregation, nanoparticle concentration, and alternating magnetic field conditions. These parameters govern specific absorption rate, intrinsic loss power, biofilm penetration, bacterial association, reactive oxygen species generation, and host-cell compatibility. Importantly, SPION-mediated treatment need not rely exclusively on high-temperature ablation. Mild hyperthermia can destabilize extracellular polymeric substances, increase membrane permeability, enhance antibiotic diffusion, promote biofilm dispersal, and amplify nanozyme-mediated oxidative stress while reducing injury to surrounding tissue. Multifunctional systems incorporating magneto-mechanical actuation, quorum-sensing interference, photodynamic therapy, thermoresponsive drug release, and implant coatings further expand the antibacterial potential of SPIONs. Nevertheless, translation remains limited by formulation variability, heterogeneous tissue accumulation, nonuniform thermal dosing, incomplete mechanistic resolution, inconsistent microbiological endpoints, and uncertainties concerning biodistribution, biodegradation, and long-term toxicity. Future progress will require quality-by-design manufacturing, standardized magnetic and thermal characterization, spatially resolved dosimetry, clinically relevant polymicrobial models, and integrated evaluation of antibacterial efficacy and host response. These advances could establish SPION-mediated magnetic hyperthermia as an effective adjunct for chronic wounds, dental infections, abscesses, and implant-associated biofilms.

# Nanoparticle-Based Therapeutic Strategies for Pathological Cardiac Hypertrophy: Preclinical Advances, Translational Challenges, and Future Perspectives

## Abstract
Pathological cardiac hypertrophy is a major contributor to heart failure and is characterized by complex molecular mechanisms involving transcriptional and epigenetic regulation, signal transduction, metabolic remodeling, inflammatory responses, and extracellular matrix remodeling. Although conventional pharmaceutical treatments may alleviate the progression of cardiac hypertrophy, their clinical effectiveness is limited by poor cardiac selectivity, systemic side effects, and limited efficacy in reverseing pathological remodeling. Recently, nanoparticle-based strategies have emerged as a promising therapeutic approach for cardiac hypertrophy owing to their ability to enhance cardiac-targeted drug delivery, enable controlled or stimuli-responsive drug release, and reduce off-target toxicity through improved biodistribution. This review systematically summarizes the design strategies of nanoparticle-based therapies for pathological cardiac hypertrophy, including material platforms such as inorganic, organic, and biomimetic nanoparticles, key delivery strategies such as passive targeting, active targeting, biomimetic targeting, and stimulus-responsive release, and administration routes including intravenous, intraperitoneal, intradermal, inhalation, and oral administration. In addition, this review provides a comprehensive summary of the preclinical applications of the above strategies in the fields of gene and epigenetic regulation, antioxidant, anti-inflammatory, and anti-fibrotic treatments. Finally, this review analyzes the challenges in clinical translation on the basis of critical issues, including long-term biosafety, insufficient targeting efficacy, large-scale production, and appropriate administration routes.

## Keywords
pathological cardiac hypertrophy; nanomedicine; targeted drug delivery; stimuli-responsive release; precision therapy

## Introduction

Pathological cardiac hypertrophy is a detrimental cardiac remodeling process triggered by various pathological stimuli, including persistent pressure or volume overload, abnormal activation of the neurohumoral system, and myocardial ischemia and hypoxia, as well as genetic abnormalities such as storage disease and hypertrophic cardiomyopathy ( Figure 1 ). 1 The key features of cardiac hypertrophy include an elevated volume of cardiomyocytes, alteration of the extracellular matrix, and compromised cardiac contraction and relaxation capabilities. 2 Pathological cardiac hypertrophy has been observed in various cardiovascular diseases and typically results in severe consequences, including heart failure, arrhythmia, and even sudden death. 3–5 According to the report from the American Heart Association in 2023, cardiovascular diseases remain one of the leading causes of death in the United States and globally, imposing a heavy burden on public health and the healthcare system. 6 Left ventricular hypertrophy (LVH) is the predominant structural remodeling of pathological cardiac hypertrophy and affects approximately 10–20% of the general adult population worldwide, 7 with the prevalence increasing to 36–41% among patients with hypertension. 8 LVH is an independent predictor of adverse cardiovascular outcomes. A prospective study demonstrated that the risk factor-adjusted hazard ratio (HR) for sudden death was 2.16 in LVH patients compared with those without LVH. 9 In addition, a meta-analysis reported that LVH was associated with a 2.16-fold higher risk of non-fatal cardiovascular events and a 2.58-fold higher risk of cardiovascular mortality. 10 Figure 1 Etiology of pathological cardiac hypertrophy and the therapeutic potential of nanoparticle-based treatments (created with BioRender.com). Cardiac hypertrophy arises from diverse stimuli such as pressure overload, neurohumoral activation, and genetic mutations and can progress to heart failure. Traditional treatments offer low cost and an established safety profile but are limited by side effects and inadequate reversal of hypertrophy. Nanoparticle-based treatments enable targeted delivery, stimuli-responsive release, and potential reversal of remodeling, but their high cost and preclinical status remain major translational hurdles. An arrow points from these causes to pathological hypertrophy, depicted with a heart image, leading to heart failure. Below, two treatment options are shown. Pathological cardiac hypertrophy can be categorized into concentric and eccentric hypertrophy. Concentric hypertrophy typically occurs in response to pressure overload and is characterized by increased ventricular wall thickness and decreased chamber size. Eccentric hypertrophy is more common in response to volume overload and is characterized by dilatation of the ventricular chamber and thinning of the wall. 1 The concentric hypertrophy induced by pressure overload preferentially involves activation of signaling pathways such as mitogen-activated protein kinase (MAPK), calcineurin, and β-arrestin-2, as well as more severe cardiac fibrosis and cardiomyocyte death. 11 , 12 Eccentric hypertrophy due to volume overload preferentially involves activation of signaling pathways, including protein kinase B (Akt) and calmodulin-dependent protein kinase II (CaMKII), with less fibrosis and apoptosis and more evident angiogenesis. 12 In conclusion, the two phenotypes of cardiac hypertrophy exhibit distinct patterns of preferentially activated pathways, indicating that anti-hypertrophic therapies may target the underlying signaling pathways based on their unique phenotypes.

Traditional treatments for pathological cardiac hypertrophy mainly include β-blockers, calcium channel antagonists, renin-angiotensin-aldosterone system (RAAS) inhibitors, and sodium-glucose cotransporter 2 inhibitors. 13 Despite their low cost and established safety profile, these pharmacological therapies often lack cardiac specificity, and the systemic side effects cannot be ignored. Depending on the specific category of the drugs, systemic adverse side effects mainly include hypotension, bradycardia, electrolyte disturbances, and urinary tract infections. 14 , 15 Importantly, current pharmacological therapies mainly relieve hemodynamic overload and neurohormonal activation rather than directly regulating the molecular mechanisms underlying pathological cardiac hypertrophy. As a result, their ability to reverse established pathological cardiac remodeling remains limited. Moreover, the small-molecule drugs also exhibit limited intrinsic cardiac specificity. 16 The cellular uptake occurs predominantly via passive diffusion across biological membranes in a non-selective manner. Consequently, cardiac distribution is largely governed by regional perfusion rather than active uptake by cardiomyocytes. Furthermore, cardiac delivery of conventional pharmaceuticals is impeded by various pharmacokinetic hurdles, including hepatic first-pass metabolism following oral administration and fast systemic clearance caused by short plasma half-lives, consequently limiting local bioavailability and therapeutic efficacy. 17 Moreover, surgical and device therapies including aortic valve replacement surgery 18 , 19 and left ventricular assist device therapy 20 , 21 are often used to correct hemodynamic abnormalities and relieve cardiac hypertrophy. However, they are only applicable to patients with specific indications and have difficulty intervening in pathological cardiac hypertrophy at the molecular level. Hence, the development of new treatments for cardiac hypertrophy is an urgent issue.

Nanoparticle-based therapies have recently emerged as a novel therapeutic method for cardiac hypertrophy. Many therapeutic agents, such as small molecule medications, 22 nucleic acids, 23 proteins, 24 and peptides, 25 can be delivered by nanoparticles. In addition, by achieving cardiac targeting and exhibiting controlled release in diseased regions, nanoparticles may enhance drug accumulation while reducing systemic side effects. Figure 1 illustrates the principal etiologies of pathological cardiac hypertrophy and compares traditional treatments with nanoparticle-based treatments. It highlights the key advantages of nanoparticle-based treatments, including targeted drug delivery, stimuli-responsive release, and the potential to reverse cardiac hypertrophy.

In addition to enhancing the efficiency of targeted drug delivery, the nanoparticle-based delivery systems can also overcome the limitations of free drugs by controlling the drug release behaviors and optimizing the drug exposure characteristics. 26 The free drugs generally lack the protection and drug release regulation mechanisms, and many therapeutic agents have a limited systemic half-life due to the rapid distribution, metabolism, and clearance. 27 Therefore, the plasma drug concentrations usually peak shortly after administration and subsequently decrease, which makes it difficult to maintain the therapeutic concentrations over time and increases the risk of adverse effects associated with peak drug concentrations. 28 Conversely, nanoparticle-based delivery systems can protect therapeutic agents through drug encapsulation, structural engineering, and surface modification strategies, thus enabling controlled drug release. 29 As conceptually illustrated in Figure 2 , under ideal design conditions, nanoparticle-based systems can transform the rapid release profile of free drugs to a slower and sustained release profile. 29 Thus, the plasma concentration-time profile can be theoretically shifted from the sharp peak and rapid decline observed with free drugs to a more stable exposure pattern with reduced peak concentrations, slow elimination, and prolonged maintenance within the therapeutic window. 30 This modulation not only reduces the risk of toxicity associated with peak concentrations but also enables sustained drug exposure within the therapeutic range, thereby improving therapeutic efficacy and enhancing the overall safety profile. Nonetheless, the nanoparticle-based delivery system is still facing significant challenges in the treatment of pathological cardiac hypertrophy. Firstly, the long-term biosafety of nanoparticles remains unclear, largely because most nanoparticle-based therapeutic strategies are still at the preclinical stage and lack sufficient long-term clinical safety data. Their potential toxicity and long-term accumulation are particularly concerning. 31 , 32 Secondly, hypertrophic myocardium lacks the typical enhanced permeability and retention effects, 33 , 34 as well as the formation of a protein corona, 35 limiting the efficient accumulation of nanoparticles in the cardiac tissue. Thirdly, the large-scale production of nanoparticles is limited by significant batch-to-batch variations, 36 complex and costly preparation processes, 37 and the absence of quality control standards. In addition, the administration route of nanoparticles is mainly intravenous injection. Long-term and repeated administration may reduce patient compliance. Alternative routes such as oral administration and inhalation still need to be further verified.

Despite the existence of multiple publications addressing the molecular mechanisms of pathological cardiac hypertrophy and the development of nanoparticle-based delivery systems, a comprehensive summary that integrates both aspects remains rather scarce. This review systematically summarizes recent advances in nanoparticle-based delivery systems, with a particular focus on material platforms, targeting strategies, stimuli-responsive drug release, and preclinical applications.

## The Molecular and Cellular Mechanisms of Pathological Cardiac Hypertrophy

As a crucial pathological process underlying various cardiovascular disorders, pathological cardiac hypertrophy is driven by highly complex molecular and cellular mechanisms. 1 Figure 3 illustrates the key pathological mechanisms that contribute to cardiac hypertrophy, including fetal gene reactivation, 38 , 39 activation of hypertrophic signal transduction pathways, 2 metabolic remodeling, 40 inflammatory responses, 41 , 42 and extracellular matrix remodeling. 43 Moreover, nanoparticle-based therapeutic strategies were also described in Figure 3 , including gene and epigenetic nanotherapy, anti-oxidative nanotherapy, anti-inflammatory nanotherapy, and anti-fibrotic nanotherapy. ### Transcription and Epigenetic Regulation

Transcription and epigenetic regulation contribute to the gene expression alterations in pathological cardiac hypertrophy. Among them, one of the most typical alterations is fetal gene reactivation, including Atrial Natriuretic Peptide (ANP), Brain Natriuretic Peptide (BNP), and Beta-Myosin Heavy Chain (β-MHC). 38 , 39 Nuclear factor of activated T cells (NFAT) is recognized as a significant transcription factor in pathological cardiac hypertrophy. 46 Calcium signal-dependent calcineurin induces the dephosphorylation of NFAT, promoting its translocation into the nucleus and triggering the transcription of downstream target genes, including hypertrophy-related genes and fetal genes. 47 , 48 Given its central role in pathological hypertrophy and its relatively well-characterized regulatory mechanism, the NFAT pathway represents an attractive candidate for targeted therapeutic intervention. Additionally, myocyte enhancer factor 2 (MEF2) functions as a central node in multiple signaling pathway networks, and MEF2 promotes the transcription of hypertrophy-associated genes by synergy with NFAT and GATA4. 49 MEF2 acetylation is essential for the activation of hypertrophy-related gene expression, while class IIa histone deacetylases (HDACs) suppress MEF2 activity. 50 Blocking MEF2 acetylation is a highly promising target for nanoparticle-based therapies in reversing cardiac hypertrophy. 50 Another essential transcription factor, GATA binding protein 4 (GATA4), is highly expressed in cardiomyocytes. Accumulating evidence indicates that GATA4 is indispensable in the reactivation of fetal genes in pathological cardiac hypertrophy. 51 , 52 However, GATA4 also contributes to the survival of cardiomyocytes and the maintenance of normal cardiac function. 53 Inhibition of GATA4 may cause potential safety challenges. In contrast to the aforementioned pro-hypertrophic transcription factors (NFAT, MEF2, and GATA4), forkhead box protein O1 (FOXO1) exerts context-dependent effects on hypertrophic remodeling by regulating stress adaptation and metabolic homeostasis. Moderate FOXO1 activity generally exerts anti-hypertrophic effects, while sustained FOXO1 activation may promote cardiac hypertrophy. 54 Therefore, therapeutic modulation of FOXO1 may require precise control of its activation intensity and duration rather than complete inhibition. Collectively, NFAT- and MEF2-associated networks may represent promising targets for nanoparticle-based therapies, whereas GATA4 and FOXO1 may require more selective and spatiotemporally controlled delivery to enhance efficacy and reduce off-target effects.

Alongside transcription factor-mediated regulation, the role of epigenetic regulation cannot be overlooked. In pathological cardiac hypertrophy, histone modifications such as acetylation, methylation, lactylation, and ubiquitination are involved in regulating hypertrophy-related gene expression. 55–58 Among these modifications, histone acetylation has drawn particular interest owing to its recognition by epigenetic reader proteins, such as bromodomain-containing protein 4 (BRD4), which governs enhancer activity and drives hypertrophic gene transcription. 59 For instance, the BRD4 inhibitor JQ1 has shown anti-hypertrophic effects in preclinical models, providing a rationale for the development of BRD4-targeted nanoparticle-based strategies. 22 Moreover, DNA methylation has been extensively investigated for its role in regulating hypertrophy-related gene expression and contributing to the progression of cardiac hypertrophy. 60 , 61 However, therapeutic modulation of DNA methylation is still challenging, because DNA methylation patterns influence broad genomic programs beyond hypertrophy-associated pathways. 62 Therefore, precise and disease-specific control of DNA methylation is a major challenge for nanoparticle-based therapeutic strategies. Furthermore, non-coding RNA is an important post-transcriptional and epigenetic regulatory factor in pathological cardiac hypertrophy. 63 Among them, microRNAs (miRNAs) mainly bind with the 3’ non-translated region of target mRNAs, inhibiting the translation or promoting the degradation of mRNA, thereby regulating the expression of genes related to hypertrophy. 64 , 65 Long non-coding RNAs (lncRNAs) act as miRNA sponges through the competitive endogenous RNA (ceRNA) mechanism, regulating the expression of downstream genes. 66 Due to their ability to precisely regulate disease-associated gene networks through specific molecular interactions, miRNAs and lncRNAs provide promising potential for nanoparticle-based therapies. 67

Nanoparticle-based therapies have been employed to modulate the lncRNA/miRNA regulatory network and have demonstrated therapeutic effects in pathological cardiac hypertrophy. For example, neutrophil membrane-coated mesoporous silica nanoparticles have been applied to deliver siRNA of lncRNA AAB, a known sponge of miR-30b-5p. In a rat model of cardiac hypertrophy, this nanoparticle was given via intravenous injection at a dose of 50 nM siRNA per rat, once every two days over a four-week treatment period. As a result, miR-30b-5p activity was restored, which suppressed ferroptosis in cardiac microvascular endothelial cells and ultimately alleviated the hypertrophic phenotype. 67 Furthermore, the above nanoparticles integrate precise targeting, excellent biocompatibility, and biodegradability, thereby providing an effective and safe platform for therapeutic delivery. 67

### Signal Transduction

A number of signal transduction pathways contribute to pathological cardiac hypertrophy, with the NFAT, phosphatidylinositol 3-kinase (PI3K)/protein kinase B (AKT)/mammalian target of rapamycin complex 1 (mTORC1) pathway, and MAPK pathways being regarded as the major signaling pathways. 13 , 68 Persistent pathological stimulation results in a prolonged elevation of intracellular calcium concentrations in cardiomyocytes, consequently activating calcineurin. Activated calcineurin dephosphorylates NFAT, facilitating its translocation into the nucleus and directly promoting the reactivation of hypertrophy-related genes and fetal genes. 47 , 48 The NFAT pathway connects pathological signaling to hypertrophic gene transcription and has well-characterized regulatory mechanisms, which makes it a promising target for nanoparticle-based interventions. Additionally, the phosphatidylinositol 3-kinase (PI3K)/protein kinase B (AKT)/mammalian target of rapamycin complex 1 (mTORC1) pathway is another central regulator of pathological cardiac hypertrophy. Under pathological stress, PI3K activation results in phosphorylation and activation of AKT, which therefore activates mTORC1 signaling. Activated mTORC1 subsequently phosphorylates downstream effectors, including ribosomal protein S6 kinase (S6K) and eukaryotic translation initiation factor 4E-binding protein 1 (4E-BP1), which enhances protein synthesis and promotes cardiomyocyte growth, ultimately leading to pathological cardiac hypertrophy. 69 , 70 The PI3K/AKT/mTORC1 pathway is a direct regulator of cardiomyocyte growth and a potential therapeutic target. However, its broad involvement in systemic physiological growth and metabolism across multiple tissues poses a challenge to the design of selective and spatiotemporally controlled delivery strategies of nanoparticles for therapeutic efficacy with minimal off-target effect. 71 Moreover, the MAPK pathway mainly consists of three main pathways, including extracellular signal-regulated kinase (ERK), p38, and c-Jun N-terminal kinase (JNK). 72 The MAPK signaling system facilitates cardiac hypertrophy by regulating cardiomyocyte proliferation, apoptosis, and the expression of hypertrophic genes. 73 However, its involvement in diverse physiological and pathological processes may complicate selective therapeutic targeting and raise concerns about pathway-wide inhibition. 74

### Metabolic Remodeling and Mitochondrial Dysfunction

Metabolic remodeling is a hallmark of pathological cardiac hypertrophy and an important basis for the decline of cardiac function. 1 Metabolic remodeling in pathological cardiac hypertrophy is defined by alterations in substrate use patterns. The capacity for oxidation of the fatty acids is reduced, whereas the extent of glycolysis is relatively increased. 75 This switch of metabolism is similar to the cardiac fetal metabolic phenotype and is called fetal-type metabolism. 76 Glycolysis is less efficient in energy transformation than fatty acid oxidation, which may contribute to the imbalance of energy supply and demand. 40

Mitochondrial dysfunction is another characteristic of metabolic remodeling. Chronic pathological stimulation impairs the efficiency of oxidative phosphorylation and ATP production by dysregulation of mitochondrial autophagy and mitochondrial biogenesis, 77 and imbalance in mitochondrial fusion and fission. 78 Metabolic remodeling and mitochondrial dysfunction synergistically contribute to excessive production of reactive oxygen species (ROS). 79 Excessive ROS not only aggravates mitochondrial injury but also acts as signaling molecules to activate hypertrophic-related signaling pathways, thus forming a vicious cycle to accelerate pathological cardiac remodeling. 80

To break this vicious cycle, nanoparticle-based antioxidant delivery has emerged as a promising therapeutic strategy. For example, a ROS-responsive nanoparticle encapsulated with the death receptor 5 fusion protein (sDR5-Fc) was given intravenously in rats (200 μL/dose, twice weekly for 14 days, specific drug loading not provided). This approach permitted sDR5-Fc release and ROS scavenging at the site of myocardial infarction, thereby lowering infarct size, attenuating fibrosis, and inhibiting cardiac hypertrophy. 81

### Inflammation

Previous studies showed that the expression levels of pro-inflammatory factors were increased in hypertrophic cardiac tissue, including tumor necrosis factor-alpha (TNF-α), interleukin-1 beta (IL-1β), and interleukin-6 (IL-6). 41 , 42 Pro-inflammatory factors are generated not just by immune cells but also by cardiomyocytes and fibroblasts. 82 These cytokines increase the expression of genes associated with cardiac hypertrophy directly via the activation of signaling pathways such as nuclear factor kappa-B (NF-κB) and MAPK. 83 , 84 Particularly, macrophages are key mediators in cardiac remodeling, 85 and they secrete pro-inflammatory and pro-fibrotic mediators, thereby linking cardiac inflammation to hypertrophic remodeling. 86 , 87 Collectively, inflammatory factors work in synergy with immune cells to accelerate the progression of pathological cardiac hypertrophy.

### Extracellular Matrix Remodeling and Fibrosis

Continuous pathogenic stimulation causes excessive deposition and cross-linking of collagen, particularly type I and type III collagen, 88 , 89 which enhances cardiac stiffness, diminishes cardiac compliance, and promotes diastolic dysfunction. 90 Cardiac fibroblasts are the primary effector cells in extracellular matrix remodeling. Under pathological stimulation, resting fibroblasts activate and differentiate into α-smooth muscle actin-expressing myofibroblasts, which synthesize and secrete large amounts of ECM proteins, continuously driving myocardial fibrosis and maladaptive remodeling. 43 The above pathological process is principally regulated by the transforming growth factor-beta 1 (TGF-β1)/suppressor of mothers against decapentaplegic (Smad) signaling pathway. The expression level of TGF-β1 is proven to be upregulated in the hypertrophic myocardium. Upon ligand binding, TGF-β receptors phosphorylate and activate Smad2/3, which form a complex with Smad4 and translocate to the nucleus. This leads to increased transcription of genes associated with cardiac hypertrophy and fibrosis. 91 In addition to excessive ECM production, an imbalance between matrix metalloproteinases (MMPs) and their tissue inhibitors (TIMPs) further disrupts ECM homeostasis, contributing to abnormal matrix turnover and structural disorganization. 92

Nanoparticle‑mediated delivery of antifibrotic agents has demonstrated considerable potential in reducing ECM remodeling and fibrosis. For instance, engineered extracellular vesicles (EVs) loaded with the TGF‑β1 receptor inhibitor GW788388 were administered via tail vein injection at 100 μg of EVs every 3 days for a total of four doses in an isoproterenol‑induced mouse model of cardiac fibrosis. This system effectively suppressed fibroblast activation and attenuated collagen deposition. 93

## Design Strategies of Nanoparticles in Pathological Cardiac Hypertrophy

### Biological Barriers of Nanoparticle Delivery in Pathological Cardiac Hypertrophy

The therapeutic efficacy of nanoparticle-based therapies for pathological cardiac hypertrophy depends not only on the biological activity of the therapeutic agents but also on the efficiency of their delivery to the myocardium. After systemic administration, the nanoparticles undergo a series of processes that impact the delivery efficiency, including impaired vascular extravasation, 44 the formation of protein corona, 35 and in vivo clearance 30 ( Figure 4A ). These factors influence the circulation time and the efficiency of cardiac accumulation of the nanoparticles. conclusions:
In this review, we have highlighted the therapeutic potential of nanoparticle-based therapeutic strategies in pathological cardiac hypertrophy. The therapeutic advantages of nanoparticle-based strategies in pathological cardiac hypertrophy can be categorized into three major aspects. First, in terms of pathological mechanism modulation, nanoparticles possess the capacity to target the key processes involved in cardiac hypertrophy, including transcriptional regulation, 22 signaling pathways, 119 oxidative stress, 261 inflammatory responses, 266 and fibrosis. 179 Such wide regulatory capacity might overcome the limitations of conventional therapies that are often unable to precisely intervene at the molecular scale. Second, both active targeting and biomimetic targeting strategies may enhance the accumulation of therapeutic agents in hypertrophic myocardial tissues for myocardial targeting, thus overcoming the limitations of conventional treatments, such as poor cardiac distribution and high systemic exposure. 23 , 125 In the therapeutic efficacy aspect, nanoparticle-based strategies have shown the potential to promote the restoration of myocardial structure and function, providing a promising way to reverse pathological cardiac remodeling, which is difficult to achieve by conventional therapies.

However, the above findings need to be interpreted with caution. All the studies discussed in this paper have been conducted in mouse or rat models, and no nanoparticle-based therapy for pathological cardiac hypertrophy has been brought to clinical trials. 300 There are noteworthy differences in heart rate, calcium ion handling, 301 myosin subtypes, 302 and immune metabolism 303 between rodents and humans. This situation might mean that conclusions based on animal experiments cannot be transferred to humans. Existing studies tend to have relatively small sample sizes of animals and short observation periods. Furthermore, there is great diversity among studies in terms of animal models, administration methods, and efficacy evaluation indicators. Such variability limits the comparability of research results and the evaluation of long-term safety. 304

Moreover, different design strategies of nanoparticles exhibit distinct advantages and limitations, and the selection depends on specific therapeutic needs. For material platforms, organic nanoparticles usually have good biocompatibility and a comparatively mature foundation for clinical translation. 184 However, despite these favorable characteristics, challenges including formulation stability and manufacturing complexity, remain to be addressed to achieve broader clinical application. 172 In contrast, inorganic nanoparticles have unique advantages owing to their intrinsic antioxidant properties and enzyme-mimetic activities. 119 However, concerns regarding long-term biosafety, biodegradation, and potential accumulation may restrict their clinical translation. 32 Biomimetic nanoparticles combine good biocompatibility with inherent targeting properties of biological components. 22 Nevertheless, challenges related to large-scale manufacturing, batch consistency, and quality control remain important barriers for their clinical application. 181 , 182 For the targeting strategies, active targeting improves the specificity of delivery via ligand-receptor recognition, although its efficiency may be influenced by factors such as protein corona formation. 35 Biomimetic targeting utilizes natural biological components for multivalent recognition and reduced immune recognition. These strategies have complementary advantages, and they can be further optimized by rational integration. 198 In addition, stimuli-responsive release strategies enable spatiotemporally controlled drug delivery by leveraging pathological microenvironmental cues, thus improving therapeutic efficacy and reducing nonspecific exposure. 81 However, pathological cardiac hypertrophy involves complex pathological processes, and a single design strategy is unlikely to comprehensively address the complex nature of the disease. Based on current evidence, the combination of advantageous material platforms, complementary targeting strategies, and stimuli-responsive release mechanisms to construct multifunctional nanoparticle platforms may be a highly promising direction for improving therapeutic efficacy and facilitating future clinical translation.

Future efforts should focus on the following three key aspects. First, systematic evaluation of nanoparticle-based therapies in large animal models is essential, along with comprehensive evaluations of pharmacokinetics, biodistribution, and long-term biosafety. Second, further optimization of cardiac targeting strategies and administration routes, coupled with the development of scalable manufacturing methods and standardized quality control systems, is required to bridge the gap between preclinical promise and clinical practice. Third, emerging artificial intelligence (AI)-assisted approaches may provide new opportunities for the rational design and optimization of nanomedicine platforms for cardiac therapy. By integrating multidimensional information, including nanoparticle physicochemical properties, biological interactions, pharmacokinetic profiles, and therapeutic outcomes, AI-driven computational models, including machine learning and deep learning algorithms, could facilitate the prediction of nanoparticle performance, optimization of formulation parameters, improvement of targeting strategies, and acceleration of clinical translation. 305–307

title: Bio-interfacial engineering of electrophoretic coacervate microcapsules for cytocompatible on-skin displays
abstract: Electrophoretic ink (e-ink) holds significant potential for energy-efficient displays and sustainable alternatives to print media. However, their use in wearables is hindered by hazardous materials which are cytotoxic and sensitizing to human tissue. While commercial e-inks encapsulate these fluids in rigid, synthetic microplastics, such as melamine-formaldehyde, they lack the mechanical conformability and environmental safety required for epidermal contact. We thus present a novel approach for producing e-ink microcapsules (EIMCs) for integration into biocompatible and free-form digital devices. Spherical, core–shell EIMCs were fabricated via complex coacervation (pH 4.1), using user-friendly biopolymers (gum acacia and gelatin). A core of white electrophoretic TiO 2 particles (diameter approx. 30 nm) was marked with a darker violet dye, while being homodispersed in hexylsalicylate-tetrachloroethylene (HS-PCE), as the liquid medium. Characterization of the physico-chemical and performance properties of EIMCs showed remarkable nominal compression stress at rupture (3.9 ± 0.9 MPa). When subjected to a DC voltage of 20 V, the microcapsules created a writable display, potentially enabling users to write and rewrite. The response time was approximately 0.5 seconds (2 Hz refresh rate), comparable to commercial products. In vitro cytotoxicity and CD54 expression (h-CLAT) assays demonstrated that the microcapsule shell successfully mitigated solvent-induced immunotoxicity, maintaining high cellular viability (approx. 70%) and minimal sensitization (approx. 1.7%).

# Bio-interfacial engineering of electrophoretic coacervate microcapsules for cytocompatible on-skin displays

## Abstract
Electrophoretic ink (e-ink) holds significant potential for energy-efficient displays and sustainable alternatives to print media. However, their use in wearables is hindered by hazardous materials which are cytotoxic and sensitizing to human tissue. While commercial e-inks encapsulate these fluids in rigid, synthetic microplastics, such as melamine-formaldehyde, they lack the mechanical conformability and environmental safety required for epidermal contact. We thus present a novel approach for producing e-ink microcapsules (EIMCs) for integration into biocompatible and free-form digital devices. Spherical, core–shell EIMCs were fabricated via complex coacervation (pH 4.1), using user-friendly biopolymers (gum acacia and gelatin). A core of white electrophoretic TiO 2 particles (diameter approx. 30 nm) was marked with a darker violet dye, while being homodispersed in hexylsalicylate-tetrachloroethylene (HS-PCE), as the liquid medium. Characterization of the physico-chemical and performance properties of EIMCs showed remarkable nominal compression stress at rupture (3.9 ± 0.9 MPa). When subjected to a DC voltage of 20 V, the microcapsules created a writable display, potentially enabling users to write and rewrite. The response time was approximately 0.5 seconds (2 Hz refresh rate), comparable to commercial products. In vitro cytotoxicity and CD54 expression (h-CLAT) assays demonstrated that the microcapsule shell successfully mitigated solvent-induced immunotoxicity, maintaining high cellular viability (approx. 70%) and minimal sensitization (approx. 1.7%).

## Keywords
e-ink microcapsules; electrochromic displays; on-skin digital devices; flexible electronics; micromanipulation; biocompatibility graphical

## Introduction

Electronic papers have emerged as a revolutionary, sustainable display technology, offering bistability, flexibility and ultra-low power dissipation, with their global market projected to reach beyond $5.5 billion by 2030 [ 1 , 2 ]. Unlike conventional emissive screens, they mimic the optical properties of traditional ink on paper, which is leveraged by the presence of an electrophoretic ink [ 3 ]. At the heart of the e-ink system lies the microcapsules in which charged pigmented particles (CPPs) are entrapped while suspended within a colourless dielectric liquid medium. When an electric field is applied, CPPs move negentropically, yielding changes in microcapsule coloration [ 4 ].

Historically, the fabrication of electrophoretic microcapsules has relied on synthetic polymer shells and industrially engineered pigments [ 3 ]. While these materials provide durability, they pose challenges to broader-spectrum applications owing to insufficient contrast and slow response speed, alongside concerns regarding their environmental sustainability, cost-effectiveness and manufacturing complexity [ 5 ]. More critically, for emerging wearable electronics, the shell of the electrophoretic microcapsule no longer acts solely as a passive CPP-retaining barrier, but rather as the primary biological interface between electrophoretically active fluids and human tissue. As such, shell composition and interfacial engineering become central determinants of both electrophoretic functionality and biological safety.

Dyes and pigments play a pivotal role in the optical properties of electrophoretic displays. Titanium dioxide (TiO 2 ) has been widely adopted owing to its superior reflectivity and brightness. However, its high specific density (approx. 4 g cm − 3 ), and thus its tendency to sediment, introduce hurdles in maintaining long-term suspension stability [ 6 , 7 ]. Darker pigments, such as carbon black and phthalocyanine-based dyes, provide strong contrast but require heavy surface modifications to ensure optimal electrophoretic behaviour [ 7 ]. Strategies to enhance white pigment performance are being explored, with special emphasis on particle size reduction, charge-control additives and polymeric coatings to ease the density mismatch between the dielectric medium and titanium dioxide [ 4 , 7 ]. The dielectric medium should facilitate the movement of CPPs, ensuring rapid response to the applied voltage. However, commonly used aliphatic hydrocarbons or silicone-based media face shortcomings in viscosity and environmental sustainability [ 3 ]. Nevertheless, the trade-off among CPP stability/mobility, highly performing dielectric medium and optical clarity remains an ongoing technical challenge towards enhancing display longevity and performance.

Beyond conventional e-paper applications, wearable on-skin displays are transforming biomedical research by providing unique platforms for health monitoring, diagnostics and therapeutic applications [ 8 ]. A critical component of these devices is the display material, which enables dynamic data streaming directly on the skin [ 9 ]. While electrophoretically active e-ink microcapsules (EIMCs), with a shell made of melamine/urea-formaldehyde [ 10 ], have been proposed for e-papers, their adaptation for on-skin biomedical devices faces challenges, including poor microcapsule suspendability, impaired biocompatibility and/or pigment clumping [ 3 , 11 ]. Therefore, the microcapsule shell material is the critical biological interface, which influences the stability and electrophoretic performance of EIMCs, provides mechanical strength, while mitigating any related human immunogenic response (e.g. skin sensitization).

Traditionally, the fabrication of electrophoretic microcapsules relies on petroleum-sourced polymers, such as polyurea [ 12 ], urea-formaldehyde [ 4 ] and melamine-formaldehyde, featuring poly(methyl methacrylate) (PMMA) [ 13 ], but they pose severe limitations for wearable applications. They lack the mechanical compliance required to withstand dynamic human joint deformation, and their synthetic nature raises stringent regulatory and biocompatibility concerns for prolonged skin contact [ 14 , 15 ]. Consequently, ideal encapsulation for on-skin devices requires sustainable materials that provide high mechanical resilience and electrical insulation without relying on immunogenic synthetic precursors [ 11 ]. To this end, biopolymeric encapsulation using gelatin and gum acacia presents a promising approach [ 16 , 17 ], offering biodegradability, interfacial stability, mechanical strength, and cost-effectiveness while preserving the functional integrity and electrophoretic activity of the microcapsules [ 18 ].

Recent work has begun to explore this direction within the human–computer interaction (HCI) community, where the challenge of democratizing access to e-ink microcapsules has been identified as an important step towards enabling new forms of interactive display fabrication [ 7 , 11 ]. That work introduced a simplified coacervation-based process to synthesize electrophoretically active capsules and highlighted its potential for design-oriented prototyping. But it addressed accessibility from a fabrication perspective, with limited attention to deeper materials analysis or biomedical applicability [ 19 ]. In contrast, the present work advances scientific understanding on the bio-interfacial properties provided by the coacervate shells towards effective cytocompatibility, immune shielding and compliant integration with epidermal systems.

Herein, we present an engineering strategy to overcome this electric and cytotoxicity trade-off. We demonstrate that core-shell biopolymer microcapsules, fabricated via complex coacervation of gelatin and gum acacia, can be cross-linked to act as a highly impermeable immune-toxicological shield. Rather than merely containing the ink, this biopolymer architecture is deliberately engineered to segregate a highly active, immunogenic electrophoretic core (comprising highly charged, surface-modified TiO 2 nanoparticles and gentian violet in a hexylsalicylate-tetrachloroethylene (HS-PCE) medium) from the surrounding biological environment. We detail the solid–liquid interfacial phenomena driving nanoparticle stability, the superior mechanical resilience of the cross-linked coacervate shell under compression, and explicitly validate its biological safety via rigorous in vitro cytotoxicity and CD54 expression (human cell line activation test; h-CLAT) assays. Ultimately, this approach establishes a robust framework for safely integrating high-performance electrophoretic fluids into flexible, human–machine interfaces.

## Results

All experiments were performed in triplicate unless stated otherwise. Data variability is expressed as the mean value ± standard error (s.e.).

### E-ink microcapsules scanning electron microscopy observation

Both morphological and surface topographical properties of cross-linked EIMCs ( D nb,J = 22.4 ± 0.4 µm; n = 200; supplementary material, table S1) were investigated by scanning electron microscopy (SEM). Figure 1a presents an overview of heterodisperse EIMC microcapsules, predominantly exhibiting a spherical morphology. While the microcapsules appear self-isolated, some areas show signs of agglomeration, probably owing to the presence of the cross-linking agent. This enhances the structural integrity of the EIMCs, preventing premature degradation in the vacuumed SEM chamber, but may also induce colloidal aggregation, leading to capsule-to-capsule bridging/gluing phenomena [ 20 ]. Figure 1. SEM images of EIMC microcapsules highlighting their morphology and surface characteristics: (a) overview of heterodisperse cross-linked microcapsules with a relatively spherical morphology; close-up of (b1) an intact spherical microcapsule with a smooth outer shell (b2) after bursting, revealing its hollow core-shell structure; (c) microcapsule with a relatively rough surface owing to embedded TiO 2 nanoparticles, deploying at its surface; (d) damaged microcapsule with visible cracks confirming a core–shell structure; SEM micrographs of electronic ink microcapsules before (e1) and after (e2) exposure to a 15 kV electron beam for over 120 s. Post-exposure, significant microparticle rearrangement is observed, probably owing to surface charging and thermal effects, triggering chromatic response of the ink system.

A close-up of a spherical microcapsule with a core–shell configuration is shown in figure 1b . The smooth outer shell in figure 1b1 indicates an intact structure, essential for effectively encapsulating the electrophoretic core. In contrast, figure 1b2 depicts a partially damaged or ruptured capsule, probably owing to prolonged exposure to the SEM electron beam under high vacuum conditions, at a reduced working distance (10 mm) and a relatively high accelerating voltage (15 kV) [ 21 ]. This damage confirms the internal hollow structure of the EIMC. For electrophoretic applications, the core–shell configuration is a desirable design, ensuring effective containment of the electrophoretic medium while providing mechanical and structural stability, which is essential for long-term performance in display or optical applications [ 22 ].

The micrograph in figure 1c depicts a microcapsule with a rough, textured surface, probably resulting from the inhomogeneous adhesion of TiO 2 nanoparticles (NPs) onto the shell [ 23 ]. The uneven surface morphology suggests that these NPs may have been embedded during the encapsulation process or attached post-formation owing to electrostatic interactions, van der Waals forces or capillary-driven deposition [ 24 ].

In figure 1d , a fractured microcapsule is shown, exhibiting visible cracks across its surface. The rupture probably resulted from a combination of electromechanical and thermal stress, induced by continuous exposure to the electron beam and vacuum pressure during SEM imaging [ 25 ]. This also appears to have led to the vaporization of the liquid electrophoretic content. Yet, the modified TiO 2 NPs are possibly accumulating near the cracked regions. Energy dispersive X-ray spectroscopy (EDX) analysis of the white clump on the uneven surface confirmed the presence of TiO 2 , with a high atomic concentration of titanium (approx. 17%). This concentration increases to over 50% when measured on the inner side of the crack (supplementary material, figure S4, table S2), where the density of nanoparticles is highest, as expected. Overall, the incorporation of TiO 2 NPs within the shell matrix is conducive to the overall structural integrity of the microcapsules and may contribute to their functional properties, such as improved mechanical strength and stability, and optical performance [ 26 , 27 ].

In figure 1e , the SEM micrographs depict EIMCs, containing violet dye in conjunction with TiO 2 NPs, before (e1) and after (e2) exposure to a 15 kV electron beam for a relatively prolonged period (greater than 120 s). The images reveal a distinct rearrangement of microparticles following electron beam exposure, indicative of potential physical changes. Specifically, in figure 1e1 , the microcapsules exhibit a compact and aggregated morphology, with well-defined clusters. TiO 2 NP-dominated regions appear bright, densely embedded within the microcapsule structures. Following exposure to the electron beam ( figure 1e2 ), significant rearrangement of the microparticles was observed. This probably resulted from localized charging effects, thermal energy or alterations in interparticle adhesion owing to the high-energy electron interactions [ 25 , 28 ]. The redistribution of EIMCs suggests potential surface charging may be triggered by electrostatic effects, thereby perturbing the quiescence of the encapsulated ink.

Interestingly, the microcapsule morphology remained largely intact, despite the redistribution of EIMC, which appeared darker and more randomly spread out ( figure 1e2 ). This provides clear evidence of their effective chromatic response.

This observation underscores the sensitivity and dynamic behaviour of EIMCs under electron beam exposure, with potential implications for their structural stability in electron-rich/high-energy environments (greater than 15 kV), under prolonged operations. However, it is important to note that typical e-paper and e-display technologies operate at no/minimal voltages (0–20 V), unveiling the potential of our EIMCs for practical applications [ 29 ].

### Applied electric field: observation of e-ink microcapsules

Upon applying an electric field, the negatively charged TiO 2 NPs suspended within the dielectric medium exhibited an instantaneous response, migrating toward the positively charged electrode ( figure 2 ). Figure 2a1 schematically represents the fundamental principle, illustrating how the NPs concentrate near the oppositely charged electrode, forming a dense layer stacking along the curvature of the microcapsule inner shell. This migration follows the electrostatic force lines, which are maximized in regions where the electrode–particle optical pathway is minimized. The real-time microscopic observation shown in figure 2a2 provides direct evidence of this rapid response, occurring within a timeframe of less than 0.5 s. It became evident that the accumulation of TiO 2 NPs effectively blocked light transmission in regions where they are densely packed, while areas devoid of particles remained transparent. Indeed, this behaviour is pivotal to electrophoretically activated e-ink technologies, where nanoparticle displacement alters the optical appearance of the microcapsule [ 3 ]. Key insights are the curvature of the microcapsule inner shell and its structural configuration (core–shell), which played a crucial role in guiding NP migration. Conversely, irregularly shaped and/or multinuclear microcapsules may alter the dielectric properties of the suspension medium, impairing the response speed and/or contrast ratio in practical applications. Figure 2. Electrophoretic behaviour of TiO 2 NPs within microcapsules under an applied electric field: (a1) schematic representation of TiO 2 NP migration toward the positively charged electrode, forming a dense layer along the inner shell of the microcapsule; (a2) real-time microscopic observation demonstrating the rapid response (less than 0.5 s) of NPs, where densely packed regions block light transmission, while particle-depleted areas remain transparent. This behaviour underpins the electrophoretic principle in electronic e-ink technology.

### Actuation tests: electrophoretic writing and display applications

In figure 3 , the principle of a dynamic, electrophoretically driven writing display is presented. This enables users to write and erase freely using a stylus connected to a low-power source. This system leverages an indium tin oxide (ITO) conductive film (10 3 –10 4 S cm −1 , optical transmittance greater than 80%) beneath the EIMC layer, where an applied voltage induces localized nanoparticle migration [ 30 ]. This movement results in high-contrast, rewritable text or drawings, potentially rendering the display helpful for interactive workspaces, or real-time brainstorming sessions. Figure 3. Electrophoretic freehand e-ink writing and display applications: (a1) schematic of the writing display, where a stylus connected to a power source modulates the electric field, redistributing NPs to create visible emoji (a2); (b) practical demonstration of the system, showing the inscription of numbers (e.g. 1, 2, 3, 4, 5) with high contrast and rapid response; (c) stencilled shape with predefined patterns (e.g. arrow) toggled on and off using controlled electrical stimulation; (d) a rudimentary 3×3 matrix display, demonstrating individually addressable cells for differential data streaming (e.g. digital indicators).

Figure 3a1 illustrates the fundamental operating principle: a stylus, acting as an electrode, modulates the electric field at the point of contact, selectively redistributing electrophoretic NPs within the microcapsules to inscribe a clear emoji ( figure 3a2 ). This effect produces visible writing with high resolution and short response times. Figure 3b demonstrates this mechanism in practice, where numbers (1, 2, 3, 4, 5) are visibly inscribed, confirming the responsiveness and functionality of our system, comparable to other commercial e-ink technologies. Figure 3c showcases other examples of freehand writing into well-defined shapes (e.g. arrow). These, defined by tape stencils, can be selectively toggled on/off via controlled electrical stimulation. This system has potential for customizable signage, yielding crisp, high-contrast patterns without blurring or smudging. Additionally, figure 3d displays a rudimentary matrix display, where a 3 × 3 grid of individually addressable cells was created using tape to partition the microcapsule layer. This demonstrated the feasibility of electrophoretic microcapsules for low-power digital signage, clocks or notification panels, where each electrophoretic cell can independently stream a different set of information. While the current system is a proof of concept, it highlights the potential for scalable, energy-efficient matrix displays, pending further development of addressing circuitry and control mechanisms.

To quantitatively assess the display performance, the drawing precision of the prototype was analysed. The theoretical minimum feature size of the display is approximately 25–50 µm (representing 1–2 microcapsule widths). In practice, the line resolution is dictated by the stylus geometry (size of electrode) and electric field fringing. The drawn line with a standard multimeter electrode is recorded and measured in imageJ, and the drawn line with 6033 ± 705 µm width was achieved. Edge sharpness was quantified via optical greyscale profiling, yielding a robust contrast ratio of 1.94 between the actuated regions and background. Furthermore, to validate the ‘flexible writing’ capability and mechanical durability, the EIMC layer was subjected to cyclic write–erase testing. After 100 continuous cycles driven at 20 V, the display exhibited no visible capsule rupture, maintaining a contrast ratio of 1.58, confirming the reversibility and mechanical resilience of the cross-linked coacervate shell under repeated electromechanical stress.

### Mechanical performance of e-ink microcapsules

The mechanical performance of gum acacia–gelatin EIMCs encapsulating electrophoretically active gentian violet dye (GVD) with surface-modified TiO 2 NPs was assessed through a micromanipulation technique [ 31 , 32 ]. The average D nb,m = 23.2 ± 1.5 µm ( n = 30) obtained by micromanipulation was in excellent agreement with D nb,J (22.4 ± 0.4 µm). The typical force–displacement curve ( figure 4a ) reveals a progressive force increase until rupture, occurring at an average displacement of 1.9 ± 0.3 µm, and marked by a sharp force drop (see the vertical orange dashed line). This highlights that the microcapsules can withstand significant compression before fracturing (average rupture force 1.14 ± 0.13 mN), which is a crucial property for durable applications, especially in electrophoretic displays/cells. Figure 4. (a) Force–displacement curve of gum acacia–gelatin microcapsules under compression, showing a rupture event followed by a residual mechanical response; (b) nominal rupture stress as a function of diameter, indicating higher stress in smaller capsules; (c) apparent Young's modulus versus diameter; (d) typical experimental force–displacement curve fitted to the Hertz model ( R 2 ∼ 0.963).

Figure 4b illustrates the relationship between the nominal rupture stress of EIMCs and their diameter, which appears to be inversely proportional to each other. Similar behaviours were described by Hu et al. [ 33 ]. The mean rupture stress was found to be 3.9 ± 0.8 MPa, significantly higher than commercial, microplastic-based melamine-formaldehyde microcapsules, used in a number of consumer products (1.2–1.8 MPa) [ 34 ]. This enhancement in mechanical strength can be attributed to the cross-linked shell structure and the reinforcing effect of TiO 2 NPs. It cannot be excluded that some NPs may have got integrated within the coacervated shell matrix during encapsulation [ 26 , 35 ].

Compared with other microcapsules reported in the literature, such as those with polydopamine (PDA)-coated calcium carbonate (2.2 ± 0.3 MPa) shells, these new EIMCs exhibited superior rupture stress, rendering them probably suitable for high-stability electronic ink applications where mechanical strength is pivotal.

The Young's modulus of the whole EIMCs, which is a measure of their apparent stiffness [ 36 ], was found to be 0.17 ± 0.03 GPa ( figure 4c ), determined by the Hertz model [ 31 ]. Interestingly, this value suggests that EIMCs are relatively rigid prior to rupturing, and then plastically deforming, under compression (deformation at rupture approx. 18% ± 2%). Furthermore, there appeared to be a tentative correlation between the elastic modulus of EIMCs and their diameter. This probably indicates less stiff microcapsules at larger diameters, which is possibly owing to their ratio of shell thickness to diameter becoming smaller. Similar considerations were reported elsewhere [ 17 ]. Typical experimental force–displacement data fitted by the classical Hertz model is displayed in figure 4d , featuring a coefficient of determination ( R 2 ) greater than 0.96.

Overall, the analysis of the mechanical properties of EIMCs suggests that they may be well-suited for electrophoretically assisted applications, especially for on-skin digital interfaces, where dynamic NP movement within an electric field and resilience against mechanical fatigue are required.
