The colon provides several engineering opportunities. The distal gastrointestinal pH profile can trigger dissolution of enteric coatings, whereas pectinase, azoreductase, nitroreductase, and other microbiota-derived enzymes can activate degradable matrices. 14–16 , 42 , 43 Mucus thickness and composition, epithelial permeability, local reactive oxygen species, and matrix metalloproteinases differ between healthy and diseased tissue and can be exploited for mucoadhesive, mucus-penetrating, inflammation-responsive, or enzyme-cleavable designs. At the cellular level, receptors such as integrin α4β7 in intestinal inflammation, and CD44, folate receptor, A33 antigen, EGFR, and selected integrins in CRC, offer opportunities for ligand-directed uptake 44–48 Because each signal is variable and rarely disease-exclusive, robust colon targeting is more likely to require layered design—regional protection, lesion recognition, and intracellular release—rather than reliance on a single trigger.

Recent reviews have separately examined extracellular-vesicle engineering across multiple physiological barriers, 23 plant-derived vesicle-like nanoparticles for oral ulcerative-colitis therapy, 25 and mesenchymal stem/stromal cell-derived extracellular vesicles in inflammatory bowel disease. 29 , 49 Taken together, these reviews do not provide a unified colon-specific engineering framework that links gastrointestinal regional barriers and triggers—including pH, transit time, mucus, microbiota-derived enzymes, reactive oxygen species (ROS), and matrix metalloproteinases (MMPs)—to surface and cargo engineering, disease-specific target-cell biology in IBD versus CRC, administration route, manufacturability, and clinical-regulatory readiness. The distinctive aim of the present review is therefore not simply to catalogue sEV engineering methods, but to organize them into a disease- and route-oriented decision framework for colon-targeted delivery. Important unresolved questions include how sEVs terminology and source heterogeneity should be standardized; which targeting strategy is most appropriate for a given disease, cargo, and route; how microbiome variability alters release and response; which potency assays predict clinical benefit; and whether added engineering complexity produces sufficient benefit to justify scale-up and cost. Accordingly, this review critically synthesizes sEVs biology, preparation and characterization, cargo loading, surface engineering, colon-specific targeting and responsive release, microbiome interactions, disease mechanisms, clinical evidence, and regulatory considerations. Comparative tables and a rational design matrix are used to identify trade-offs and to provide a practical roadmap for development of safe, reproducible, and clinically relevant colon-targeted sEV systems ( Figure 1 ). ## Overview of sEVs

### Biogenesis, Molecular Composition, and Functional Mechanisms of sEVs

Extracellular vesicles comprise heterogeneous lipid-bilayer particles released by cells. Operationally, the International Society for Extracellular Vesicles recommends describing vesicles by physical characteristics, biochemical composition, or experimental source when endosomal origin has not been directly demonstrated. Exosomes are generated as intraluminal vesicles within multivesicular bodies and are released after fusion with the plasma membrane, whereas microvesicles arise predominantly by outward budding of the plasma membrane; apoptotic bodies are generated during programmed cell death. 50–52 Because common isolation methods do not completely separate these populations, the operational term “sEVs” is used throughout this review for particles within the small-size range unless biogenesis has been established.

sEVs biogenesis and cargo sorting involve endosomal sorting complex required for transport (ESCRT)-dependent machinery, ESCRT-independent lipid pathways, tetraspanins, Rab GTPases, and SNARE proteins. 53 Cargo selection is not random: RNA-binding proteins, sequence motifs, post-translational modifications, membrane microdomains, and donor-cell state influence enrichment of proteins, lipids, messenger RNAs, microRNAs, long non-coding RNAs, and DNA fragments. 54 , 55 The membrane is enriched in cholesterol, sphingomyelin, ceramide, and proteins including CD9, CD63, CD81, Alix, and TSG101, although marker abundance varies by source and preparation. Recipient cells internalize sEVs through clathrin- or caveolin-dependent endocytosis, macropinocytosis, phagocytosis, receptor-ligand binding, or direct membrane fusion. Subsequent endosomal escape or lysosomal processing determines whether cargo reaches the cytosol and remains functional. 56–59

### Comparison of sEV Isolation and Purification Technologies

Preparation of therapeutic sEVs is a multistep process rather than a single isolation step. A concise workflow comprises: selection and qualification of the donor source; controlled cell or biological-fluid collection; removal of cells, debris, and large vesicles; enrichment by ultracentrifugation, filtration, size-exclusion chromatography, precipitation, immunoaffinity, or microfluidics; orthogonal characterization of particle number, size, morphology, markers, purity, and biological activity; cargo loading or surface engineering; removal of unincorporated reagents; sterile formulation; and stability testing. Since high recovery, high purity, preserved functionality, throughput, and scalability are seldom achieved simultaneously, the choice of methods should be carefully aligned with the intended application ( Table 2 and Figure 2 ). Beyond the isolation protocol, storage buffer, temperature, freeze-thaw exposure, and sample concentration are additional critical variables that substantially influence sEV recovery and potency. 41 , Ultracentrifugation (100,000–150,000 g) remains one of the most widely used methods for bulk sEV enrichment because it can process relatively large sample volumes using well-established workflows. 84 However, it is time-consuming, requires specialized equipment, and high shear forces can damage vesicles, while co-pelleted protein aggregates limit purity. 85 , 86 By comparison, size-based methods (ultrafiltration and size-exclusion chromatography) offer milder conditions—especially SEC, which preserves vesicle integrity—but neither fully removes similarly sized lipoproteins, and SEC suffers from low throughput and diluted eluates. 87–89 Polymer precipitation (eg, PEG) is even simpler and faster, ideal for small volumes, yet it yields the lowest purity because reagents co-precipitate abundant proteins and lipoproteins, and residual polymers interfere with downstream assays. 90 Stimuli-responsive polymers have emerged to improve purity and recovery but remain laboratory-stage. 91

Immunoaffinity capture can provide high-purity, subset-selective isolation by targeting exosomal surface markers (CD63, CD81, EpCAM), making it uniquely suited for diagnostic applications requiring origin discrimination. 92 In contrast, its high cost, limited capture capacity, potential elution-induced activity loss, and restriction to marker-positive subsets hinder large-scale use. Microfluidic technologies integrate multiple principles (immunoaffinity, size, acoustics, dielectrophoresis) on miniaturized chips, enabling automated, low-consumption isolation directly from whole blood with preserved bioactivity. 79 , 80 , 93 While microfluidics holds great promise for clinical diagnostics and point-of-care testing, its processing throughput remains lower than ultracentrifugation or precipitation, and scale-up poses significant engineering challenges—mirroring the scalability limitations of immunoaffinity but offering greater flexibility in sample type and labeling options.

Advances in kits and novel platforms have aimed to bridge the gap between purity, speed, and scalability. Early kits like ExoQuick (polymer precipitation) prioritized speed, whereas Qiagen’s membrane affinity improved reproducibility for GMP compliance, and MagCapture enabled clinical throughput via magnetic beads. Newer designs such as Exodisc integrate filtration for efficient urine processing; ultrathin membranes support continuous low-cost production; ExoSearch offers closed-loop analysis; and iKnife uses AI to optimize parameters and reduce variability. 94 , 95 None of these emerging techniques, however, completely resolve all trade-offs between purity, yield, vesicle integrity, and throughput—highlighting the need for method selection based on specific research or production goals.

In summary, sEVs isolation requires trade-offs among purity, yield, throughput, and vesicle integrity. No single method is optimal for all applications. Future development should prioritize scalable, standardized isolation systems that preserve structural and functional integrity and are compatible with clinical translation.

conclusions:
Engineered sEVs combine a natural lipid bilayer, cargo protection, cellular uptake, and programmable modification of their surfaces and cargo. These features make them suitable for overcoming the sequential barriers encountered during oral delivery to the colon. Within a single system, they can provide protection during gastrointestinal transit, regional release, recognition of diseased tissue, delivery into target cells, and biological signaling. Nanovesicles derived from edible plants further expand this design space because their sources are abundant, renewable, and potentially scalable. Several preparations tolerate gastrointestinal conditions and contain components that suppress inflammation, reduce oxidative stress, or regulate the intestinal microbiota. However, these properties depend on the source and preparation method. The most immediate opportunities lie in applications with clearly defined mechanisms, including restoration of epithelial barrier integrity and immune homeostasis in IBD and targeted delivery of cytotoxic or immunomodulatory agents in CRC.

Clinical translation now depends on resolving three priorities. First, heterogeneity among sources and uncertainty in potency require nomenclature that identifies the source, benchmarks for composition, and potency assays tied to mechanisms of action. Second, variable yield and product instability require closed production systems that comply with good manufacturing practice. Tangential-flow filtration followed by size-exclusion chromatography may be used where appropriate, together with controls during production and protective formulations or lyophilization. Third, limited knowledge of biodistribution, safety over extended periods, and clinical efficacy requires quantitative fate studies, organoids and microphysiological intestinal models that reproduce relevant diseases, and early clinical trials that include pharmacodynamic measures and outcomes meaningful to patients. A development framework that integrates the route of administration, disease context, cargo, mechanism of action, and manufacturing requirements will therefore be essential. Progress in these related areas could convert promising vesicle biology into reproducible and clinically useful sEV products for delivery to the colon.

title: cRGD-Targeted Nanoparticles Co-Loaded with Ag, Quercetin and PD-L1 siRNA with Combined Antibacterial and Immunotherapeutic Functions Against Fusobacterium nucleatum -Associated Triple-Negative Breast Cancer
abstract:
### Introduction

Triple-negative breast cancer (TNBC) is an aggressive malignancy with poor prognosis, and Fusobacterium nucleatum (Fn) colonization further aggravates tumor progression, immunosuppression and therapeutic resistance. Conventional monotherapies are limited by insufficient tumor targeting, rapid drug clearance and failure to reverse immune suppression. Here, we fabricated cRGD-modified nanoparticles (Ag@GQDs/QUE-siP-c-L) for co-delivery of AgNPs, quercetin (QUE) and PD-L1 siRNA (siP).

### Methods

The morphology, particle size, surface metal elements, drug content and QUE entrapment efficiency of Ag@GQDs/QUE-siP-c-L were obtained using particle size analysis, SEM, inductively coupled plasma-optical emission spectrometry (ICP-OES) and HPLC. We further detected cellular uptake, in vitro drug release, cytotoxicity, intracellular reactive oxygen species level, PD-L1 gene silencing efficiency and in vitro anti-Fn activity. Pharmacokinetics and tissue distribution of Ag and QUE were analyzed by ICP-OES and LC-MS/MS, and in vivo antitumor efficacy and biosafety were tested in Fn-colonized orthotopic 4T1 tumor mice.

### Results

Ag@GQDs/QUE-siP-c-L exhibited uniform spherical morphology (195.87± 15.96 nm) with high encapsulation of QUE. cRGD modification enhanced Ag/QUE cellular uptake in 4T1 cells, with pH-responsive release accelerated under tumor acidic conditions. The nanoparticles exhibited selective tumor cytotoxicity, induced oxidative stress, downregulated PD-L1 mRNA, and exerted potent anti-Fn activity in vitro. Pharmacokinetics revealed increased AUC 0-t and reduced clearance compared with free drugs, and cRGD modification promoted tumor accumulation and retention of drugs. In vivo preliminary experiments proved the Ag@GQDs/QUE-siP-c-L formulation suppressed tumor growth with a tumor inhibition rate of 45%, and effectively modulated the tumor immune microenvironment: it increased tumor-infiltrating CD3⁺CD4⁺ T cells, reduced PD-L1⁺CD11c⁺ dendritic cells, and decreased the proportions of immunosuppressive Tregs and MDSCs. Hematoxylin-eosin staining and serum liver-kidney biochemistry confirmed no obvious systemic toxicity.

### Conclusion

Ag@GQDs/QUE-siP-c-L serves as a multimodal nanoplatform for Fn -associated TNBC with combined in vitro antibacterial, gene silencing and in vivo antitumor immunomodulatory effects, showing great potential for future translational research.

## Keywords
silver nanoparticles; PD-L1 siRNA; Fusobacterium nucleatum; breast cancer; quercetin; combined therapy

## Introduction

Breast cancer remains the most prevalent malignant tumor and leading cause of cancer-related mortality in women worldwide, among which triple-negative breast cancer (TNBC) represents the most aggressive subtype with high metastasis, strong drug resistance, and extremely poor prognosis due to the lack of effective therapeutic targets. Clinical mainstream strategies including surgery, chemotherapy, and radiotherapy are severely limited by poor tumor specificity, rapid drug clearance, off-target toxicity, and high recurrence risk, failing to meet the clinical demand for precise and efficient treatment of TNBC. 1 In recent years, emerging evidence has confirmed that tumor-associated microbiota, especially Fusobacterium nucleatum (Fn), is highly enriched in breast cancer tissues and plays a critical oncogenic role. 2 Fn colonizes in tumor parenchyma, remodels the tumor microenvironment (TME) into an immunosuppressive niche, inhibits cytotoxic T-cell infiltration, accelerates tumor proliferation and distant metastasis, and further reduces the sensitivity of TNBC to conventional therapy, which has become a new key target for breast cancer treatment. 3 Therefore, the development of a novel therapeutic platform that can simultaneously kill tumor cells, reverse immunosuppression, and eliminate tumor-resident Fn is of great significance to break through the treatment dilemma of TNBC.

Combination therapy has become a core strategy for cancer treatment, which exerts synergistic antitumor effects through multi-target and multi-mechanism intervention, reduces toxic side effects, and overcomes the limitations of single-drug therapy. 4 In our previous study, we constructed a lipid-coated silver nanoparticle (AgNP)-single-stranded DNA (ssDNA)-graphene quantum dot (GQDs) delivery system, which achieved favorable antitumor efficacy against cervical cancer and enabled real-time fluorescence imaging tracking owing to the excellent optical properties of GQDs. 5 Inspired by multi-modal combination therapy and tumor bacteria-targeted strategies, we further optimized this delivery system by introducing GQDs as a fluorescent tracking module and structural stabilizer to construct a stable AgNP-GQDs composite core. To endow the carrier with multifunctions of bacteriostasis, tumor growth suppression and immune checkpoint blockade, we incorporated natural flavonoid quercetin (QUE) and PD-L1 siRNA (siP) into cyclic arginine-glycine-aspartic acid (cRGD)-functionalized AgNP-GQDs-cored nanoparticles for synchronous co-delivery.

In summary, we designed a novel targeted nanoparticle Ag@GQDs/QUE-siP-c-L for the co-delivery of AgNPs, QUE, and siP. This study aimed to systematically evaluate the physicochemical properties, in vitro performance, in vivo pharmacokinetics, antitumor efficacy, and biosafety of Ag@GQDs/QUE-siP-c-L, and explore its synergistic therapeutic mechanism against TNBC, so as to provide a novel and effective multi-functional targeted strategy for the clinical treatment of TNBC.

## Materials and Methods

### Materials

Silver nitrate (≥99.7%) and poly(allylamine hydrochloride) (PAH, ≥99.7%) were obtained from Shanghai Aladdin Bio-Chem Technology Co., Ltd. (Shanghai, China). Graphene quantum dots (GQDs) were purchased from Jiangsu XFNANO Materials Tech. Co., Ltd. (Nanjing, China). Quercetin (QUE, purity≥99%) was purchased from Shanghai Yuanye Bio-Technology Co., Ltd. (Shanghai, China). The siP (sequence: GAGGTAATCTGGACAAACA) and nonsense siRNA (target sequence: CAATCGTCGTAACTAGACT) was purchased from Guangzhou Ribo Bio Co., Ltd. (Guangzhou, China). The lipids for drug encapsulation including: the 1,2-distearoyl-sn-glycero-3-phosphoethanolamine-N-(polyethylene glycol)-1000-NHS (DSPE-PEG1000-NHS, Catalog No. R-0042-K) and 1,2-dipalmitoyl-sn-glycero-3-phosphoethanolamine-N-(polyethylene glycol)-3400-cRGD (DSPE-PEG3400-cRGD, Catalog No. R-BGV451) were purchased from Xi’an Ruixi Biotechnology Co., Ltd. (Xi’an, China). Polyamidoamine dendrimer (PAMAM, Generation 4) was purchased from Sigma-Aldrich Co. LLC (Catalog No. 412449-10G; St. Louis, MO, USA). DSPE-PEG1000-PAMAM was synthesized according to previously reported methods. 6 The 1,2-distearoyl-sn-glycero-3-phosphoethanolamine-N-(polyethylene glycol)-2000 (DSPE-PEG2000) were purchased from AVT (Shanghai) Pharmaceutical Tech Co., Ltd. (Catalog No. F01008 ; Shanghai, China). Quantitative reverse transcription polymerase chain reaction (qRT-PCR) PrimerSets (one RT primer and a pair of qPCR primers for each set) specific for PD-L1 and the primer for β-actin (targeting sequence: forward 5′-AGATGACCCAGATCATGTTTGAGA-3′; reverse 5′-GCATGAGGGAGCGCGTAA-3′) are designed by RiboBio Biotechnology Co., Ltd. (Guangzhou, China). Kaempferol (purity≥98%) was from Beijing Solarbio Science and Technology Co., Ltd. Xin’erjin ® Paclitaxel Injection (Approval No. H20066640, Beijing Shuanglu Pharmaceutical Co., Ltd.). Isoflurane was from RWD Life Science Co., Ltd. (Shenzhen, China, GMP Certificate for Veterinary Drugs No. 030189). Analytical-grade chemicals and reagents were used in this study unless specified otherwise.

### Cells

The 4T1 mouse breast cancer cell line and embryonic fibroblast NIH3T3 cell line were purchased from Beijing Dingguo Changsheng Biotechnology Co., Ltd. 4T1 cells were inoculated in complete medium consisting of Roswell Park Memorial Institute 1640 basal medium, 10% (v/v) fetal bovine serum (FBS) and 1% penicillin-streptomycin (PS), and incubated in a humidified incubator at 37 °C under 5% CO 2 atmosphere. NIH3T3 cells were cultured in high-glucose Dulbecco’s modified Eagle’s medium (DMEM) supplemented with 10% fetal bovine serum (FBS) and 1% penicillin-streptomycin solution, and maintained at 37 °C in a humidified incubator with 5% CO 2 . Cells in the logarithmic growth phase were harvested for subsequent cytotoxicity assays.

### Bacteria

Fusobacterium nucleatum (Fn) strain was purchased from BeNa Culture Collection (BNCC305282, Beijing, China). The strain was resuscitated and cultured on Colombia blood agar plates supplemented with 5% defibrinated sheep blood, and incubated at 37 °C for 48–72 h in an anaerobic workstation (80% N 2 , 10% H 2 , 10% CO 2 ). Single colonies were selected and subcultured to logarithmic phase for subsequent in vitro antibacterial assays and in vivo intratumoral inoculation.

### Animals

Specific pathogen-free female BALB/c mice (16–18 g) and male Sprague-Dawley rats (200±20 g) were provided by SPF (Beijing) Biotechnology Co., Ltd. The animal experiments were conducted according to the ethical policies and procedures approved by the Medical Ethics Committee of Jiangxi University of Chinese Medicine (Approval No. JZLLSC20250503). The animal room was well-ventilated and had a regular 12 h light-dark cycle throughout the experimental period.

### Synthesis of AgNPs

Silver nanoparticles (AgNPs) were prepared via a redox method using polyallylamine hydrochloride (PAH) as the reducing agent. Briefly, PAH and AgNO 3 solutions were prepared at concentrations of 0.03 M and 8×10 −3 M, respectively. Under ice‑water bath at 0 °C and 900 rpm stirring, AgNO 3 solution was slowly added dropwise to PAH solution. The reaction was kept in the dark for 15 min.

After the reaction, the resulting solution was divided into two portions. One portion was dialyzed in a 3.5 kDa dialysis bag for 4 h to remove unreacted reagents, and the purified AgNPs obtained were used as the control group in subsequent in vitro and in vivo assays, and stored at 4 °C. Particle size and zeta potential of the dialyzed AgNPs were measured using a Malvern particle size analyzer (Nano ZS90, Malvern, UK).

The other portion of freshly prepared AgNPs was used directly for the preparation of the final Ag@GQDs/QUE-siP-c-L without intermediate dialysis.

### Synthesis of Ag@GQDs/QUE-siP-c-L

One milliliter of the as-synthesized AgNPs solution (without intermediate dialysis) was mixed with 20 μL of 100 μM citrate solution (adjusted to acidic pH) and incubated at 37 °C for 5 min. Then 5 μL of 100 μM PD-L1 siRNA (siP) was added and incubated for another 5 min. Subsequently, 167 μL of 1 mg/mL graphene quantum dots (GQDs) solution was slowly added dropwise into the above mixture, and incubated at 37 °C with 200 r/min stirring for 30 min to form siP-loaded Ag@GQDs cores (Ag@GQDs/siP).

To prepare Ag@GQDs/QUE-siP-L, ethanol injection method was applied. Lipid materials including DSPE-PEG1000-PAMAM, DSPE-PEG2000 and DSPE-PEG3400-cRGD with a molar ratio of 1:3.5:0.3 were mixed with QUE at a lipid‑to‑drug ratio (total phospholipids: QUE) of 20:1 in ethanol solution. This solution was slowly injected into the Ag@GQDs/siP core solution under 800 rpm stirring, and reacted at 50 °C for 30 min. Finally, the mixture was transferred into a dialysis bag (Mw: 3.5 kDa) and dialyzed for 4 h to obtain the final targeted nanoparticle Ag@GQDs/QUE-siP-c-L. To prepare Ag@GQDs/QUE-siP-L, the same procedure was followed, with the addition of DSPE-PEG3400-cRGD replaced by DSPE-PEG2000 in the total phospholipids. Ag@GQDs/QUE-sis-L was prepared by replacing siP with an equal amount of scrambled siRNA (sis) in accordance with the aforementioned procedures of Ag@GQDs/QUE-siP-L.

For the preparation of various control formulations, all operations were performed in accordance with the aforementioned procedures of Ag@GQDs/QUE-siP-c-L with corresponding adjustments: Ag@GQDs/siP-c-L was prepared without the addition of QUE, Ag@GQDs/QUE-c-L was prepared without siP, Ag@GQDs-c-L was prepared without the addition of siP and QUE.

Ag@GQDs/siP-L was prepared in accordance with the aforementioned procedures of Ag@GQDs/QUE-siP-L without QUE, Ag@GQDs/QUE-L was prepared without any siRNA, Ag@GQDs/L was prepared without siP and QUE.

### Characterization of Ag@GQDs/QUE-siP-c-L

#### Size, Zeta Potential, Morphology, and Surface Metal Analysis

The particle sizes and zeta potentials of AgNPs, Ag@GQDs/siP-L, and Ag@GQDs/QUE-siP-c-L were determined using a Laser Nanometer Particle Size Analyzer (Nano ZS90, Malvern, UK). AgNPs and Ag@GQDs/QUE-siP-c-L was observed by field-emission scanning electron microscopy (FE-SEM, HITACHI SU8010, Hitachi, Japan) equipped with an energy-dispersive X-ray spectrometer (EDS, HORIBA X-MaxN20 011, Horiba, Japan). Prior to observation, samples were coated with gold (sputter coater, GEVEE GVC-2000) and dried (critical point dryer, HAPVENT Himatic-250). SEM images were captured at 3 kV or 5 kV, and EDS was performed at 20 kV (resolution: 1.0 nm@15 kV for SEM, 127 eV for EDS).

#### Entrapment Efficiency and Content of QUE

The entrapment efficiency (EE%) of QUE was determined using ultrafiltration. One milliliter of the Ag@GQDs/QUE-siP-c-L solution was loaded into a 10 kDa MWCO ultrafiltration tube, centrifuged at 10,000 r/min for 20 min, and the filtrate was collected to measure the amount of free drug (W 1 ). The total drug content (W 2 ) was determined by diluting an equal volume of Ag@GQDs/QUE-siP-c-L to 10 mL with methanol and analyzing it via high-performance liquid chromatography (HPLC). The QUE content was quantified using an HPLC system (1260, Agilent, Japan) with a Diamonsil ODS-C 18 column (250 mm × 4.6 mm, 5 μm) at 30°C. The mobile phase was methanol-0.4% phosphate buffer (V: V=7:3) at a flow rate of 1.0 mL/min. The detection wavelength was 372 nm, and the injection volume was 10 μL. EE% was calculated using the formula. \documentclass[12pt]{minimal} \usepackage{wasysym} \usepackage[substack]{amsmath} \usepackage{amsfonts} \usepackage{amssymb} \usepackage{amsbsy} \usepackage[mathscr]{eucal} \usepackage{mathrsfs} \DeclareFontFamily{T1}{linotext}{} \DeclareFontShape{T1}{linotext}{m}{n} {linotext }{} \DeclareSymbolFont{linotext}{T1}{linotext}{m}{n} \DeclareSymbolFontAlphabet{\mathLINOTEXT}{linotext} \begin{document}$$EE{\mathrm{\%=}}{{{W_{\mathrm{2}}} - {W_{\mathrm{1}}}} \over {{W_{\mathrm{2}}}}}{\mathrm{\times100}}$$\end{document}

#### Silver Content Determination

The silver content of the samples was determined using inductively coupled plasma optical emission spectroscopy (ICP-OES) (700ES, Varian, USA). Briefly, the samples were completely digested by nitric acid and diluted to volume with 1% nitric acid until analysis. 7 The instrument parameters were set with a radio frequency power of 1.0 kW, the plasma gas flow rate was set to 15 L/min, the auxiliary gas flow rate was controlled at 1.5 L/min, the nebulizer gas pressure was maintained at 200 kPa, the rotational speed of the peristaltic pump was tuned to 15 rpm, and the sample introduction rate was kept at 1 mL/min. The instrument dwell time for each test sample was set to 30s. Each sample was analyzed in triplicate, and the final results were calculated using the average of the three replicate measurements.

#### Gel Retardation Assay

The siRNA loading in Ag@GQDs/QUE-siP-c-L was evaluated using agarose gel electrophoresis. The suspension was added to the pre-prepared siRNA solution at different N:P ratios (1:1, 2:1, 3:1, 4:1, 5:1, 6:1, 7:1 and 8:1). The N:P ratio is defined as the molar ratio of nitrogen atoms from the amine groups of the cationic lipid DSPE-PEG1000-PAMAM in the formulation to phosphorus atoms in the phosphate backbone of siRNA. The mixture was then loaded into the wells of a precast 1.2% agarose gel supplemented with SYBR Safe dye (Invitrogen, Thermo Fisher Scientific). Free siP (20 μmol/L) was used as a positive control, while Ag@GQDs/QUE-c-L without siP addition served as a blank control. Electrophoresis was conducted and visualized using an Invitrogen E-Gel Power Snap Electrophoresis Device (ThermoFisher Scientific) at a constant voltage of 65 V for 30 min.

#### Cell Uptake

4T1 cells were seeded in 6-well plates at 1×10 6 cells/well and incubated for 8 h. After washing, cells were treated with various Ag-containing and QUE-cotaining formulations, including AgNPs, Ag@GQDs/siP-L, Ag@GQDs/QUE-siP-L, and Ag@GQDs/QUE-siP-c-L with an Ag concentration of 3 µg/mL, as well as Ag@GQDs/QUE-siP-L, Ag@GQDs/QUE-siP-c-L and QUE suspension with a QUE concentration of 2 µg/mL.

After incubation for 2, 5, 10, and 15 min, the drug-containing medium was removed, and cells were washed three times with serum-free medium again. Cells at each time point were collected and divided into two aliquots. One part was digested with aqua regia, and the digested solution was diluted to 5 mL with 1% nitric acid for silver content determination by ICP-OES. The other part was treated with acetonitrile, centrifuged at 12,000 r/min for 10 min at 4 °C to remove protein precipitates, and the supernatant was collected and analyzed by liquid chromatograph-tandem mass spectrometry (LC-MS/MS) for QUE content with the following analysis condition.

#### Release Behavior

Dialysis was performed to evaluate the in vitro release of QUE and Ag from Ag@GQDs/QUE-siP-c-L under pH 7.4 (normal physiological condition) and pH 5.0 (tumor acidic microenvironment), respectively. A dialysis bag with a molecular weight cutoff of 20 kDa was filled with 1 mL of Ag@GQDs/QUE-siP-c-L and immersed in 100 mL of release medium (PBS containing 0.5% Tween-80) at pH 5.0 or pH 7.4. The release system was incubated at 37 °C with continuous shaking at 100 rpm. Samples were taken at 0.5, 1, 2, 4, 8, 12, and 24 h, and an equal volume of fresh pre-warmed release medium was immediately replenished to maintain a constant volume. The concentrations of released Ag and QUE were determined by corresponding analytical methods, and the cumulative release rate was calculated using the following equation: \documentclass[12pt]{minimal} \usepackage{wasysym} \usepackage[substack]{amsmath} \usepackage{amsfonts} \usepackage{amssymb} \usepackage{amsbsy} \usepackage[mathscr]{eucal} \usepackage{mathrsfs} \DeclareFontFamily{T1}{linotext}{} \DeclareFontShape{T1}{linotext}{m}{n} {linotext }{} \DeclareSymbolFont{linotext}{T1}{linotext}{m}{n} \DeclareSymbolFontAlphabet{\mathLINOTEXT}{linotext} \begin{document}$${\mathrm{Cumulative\ release\ rate }}\left({\mathrm{\% }} \right){\mathrm{=}}{{{V_{total}}{\mathrm{\times}}\mathop \sum \nolimits_{i{\mathrm{=1}}}^n {C_{i}}{\mathrm{+}}{V_i}{\mathrm{\times}}\mathop \sum \nolimits_{i{\mathrm{=1}}}^{n{\mathrm{-1}}} {C_i}} \over {{M_{\mathrm{0}}}}}{\mathrm{\times100}}$$\end{document}

Where V total is the initial total volume of release medium, n is the sampling number, C i is the mass concentration of Ag or QUE at the n-th sampling, V i is the volume of each sampling, and M 0 is the initial total mass of Ag or QUE inside the dialysis bag. Subsequently, the release curves were fitted with zero-order kinetics, first-order kinetics and Higuchi models to explore the drug release mechanism.

### Cell Viability

The cytotoxicity of AgNPs, Ag@GQDs/siP-L, Ag@GQDs/QUE-siP-L and Ag@GQDs/QUE-siP-c-L against 4T1 and NIH3T3 cells was evaluated using the CCK-8 assay. Briefly, cells were seeded into 96-well plates at a density of 2×10 4 cells per well and cultured overnight for adherence. Cells were then treated with serial dilutions of these Ag-containing formulations with Ag concentrations of 37.5, 18.75, 9.37, 4.68, 2.34, 1.17, 0.58, 0.29 µg/mL for 12 h. According to the manufacturer’s instruction, 10 μL of CCK-8 reagent was added to each well and incubated for another 2 h. The absorbance at 450 nm was measured by an M200 PRO microplate reader (Tecan, Switzerland). Cell viability was calculated relative to the untreated control group, and the half-maximal inhibitory concentration (IC 5 0 ) was determined using GraphPad Prism software (Version 10).

### Intracellular Reactive Oxygen Species Detection

The intracellular reactive oxygen species (ROS) level in 4T1 cells treated with Ag@GQDs/QUE-siP-c-L was detected by the Reactive Oxygen Species Assay Kit (Beyotime Biotechnology Co., Ltd., Shanghai, China) using 2′,7′-Dichlorofluorescin diacetate (DCFH-DA) as the fluorescent probe. Briefly, 4T1 cells were seeded into 6-well plates at a density of 2×10 6 cells/well and incubated for 12 h. Then cell culture medium was removed. Diluted DCFH-DA (10μmol/L) was added and incubated for 20 minutes in a 37°C-cell incubator. Then the medium was replaced with fresh medium containing AgNPs, Ag@GQDs/siP-c-L, and Ag@GQDs/QUE-siP-c-L at a final concentration of 1 μg/mL, while the control group received an equal volume of serum-free medium. After 2 h incubation, cells were washed and harvested. Intracellular fluorescence intensity was measured at an excitation wavelength of 488 nm and emission wavelength of 525 nm using a M200 PRO microplate reader (Tecan, Switzerland).

### Gene Silencing Assay

4T1 cells in logarithmic growth phase were seeded into 24-well plates at a density of 1×10 5 cells per well and cultured in complete medium containing 10% FBS overnight. After washing twice with PBS, cells were divided into five groups: blank group (untreated), free siP group, empty nanocarrier group (siP-free nanoparticles at the same particle concentration, Ag@GQDs/QUE-c-L), Ag@GQDs/QUE-siP-L group, and Ag@GQDs/QUE-siP-c-L group. All siRNA-containing groups were dosed at an equivalent final siRNA concentration of 20 nM. After 4 h of transfection incubation, the drug-containing medium was aspirated, cells were rinsed once with pre-warmed PBS, and fresh complete medium was added to continue culture. At 48 h after the initial administration, total cellular RNA was extracted using a commercial RNA extraction kit (Yeasen Biotechnology (Shanghai) Co., Ltd.) following the manufacturer’s protocol., and equal amounts of total RNA were reverse-transcribed into cDNA following the protocol of the HiFiScript cDNA Synthesis Kit. Quantitative real-time PCR was then performed using Hieff ® qPCR SYBR Master Mix on a real-time PCR system, with β-actin as the endogenous reference gene. The relative expression level of PD-L1 mRNA was calculated via the 2 −ΔΔCT method. 8 All experiments were carried out in three independent replicates.

### Antibacterial Assay

The in vitro antibacterial activity of Ag@GQDs/QUE-siP-c-L against Fusobacterium nucleatum (Fn) was evaluated by using colony counting assay. Fn in the logarithmic growth phase was adjusted to a concentration of 3×10 8 CFU/mL in anaerobic broth. Serial dilutions of AgNPs, Ag@GQDs/siP-L, Ag@GQDs/QUE-siP-L, and Ag@GQDs/QUE-siP-c-L were prepared in anaerobic medium (concentration of Ag at 50 μg/mL), using PBS solution as negative control, and then mixed with an equal volume of the above bacterial suspension in tubes, followed by anaerobic incubation at 37 °C for 4 h.

For quantitative analysis, 100 μL of each culture suspension was collected, gradient-diluted, and spread on Colombia blood agar plates supplemented with 5% defibrinated sheep blood. After continuous anaerobic incubation at 37 °C for 48 h, the number of colonies on each plate was counted, and the bacterial survival rate and inhibition rate were calculated accordingly. All experiments were performed in triplicate under strict anaerobic conditions (80% N 2 , 10% H 2 , 10% CO 2 ).

### Pharmacokinetic Evaluation

Nine Sprague-Dawley rats were randomly divided into three groups: QUE suspension, Ag@GQDs/QUE-siP-L, and Ag@GQDs/QUE-siP-c-L. After fasting for 12 h before the experiment, the corresponding formulation was administered to each group via tail vein injections at a dose normalized to 3.0 mg/kg for QUE. Blood samples (around 500 μL) were gathered from the retro-orbital venous plexus at scheduled time points: 0.017, 0.083, 0.25, 0.5, 1, 2, 4, 8, 12, 24, and 48 h post-injection. Collected blood was immediately transferred into heparin-coated tubes, followed by centrifugation at 2000 rpm for 15 min under 4 °C to obtain plasma. For sample pretreatment, 50 μL plasma was mixed with 30 ng Kaempferol (purity≥98%) in 150 μL acetonitrile for protein precipitation. After vortex blending for 5 min and centrifugation at 12,000 rpm for 10 min at 4 °C, the supernatant was collected and subjected to liquid chromatography-tandem mass spectrometry (LC-MS/MS) (QTRAP ® 4500, AB Sciex, USA) for analysis. Pharmacokinetic parameters were calculated by fitting the concentration-time data using PK solver software (version 2.0).

### LC-MS/MS Analysis of QUE

#### Chromatographic Conditions

Chromatographic separation was performed on a ZORBAX Eclipse XDB-C18 column (2.1×50 mm, 5 μm) maintained at 40 °C. The mobile phase consisted of 0.1% formic acid in water (A) and acetonitrile (B) at a flow rate of 0.5 mL/min, with an injection volume of 5 μL. Gradient elution was carried out as follows: 0.00–1.00 min, 5% B; 1.00–2.00 min, 5–20% B; 2.00–3.00 min, 20–80% B; 3.00–3.50 min, 80–95% B; 4.00–4.50 min, 95–5% B; 4.50–5.50 min, 5% B.

#### Mass Spectrometric Conditions

Mass spectrometry was operated in electrospray ionization (ESI) negative mode with multiple reaction monitoring (MRM). The ion spray voltage was set to 4500 V; curtain gas, nebulizing gas, and auxiliary gas were all nitrogen, at 25 psi, 55 psi, and 55 psi, respectively. The nebulization temperature was 550 °C, declustering potential (DP) was 100 V, and collision energy (CE) was 30 eV.

The MRM transitions were m/z 301.0→150.7 for QUE (DP: −116.94 V; CE: −28.20 eV) and m/z 284.9→184.8 for kaempferol (internal standard, DP: −132.01 V; CE: −36.90 eV).

### Tissue Distribution

When the tumor volume of mice reached approximately 300 mm 3 , BALB/c mice were randomly divided into the Ag@GQDs/QUE/siP-L and Ag@GQDs/QUE/siP-c-L groups as experimental groups, with the same concentration of AgNPs and QUE-suspension as the control group. Each formulation was administered to each group via tail vein injections at a dose of 3.0 mg/kg for QUE. All tail vein injection procedures were performed under isoflurane inhalation anesthesia. Mice were induced with 3–5% isoflurane in 100% oxygen at a flow rate of 1 L/min in an induction chamber, and anesthesia was maintained at 1.5–2% isoflurane during the operation. The depth of anesthesia was confirmed by the loss of the pedal withdrawal reflex to ensure the comfort of animals.

Mice were humanely euthanized at 0.5, 6, and 24 h after injection. Then the heart, liver, spleen, lungs, kidneys, and tumor tissues were excised. After rinsing, drying, and weighing, the tissue samples were sectioned. ICP-OES was used to measure the Ag content in the major organs and tumors as aforementioned. LC-MS/MS was used to detect QUE content in the major organs and tumors as aforementioned. For quantitative analysis, tissue Ag and QUE levels were further normalized relative to their corresponding free formulations (free AgNPs and free QUE suspension, respectively) to compare the tissue distribution performance of Ag@GQDs/QUE/siP-L and Ag@GQDs/QUE/siP-c-L.

### In vivo Anti-Tumor Efficacy

#### Tumor Model Establishment

Female BALB/c mice were used to establish orthotopic 4T1 breast cancer models colonized with Fn. Briefly, 1×10 6 4T1 cells suspension was inoculated into the mammary fat pad of mice, and a round, white, raised bleb on the mammary surface confirmed successful in-situ retention of cells. Tumor volume was measured, and the experiment was initiated when tumor volume reached 80–100 mm 3 .

Tumor volume was calculated by measuring the longest diameter (D) and shortest diameter (L) with a vernier caliper, using the following formula: \documentclass[12pt]{minimal} \usepackage{wasysym} \usepackage[substack]{amsmath} \usepackage{amsfonts} \usepackage{amssymb} \usepackage{amsbsy} \usepackage[mathscr]{eucal} \usepackage{mathrsfs} \DeclareFontFamily{T1}{linotext}{} \DeclareFontShape{T1}{linotext}{m}{n} {linotext }{} \DeclareSymbolFont{linotext}{T1}{linotext}{m}{n} \DeclareSymbolFontAlphabet{\mathLINOTEXT}{linotext} \begin{document}$${\mathrm{V }} = {\mathrm{ D}} \times {{\mathrm{L}}^2}/2$$\end{document}

Tumor-bearing mice were randomly divided into nine groups: bacteria-colonized model group, AgNPs group, QUE suspension group, Ag@GQDs/L group, Ag@GQDs/QUE-L group, Ag@GQDs/QUE-sis-L group, Ag@GQDs/QUE-siP-L group, Ag@GQDs/QUE-siP-c-L group, and Paclitaxel (PTX) Injection group. Fn suspension was prepared by picking single colonies of the 2nd generation with a sterile inoculation loop, mixing gently in PBS buffer, and adjusting to a concentration of 1.2×10 7 CFU per mouse. Intratumoral injection of Fn was performed in all groups to construct the Fn-infected orthotopic breast cancer mouse model. 9 All groups were administered via tail vein injection every 2 days for a total of 7 administrations at a dose of 1.5 mg/kg (QUE-equivalent) for nanoparticle formulations; PTX 20 mg/kg was injected once a week.

Body weight and tumor volume were recorded throughout the experiment to evaluate antitumor efficacy and in vivo toxicity. Three days after the last treatment, the mice were humanely euthanized with the same two-step protocol as aforementioned. Then the tumors were collected, weighed, and then processed for the following detection.

#### Flow Cytometry Detection

The tumor tissue was digested and gently rubbed through a 70-μm cell strainer on ice. After diluting with cell staining buffer (Elabscience Biotechnology Co., Ltd., Wuhan, China), the cells were centrifuged at 1000 r/min for 5 min and resuspended to form a single-cell suspension for staining. Cells were stained using fluorophore-labeled antibodies purchased from Elabscience Biotechnology Co., Ltd. (Wuhan, China), including PE anti-mouse CD3 (E-AB-F1013D), FITC anti-mouse CD4 (E-AB-F1353C), PE/Cy7 anti-mouse CD8a (E-AB-F1104H), APC anti-mouse CD25 (E-AB-F1102E), PE anti-FoxP3 (E-AB-F1238D), PE anti-mouse CD11b (E-AB-F1081D), APC anti-mouse Gr-1 (E-AB-F1120E), APC anti-mouse CD274/PD-L1 (E-AB-F1132E), and FITC anti-mouse CD11c (E-AB-F0991C). Fixation and permeabilization are required for the staining of FoxP3. Each antibody was used at the manufacturer’s recommended concentration of 5 μL per staining reaction, corresponding to 1 × 10 6 cells suspended in 100 μL of cell staining buffer. Mix thoroughly at room temperature, followed by 30 minutes of incubation in the dark. Cells were washed and resuspended in 500 µL PBS with adequate mixing prior to flow cytometric analysis. All samples were analyzed using a NovoCyte™ flow cytometer (NovoCyte 2060R, ACEA Biosciences (Hangzhou) Co., Ltd.), and the data were analyzed using NovoExpress (version 1.5.0) with the gating strategy was organized as Figure S1 in the supplementary materials .

### Hematoxylin and Eosin Staining

The heart, liver, spleen, lung, kidney, and tumor tissues were collected and fixed in 4% paraformaldehyde for 24 h, dehydrated, embedded in paraffin, and cut into 5 μm sections. For hematoxylin and eosin (H&E) staining, sections were dewaxed and rehydrated, stained with hematoxylin for 5 min, differentiated in 1% hydrochloric acid-ethanol for 15s, blued in running tap water for 2 min, counterstained with eosin for 1 min, then dehydrated, cleared and mounted with neutral balsam. Histopathological observation and image acquisition were performed using a DM2500 biological microscope (Leica Microsystems, Shanghai, China).

# Ex vivo Evaluation of Live-MB2 and CX-2 Biotic Strains on Inflammatory and Barrier-Related Biomarkers in a Human Skin Atopic Dermatitis–Like Model

## Abstract
### Objective

Atopic dermatitis (AD) is a chronic inflammatory skin condition characterized by epidermal barrier disruption and immune dysregulation. Live-MB2 and CX-2 were used in an ex vivo human skin AD-like model, which provides a biologically relevant platform for assessing cosmetic ingredients targeting AD-like features.

### Methods

An AD-like condition was induced in ex vivo human skin explants by repeated tape stripping followed by 2,4-dinitrochlorobenzene stimulation. Skin tissues were treated with Live-MB2 or CX-2 via topical or dermal exposure. Epidermal thickness, IgE, and filaggrin levels were evaluated using hematoxylin and eosin, immunofluorescence, and Enzyme-Linked Immunosorbent Assay analyses.

### Results

Topical application of Live-MB2 and CX-2 significantly reduced epidermal thickness compared with AD-induced controls. IgE levels were significantly reduced, while filaggrin expression indicated a marked increase, indicating barrier recovery. No treatment-related tissue damage was observed.

### Conclusion

Live-MB2 and CX-2 showed favorable effects on inflammatory and barrier-related parameters in an ex vivo human skin AD-like model, supporting their potential application as cosmetic ingredients for sensitive and atopic-prone skin.

## Keywords
Ex vivo human skin; atopic dermatitis; live biotics; skin barrier; filaggrin; cosmetic ingredients

## Introduction

Atopic dermatitis (AD) is a multifactorial inflammatory skin disorder involving epidermal barrier impairment, immune imbalance, and environmental triggers. 1 , 2 The pathogenesis of AD is largely explained by defects in epidermal barrier function and immune system dysregulation. Notably, mutations and reduced expression of the epidermal barrier protein filaggrin (FLG) decrease the stratum corneum’s water-retention capacity and increase trans epidermal water loss. 3 This weakening of the physical barrier facilitates the penetration of allergens and pathogens into the epidermis, thereby triggering an “outside-in” pathogenesis that induces Th2-skewed immune responses and excessive immunoglobulin E (IgE) production. 2 In addition to epidermal barrier disruption, AD is strongly associated with type 2 immune inflammation. Key cytokines such as interleukin (IL)-4, IL-13, and IL-31, along with epithelial mediators including thymic stromal lymphopoietin (TSLP), contribute to pruritus, inflammation, and further deterioration of skin barrier function. 4 , 5

Recent studies have shown that the skin of patients with AD exhibits a severe reduction in microbial diversity. In particular, the overgrowth of Staphylococcus aureus is closely associated with epidermal barrier damage and the exacerbation of inflammation. 6–8 Consequently, topical application of probiotics to restore the skin microbiome and modulate inflammation has emerged as a promising therapeutic strategy. Topical probiotics and microbiome-based ingredients contribute to suppressing harmful bacteria by secreting antimicrobial peptides and regulating the innate immune responses of the epidermis. 9

While many topical microbiome interventions currently rely on non-viable bacterial lysates or postbiotics, these inactive derivatives lack the dynamic ability to colonize, continuously secrete active metabolites, and engage in active host-microbe cross-talk. 10 , 11 Therefore, there is a critical need to investigate the direct immunomodulatory and barrier-restoring effects of viable live biotics on human skin. 12–14

Conventional in vitro models using keratinocytes provide mechanistic insights but lack the structural complexity of human skin. 15 Compared with conventional two-dimensional keratinocyte models, an ex vivo human skin model preserves native tissue architecture and epidermal-dermal interactions, thereby providing a more biologically relevant platform for evaluating inflammatory and barrier-related changes in human skin. Therefore, this study aimed to investigate the effects of two candidate live biotic strains, Live-MB2 ( Epidermidibacterium keratini ; previously referred to as EPI-7) and CX-2 ( Streptococcus thermophilus ), on inflammatory and barrier-related parameters using an ex vivo human skin AD-like model. 16 , 17 Live-MB2 is a skin-derived strain isolated from the human skin microbiome and reported to be more prevalent in younger individuals, with potential relevance to skin homeostasis and microbiome-associated skin function. 18 CX-2 is a skin-associated strain with reported potential to support dermal recovery, barrier function, and sensitive-skin normalization. 19 Ultimately, we aimed to evaluate their potential application as cosmetic ingredients for sensitive and atopic-prone skin.

## Methods

### Human Skin Explants

Human skin explants were obtained from the Korea Biomedical Research Institute (KBI) under the approval of the Institutional Review Board (IRB No. 2023–0247 and 2023–0210). Korean females (ages 35, 48, 48, 49 years old) were collected from surgical discards with written informed consent in compliance with the Declaration of Helsinki and relevant national bioethics regulations. Subcutaneous fat was removed, and the skin was sectioned using biopsy punches before culture. The ex vivo skin explants were maintained in a sterile culture system at 37 °C in a 5% CO 2 humidified incubator, as previously described in established models. The tissues were placed on Transwell ® inserts (Corning Inc., Corning, NY, USA) with the epidermal surface exposed to air to reproduce the physiological air–liquid interface of human skin. The culture medium was replaced every 48 hours.

### Induction of AD-Like Condition in Human Skin Explants

To mimic the structural and immunological characteristics of AD ex vivo, an acute AD-like inflammatory state was induced using a combination of mechanical and chemical barrier disruption. After allowing the human skin explants to equilibrate in an air-liquid interface culture for 24 hours, the stratum corneum was mechanically disrupted by repeated tape stripping (30 consecutive times) using standard adhesive discs (D-Squame; CuDerm Co., Dallas, TX, USA). Immediately following the mechanical disruption, the skin explants were topically stimulated with 0.001% 2,4-dinitrochlorobenzene dissolved in an appropriate vehicle (eg, acetone and olive oil, 3:1 v/v) to induce a robust allergic inflammatory response. The explants were then incubated at 37°C in a 5% CO 2 humidified atmosphere. This short-term induction protocol, followed by a 48-hour treatment period, was designed to model an acute rather than chronic AD-like response.

### Treatment with Live Biotics

E. keratini Live-MB2 and S. thermophilus CX-2 strains were obtained from the COSMAX Microbiome Bank (Seongnam, South Korea) and had been previously identified by 16S rRNA sequencing. For inoculum preparation, a single colony grown on an agar plate was inoculated into seed culture medium, followed by a 1% secondary inoculation and further cultivation. Live-MB2 and CX-2 were cultured into Tryptic Soy Broth (TSB; MB Cell, Seoul, South Korea) and de Man, Rogosa and Sharpe broth (MRS broth; MB Cell), respectively, and cultured at 37°C for 48 hours. Following incubation, the bacterial cells were harvested by centrifugation at 15,000 rpm for 3 minutes. The supernatants were carefully discarded, and the remaining cell pellets were washed twice with phosphate-buffered saline (PBS) to remove any residual culture media. The washed bacterial cells were then resuspended in PBS for subsequent ex vivo experiments. Bacterial concentration was determined by serial dilution plating (10 −3 , 10 −4 , and 10 −5 ), and CFU/mL was calculated using plates within the countable colony range. Following acute AD induction, Live-MB2 and CX-2 were applied to the skin explants either by topical (epidermal) application or by dermal exposure via the culture medium at a designated concentration for each treatment group. The explants were cultured for an additional 48 hours prior to harvest.

### Experimental Design

Skin explants obtained from four independent donors were allocated across all experimental conditions after induction of an acute AD-like state. A total of 11 experimental groups were established: an untreated control (without AD-like induction), a negative control (with AD-like induction), three vehicle-control groups, three Live-MB2 treatment groups, and three CX-2 treatment groups. For each strain, treatment conditions comprised 1×10 6 CFU/mL applied via the dermal-side culture medium, 1×10 3 CFU/mL applied via the dermal-side culture medium, and 1×10 6 CFU/mL applied topically to the epidermal surface, with corresponding vehicle-control conditions. Each donor contributed one skin punch to each of the 11 groups; therefore, each experimental group contained four explants (n = 4 biological replicates, one explant per donor). This donor-matched allocation ensured that tissues from all four donors were represented across all experimental conditions and minimized donor-dependent bias.

### Hematoxylin and Eosin (H&E) Staining

To assess morphological changes and epidermal thickness, the harvested tissue samples were immediately fixed in 4% paraformaldehyde for 24 hours and embedded in paraffin blocks. The blocks were sectioned into 4–5 μm thick slices using a microtome. After deparaffinization and rehydration, the sections were stained with hematoxylin and eosin (H&E) according to standard protocols. Histological images were captured using a light microscope (original magnification×100). Epidermal thickness was quantitatively measured from the granular layer to the basal layer using image analysis software (ImageJ; National Institutes of Health, Bethesda, MD, USA). For each explant, measurements were obtained from three randomly selected fields, and the mean value was used for analysis.

### Enzyme-Linked Immunosorbent Assay (ELISA) for IgE and FLG Quantification

To quantify specific protein levels, the skin tissues were homogenized in RIPA lysis buffer supplemented with a protease and phosphatase inhibitor cocktail. The lysates were centrifuged at 12,000 rpm for 15 minutes at 4°C, and the supernatants were collected. Total protein concentration was determined using a BCA Protein Assay Kit. The levels of IgE and FLG in the tissue lysates were then measured using commercially available human-specific ELISA kits strictly following the manufacturer’s instructions. The optical density was read at 450 nm using a microplate reader. Each sample was assayed in duplicate, and the mean value was used for analysis. The mean of the duplicate wells was treated as a single technical measurement for each donor-derived explant. For IgE quantification, one donor-derived sample produced no detectable signal and was therefore excluded from the IgE analysis, resulting in n = 3 biological replicates for this endpoint; all other endpoints included n = 4 biological replicates.

### Immunofluorescence (IF) Staining

For the spatial localization and expression analysis of FLG, tissue sections were deparaffinized and subjected to heat-induced epitope retrieval using a citrate buffer (pH 6.0). Sections were blocked with 5% bovine serum albumin for 1 hour at room temperature to prevent non-specific binding. Subsequently, the sections were incubated overnight at 4°C with a primary antibody targeting human FLG. After washing, sections were incubated with a fluorophore-conjugated secondary antibody for 1 hour in the dark. Nuclei were counterstained with 4′,6-diamidino-2-phenylindole. Fluorescence images were obtained using a fluorescence microscope (original magnification ×100). For each explant, three representative fields were analyzed under identical imaging conditions, and the mean signal intensity was used for analysis.

### Statistical Analysis

Unless otherwise specified, analyses were performed using four independent biological replicates (n = 4; one explant per donor per experimental condition). The IgE analysis included three biological replicates (n = 3) because one donor-derived sample yielded no detectable signal. Quantitative data are expressed as the mean ± standard error of the mean (SEM). Statistical analyses were performed using GraphPad Prism software (GraphPad Software, San Diego, CA, USA). The normal distribution of the data was assessed, and statistical significance was determined using one-way analysis of variance followed by an appropriate post-hoc test (Tukey’s or Dunnett’s multiple comparisons test) or paired Student’s t -test for two-group comparisons. A two-sided p-value of less than 0.05 was considered statistically significant.

## Results

### Tissue Safety and Epidermal Thickness

No treatment-related tissue damage was observed, indicating the safety of the live biotics on human tissue ( Figure 1 ). In the AD-induced control group, epidermal thickness increased markedly to 112.27 μm compared with 56.87 μm in the untreated control group. However, this AD-induced hyperproliferation was significantly reduced following topical application of 41.15% in the Live-MB2 (epidermal thickness, 66.07 μm) and 47.42% in the CX-2 group (59.04 μm) compared with the AD-induced control group, restoring the tissue closer to a normal state ( Figure 2 ). ## Discussion

### Key Findings

This study evaluated the effects of novel probiotic ingredients, including Live-MB2 and CX-2, utilizing an ex vivo human skin AD-like model. Live-MB2 and CX-2 treatment was not associated with tissue damage. Epidermal thickness was significantly reduced in both topically treated groups. IgE protein expression significantly reduced in both the topically treated Live-MB2 and CX-2 groups compared to AD-induced control group. FLG protein expression significantly recovered in the topical CX-2 group. The novelty of the present study lies in the evaluation of these two candidates live biotic strains in a human ex vivo AD-like skin model that preserves native tissue architecture and epidermal–dermal interactions. These findings suggest that Live-MB2 and CX-2 may contribute to barrier-repairing and anti-inflammatory functions, without evidence of overt tissue damage under the present experimental conditions.

### Plausible Underlying Mechanisms

The reduction in epidermal thickness and the enhancement of FLG expression observed in this study suggest that Live-MB2 and CX-2 may contribute to barrier-related improvement in AD-like skin. A pathological hallmark of AD is the overexpression of Th2 cytokines (eg, IL-4, IL-13), which inhibits the synthesis of FLG in the epidermis, thereby contributing to barrier dysfunction and inflammation. 20–22 The decreasing trend in IgE levels and the recovery of FLG expression, particularly in the topical CX-2 group, suggest that live biotic treatment may influence processes associated with barrier impairment and inflammatory dysregulation in AD-like skin, although the underlying molecular mechanisms were not directly examined in the present study. 4

The observed reductions in epidermal thickness and the enhancement of FLG expression further support the potential relevance of both Live-MB2 and CX-2 to barrier-related changes in AD-like skin. Topically applied live biotics may interact with keratinocytes at the skin surface to induce local immune tolerance or stimulate the production of essential skin barrier proteins. 23 , 24 In this regard, previous studies reported that metabolites and antimicrobial peptides secreted by skin commensal bacteria inhibit inflammatory microbes and protect the physical barrier. 6 , 25 , 26 These findings are consistent with previous reports on the efficacy of topical microbiome modulators.

### Comparisons with Previous Studies

This study utilized an ex vivo model to evaluate probiotic ingredients. Compared with conventional 2D in vitro keratinocyte cultures, the ex vivo human skin model provides a more physiologically relevant platform by preserving native tissue architecture and epidermal–dermal interactions. 16 , 17 Within this experimental context, the observed effects of Live-MB2 and CX-2 support their potential relevance to barrier-related and inflammatory changes in AD-like skin.

Although conventional immunosuppressive therapies, including topical corticosteroids, are widely used in AD management, the present findings should be interpreted cautiously because this study was performed in an ex vivo model without a positive control or direct mechanistic analyses. 27 , 28 Accordingly, Live-MB2 and CX-2 may be considered candidate live biotic ingredients with potential relevance to skin barrier- and inflammation-related applications, rather than established therapeutic alternatives at this stage. The observed restoration of epidermal barrier-related readouts by CX-2 and Live-MB2, together with the absence of overt tissue damage under the present experimental conditions, supports their potential relevance to microbiome-based approaches for AD-like skin. 4 Beyond their mechanistic benefits, the direct topical application of live biotics represents a complementary strategy from transient symptom management to proactive skin ecosystem restoration. 13 , 14 Because viable strains like Live-MB2 and CX-2 can continuously secrete functional metabolites and dynamically engage in host-microbe cross-talk, they could offer sustained barrier-enhancing efficacy compared to non-viable postbiotics. 29 Practically, these findings underscore the high industrial and medical applicability of live biotics as next-generation dermo cosmetics (cosmeceuticals) and adjunctive treatments in clinical dermatology for sensitive and atopic-prone skin. 30

### Strengths and Limitations

There are several limitations to our study. First, donor-to-donor variation inherent to ex vivo human skin AD-like models may introduce variability in outcomes attributable to intrinsic genetic differences across donated skin tissues. 31 In particular, donor-specific characteristics such as sex, age, and ethnicity represent important variables that should be carefully considered in future investigations to elucidate differential immune responses in the skin. 31 , 32 In this study, tissue samples were collected from four donors of varying ages, with deliberate emphasis placed on ensuring donor diversity. Nevertheless, further studies incorporating a larger donor cohort will be required to comprehensively assess the potential confounding influence of sex and ethnicity on the observed outcomes. In addition, no positive control, such as an established AD treatment or a previously validated probiotic/postbiotic formulation, was included in the present study; therefore, the relative efficacy of Live-MB2 and CX-2 could not be determined. Second, the immune responses observed in ex vivo human skin AD-like models are inherently limited in their ability to reflect in vivo conditions, particularly because these systems lack systemic immune responses, circulating immune cells, vascular components, and long-term microbiome interactions that are relevant to AD pathophysiology. 31 Moreover, the current study primarily evaluated phenotypic endpoints, including epidermal thickness, IgE, and FLG-related readouts, and did not directly assess key AD-associated inflammatory mediators such as IL-4, IL-13, IL-31, TSLP, or related signaling mechanisms. Future investigations employing randomized controlled trials in in vivo settings would be warranted to further validate and extend the explanatory power of the findings reported in the present study. 33 Although the strains used in this study had been previously identified by 16S rRNA sequencing, no additional sequencing was performed immediately before the experiment. In addition, viability was not re-confirmed immediately prior to tissue application, and stability during the experimental period was not separately evaluated.

Despite these limitations, our study has important strengths. This study provides the first comprehensive ex vivo assessment of the effects of two novel live biotics, Live-MB2 and CX-2, on AD-induced skin. These findings provide preliminary ex vivo evidence supporting the potential of live biotics as microbiome-based candidate active ingredients for sensitive and atopic-prone skin. In particular, the observed changes in epidermal thickness, IgE, and FLG-related readouts support the further evaluation of these strains in skin barrier- and inflammation-related applications.
