conclusions:
Osteoporosis should be understood beyond the traditional paradigm of “bone formation-resorption imbalance” as a systemic bone remodeling disorder driven by immunometabolic dysregulation. Upstream risk factors, including estrogen deficiency, aging, gut microbiota dysbiosis, lipid and glucose metabolic disturbances, and chronic low-grade inflammation, continuously generate pathological signals that are locally translated within the bone marrow immunometabolic microenvironment. As a pivotal hub, this niche regulates hematopoietic lineage output, BMSC osteogenic-adipogenic fate decisions, BMAT expansion, local immune tone, metabolic buffering capacity, and bone cell function. When the marrow microenvironment shifts from a homeostasis-supportive state toward a pro-inflammatory and osteoclastogenic phenotype, Th17/Treg imbalance, inflammatory monocyte/macrophage polarization, enhanced osteoclast precursor recruitment, osteoclast glycolytic reprogramming, lipotoxic accumulation, and inflammasome activation mutually reinforce one another, ultimately driving a remodeling pattern characterized by enhanced bone resorption, impaired bone formation, and aggravated marrow adiposity. Thus, osteoporosis does not arise from isolated terminal bone cell dysfunction, but from a continuous pathological cascade linking risk factor signaling, marrow niche translation, immunometabolic network remodeling, and persistent bone remodeling imbalance.

Current anti-resorptive and osteoanabolic agents remain essential because they improve bone mineral density and reduce fracture risk; however, their effects are largely confined to terminal osteoclast or osteoblast modulation, with limited capacity to correct upstream drivers, marrow immune ecological disruption, pathological BMAT expansion, BMSC fate shift, or metabolic checkpoint dysregulation. Future strategies should therefore evolve from single bone-cell targeting toward mechanism-stratified interventions, including subtype-specific immunometabolic profiling, microecological remodeling, immunophenotypic correction, macrophage metabolic reprogramming, BMAT control, BMSC fate modulation, and local biomaterial-based niche repair. The major therapeutic opportunity may therefore lie not simply in further intensifying terminal effector inhibition, but in establishing subtype-tailored strategies capable of reconstructing systemic immunometabolic equilibrium.

Within this translational agenda, two priorities are particularly important. First, prospective human studies integrating longitudinal clinical phenotyping with single-cell, spatial, and multi-omics analyses are needed to validate causal immunometabolic subtypes and identify clinically actionable biomarkers. Second, mechanism-guided intervention studies should determine whether correcting pathological marrow niche states provides additional skeletal benefit when combined with established anti-resorptive or osteoanabolic therapies. Together, these efforts will be essential for translating the proposed immunometabolic framework from a mechanistic model into a clinically testable strategy for precision osteoporosis management.

# The Multiorgan Complications of Stevens-Johnson Syndrome and Toxic Epidermal Necrolysis: A Systematic Review

## Abstract

Numerous internal organ systems are impacted by SJS-TEN, encompassing the skin, ocular, ear, nose, and throat (ENT), pulmonary, gastrointestinal (GIT), and genitourinary systems. The terms “Stevens-Johnson syndrome”, “toxic epidermal necrolysis”, “organ complication”, “multiorgan involvement”, and “sequelae” were used as keywords. We included 38 articles reporting SJS-TEN patients with multiorgan complications, comprising 15 reviews, 11 original studies, 9 case reports, and 3 case series; data were synthesized descriptively, and no quantitative meta-analysis was performed. Reported percentages therefore reflect the proportion of included studies reporting a given complication, not patient-level prevalence. Among studies providing extractable patient-level data, the mean age of the subject population was 36.72 ± 26.58 years, with female predominance (88.2%). Ocular involvement was the complication most frequently reported across the included studies (65.8% of studies), followed by pulmonary and genitourinary involvement (26.32% of studies each) and skin complications (21.05% of studies). ## Keywords
organ involvement; Stevens-Johnson syndrome; toxic epidermal necrolysis

## Introduction

Stevens-Johnson syndrome (SJS) and toxic epidermal necrolysis (TEN) are acute, life-threatening mucocutaneous reactions characterized by extensive necrosis and detachment of the epidermis and mucosal epithelium. SJS-TEN is an uncommon condition, impacting two to seven individuals per million annually. 1 The exact pathophysiology of SJS-TEN remains elusive. However, it is understood that SJS-TEN develops as a consequence of immune system activation, primarily initiated by specific medications, including their metabolites, and less frequently by infections through delayed-type hypersensitivity reactions. 2 , 3 They are marked by extensive keratinocyte apoptosis, leading to complete denudation of the skin and mucosa, rendering patients vulnerable to sepsis, with an approximate mortality rate of 30%. 4 The defining clinical features comprise mucocutaneous pain, haemorrhagic erosions, mucous membrane erosion, erythematous macules, blisters, and denuded skin resulting from significant epidermal-dermal separation. 5

Given the similarities in clinical presentation, histopathological findings, etiology, risk factors, and underlying mechanisms, SJS-TEN are considered severe variants within a single disease entity, differing primarily in the extent of epidermal detachment relative to the body surface area. 1 SJS represents the milder end of the spectrum, accounting for fewer than 10% of epidermal detachment and exhibiting a high mortality rate of 1–5%. TEN involves more than 30% of the body surface area and has a mortality rate of 25–35%. Epidermal detachment of 10 to 30% signifies SJS-TEN overlap. 2 , 3 , 6 SJS-TEN is generally severe and potentially lethal in the acute phase due to necrosis of external and internal body surfaces, predisposing the patient to life-threatening consequences such as sepsis and multiple organ failure. Healing of ulcerative mucosal lesions may result in extensive scarring, which can interfere with organ function. 7 The spectrum of acute and chronic organ complications associated with SJS-TEN remains incompletely characterized. Numerous internal organ systems are impacted by SJS-TEN, encompassing the skin, ocular, ear, nose, and throat (ENT), pulmonary, gastrointestinal (GIT), and genitourinary systems. 2 , 3 , 8

The objective of this systematic review was to delineate the organ systems involved in SJS-TEN complications and to identify the key responsibilities of a multidisciplinary team in ensuring optimal patient management. Although several prior reviews have addressed individual aspects of SJS-TEN sequelae — for example, ocular complications specifically, or long-term sequelae in general — few have consolidated acute and long-term complications across all major organ systems within a single, systematically conducted review. 2 This review therefore aims to fill this gap by systematically mapping both acute and long-term/chronic multiorgan complications of SJS-TEN, as reported across the recent (2019–2024) literature, while distinguishing the primary cutaneous and mucosal involvement that defines the acute disease from the secondary internal-organ complications that are the principal focus of this review.

## Methods

This review was conducted and reported in accordance with the Preferred Reporting Items for Systematic Reviews and Meta-Analyses (PRISMA) guidelines, with the aim of investigating multiorgan complications associated with SJS-TEN ( Figure 1 ). Figure 1 Steps in articles selection. A flowchart of article selection for a review process with identification, screening and inclusion steps. The flowchart outlines the article selection process for a review. It begins with the identification phase, where 310 records are identified from databases: 40 from PubMed and 270 from Scopus. Seven duplicate records are removed before screening, leaving 303 records. During the screening phase, 238 non-English records are excluded, resulting in 65 reports sought for retrieval. Of these, 21 reports are not retrieved. In the eligibility assessment, 44 full-text reports are evaluated, with 6 excluded for not meeting inclusion criteria. Finally, 38 studies are included in the review.

### Literature Search Strategies

#### Electronic Database

We conducted a comprehensive search of electronic databases for relevant studies, narrowing the publication dates to 2019–2024. The systematic review included a range of publication types, including review articles, original studies, case reports, and case series. The primary databases used for the articles in this study were PubMed and Scopus, as they are widely used and easily accessible within the academic research community. Duplicate records were removed through cross-referencing between databases. Two reviewers independently screened titles, abstracts, and full-text articles according to the predefined inclusion and exclusion criteria, with disagreements resolved by consensus. The subsequent search parameters were employed, utilizing the following key terms: (“Stevens-Johnson Syndrome” OR “toxic epidermal necrolysis”) AND (“organ complication” OR “multiorgan involvement” OR “sequelae”). The study methodology was designed in accordance with a systematic and organized process, as illustrated in the flowchart presented in Figure 1 . This methodology encompassed a comprehensive range of steps, from the initial database search to the final selection of pertinent articles, and included the elimination of duplicate entries.

The complete search strategy for each electronic database, including the filters and limits applied, is reported below:

PubMed: (“Stevens-Johnson Syndrome” [Title/Abstract] OR “Stevens Johnson Syndrome” [MeSH Terms] OR “toxic epidermal necrolysis” [Title/Abstract] OR “Toxic Epidermal Necrolysis” [MeSH Terms]) AND (“organ complication” [Title/Abstract] OR “multiorgan involvement” [Title/Abstract] OR “sequelae” [Title/Abstract] OR “sequela” [MeSH Terms]). Filters applied: Publication date 1 January 2019–31 December 2024; Language: English.

Scopus: TITLE-ABS-KEY (“Stevens-Johnson Syndrome” OR “toxic epidermal necrolysis”) AND TITLE-ABS-KEY (“organ complication” OR “multiorgan involvement” OR “sequelae”) AND PUBYEAR > 2018 AND PUBYEAR < 2025 AND (LIMIT-TO (LANGUAGE, “English”)). Filters applied: Publication years 2019–2024; Language: English.

Both search strings used identical core concepts and Boolean logic, adapted to the indexing syntax of each database (title/abstract and MeSH-term fields for PubMed; TITLE-ABS-KEY field for Scopus), with the same publication-date window (2019–2024) and English-language restriction applied consistently across both. Both databases were last searched, and the search results retrieved, during the period 1 October 2024 to 31 December 2024, with the final search conducted on 31 December 2024.

#### Inclusion Criteria

Studies included in the analysis met the following criteria: (1) documented and diagnosed with SJS-TEN; and (2) demonstrated the presence of multiorgan complications with at least one identifiable abnormality by clinical assessment and/or additional supportive investigations.

#### Exclusion Criteria

The studies were excluded if they were unavailable in an accessible form, duplicated, had no abstract, used animal subjects, or were published in languages other than English. Any disagreements were resolved by consensus with involvement of a third reviewer when necessary.

### Outcome Measures

The specific outcome of interest was detecting at least one organ abnormality as well as describing the clinical manifestations involved. The following data were extracted from the studies and entered into an electronic database: age, gender, diagnosis classification (SJS, SJS-TEN overlap, and TEN), and organ involvement type ( Table 1 ). Descriptive statistics were performed using Microsoft Excel for Office Home and Student, 2021. Data extraction was performed by one reviewer using a standardized electronic data-collection form, with the extracted data independently verified for accuracy and completeness by a second reviewer; discrepancies were resolved by discussion. Table 1 Clinical Characteristics of SJS-TEN with Multiorgan Complications Variable Mean (SD) or N (Studies Reporting) Age 36.72 ± 26.58 Gender distribution Female sex 15 Male sex 2 Diagnosis classification SJS 34 SJS-TEN overlap 3 TEN 36 Complications (type of organ involvement) Ear, nose, and throat (ENT) 3 Gastrointestinal (GIT) 7 Ocular 25 Pulmonary 10 Skin 8 Urogenital 10 Notes : N denotes the number of included studies reporting each variable among the total of 38 included articles. Demographic variables were synthesized only from studies providing extractable patient-level data, while review articles were excluded from pooled demographic assessment to minimize duplication and reporting bias. Studies may report more than one SJS-TEN diagnostic category or organ involvement type.

Because the included literature was dominated by case reports, case series, and narrative reviews rather than comparative interventional or observational studies, a formal risk-of-bias or quality-appraisal tool was not applicable to the dataset as a whole. Instead, the publication type of each included article (review, original study, case report, or case series) was recorded ( Table 1 ) and used to contextualize the certainty of the evidence; pooled demographic and organ-involvement figures were calculated only from studies with extractable, non-duplicated patient-level data, and review articles were excluded from these pooled counts to minimize double-counting of the same underlying patients or complications. Throughout the Results, “N” denotes the number of included studies reporting a given variable or complication, not the number of individual patients, and reported percentages reflect the proportion of studies reporting a finding rather than patient-level prevalence.

## Results

### Study Selection

The study selection is illustrated in Figure 1 . The preliminary database and reference list searches yielded a total of 310 articles. Following the removal of duplicates, and the exclusion of languages other than English, 94 articles were selected for full-text review. The following studies were then excluded from the total articles for the subsequent reasons: the absence of abstracts (n = 50) and the irrelevance of topics (n = 6). The remaining articles were included in the systematic review. A total of 38 relevant articles were used for data collection, and the screening process resulted in a combination of 15 reviews, 11 original studies, 9 case reports, and 3 case series. Detailed characteristics of the included studies and organ-specific clinical manifestations are provided in Supplementary Table S1 .

### General Comparison Result

As shown in Table 1 , the mean age associated with multiorgan complications of SJS-TEN was 36.72 ± 26.58 years, with female predominance (88.2%). Most of the reported complications were related to TEN (94.7%). Ocular involvement was the most frequently reported complication, identified in 25 of 38 included studies (65.8%), followed by pulmonary and genitourinary involvement, each reported in 10 studies (26.3%).

## Discussion

### Age and Gender

Multiorgan complications of SJS-TEN were associated with a mean age of 36.72 ± 26.58 years. The female to male ratio was 15:2. The mechanisms underlying this gender difference are not yet fully understood. Specifically, the pathogenesis of idiosyncratic reactions is complex and remains to be comprehensively delineated. The observed risk difference between the sexes may be attributable to physiological and hormonal differences in immunological characteristics. 40 The existence of gender disparities in factors that affect pharmacokinetics, such as body mass, renal, and hepatic functions, may be a contributing factor to the observed differences in drug metabolism between the genders. In general, females exhibit lower lean body mass, decreased hepatic clearance, and reduced renal clearance due to lower glomerular filtration. 40 In addition, Giefing-Kroell et al had proposed a potential link between sex hormones and the immune system, as reported in the literature. Gonadal hormones, such as estrogen, have been demonstrated to exert specific effects on female immunocompetence at both the cellular and the molecular level. 41 Estrogen receptors have been identified in a variety of immune system cells, including T cells, B cells, neutrophils, macrophages, dendritic cells (DCs), and natural killer (NK) cells. Elevated levels of estradiol have been demonstrated to encourage the development of conventional IL-12-producing dendritic cells (DCs), the production of IL-6, IL-8, and chemokine (C-C motif) ligand 2 (CCL2) by immature DCs, and the expansion of IFN-γ-producing killer DCs. In addition, estrogen has been demonstrated to enhance immune function, while progesterone and androgens, including testosterone, have been observed to primarily exert immunosuppressive effects. 40 , 41 Adegbenro et al reported that SJS-TEN can manifest in any age group. However, the majority of cases were observed in females, with a female-to-male ratio of approximately 3:2. 5

### Diagnosis Classification

According to the diagnostic classification of SJS-TEN, the majority of cases were TEN (94.73%), followed by SJS (89.47%), and the least were SJS-TEN overlap (7.89%). This discrepancy may be due to the fact that some data sources did not include SJS-TEN overlap in the classification. Although the majority of cases were associated with TEN, based on the journal review, no specific associations were found between the classification of SJS-TEN diagnosis and the rate of multiorgan complications, except for ocular complications. According to Ganekal et al, the severity of ocular complications was significantly greater in TEN cases than in SJS cases. 18

### Multiorgan Complications in SJS-TEN

#### Skin

A variety of clinical manifestations of skin complications were documented ( Table 2 ). The most prevalent manifestations were pigmentation disorders, encompassing hyperpigmentation and hypopigmentation (31.82%), hypertrophic scarring tissue formation (22.72%), and xerosis cutis with chronic pruritus (9.09%). This finding was consistent with the research conducted by Cristina et al, which indicated that post-inflammatory skin changes (77%), as well as cutaneous scars (46%), were the most prevalent physical complications observed in SJS-TEN. 13 Table 2 Skin Complications Variable N (Studies Reporting) Clinical Manifestations Anetoderma 1 Chronic eczema 1 Ectopic sebaceous glands 1 Eruptive naevi 1 Hypertrophic scar 5 Milia and urticaria 1 Photosensitivity 1 Pigmentation disorder 7 Verrucous hyperplasia 1 Xerosis cutis with chronic pruritus 2 Note : N denotes the number of included studies reporting each complication.

According to a Canadian follow-up study of 13 adult survivors of SJS-TEN, 75% of participants had persistent abnormalities in their skin pigmentation, with a mean time of 38 ± 27 months after onset of SJS-TEN. These complications had the potential to significantly impair the patient’s quality of life. 22 Most SJS-TEN erosions heal without scarring. However, hypertrophic scars had been described. 14 , 22 , 23 Risk factors include prolonged immobility, unrelieved skin pressure, delayed epithelialization, and secondary infections. 23

Furthermore, H.Y. Lee et al reported that survivors of SJS-TEN might develop eruptive naevi post-exposure as well as sebaceous gland proliferation. 23 These tended to occur between 3 weeks and 3 years following the acute episode, with the majority of cases occurring in children and young adults. The exact pathogenesis is unclear, but it is postulated that the microenvironment of epidermal regeneration following SJS-TEN fosters the development of these lesions. 23 A disseminated eruption of ectopic sebaceous glands represents a rare complication, observed in a patient 4 months after the development of SJS-TEN. The diagnosis was confirmed by histopathology, which differentiates it from sebaceous gland hyperplasia. 23 , 42 The presence of numerous enlarged gland lobules in proximity to a hair follicle is a characteristic feature of sebaceous gland hyperplasia. However, in ectopic sebaceous glands, there is an opening directly onto the epidermis, which lacks a connection to hair follicles. 42 The underlying mechanism responsible for the dissemination of ectopic sebaceous glands following SJS-TEN remains unclear. Damage to the pilosebaceous unit and destruction of hair follicles are evident. It is proposed that cytokines and growth factors associated with cutaneous healing in SJS-TEN may contribute to sebaceous gland proliferation and also the development of eruptive nevi. 42 Additional skin complications associated with SJS-TEN have been documented, including verrucous hyperplasia diagnosed histopathologically as seborrheic keratosis type, photosensitivity, anetoderma, chronic eczema, milia, and urticaria. However, these manifestations were reported in only a limited number of cases (12.5%).

A consensus was reached on the importance of prolonged sun protection and daily use of emollients for the management of skin complications. 23 Sun avoidance and use of sunscreens should be observed to minimize pigmentary changes. The regular use of an emollient will improve xerosis and pruritus. Additionally, laser procedures were identified as a necessary treatment for disabling hypertrophic scars and ectopic sebaceous glands. It is recommended that all skin surfaces be examined during the follow-up period. 13 , 23

#### Ocular

Ocular complications were the most prevalent cases among those associated with SJS-TEN, manifesting in a multitude of clinical presentations ( Table 3 ). A study from Hua-Ching et al revealed that 59.5% of cases had physical sequelae related to SJS-TEN, including ocular problems. 14 Ocular complications are the result of a multifactorial etiology, with the pathogenic processes classified based on anatomic structures. 23 The most prominent complications associated with the eyelid were trichiasis/distichiasis (60%), meibomian gland destruction (36%), and lid margin keratinization (32%); while symblepharon (60%), persistent conjunctival inflammation/chronic conjunctivitis (24%), and membrane/pseudomembrane formation were observed in 20% of cases related with conjunctival manifestation. The most frequently observed complications in the cornea were corneal neovascularization (10%), conjunctivalization of the cornea (9%), corneal keratinization, and stromal opacification (8%), along with other complications such as limbal stem cell deficiency (LSCD), which was present in 12% of cases. Table 3 Ocular Complications Variable N (Studies Reporting) Clinical Manifestations Eyelid Entropion/ectropion 7 Lacrimal punctal occlusion 7 Lid margin keratinization 8 Meibomian gland destruction 9 Trichiasis/distichiasis 15 Conjunctival Ankyloblepharon 2 Conjunctival keratinization 1 Membrane and pseudomembrane formation 5 Persistent conjunctival inflammation/chronic conjunctivitis 6 Scarring 3 Subconjunctival fibrosis 1 Symblepharon 15 Ulceration 1 Corneal Conjunctivalization of cornea 9 Corneal keratinization 8 Corneal neovascularization 10 Corneal/stromal scarring 5 Loss of palisades of Vogt 4 Stromal opacification 8 Superficial punctate keratitis/keratopathy (SPK) 3 Others Abnormal corneal nerves 1 Limbal stem cell deficiency (LSCD) 3 Note : N denotes the number of included studies reporting each complication.

However, in general, the most prevalent ocular complications were trichiasis, distichiasis, and symblepharon which were observed in 60% of cases, followed by corneal neovascularization in 40% of cases, meibomian gland destruction, and conjunctivalization of the cornea in 36% of cases. This result was in accordance with the findings of Gueudry et al, who identified trichiasis/distichiasis and symblepharon among the most prevalent ocular sequelae of SJS-TEN in France. The clinical manifestations may manifest within the initial 2-week period following the onset of the disease. 6 However, it was notable that a considerable proportion of patients (41–66%) developed ocular complications more than 1 year after the acute phase of SJS-TEN. 2

Disruption of ocular surface homeostasis, observed in ocular SJS-TEN, is linked to the underlying mechanisms of these ocular complications. The healthy ocular surface exhibits a diverse range of microbiomes, with Streptococcus sp . and Lactobacillus sp . being the most commonly identified bacteria. 10 , 23 Conversely, the ocular surface of individuals with chronic SJS-TEN displays a reduction in bacterial diversity, with a predominance of Staphylococcus sp ., which can readily become pathogenic. Consequently, the incidence of infective ocular inflammation is elevated in individuals with SJS-TEN compared to those without this condition. 10

The ocular inflammatory response ranges from mild conjunctivitis to suppurative membranous conjunctivitis, which is often followed by fibrosis. Severe inflammation of the ocular surfaces during the acute phase can result in the formation of pseudomembranes and corneal epithelial defects. The tear film, which is essential for maintaining corneal clarity, is compromised by the depletion of conjunctival goblet cells and a reduction in mucin production. 23 Furthermore, the healing process is impeded by the loss of limbal corneal stem cells. The ongoing damage is manifested as cicatricial alterations in the conjunctiva and lid margin. Conjunctival drying is a consequence of scarring in the fornix, which obstructs the ductal openings of the lacrimal glands. 7 , 23 The formation of symblepharon or ankyloblepharon due to bulbar and forniceal scarring impairs the tear meniscus, resulting in insufficient eye blinking or closure and restricting ocular mobility. Furthermore, microtrauma resulting from eyelid anomalies can lead to a number of complications, including corneal neovascularization, loss of the palisades of Vogt, 10 LSCD, persistent epithelial defects, conjunctivalization, keratinization, and ulceration. Additionally, the development of abnormal corneal nerves, punctate corneal staining, ectropion, entropion, and misdirected eyelashes (trichiasis and distichiasis) is caused by scarring of the lid margins. 6 , 7 , 23

The precise manner by which systemic and ocular treatments administered during the acute phase of the illness can mitigate long-term ocular complications remains uncertain. A recent retrospective multicentre study found that supportive care and different immunomodulatory treatments, including systemic corticosteroids, intravenous immunoglobulin (IVIG), or a combination of both, were comparable in terms of long-term ocular complications and final visual outcome. 23 , 40 IVIG has been demonstrated to potently impede the interaction of the Fas receptor with Fas ligand, a reported pathway of keratinocyte death. A preceding single-centre study exhibited outcomes for patients with SJS-TEN treated at a dose of IVIG (0.4–1 g/kg dose). This study, which encompassed 16 consecutively treated patients, exhibited a significant decreased in mortality rate. 4 In a case series of five patients with SJS-TEN who had acute ocular involvement, Lee et al demonstrated the efficacy of methylprednisolone in preventing ocular complications. The treatment regimen involved the administration of 500–1000 mg of pulsed methylprednisolone daily for three to four days, commencing within four days of disease onset. The outcome was the preservation of 20/20 vision in all patients. 23 Magone MT et al discovered that early application of topical steroids led to markedly enhanced visual outcomes in a cohort of 94 patients diagnosed with SJS. Furthermore, the administration of preservative-free artificial tears at hourly intervals is essential to mitigate the concentrations of proinflammatory agents and facilitate epithelial regeneration. 33

As a preventative measure and to facilitate further monitoring, Ganekal et al proposed that at the time of hospital discharge, patients should be advised to attend follow-up appointments on a weekly basis for a month, and then on a monthly basis for six months. Given that chronic ocular disease may develop several months after hospital discharge, all patients with SJS-TEN should be monitored by an ophthalmologist for at least a year following the acute episode. 18

#### Ear, Nose, and Throat (ENT)

The ENT complications associated with SJS-TEN manifest in a number of clinical manifestations, as outlined in Table 4 . These include endobuccal synechiae, severe gingivolabial adhesions, retrocricoid ulceration and fistula, hypopharyngeal stenosis, external auditory canal stenosis, and synechiae between the pinna and scalp in 33.3% of cases. The ENT complications frequently represent an extension of the oral and oropharyngeal mucosal involvement. The evolution of these mucosal lesions resulted in the formation of multi-site mucosal synechiae, such as between the epiglottis and the base of the tongue, the floor of the mouth and the tongue, as well as severe gingivolabial adhesions. Moreover, some cases exhibited a retrocricoid fistula. 2 Table 4 ENT Complications Variable N (Studies Reporting) Clinical Manifestations Endobuccal synechiae 1 External auditory canal stenosis 1 Hypopharyngeal stenosis 1 Retrocricoid fistula 1 Retrocricoid ulceration 1 Severe gingivolabial adhesion 1 Synechiae between the pinna of the ear and scalp 1 Note : N denotes the number of included studies reporting each complication.

As reported by Glasson et al, there appeared to be a correlation between the formation of mucosal synechiae, particularly in the hypopharynx, and the intubation event, especially in terms of the duration. Following prolonged intubation, which lasted an average of 15 to 27 days, one in five patients exhibited long-term ENT sequelae. At 3, 4, and 10 months post-diagnosis of SJS-TEN, cases of hypopharyngeal synechiae were identified due to persistent dysphagia complaints. 3 , 43

Additionally, it was reported that the severity of the oral adhesions was likely a consequence of inadequate nursing care, which could have been averted. In this case, daily manual digital mobilization of the lips and tongue with steroid ointments (eg, betamethasone) may prove an effective method of preventing the complications, such as gingivolabial adhesions and cicatricial adhesions between the tongue and the floor of the mouth. 3 The French national protocol for diagnosis and care (PNDS; protocole national de diagnostic et de soins ) recommends daily examination of accessible mucosal membranes, including the outer ear and a complete specialized ENT examination once a week. Periodic examinations of the ENT could potentially prevent the formation of mature synechiae. 43

#### Pulmonary

The pulmonary complications were described in several clinical manifestations ( Table 5 ), with the most common being bronchiolitis obliterans (BO) at 70%, followed by respiratory tract obstruction/obliteration at 60%, interstitial lung disease (ILD), bronchiectasis, acute respiratory distress syndrome (ARDS), and/or respiratory failure at 30% of cases. The mechanism underlying the development of BO in patients with SJS-TEN remains unclear. One potential mechanism is immune complex deposition, which may result in damage to bronchial epithelial cells and mucosa, including subepithelial structures, as well as dysregulated repair. It was postulated that the alterations in necrosis and shedding of bronchiolar epithelial cells were initiated by some form of injury, subsequently resulting in exudation of inflammatory cells, including lymphocytes, macrophages, and the proliferation of myofibroblasts and capillary vessels. # Enhancing the Safety of Nanoparticles in Medicine: Highlights of Progress and Critical Objectives

## Abstract
Nanoparticles have transformed drug delivery, imaging, vaccination, and precision therapeutics, but their clinical translation remains constrained by safety profiles that are inseparable from material design, biological identity, host factors, and manufacturing. This review critically evaluates recent progress, persistent limitations, and priority objectives for safer nanomedicine. Unlike reviews organized primarily by material class or isolated toxicology endpoints, we integrate physicochemical determinants, protein corona formation, immune recognition, organ disposition, preclinical models, chemistry-manufacturing-controls (CMC), regulatory expectations, disease context, and patient heterogeneity into a translational safety-by-design framework. We distinguish clinically established risk-mitigation strategies from emerging approaches and examine why apparently favorable preclinical performance may fail to predict human safety. Particular attention is given to complement activation, repeat-dose immunogenicity, long-term retention, blood-brain barrier delivery, oncology and inflammatory disease, assay interference, quantitative biodistribution, and scale-up. Artificial intelligence, physiologically based pharmacokinetic modeling, multi-omics, organ-on-chip systems, imaging, and digital-twin concepts are evaluated as emerging tools for predictive safety, while their present validation limitations are emphasized. Overall, the evidence supports early integration of efficacy, mechanistic toxicology, CMC, and patient-specific risk rather than downstream safety testing alone. Harmonized characterization, clinically relevant models, long-term fate studies, and lifecycle surveillance remain central priorities for the next generation of nanomedicines.

## Keywords
nanoparticle safety; nanotoxicology; biological interactions; immunotoxicity; translational nanomedicine

## Introduction

Nanoparticles have become one of the most influential enabling technologies in modern medicine because they allow therapeutic and diagnostic agents to be formulated, protected, transported, and presented to biological systems in ways that are not achievable with conventional molecular dosage forms alone. 1–4 By controlling size, shape, composition, deformability, surface chemistry, and interfacial behavior, nanoparticle-based systems can modify solubility, circulation half-life, tissue distribution, intracellular trafficking, and release kinetics, thereby widening the therapeutic index of potent but otherwise limited payloads. 1 , 2 These advantages are not merely conceptual. Over the past three decades, nanomedicine has generated clinically used liposomes, lipid nanoparticles, polymer conjugates, protein nanoparticles, iron-carbohydrate nanocolloids, and nanocrystal formulations that have altered standards of care in oncology, infectious disease, metabolic disorders, vaccination, imaging, and supportive care. 2 , 5 , 6 The field therefore occupies a distinctive translational position: unlike many platform technologies that remain largely aspirational, nanoparticle systems have already demonstrated that nanoscale engineering can produce regulatory approvals, industrial adoption, and measurable patient benefit. 2 , 3 , 5 , 6

The clinical promise of nanoparticles in medicine arises from a convergence of pharmacologic and biologic principles. First, nanoparticles can rescue otherwise unmanageable active pharmaceutical ingredients by increasing apparent solubility, improving chemical stability, reducing premature metabolism, and limiting nonspecific exposure. 1 , 2 Second, they can decouple systemic exposure from target exposure by altering biodistribution and organ partitioning, which is particularly relevant for cytotoxic drugs, nucleic acids, immunomodulators, radionuclides, and imaging agents. 1–4 Third, they permit multifunctionality: the same carrier can integrate stealth properties, targeting ligands, triggered-release mechanisms, imaging labels, and immune-modulating features. Fourth, nanoparticles can be designed to engage biological transport processes at several scales, including vascular extravasation, lymphatic trafficking, endocytosis, endosomal escape, and interstitial penetration. 3 , 4 , 7 , 8 In principle, these capabilities support a transition from passive formulation science toward programmable therapeutic systems that are matched to the pathophysiology of specific diseases and even to the heterogeneity of individual patients. 3 , 4 , 7

This promise has been especially visible in cancer. Nanoparticles were embraced in oncology because they offered solutions to several chronic limitations of anticancer pharmacology: poor aqueous solubility, dose-limiting systemic toxicity, low tumor selectivity, and the need to combine multiple agents with incompatible physicochemical properties. 3 , 4 , 7 , 8 Clinically approved systems such as PEGylated liposomal doxorubicin and albumin-bound paclitaxel showed that nanoparticle reformulation could reduce selected toxicities, change infusion behavior, improve tolerability, and create viable commercial products. 3 , 4 , 7 More recently, the success of lipid nanoparticle-enabled nucleic acid delivery, including globally deployed mRNA vaccines, has expanded the perceived scope of nanomedicine beyond oncology and has demonstrated that nanoparticle systems can support rapid manufacturing scale-up, cold-chain distribution, and worldwide clinical deployment. 2 , 6 This broadening of indication space matters for safety because it shifts the field from relatively controlled specialist settings toward larger, more heterogeneous patient populations, repeated dosing paradigms, preventive applications, and combinations with biologics, devices, and immunotherapies. 2 , 6 , 9

Yet the same features that confer therapeutic opportunity also create safety complexity. Nanoparticles are not simply small versions of conventional formulations. Their clinical behavior is governed by emergent properties produced by the coupling of material composition, nanoscale architecture, colloidal stability, interfacial adsorption, dynamic restructuring in biological fluids, and interaction with immune and clearance systems. 1 , 6 , 9–14 Accordingly, nanoparticle safety cannot be reduced to the toxicology of the free drug or the bulk material alone. The relevant hazard profile is a system-level property of the entire nanoscale construct, including its excipients, degradation products, adsorbed biomolecular corona, process-related impurities, storage-dependent transformations, and dose- and route-specific biological interactions. 6 , 9–11 This principle is now well recognized in translational nanomedicine, but it remains imperfectly implemented in discovery pipelines, where efficacy-oriented optimization often still precedes robust mechanistic safety evaluation. 5 , 6 , 10

Safety has therefore become the central barrier to translation not because nanoparticle systems are uniformly unsafe, but because their risk profiles are frequently difficult to predict, compare, standardize, and regulate across platforms. 5 , 6 , 10 The problem is compounded by the historical mismatch between the sophistication of nanoparticle engineering and the maturity of the corresponding safety science. A formulation can be exquisitely optimized for encapsulation efficiency, targeting ligand density, or stimulus-responsive release, yet still fail clinically because of unanticipated complement activation, infusion reactions, altered pharmacokinetics after repeat dosing, off-target accumulation in mononuclear phagocyte system organs, unexpected degradation behavior, assay interference, manufacturing drift, or poor reproducibility across scales. 5 , 6 , 9–14 Translation is further constrained by the reality that preclinical models often overestimate delivery performance and underestimate safety liabilities, particularly when tumor biology, vascular permeability, immune competence, protein composition, and sex- or ancestry-related host variables diverge from those in the intended human population. 7–9 , 11 , 12 , 15

A major conceptual advance in the field has been the recognition that nanoparticle safety and efficacy are inseparable. The traditional translational paradigm treated safety primarily as a downstream gatekeeping exercise that follows proof-of-concept efficacy. In nanomedicine, however, the material features that determine efficacy often also determine toxicity. For example, increasing circulation time through PEGylation can improve exposure and enable tumor accumulation or extrahepatic delivery, but it can also influence anti-PEG immunogenicity, complement activation, and accelerated blood clearance on repeat administration. 13 , 14 , 16 Enhancing cellular uptake by increasing cationic character may improve transfection or endosomal escape, yet at the same time increase membrane disruption, protein adsorption, hemolytic potential, and innate immune activation. 9 , 10 Optimizing size for tissue penetration may change renal clearance thresholds, hepatosplenic sequestration, or placental transfer. Similarly, pursuing multifunctionality through ligand decoration, image-enabling components, or responsive coatings can intensify compositional complexity, increase batch-to-batch variability, and complicate analytical comparability, thereby widening both regulatory uncertainty and toxicologic ambiguity. 5 , 6 , 8 , 10 , 11

This tight coupling is especially important in cancer nanomedicine, where early enthusiasm was strongly shaped by the enhanced permeability and retention (EPR) effect. The EPR framework provided an appealing mechanistic basis for selective tumor delivery, and it helped justify extensive investment in passively targeted nanoparticles. 3 , 4 , 8 , 15 However, subsequent work has shown that EPR is highly heterogeneous across tumor types, anatomical sites, disease stages, and individual patients; moreover, the magnitude and clinical utility of passive accumulation in human solid tumors are often much less predictable than in rodent xenograft models. 8 , 15 This does not negate the value of nanoparticles in oncology, but it changes the safety discussion in a fundamental way. When tumor delivery is variable and often modest, the balance between intended and unintended exposure becomes more dependent on systemic disposition, immune recognition, stromal barriers, vascular physiology, and patient selection. In other words, safety cannot be considered independently of delivery realism. A nanoparticle that performs well in a permissive animal model may expose patients primarily through liver, spleen, blood, or infusion-related pathways rather than through therapeutically meaningful tumor deposition. 7 , 8 , 15

A second major realization is that the biological identity of a nanoparticle is not fixed at the time of manufacture. Once introduced into blood or other biological fluids, nanoparticles rapidly acquire a biomolecular corona composed of proteins, lipids, metabolites, and other macromolecules. 11 , 12 This adsorbed layer can profoundly alter colloidal stability, opsonization, immune recognition, cell-surface interactions, trafficking, and clearance. As a result, the in vivo behavior of a nominally identical formulation may vary across species, disease states, and patient subpopulations as a function of the surrounding biological milieu. 11 , 12 The translational implications are substantial. Protein corona composition is influenced by methodological factors such as sample preparation and analytical workflow, but also by patient-specific variables including inflammation, sex, ancestry, hormonal state, metabolic status, and comorbidities. 11 , 12 Safety assessment that ignores these dynamic interfaces risks both false reassurance and poor reproducibility. The growing emphasis on corona standardization and patient-dependent corona biology represents one of the clearest examples of the field moving from descriptive nanotoxicology toward mechanistically informed translational safety science. 11 , 12

Immunological interactions remain among the most consequential and incompletely resolved safety issues in nanomedicine. Nanoparticles can engage complement pathways, coagulation cascades, platelets, monocytes, macrophages, dendritic cells, mast cells, and pattern-recognition systems in ways that depend on composition, curvature, surface charge, PEG density, impurity burden, and aggregation state. 9 , 13 , 14 These responses can manifest as cytokine release, altered innate and adaptive immunity, changes in biodistribution, or acute infusion reactions. Complement activation-related pseudoallergy (CARPA) is a paradigmatic concern for liposomes and certain other lipid-based or colloidal products, because it demonstrates how a nanoparticle can trigger clinically relevant reactions that are neither classical IgE-mediated allergy nor easily predicted by conventional toxicology alone. 13 The persistence of this issue across decades of liposomal development underscores a broader lesson: in nanomedicine, safety barriers are not always exotic or late-stage; some are recurrent, mechanistically understandable, and therefore potentially preventable if incorporated early into platform design and translational testing. 9 , 13 , 14

Repeat dosing introduces an additional layer of complexity. Many therapeutic contexts require chronic or cyclical administration, yet repeated exposure can change nanoparticle disposition through adaptive immune responses, altered corona formation, saturation or priming of clearance pathways, and anti-carrier antibodies. 14 , 16 Anti-PEG immunity has become the most widely discussed example, reflecting the extensive use of PEG in liposomes, lipid nanoparticles, protein conjugates, and other long-circulating systems. 14 , 16 Although PEG remains an important technology, its benefits are now understood to coexist with liabilities related to pre-existing antibodies, de novo antibody induction, accelerated blood clearance, and potential hypersensitivity. 14 , 16 This tension is highly instructive for the broader field. It illustrates that excipients once considered largely inert may become critical determinants of clinical performance and safety when deployed repeatedly, at scale, and in immunologically diverse populations. Thus, contemporary nanoparticle safety evaluation must consider not only acute tolerability but also immunologic memory, sequence effects, and the consequences of prior exposure to structurally related materials. 9 , 14 , 16

In parallel with biologic complexity, the chemistry, manufacturing, and controls (CMC) dimension of nanoparticle safety has assumed increasing importance. For many nanomedicines, critical quality attributes extend beyond the conventional identity-purity-potency triad to include size distribution, morphology, lamellarity, drug localization, surface composition, corona susceptibility, aggregation tendency, residual solvents, endotoxin burden, free versus encapsulated payload, and time-dependent instability during storage or handling. 6 , 10 Minor shifts in these variables can alter biodistribution, immunoreactivity, or release kinetics enough to change clinical safety. As nanomedicine products become more complex, developers increasingly rely on advanced analytical technologies, orthogonal characterization, and platform-specific comparability strategies. 6 , 10 The importance of this evolution cannot be overstated. Translation failures are often attributed to biology, but a substantial fraction of safety uncertainty arises upstream from insufficiently controlled material definition or from the inability to show that the material used in pivotal studies is analytically and functionally comparable to the material manufactured at larger scale. 6 , 10 In this sense, nanoparticle safety is not only a toxicology problem; it is also a materials science, process engineering, and regulatory science problem. 5 , 6 , 10

Encouragingly, the field has made real progress. First, there is now broad consensus that nanosafety must be integrated into design rather than appended after optimization. 5 , 6 , 9 ,10 Second, clinically informative case studies, especially from liposomes, albumin nanoparticles, LNPs, and iron-based nanocolloids, have clarified which properties are most consequential for tolerability and regulatory acceptability. 2 , 5 , 6 , 13 Third, translational frameworks have shifted toward more realistic disease models, improved bioanalytical methods, and stronger emphasis on patient stratification, imaging-based pharmacology, and mechanism-aware trial design. 3 , 5 , 7 , 8 Fourth, reproducibility efforts are beginning to address long-standing heterogeneity in corona analysis, material characterization, and interlaboratory comparability. 6 , 11 Finally, the recent industrial and regulatory maturation of nucleic acid nanomedicines has strengthened the notion that scalable, clinically acceptable nanoparticle platforms can be developed when platform engineering, process control, analytical depth, and risk assessment evolve together. 2 , 6 , 9 The central challenge now is to convert these lessons from isolated successes into generalizable translational principles.

The next phase of the field therefore depends less on proving that nanoparticles can work and more on demonstrating when, why, and in whom they can work safely. This requires moving beyond generalized claims of “biocompatibility” toward mechanistic, indication-specific, and patient-aware safety definitions. It also requires distinguishing platform-intrinsic hazards from modifiable design liabilities; separating transient, manageable on-target effects from unpredictable off-target reactions; and recognizing that successful translation often rests on selecting the right clinical problem for a given nanoparticle architecture rather than forcing a versatile platform into biologically incompatible settings. 3 , 5 , 7 , 8 Particularly in oncology, future progress will likely depend on aligning carrier design with realistic delivery constraints, measurable biomarkers of accumulation or response, and combination strategies that justify the added complexity of nanoscale formulations. 3 , 4 , 7 , 8 , 15 More broadly, the field must address chronic exposure, special populations, immunogenic memory, degradation fate, and long-term organ retention with the same rigor that it has historically applied to short-term efficacy.

Against this background, the present review examines the safety of nanoparticles in medicine from a translational perspective. Its purpose is not to restate the generic advantages of nanomedicine, but to critically assess what has been learned from approved products, clinical candidates, mechanistic safety studies, and emerging analytical frameworks. The review is organized around three overarching questions. First, what genuine progress has been made in understanding and mitigating the safety liabilities of medical nanoparticles? Second, which limitations remain unresolved despite technological and regulatory advances? Third, what critical objectives should guide the next generation of safer, more clinically reliable nanomedicines? By focusing on the interface between physicochemical design, biological identity, immunological reactivity, manufacturing control, and patient heterogeneity, this review argues that nanoparticle safety should be treated not as a late-stage hurdle, but as the organizing principle of clinically meaningful nanomedicine development. 5 , 6 , 9–14

More specifically, the review highlights progress in platform characterization, standardization of nanosafety-relevant assays, improved recognition of immune-mediated adverse events, deeper understanding of protein corona biology, and growing appreciation of the mismatch between permissive preclinical models and heterogeneous human disease. 6 , 8–12 , 15 At the same time, it addresses persistent limitations: insufficient mechanistic comparability between formulations, incomplete prediction of infusion and repeat-dose toxicities, inadequate representation of susceptible populations, underdeveloped strategies for long-term fate assessment, and the continuing tendency to frame translational failure primarily as a delivery problem rather than as a coupled delivery-safety problem. 5 , 6 , 8–16 The future priorities emerging from this analysis include safe-by-design formulation paradigms, clinically relevant exposure models, patient-stratified evaluation, integrated CMC-toxicology frameworks, and prospective use of biomarkers and imaging to identify the patients most likely to achieve benefit without disproportionate risk. 3 , 5–8 , 11 , 12 , 15 In this sense, enhancing nanoparticle safety is not a defensive or restrictive agenda. On the contrary, it is the most direct route to making nanomedicine more precise, more reproducible, and more clinically transformative. To preserve a translational rather than purely descriptive focus, the literature considered in this narrative synthesis was prioritized according to clinical relevance, mechanistic contribution to nanosafety, regulatory or manufacturing significance, and the ability to clarify reproducibility, patient heterogeneity, long-term fate, or clinically important failure modes. Recent peer-reviewed studies were emphasized while landmark earlier work was retained when it remains foundational. The distinctive contribution of the present review is therefore the integration of physicochemical design, biological identity, host response, preclinical evidence, CMC, regulation, and patient context into a single safety-by-design continuum rather than the treatment of these domains as independent topics. 6 , 10 , 11 , 17–19

## Nanoparticles in Medicine: Classes and Biomedical Uses

Nanoparticles used in medicine comprise a structurally diverse family of materials whose biomedical behavior is determined not only by core composition but also by size, shape, surface chemistry, colloidal stability, protein adsorption, degradation kinetics, and cargo-release behavior. From a translational perspective, it is useful to organize them into broad material classes—lipid-based, polymeric, metallic and metal oxide, silica-based, carbon-based, and hybrid nanomaterials—because each class brings a distinct combination of advantages, limitations, manufacturing constraints, and safety considerations. Although these categories often overlap in practice, especially in multifunctional theranostic platforms, they remain conceptually valuable for understanding how nanomaterial design governs biomedical use in drug delivery, imaging, vaccines, and oncology. 2 , 3 , 20 The current clinical and preclinical landscape further shows that no single nanoparticle class is universally optimal; instead, platform selection must be aligned with the physicochemical requirements of the payload, the biological barriers of the target tissue, the intended route of administration, and the level of multifunctionality required for the therapeutic objective. 2 , 21 , 22

### Lipid-Based Nanoparticles

Lipid-based nanoparticles are the most clinically mature and commercially visible class of nanomedicines. Their central importance reflects a favorable convergence of biocompatibility, formulation flexibility, scalable manufacturing, and the capacity to encapsulate a wide spectrum of payloads ranging from hydrophobic small molecules to fragile nucleic acids. This category includes classical liposomes, solid lipid nanoparticles (SLNs), nanostructured lipid carriers (NLCs), nanoemulsions, niosomes in broader colloidal discussions, and, most prominently in current translational medicine, lipid nanoparticles (LNPs) designed for RNA and other nucleic acid delivery. 2 , 20 , 23 , 24 Across these subclasses, lipids serve not merely as inert carriers but as functional structural elements that determine membrane fusion behavior, endosomal escape, circulation half-life, storage stability, and cell-type selectivity. 20 , 23

The biomedical utility of lipid-based nanoparticles arises from their amphiphilic organization. Liposomes and related vesicular systems can accommodate hydrophilic cargo in aqueous cores and hydrophobic compounds within bilayers, enabling unusually broad formulation versatility. SLNs and NLCs, by contrast, exploit solid or mixed solid–liquid lipid matrices to stabilize loaded agents and modulate release kinetics. Contemporary LNPs for nucleic acid delivery rely on multicomponent formulations that typically include an ionizable lipid, a phospholipid, cholesterol, and a PEG-lipid. The ionizable lipid is especially important because it permits low-to-neutral surface charge under physiological conditions while acquiring positive charge in acidic endosomes, thereby facilitating endosomal escape and intracellular payload release. 20 , 23 , 25 This structure–function logic has become foundational in modern nanomedicine, particularly after the successful deployment of LNP-enabled mRNA vaccines and the broader expansion of RNA therapeutics. 20 , 25 , 26

A major strength of lipid-based nanoparticles is their capacity to improve the pharmacology of otherwise problematic drugs. Lipid encapsulation can increase the apparent solubility of poorly water-soluble compounds, shield labile cargos from hydrolysis or enzymatic degradation, reduce premature systemic exposure, and alter tissue distribution in ways that improve tolerability or efficacy. In oncology, these effects have been exploited to reformulate cytotoxic agents with the goal of reducing off-target toxicity and modifying biodistribution. In nucleic acid therapeutics, lipid nanocarriers protect RNA from extracellular nuclease degradation and promote intracellular delivery, thereby converting a highly unstable macromolecule into a clinically viable platform. 2 , 23 , 25 , 26 The translational significance of this class is therefore not limited to one disease area; instead, lipid-based systems have become enabling technologies across infectious disease, oncology, inflammatory disease, and regenerative medicine. 2 , 20 , 26

Liposomes remain the archetypal lipid nanocarrier and continue to be highly relevant because they illustrate the central design principles of lipid-based drug delivery. Their bilayer architecture permits passive loading, active loading, ligand functionalization, and tuning of rigidity or fusogenicity through lipid composition. The historical success of liposomal formulations demonstrated that nanoscale lipid engineering could translate into approved medicinal products, but the platform has also revealed enduring constraints such as limited loading for some cargo classes, leakage during storage, uptake by the mononuclear phagocyte system, complement activation, and modest target-site delivery in many solid tumors. 2 , 3 , 27 These issues have not displaced liposomes from the field; rather, they have driven increasingly sophisticated lipid selection, PEG-lipid optimization, surface decoration, and trigger-responsive designs.

SLNs and NLCs were developed partly to address some of the limitations associated with conventional emulsions and liposomes, especially in relation to physical stability and sustained release. Their solid or partially solid lipid matrices can enhance drug retention and improve formulation robustness, while their use of physiologically acceptable lipids supports broad interest in oral, topical, pulmonary, and parenteral applications. Recent literature continues to emphasize their suitability for antibacterial agents, chemotherapeutics, nucleic acids, and phytoconstituents, as well as their relative manufacturing simplicity and biocompatibility. 24 Nevertheless, SLNs and related systems are not free of constraints. Drug expulsion during storage, polymorphic lipid transitions, limited loading of certain molecules, and scale-sensitive process variability remain important formulation concerns. 24

The most transformative recent development in lipid nanotechnology has been the rise of LNPs for nucleic acid delivery. These systems differ from classical liposomes in both compositional philosophy and functional purpose. Rather than serving mainly as passive vesicles, LNPs are typically engineered as dynamic condensed assemblies in which the ionizable lipid plays a decisive role in nucleic acid complexation, intracellular trafficking, and endosomal disruption. Their success in clinically deployed mRNA vaccines and siRNA therapeutics has established LNPs as one of the clearest demonstrations that nanoparticle platforms can achieve industrial-scale manufacturing, regulatory acceptance, and global medical impact. 20 , 23 , 25 , 26 At the same time, this success has intensified scrutiny of their immunological and toxicological profiles, including the influence of ionizable lipid chemistry, PEG-lipid immunogenicity, reactogenicity, biodistribution to liver and spleen, and the consequences of repeated administration. 25 , 28

Beyond vaccines and RNA therapeutics, lipid-based nanoparticles are being intensively developed for cancer immunotherapy. Their ability to deliver mRNA, immunostimulatory molecules, tumor antigens, adjuvants, and combination payloads makes them attractive tools for engineering the cancer-immunity cycle. They can be designed to target antigen-presenting cells, modulate tumor-associated myeloid compartments, or support in situ vaccination strategies. In this context, lipid nanoparticles are not simply drug carriers; they are immunopharmacologic devices whose composition can shape innate sensing, antigen expression kinetics, and the spatial pattern of immune activation. 26 , 29 This is one reason why lipid-based nanocarriers occupy a central position in both prophylactic and therapeutic vaccine design.

Lipid-based nanoparticles also contribute substantially to theranostics and imaging, although they are often less intrinsically image-active than metallic or silica-based systems. Their value in this domain comes from their ability to co-load imaging probes and therapeutic agents or to encapsulate radionuclides, fluorophores, MRI-active species, or contrast enhancers together with drugs or nucleic acids. Such combinations enable image-guided drug delivery, biodistribution tracking, and pharmacodynamic readouts. In cancer, lipid-based theranostic systems are being developed to merge molecular imaging with targeted or immune-mediated intervention, though translational success still depends on solving the same core issues of circulation behavior, tumor penetration, and reproducible manufacturability that affect therapeutic-only systems. 17 , 28

Overall, lipid-based nanoparticles represent the most advanced and versatile nanomedicine class currently available. Their success derives from a balance of biological compatibility and engineering adaptability that is difficult to match. However, their maturation has also clarified an essential lesson for the broader field: clinical usability depends not only on elegant nanoparticle design but also on deep control over lipid composition, interfacial behavior, immune compatibility, storage stability, and scalable process reproducibility. 2 , 20 , 23 , 25 , 28

Polymeric nanoparticles form one of the broadest and most adaptable classes of nanocarriers in medicine. Unlike lipid systems, whose behavior is largely dictated by supramolecular assembly of amphiphilic molecules, polymeric nanoparticles are built from covalent macromolecular frameworks that can be tuned with exceptional precision in relation to molecular weight, block architecture, degradability, hydrophobicity, charge density, glass transition behavior, and functional group distribution. conclusions:
Nanomedicine has reached a decisive stage in its development. The field has moved well beyond the era in which nanoparticles were viewed mainly as elegant delivery concepts or highly flexible experimental platforms. It has now generated approved products, shaped important areas of modern therapeutics, and demonstrated that nanoscale engineering can solve clinically meaningful problems. At the same time, this progress has made one point unmistakably clear: the future of nanomedicine will depend less on how complex nanoparticles can become and more on how safely, reproducibly, and rationally they can be translated into real medical use.

One of the most important lessons to emerge from the field is that safety cannot be treated as a late checkpoint added after efficacy has already been optimized. In nanomedicine, safety is inseparable from function. The same attributes that influence circulation, targeting, uptake, intracellular delivery, and release also shape immune recognition, blood compatibility, off-target accumulation, degradation, and long-term tolerance. This means that safety is not a peripheral constraint on innovation. It is the framework that determines whether innovation becomes clinically meaningful. In many ways, the maturation of nanomedicine can be understood as a shift from designing nanoparticles that can work to designing nanoparticles that can work reliably, safely, and for the right patients.

There has been genuine and important progress. The field now has a far better understanding of how physicochemical properties govern biological behavior. It has developed safer lipid nanoparticle systems, more sophisticated stealth and biomimetic strategies, more biodegradable and responsive materials, and more advanced tools for preclinical characterization and biodistribution analysis. Regulatory thinking has also become more mature, with greater emphasis on critical quality attributes, manufacturing control, stability, and lifecycle management. These advances show that the safety of nanoparticles is not an unsolved abstraction. It is a problem that can be progressively reduced through careful design, rigorous characterization, and translational discipline.

And yet, major challenges remain. Human biodistribution is still difficult to predict with confidence. Long-term fate and clearance are still insufficiently resolved for many platforms. Immunotoxicity remains only partly understood in mechanistic terms, especially under repeated dosing and in heterogeneous patient populations. Reproducibility across studies and batch-to-batch consistency in complex products still represent major obstacles. Perhaps most importantly, the field still needs to become more selective in deciding which nanoparticle systems truly justify clinical development. Not every technically impressive nanoplatform offers a meaningful therapeutic advantage, and not every increase in sophistication leads to better medicine.

For that reason, the next decade should be guided by a more deliberate philosophy. Safer nanomedicine will not come only from inventing new materials. It will come from integrating efficacy, safety, manufacturing, and patient relevance from the earliest stages of design. It will come from better long-term studies, more predictive biological models, stronger mechanistic toxicology, clearer reporting standards, and greater willingness to abandon platforms whose complexity exceeds their clinical value. It will also come from recognizing that different diseases impose different safety demands, and that truly successful nanomedicine must be adapted not only to a target, but to a therapeutic context.

The field has therefore moved beyond the question of whether nanoparticles can contribute meaningfully to medicine. The more consequential translational question is which nanoparticle systems should advance, in which clinical settings, and with what degree of confidence in their long-term safety, manufacturing reproducibility, and patient-specific benefit-risk profile. Addressing this question requires increasingly mechanistic, quantitative, and clinically grounded evidence rather than generalized assumptions of platform biocompatibility.

Ultimately, enhancing the safety of nanoparticles in medicine should not be seen as a defensive exercise or a regulatory burden. It is the most direct route toward making nanomedicine more credible, more precise, and more useful to patients. The strongest future for the field will belong not to the most complicated systems, but to the ones whose design, biological behavior, manufacturability, and safety profile are aligned in a coherent and clinically justified way. If nanomedicine can sustain that level of rigor, it will not simply remain promising. It will become one of the most durable and transformative areas of modern therapeutic science.

Accordingly, the most consequential priorities for the next decade are harmonized characterization and reporting, mechanistic immunotoxicity and genotoxicity assessment, longitudinal fate and clearance studies, clinically relevant experimental models, quantitative exposure-based toxicology, tighter CMC-toxicology integration, and patient stratification supported by biomarkers and imaging. AI, multi-omics, PBPK modeling, microphysiological systems, and digital-twin approaches can strengthen this framework, but only when their predictions are externally validated and linked to experimentally measurable mechanisms. Progress in these areas should accelerate regulatory confidence and clinical adoption while reducing the probability that increased nanoparticle complexity produces risk without proportional therapeutic value.
