# Mesolens imaging in microbiology

## Abstract
The optical microscope has served as an essential tool for the microbiologist since van Leeuwenhoek’s observations of ‘animalcules’, yet the core design of the objective lens has changed little over the last 100 years and imparts a dichotomy between resolution and field of view. High numerical aperture objectives resolve subcellular detail but sample only small regions, whereas low-magnification objectives capture large areas with limited resolving power. Many microbial processes span the micron-to-centimetre length scales, constraining how spatial heterogeneity, microbial interaction, and rare events can be visualised in intact specimens. This review describes how the Mesolens overcomes this limitation by combining low magnification with high numerical aperture to deliver sub-micron resolution across multi-millimetre fields of view and millimetre-scale depths. We summarise the optical principles and imaging modalities that underpin the Mesolens, including widefield and confocal laser scanning mesoscopy, and emerging implementations such as light-sheet mesoscopy, mesoscopic total internal reflection fluorescence, and standing-wave mesoscopy. We highlight applications where spatial context is essential; the discovery and characterisation of biofilm nutrient transport channels in Escherichia coli , understanding the architecture of cross-kingdom Candida albicans – Staphylococcus aureus biofilms, and translational applications in clinical and environmental microbiology. Finally, we discuss specimen preparation, analysis workflows, and future opportunities in new modalities, computationally guided acquisition, and scalable optical manufacturing. Together, these advances position the Mesolens as a versatile tool to resolve microbial interactions and dynamics across length scales associated with priority areas in microbiology.

## Keywords
Biofilms; Cross-scale imaging; Microbial Communities; Multi-modal imaging; Optical Microscopy

## Introduction to optical mesoscopy

Optical microscopy remains one of the most versatile and informative tools in biochemistry and cell biology. From the discovery of cells to the visualisation of molecular interactions, the ability to image biological structures using light has transformed our understanding of living systems. However, a persistent challenge lies in bridging the scale between subcellular and tissue-level imaging. This spatial range is often known as the mesoscale. Traditional high numerical aperture (NA) objectives offer excellent resolution but only over small fields of view, whereas low-magnification optics can capture images of large areas, but resolving power is poor.

The development of the Mesolens addresses this long-standing trade-off. Designed to provide sub-micron resolution across a field of view (FOV) more than 4 mm wide and of specimens up to 3-mm thick, the Mesolens is an imaging objective that enables imaging of whole biological specimens, such as embryos [ 1 ], developing Drosophilia larvae [ 2 ], zebrafish models [ 3 ], and mature colony biofilms [ 4 ], while still resolving individual cells. To appreciate how such performance is achieved, it is useful to review the fundamental principles of optical imaging that underpin the operation of all light microscopes, including those at the mesoscale.

The Mesolens has a unique combination of a fixed low-magnification, to sample large areas, and high NA, to resolve subcellular detail. Combined, these variables break the traditional ratio between magnification and NA that limit multi-scale imaging. For example, a typical microbiologist may wish to survey their sample at low magnification using a 4×/0.10 NA objective lens and then image their chosen region of interest using a 60×/1.50 NA objective lens; both have a ratio of 1:40, precluding the ability to resolve fine spatial structures over large areas in a single acquisition. The Mesolens has a prescription of 4×/0.47 NA—a ratio of 1:8—permitting visualisation and resolution of structures on the order of 700 nm throughout a 108 mm 3 capture volume [ 1 , 2 ]. Coincidentally, this prescription is ideal to sample the spatial scales over which many microbiological processes and challenges manifest, positioning the Mesolens as an emerging and powerful tool for the microbiologist.

The basic principles of light, resolution, contrast, and FOV underpin all optical imaging, from simple microscopes to advanced mesoscale systems. The Mesolens exemplifies how careful application of these principles, combined with innovative optical design, can overcome long-standing trade-offs between resolution and FOV. By facilitating subcellular-resolution imaging across multi-millimetre-scale volumes, the Mesolens bridges the gap between microscopy and macrophotography, enabling subcellular resolution imaging with the possibility of molecular specificity.

### Fundamentals of optical imaging

While light exhibits both the properties of a wave and a particle, most optical imaging systems consider only the wave nature of light. When light interacts with matter, it can be refracted, reflected, scattered, and diffracted. These processes determine how an image is formed, and what spatial information can be captured. In microscopy, the objective lens is the key element that collects and focuses light emerging from the specimen to form a magnified image.

A crucial parameter in optical design is the NA, defined as (1) N A = n sin θ ,

where n is the refractive index of the imaging medium or specimen, and θ is the half-angle of the light cone collected by the objective ( Figure 1 A). The NA quantifies the light-collecting capacity and directly influences both image brightness and resolution [ 5 ].

To maintain image quality, optical aberrations, such as chromatic and spherical aberrations, must be minimised through precise lens design [ 6 ]. The Mesolens is distinctive in achieving diffraction-limited performance across a large FOV. More than seventeen individual lens elements are included in the prescription, with the largest lenses being more than 60 mm in diameter, and they are precisely located within the objective lens barrel to minimise optical aberrations [ 1 ]. Further reduction of optical aberrations, particularly coma, chromatic aberration, and spherical aberration, is achieved by use of correction collars [ 2 ], which can be adjusted to give diffraction-limited imaging resolution in specimens with refractive indices from n = 1.33 to n = 1.51, thus making it compatible for multi-colour imaging in three-dimensions (3D) with most biological specimens.

### Resolution

Resolution defines the smallest distance between two points that can still be distinguished as separate. The Rayleigh criterion defines the theoretical bound of lateral resolution as (2) d x , y = 0 .61 λ N A ,

where d x,y is the smallest resolvable distance and λ is the wavelength of light. The axial resolution, which is along the optical axis of the microscope, is given by (3) d z = 2 n λ N A 2 .

In practical terms, achieving high resolution depends not only on wavelength and NA but also on illumination uniformity, detector sampling, and system stability [ 5 ]. Traditional optical systems face an intrinsic compromise: high NA lenses are invariably high in magnification, meaning that the improved resolution can only be obtained within a tiny volume. The Mesolens uniquely circumvents this limitation through a low magnification (4×) yet exceptionally high NA (0.47) design, maintaining sub-micron resolution across a field exceeding 6 mm in diameter [ 1 ] ( Figure 1 ). This capability allows imaging of entire biological structures at cellular detail.

### Contrast

In biological imaging, contrast determines the visibility of structures within the specimen. Without contrast, even high-resolution systems yield little meaningful information. Contrast arises from differences in absorption, scattering, refractive index, or fluorescence emission between regions [ 7 ].

Techniques such as brightfield and phase contrast microscopy enhance image visibility by exploiting these differences. In fluorescence imaging, contrast is generated by specific fluorophores that emit light at characteristic wavelengths upon excitation, enabling molecular specificity.

The Mesolens is compatible with multiple contrast mechanisms, including brightfield transmitted light, widefield epifluorescence recording, and confocal imaging. Its high NA and wide field permit both high brightness and excellent contrast over large specimen volumes, facilitating visualisation of complex biological samples.

### Field of view and depth of field

The FOV represents the spatial extent of the sample that can be imaged at once, while the depth of field (DOF) defines the axial range within which structures appear in acceptable focus [ 5 ]. Typically, increasing magnification or NA reduces the FOV and DOF, presenting a challenge for imaging large, thick specimens. The DOF can be calculated by (4) D O F = λ ( n 2 - N A 2 ) 1 / 2 N A 2

Conventional objectives cannot easily deliver both high resolution and a large FOV because lens aberrations scale with aperture size. The Mesolens overcomes this through custom optical engineering, providing a millimetre-scale field with sub-micron resolution and a relatively long working distance. This combination allows entire specimens, such as Drosophila or whole mouse organs, to be imaged in a single dataset.

In 3D imaging, the axial resolution is equally important and depends on both NA and illumination geometry. Optical sectioning methods such as confocal scanning or lightsheet illumination can further improve depth discrimination, enabling high-quality volumetric reconstructions.

### Two-dimensional and three-dimensional imaging

Traditional light microscopy captures two-dimensional (2D) projections of a specimen. This is adequate for thin samples but is insufficient for thick, complex structures. To image in 3D, optical sectioning is required. By acquiring sequential focal planes, commonly referred to as a ‘z-stack’ and reconstructing them computationally, the full spatial organisation of the sample can be visualised without mechanical sectioning.

The PSF describes how a point source of light is represented in an image and governs both lateral and axial resolution. Deconvolution algorithms use the PSF to computationally correct blur and improve image sharpness.

The Mesolens supports several 3D imaging modalities. In confocal mode, optical sectioning is achieved through a pinhole that rejects out-of-focus light, improving axial resolution as in the original confocal laser scanning microscope. The lightsheet Mesolens, in contrast, uses planar illumination to excite only a thin optical section, reducing phototoxicity and acquisition time [ 9 ]. These methods enable rapid volumetric imaging of large biological specimens with cellular resolution.

### Imaging modalities underpinning the mesolens

#### Widefield Microscopy

Widefield microscopy illuminates the entire specimen simultaneously, capturing images in a single exposure. It offers high temporal resolution and is ideal for live or dynamic samples but suffers from out-of-focus blur when imaging thick specimens. The Mesolens widefield system leverages its large NA to maintain resolution across an extended field, producing detailed images of large specimens at the subcellular scale, and is compatible with brightfield transmission, darkfield illumination, and epifluorescence contrast. Illumination of specimens can be performed with a simple halogen bulb for brightfield and darkfield modes, and either an arc lamp or light-emitting diodes for excitation of fluorescence. Due to the high-resolution images across the large FOV of the Mesolens, a camera with an appropriate pixel size commensurate with the low magnification but high pixel number to capture the high-resolution detail is required for optimum performance. This was achieved at modest cost using a chip-shifting camera, which produced a 224-nm pixel size, satisfying the Nyquist–Shannon sampling criterion, across a 4.4 mm × 3.0 mm FOV [ 2 , 10 ]. With this camera, images can be acquired at relatively high speeds (0.55 Hz, or 1.8 seconds/image).

#### Confocal laser scanning mesoscopy

Confocal mesoscopy achieves optical sectioning by following the same principles as a confocal laser scanning microscope. A pair of galvanometer mirrors are used to produce a scanned focused laser point across the sample. Where the laser spot excites fluorescence from the specimen or reflection occurs in the specimen, causing backscattering of the incident light, the light that is emitted or reflected is collected by the Mesolens, and directed through a pinhole that is conjugate to the focal plane in the imaged specimen. This suppresses background fluorescence or reflections and enhances axial resolution. The confocal Mesolens system is slower to image specimens than widefield methods: to capture all information from a 6 mm × 6 mm FOV, with a pixel dwell time of 1 μs, each image takes 100 seconds to acquire [ 11 ].

#### Other mesolens modalities

Building on the Mesolens optical design, several additional modalities have emerged. By illuminating the specimen with a long, thin sheet of light, as is performed in lightsheet microscopy, lightsheet mesoscopy with the Mesolens can perform much faster 3D imaging of specimens than confocal laser scanning mesoscopy. Imaging speeds with the Mesolens and a lightsheet are 14 times faster than the confocal counterpart. However, specimen mounting for lightsheet mesoscopy is challenging. The specimen must be mounted in a chamber with two orthogonal optical quality windows, one suitable for introducing the illumination beam, and the other for imaging the resulting fluorescence from the specimen with the Mesolens. Moreover, the optical alignment of the optical system to produce the unusually long and thin lightsheet for compatibility with the Mesolens is amenable to misalignment, thereby reducing the practicality of this approach. Nevertheless, the Mesolens Airy lightsheet has demonstrated extended volumetric imaging over a 4.4 mm field with a lightsheet thickness of 7.8 μm over the full FOV [ 9 ].

Mesoscopic total internal reflection fluorescence (mesoTIRF) extends the principle of conventional total internal reflection (TIRF) imaging to the mesoscale regime by coupling the unique optical design of the Mesolens with an oblique, high-angle illumination geometry [ 12 ]. In standard TIRF, an evanescent electromagnetic field is generated at the interface between a high-refractive-index substrate (typically glass) and an aqueous specimen when the incident light exceeds the critical angle for TIRF. This evanescent field decays exponentially, with the thickness of the evanescent wave given by (5) δ = λ 0 4 π N 2 2 sin 2 θ C - n 1 2 - 1 2 ,

where θ c is the critical angle given by (6) θ C = sin - 1 n 2 n 1

and n 2 and n 1 are refractive indices adjacent to a boundary, e.g. a cell-coverslip interface, and n 2 ≤ n 1 .

The approximate thickness of the evanescent wave is ∼100 nm. This results in exceptional axial confinement and high signal-to-background ratio imaging of regions of the specimen in contact with the coverslip [ 13 ]. The mesoTIRF implementation achieves the same principle but over a multi-millimetre-scale FOV, exploiting the high NA (NA = 0.47) of the Mesolens to sustain critical-angle illumination across a vastly expanded area compared to the conventional light microscope (4.4 mm versus several hundred micron). The technique thus provides a powerful means of mapping cell morphology, membrane dynamics, or focal adhesion organization across entire cultures in a single high-speed imaging acquisition.

Standing-wave mesoscale imaging applies the principles of standing-wave fluorescence microscopy to the large field and high NA of the Mesolens to achieve axial super-resolution over millimetre-scale specimen areas [ 14 ]. In standing-wave fluorescence microscopy, an interference pattern is created by the superposition of two coherent light beams, typically an incident and a reflected wave, producing a series of excitation antinodes and nodes normal to the optical axis [ 15 , 16 ]. Fluorophores located within the antinodes experience enhanced excitation, generating a modulated axial fluorescence pattern with an effective periodicity of approximately (7) λ 2 n .

When used in conjunction with a fluorescent membrane stain applied to cells, standing wave imaging results in a topographical contour map of the cell, encoding 3D information in a 2D image, with an axial resolution on the order of 100 nm. Unlike TIRF, the multiplanar nature of the illuminating standing wave means that specimens can be imaged at depth using this approach, rather than with a single illuminating evanescent wave that can only map the part of the cell membrane in contact with the coverslip. While the axial resolution of standing wave microscopy is higher than that of confocal microscopy by approximately a factor of 8, there are information gaps caused by the modulated illuminating beam in standing wave imaging. Multicolour imaging has been used to fill in these gaps, and in the similar label-free method interference reflection microscopy. A sampling density of 92% was achieved in the microscale, compared to a fill-factor of approximately 50% in the conventional standing wave micrographs [ 17 , 18 ].

Standing wave mesoscopy adapts this concept to the mesoscale by combining widefield standing-wave excitation with the high NA and high collection efficiency of the Mesolens. This configuration allows the acquisition of high-contrast contour maps of the cell membrane with a single exposure. Because the standing wave pattern is formed globally across the field rather than point-by-point, standing wave mesoscopy provides rapid optical sectioning without the need for mechanical scanning. The result is a powerful modality that yields near-isotropic resolution over large areas, bridging the gap between super-resolution microscopy and large-scale tissue imaging. In addition, the technique is compatible with multi-wavelength excitation, enabling simultaneous mapping of cell structures in three dimensions at high speeds.

To illustrate the impact of mesoscopy across microbiology, we present applications by biological context, ranging from controlled model systems to complex clinical and environmental samples, and highlight the common principles by which Mesolens imaging enables new insight across these domains.

## Mesoscopic imaging of biofilm nutrient transport channels

Biofilms are microbial communities in which the constituent cells are embedded in a self-secreted extracellular matrix. This matrix is mainly composed of water, lipids, proteins and extracellular DNA [ 19 ], and it provides structural support and protection from mechanical and chemical stress [ 20 ]. Biofilms are highly dynamic and adaptable communities that can share information and collectively process external signals [ 21 ], and for this reason they constitute both a health and an environmental risk. For example, biofilms are up to 1000× more resistant to antimicrobial compounds than their planktonic counterparts [ 22 ], and they can compromise medical and industrial equipment through contamination [ 23–25 ].

Biofilms can exhibit complex morphologies and internal patterns. The structure of the biofilm itself is affected by the properties of the growth substrate [ 26 ], and specific biofilm morphologies can result from mechanical instabilities that occur during their growth and expansion [ 27 ]. For example, differences in biofilm growth rate can lead to the formation of patterns in both 2D (e.g. irregular colony edges for Bacillus subtilis [ 28 , 29 ]) and 3D, in the form of axial buckling [ 30 ]. Complex internal patterns can also arise due to heterogeneity within the bacterial population [ 31 , 32 ].

Optical microscopy has been used extensively to image biofilms both in vitro and in vivo using fluorescence and absorption-based contrast methods [ 33–35 ]. The optical sectioning capabilities of confocal microscopy have enabled 3D imaging of biofilms since 1991 [ 36 ], however the physical compromise between NA and magnification of traditional microscopes had previously limited the amount of spatial information that could easily be extracted from these micrographs. Because of this trade-off, one could either image a small region of the biofilm at high magnification and high resolution, thereby losing the overall context, or image the full size of the biofilm at low magnification and low resolution, but without being able to resolve individual bacterial cells. Lightsheet microscopy can be used to improve the acquisition speed of large volumes of data, and it has been used to image industrially relevant biofilms in microfluidic devices at cellular resolution, albeit with a limited FOV measuring approximately 100 μm 2 [ 37 ]. As discussed above, the Mesolens overcomes this limitation due to an unusual combination of NA and magnification, which allows for imaging at sub-micron resolution across whole, mature colony biofilms of up to 5 mm in diameter.

### Biofilm nutrient transport channels

#### Discovery and biochemical composition

The unique combination of low magnification and high resolution of the Mesolens enabled the discovery of a network of intra-colony channels in biofilms formed by the Escherichia coli K–12 strain JM105 [ 38 ]. The miniTn7 transposon system [ 39 ] was used to stably insert a photoprotein gene ( gfp or HcRed1 as required) into the genome of JM105, thus providing the signal for fluorescence mesoscopy. The 3D morphology of the channels was revealed through optical sectioning by confocal laser scanning mesoscopy of full, mature E. coli biofilms. This showed that intra-colony channels form complex, fractal-like patterns within the enclosed volume of macrocolony biofilms ( Figure 2 A), and they remain segregated between adjacent clonal populations. The formation of these channel networks is an emergent property of biofilm growth, as channels were observed spontaneously to reform after mechanical disruption.

Individual labelling of various structural components revealed that intra-colony channels were filled with protein-based extracellular matrix. Furthermore, channels were observed to transport small fluorescent microspheres from the surrounding environment and function as a nutrient uptake and transport mechanism, which facilitated the delivery of nutrients and key resources to the center of the biofilm. This suggests a lucrative avenue for the targeted delivery of antimicrobial compounds, which could reduce the burden of biofilms in various settings.

This was further investigated using the Mesolens, which played a crucial role in elucidating the oxygen microenvironment within biofilm transport channels. The use of a fluorescent oxygen sensor, which can be transported within the channel network, highlighted a reduction in oxygen concentration towards the centre of the biofilm compared to the edges ( Figure 2 B). The presence of this oxygen gradient was supported using an oxygen reporter plasmid expressing a strong fluorescent signal in the presence of anoxia, which was more intense in the centre of the biofilm [ 40 ]. This biochemical characterisation of the channel microenvironment marks an important step towards the exploitation of the channel architecture as a potential antimicrobial strategy.

#### Biofilm nutrient transport channel morphology

The chemical makeup of the growth substrate is known to influence the growth and internal morphology of bacterial biofilms, leading for example to branched morphologies in B. subtilis [ 41 , 42 ] and highly symmetric patterns in Vibrio cholerae [ 43 ]. The same happens for E. coli biofilms intra-colony channels, which expand radially outwards when grown on nutrient-deficient substrates and adopt intricate, fractal-like patterns when nutrients are abundant [ 44 ] ( Figure 2 C). It was initially assumed that channels were open to the surrounding environment at the biofilm edge to facilitate nutrient uptake; however, orthogonal visualisation of paraffin-embedded thin sections revealed that the channels were capped by a thin apical layer of cells. Instead, the nutrient uptake likely occurs from the base of the biofilm, where channels are often open to the growth medium containing the nutrients [ 40 ].

Biofilm fractal patterns have been observed in boundaries between isogenic strains of E. coli [ 45 ] and B. subtilis [ 46 ], where the specific geometry of the boundaries is affected by constituent cell properties such as cell shape and length [ 47 ] as well as by their metabolism [ 48 ]. In transport channels formed by the E. coli wide cell-shape mutant strain BW25113 Δ ompR ::kan, the fractal complexity is affected by the chemical makeup of the growth substrate, and in particular by osmotic stress (which was investigated by altering the concentration of NaCl in the medium and by adding various amounts of iodixanol) [ 49 ].

The fractal morphology of the channels was quantified using an open-source fractal dimension image analysis package, and no relationship was established between the shape of constituent cells and the fractal complexity of the channels they formed. However, the specific E. coli strain used to investigate this relationship is not compatible with Mesolens imaging in water immersion (which improves image resolution compared to imaging performed in air due to the higher refractive index of the immersion fluid). The BW25113 strain used for these functional studies tended to shed under liquid immersion, which was not an issue with the original JM105 strain. For this reason, these BW25113 mutant biofilms were imaged using standard confocal laser scanning microscopy. Genetic engineering of the original JM105 strain would produce cell-shape mutants compatible with Mesolens confocal laser scanning mesoscopy in water immersion, which could provide additional 3D information and significantly increase the precision of the quantification of channel fractal morphology.

## Cross-kingdom interactions

In nature, microorganisms exist as multispecies microbial communities of prokaryotic, eukaryotic, and archaeal life within protective biofilm matrices [ 50 ]. These cross-kingdom communities are crucial for the maintenance of organism and ecosystem health, with perturbations resulting in altered stress responses, immunological dysfunction, increased likelihood of diseased states [ 51–53 ], and fundamental changes in biogeochemical processes within ecosystems [ 54 ].

Cross-kingdom biofilm development involves interspecies and intraspecies interactions, and the bidirectional exchange between the microbial community and the surrounding external milieu [ 50 , 55 ]. This multivariable input into biofilm synthesis allows communities to produce optimal biofilm for a given local environment, ensuring community survival under a variety of challenging growth conditions [ 56 , 57 ]. The inherent ability of biofilms to adapt has enabled microorganisms to colonise every ecological niche on Earth; an underpinning factor in their virulence and pathogenicity [ 51 , 58 ]. Therefore, understanding the cross-kingdom interactions that drive biofilm formation is a fundamental requirement to ensure ecosystem health in the face of climate change, and for the development of new drugs, tools and methodologies that can tackle rising antimicrobial resistance and improve sustainability. Mesolens imaging enables measurement and quantification of these cross-kingdom biofilm macrostructures, cellular interactions, and biofilm–surface interactions, providing new insight into cross-kingdom communities, as has been demonstrated with the Candida albicans – Staphylococcus aureus model community.

### Mesolens imaging of a common cross-kingdom microbial community

The pleiomorphic fungus, C. albicans , and Gram-positive bacterium, S. aureus , are two components of the skin microbiome that co-infect those with underlying health conditions and form biofilm-associated infections of indwelling medical devices [ 59 ]. Their synergism in infection occurs through reciprocal augmentation of each other’s virulence through a variety of metabolic and physical interactions [ 59 ].

Use of widefield epifluorescence mesoscopy to study C. albicans–S. aureus interactions has provided unparalleled visualisation of biofilm structure and provided new understandings of C. albicans–S. aureus dual-species biofilm formation. This approach has detailed the emergence of global biofilm macrostructures arising from deposition of the original cell population and indicated the pivotal role of C. albicans cell morphotype as a major structural driver of biofilm architecture [ 60 ], as can be observed in Figure 3 A(i-ii), which displays an example of the two C. albicans–S. aureu s biofilms of differing C. albicans cell morphotype. In addition, the same imaging approach facilitated the study of C. albicans–S. aureus colonisation phenotypes on polydimethylsiloxane (PDMS), a common component of indwelling medical devices readily colonised by biofilm [ 61 ]. Mesolens imaging of C. albicans–S. aureus biofilm formation on PDMS in the presence and the absence of an agar tissue substitute revealed a critical role in surface colonisation and biofilm robustness for C. albicans hyphae ( Figure 3 B(i-ii). Taken together, these two Mesolens-based studies have shown that hyphae are pivotal in shaping C. albicans–S. aureus global biofilm formation beyond known adhesin-mediated physical interactions. Using Mesolens-based methodologies to investigate other cross-kingdom communities can address our knowledge gaps in host-biofilm dialogue, biofilm–surface interactions, and facilitate the development of biofilm-based technology platforms.

## Mesolens imaging in clinical microbiology

Clinical microbiology is inherently multiscale. Infections unfold across spatial scales, extending from subcellular host–pathogen interactions to whole-organ and systemic infections, often within specimens measuring multiple millimetres to centimetres in size. Thin tissue histology sections, cytology smears, and tissue or fluid biopsies provide high-resolution snapshots of disease, but at the cost of losing 3D context and long-range spatial relationships. Conversely, whole-organ imaging approaches routinely capture global pathology but lack the resolution required to resolve individual microorganisms or cellular interactions. This incongruity between biological scale and imaging capability presents a persistent barrier to understanding infection progression, tissue invasion, and host response.

The Mesolens addresses this gap directly by enabling subcellular resolution imaging across intact, millimetre-scale clinical specimens. Capturing large volumes in a single, continuous dataset allows host tissue, immune responses and microbial populations to be visualised simultaneously without the need for physical sectioning or computational reconstruction from tiled fields. This capability is particularly relevant for infections that exhibit spatial heterogeneity, focal invasion, or niche-specific persistence, all of which are hallmarks of chronic and systemic disease.

To illustrate the advantages of the Mesolens for clinical microbiology, we highlight applications spanning infection models, diagnostic imaging, and chronic disease, focusing on cases where mesoscopic imaging reveals spatial features that are difficult to capture using conventional approaches.

# Recent advances in Siraitia grosvenorii polysaccharides: Extraction, structural characteristics, biological activities and structure-activity relationships

## Abstract
As important bioactive macromolecular components of Siraitia grosvenorii , Siraitia grosvenorii polysaccharides (SGPs) have attracted considerable attention in the field of functional foods in recent years. This review systematically summarizes the latest research advances regarding extraction strategies, structural characteristics, gastrointestinal digestion and gut fermentation, biological activities, and structure-activity relationships of SGPs. The relationships between structural characteristics, including molecular weight, monosaccharide composition, and glycosidic linkages, and their antioxidant, hypoglycemic, and immunoregulatory activities are summarized. In addition, the major issues and challenges associated with the mechanism of biological activity, safety assessment, and industrial production of SGPs are discussed in more detail. Overall, this review provides a theoretical basis for the precise design and food-oriented application of SGPs in functional food systems, natural functional ingredients, and related health products.

## Keywords
Siraitia grosvenorii polysaccharides; Extraction; Structural characterization; Biological activities

## Introduction

Siraitia grosvenorii (Swingle) C. Jeffrey ex Lu et Z. Y. Zhang ( S. grosvenorii ), also known as “Monk fruit” or “Luo han guo,” is a perennial climbing vine belonging to the genus Siraitia of the Cucurbitaceae family ( Fig. 1 ) ( Xie et al., 2023 ). S. grosvenorii is native to the provinces of Guangxi, Guangdong, and Hunan in China, particularly the Guilin region, where it has been cultivated for more than 400 years ( Guo et al., 2024 ). According to statistics, the cultivation area of S. grosvenorii in Guilin exceeds 200,000 mu, and its annual production accounts for more than 80% of the national output, making it the largest production base worldwide ( Yang et al., 2025 ). In recent years, the market demand for S. grosvenorii has shown a continuous upward trend, primarily attributable to its unique nutritional and edible values. In 2002, S. grosvenorii was officially included by the Ministry of Health of the People's Republic of China in the “ List of Substances that are Both Food and Medicine ,” making it one of the earliest approved medicinal-food homologous species in China ( Luo et al., 2026 ). Owing to its richness in vitamins, amino acids, trace elements, and various bioactive components, S. grosvenorii is commonly consumed fresh or processed into diverse products such as dried fruits, fruit teas, and fruit wines ( Wu et al., 2022 ). Among these, mogroside V, as the principal functional component, exhibits a sweetness approximately 300 times that of sucrose, yet contains negligible calories, is not metabolized in the human body, and does not induce fluctuations in blood glucose levels. This property makes S. grosvenorii an ideal natural sugar substitute for individuals with diabetes, obese populations, and those pursuing a healthy diet ( Liao et al., 2022 ). In addition, the U.S. Food and Drug Administration (FDA) has officially recognized S. grosvenorii extract as a “Generally Recognized as Safe” (GRAS) food additive, which has greatly promoted its global market expansion( Muñoz-Labrador et al., 2024 ). In addition to serving as a rich food resource, S. grosvenorii has also been traditionally used as an empirical medicinal agent with remarkable therapeutic effects against various diseases ( Duan et al., 2023 ). Modern pharmacological studies have demonstrated that S. grosvenorii exhibits antioxidant, antitumor, hypoglycemic, and hepatoprotective activities ( Mao et al., 2025 ). In summary, as a characteristic plant resource with both edible and medicinal value, S. grosvenorii aligns well with the principles of modern healthy dietary concepts. To date, a variety of components have been isolated and identified from S. grosvenorii , mainly including triterpenoid saponins, flavonoids, polyphenols, and polysaccharides ( Liu et al., 2026 ). Among these, the triterpenoid saponin mogroside V is the most extensively studied representative compound, exhibiting significant biological activities in regulating glucose and lipid metabolism, protecting liver function, and inhibiting tumor cell proliferation ( He et al., 2025 ). However, these small-molecule components exhibit limitations such as rapid in vivo metabolism, low bioavailability, and poor targeting ability, which severely restrict their clinical efficacy ( Zhang et al., 2025 ). In contrast, S. grosvenorii polysaccharides (SGPs) exhibit considerable development potential. These macromolecules generally possess superior biocompatibility and sustained-release properties, enabling prolonged and stable pharmacological effects in vivo , thereby overcoming many limitations of small-molecule components ( Guo et al., 2022a ). Compared with mogroside V, the unique branched architecture of SGPs may confer a broader range of targets and mechanisms of action. Specifically, the complex spatial structure of SGPs can interact with the gut microbiota to generate beneficial metabolites such as short-chain fatty acids, thereby regulating the host's overall metabolic status ( Guo et al., 2022b ). Furthermore, their macromolecular nature confers notable immunomodulatory properties, enhancing host defense by activating macrophages and promoting cytokine secretion ( Jiang et al., 2026 ). Despite the distinctive structural features and diverse functional potential of SGPs, current research remains fragmented, with most studies limited to crude polysaccharide mixtures and lacking systematic elucidation of their fine structures. Moreover, studies on structure-activity relationships are largely restricted to correlative descriptions, lacking systematic validation of causal relationships between individual structural parameters and functional outcomes. Although some progress has been made in biological activity studies, the underlying molecular mechanisms remain at an early exploratory stage, and data on long-term safety evaluation are relatively scarce. These limitations significantly constrain the in-depth development and industrial application of SGPs.

Previous reviews on SGPs have primarily focused on providing a general overview of their biological activities and structural characterization, without establishing a comprehensive framework that links extraction and purification, structural elucidation, and biological activity validation ( Duan et al., 2023 ; Huang et al., 2024 ). To address this research gap, the present review establishes a more systematic and comprehensive framework by providing an up-to-date and integrated overview of recent advances in the extraction and purification techniques, structural characteristics, and biological activities of SGPs. The structure-activity relationship of SGPs is deeply analyzed to elucidate the underlying molecular mechanisms responsible for their biological functions, while the current research limitations and future perspectives are also discussed. Particular emphasis is placed on the effects of different extraction methods on polysaccharide yield and structural integrity, along with a systematic comparison of the advantages and limitations of various extraction approaches. It analyzes the intrinsic relationships between structure and biological activity, revealing how key structural parameters such as molecular weight (Mw) distribution, monosaccharide composition, and glycosidic linkage patterns regulate immunomodulatory, antioxidant, and hypoglycemic activities. Furthermore, this review provides an integrated analysis of the structural transformations, biological mechanisms, and prospects for food industrial applications of SGPs during gastrointestinal digestion and intestinal fermentation processes. In particular, the influence of SGPs structural characteristics on their functional expression during gastrointestinal processing is highlighted, and the key challenges associated with safety evaluation and large-scale production are further discussed. This review aims to provide theoretical support and references for the high-value utilization of SGPs and promote the transformation of this medicinal and edible resource from traditional empirical applications toward modern precision nutrition interventions.

## Nutritional value

As a natural low-calorie sweetening resource, S. grosvenorii has attracted extensive attention for its nutritional value in the development of functional foods. Based on nutritional data, S. grosvenorii can be regarded as a nutritionally distinctive fruit resource characterized by high dietary fiber, moderate protein, low lipid content in the flesh, abundant minerals, and high-intensity non-sugar sweet constituents. In different fruit parts, the flesh showed the highest protein content (11.46%) and the lowest fat content (2.93%), being approximately 67.3% richer in protein and 61.4% lower in fat than the peel ( Utami et al., 2024 ). Although the whole fruit exhibited the highest total sugar content (7.51%), the difference among peel, flesh, and whole fruit was not statistically significant, suggesting that the sweetness of S. grosvenorii cannot be explained solely by conventional sugars. Instead, it is mainly attributed to mogrosides, especially Mogroside V and Siamenoside I, whose sweetness is hundreds of times higher than that of sucrose ( Guo et al., 2024 ). Region- and processing-dependent analyses further showed that fresh Longsheng fruit contained higher total sugar, protein, and crude fat than fresh Yongfu fruit, whereas dried Yongfu fruit showed increased total sugar, dietary fiber, protein, ash, and crude fat, probably due to dehydration-induced concentration and processing-related compositional changes ( Liu et al., 2025 ). In particular, total dietary fiber increased from 34.97 g/100 g in fresh Yongfu fruit to 41.99 g/100 g in dried fruit, indicating the strong potential of S. grosvenorii as a fiber-rich functional food ingredient. Mineral analysis revealed that fresh Yongfu fruit contained particularly high levels of K, Mg, and Ca, reaching 13,656.5, 2254.25, and 1203.5 μg/g, respectively, which were 27.9%, 29.1%, and 23.9% higher than those in fresh Longsheng fruit.

Overall, S. grosvenorii is not merely a natural sweetener but rather a multifunctional food resource that combines low-calorie sweetness with dietary fiber, minerals, amino acids, and polysaccharides. The high-protein and low-fat characteristics of its pulp, together with the high dietary fiber content in dried fruits, provide a nutritional basis for its application in low-sugar, low-fat, and gut health-related foods. Meanwhile, the high sweetness and low-calorie characteristics conferred by mogrosides enable S. grosvenorii to partially replace sucrose and reduce the caloric burden of foods. However, existing studies have also demonstrated that the nutritional composition of S. grosvenorii is significantly influenced by cultivation region, plant part, processing method, and drying degree. Therefore, future studies should further integrate nutrigenomics, metabolomics, and food processing evaluation to establish standardized assessment systems for the nutritional quality and functional component stability of S. grosvenorii , thereby promoting its precise application in low-sugar foods, nutritional supplements, and special dietary products.

## Extraction and purification

### Extraction

Extraction is the primary step in SGPs research, and its efficiency and quality directly determine the reliability of subsequent structural characterization and bioactivity evaluation ( Wu et al., 2025 ). The selection of extraction methods for SGPs requires comprehensive consideration of raw material characteristics, target polysaccharide types, and intended applications, as different strategies exhibit significant differences in yield, structural preservation, and processing cost ( Wei et al., 2026 ). Currently, conventional methods for extracting SGPs include hot water extraction (HWE) and acid-alkali extraction. Moreover, emerging techniques such as enzyme-assisted extraction (EAE) and ultrasonic-assisted extraction (UAE) have demonstrated significant advantages in SGPs extraction. #### Hot water extraction

HWE, as the most classical and widely applied extraction method for the preparation of SGPs, possesses a solid application foundation in both laboratory research and industrial food processing due to its operational simplicity, low cost, and the absence of organic chemical reagents ( Khalil & Lukasiewicz, 2024 ). The core principle of this method is based on the enhanced permeability and solubilizing capacity of water molecules at elevated temperatures, which disrupts the cell wall structure of S. grosvenorii and facilitates the release of intracellular polysaccharides. The effectiveness of HWE for extracting SGPs has been well established, with typical extraction temperatures ranging from 70 to 100 °C, solid-to-liquid ratios ranging from 1:12 to 1:35 g/mL, single extraction times from 15 min to 6 h, extraction cycles of 2–3 times, and yields ranging from 0.5% to 18.48%. Notably, prolonging the extraction time can significantly increase the yield of SGPs, which may be attributed to enhanced cell wall swelling and more complete release of polysaccharide molecules ( Wang, Li, et al., 2023 ). Dujni et al. obtained polysaccharide fractions SGF1 (1.2%) and SGT2 (0.5%) from S. grosvenorii using HWE. Under the same extraction temperature (100 °C), the extraction time for SGF1 was 120 min, whereas that for SGT2 was 15 min ( Dujnič et al., 2021 ). However, excessively prolonged extraction may lead to the cleavage or degradation of polysaccharide chains, thereby affecting the overall yield. Under extraction conditions of 100 °C and 300 min, Lin obtained a yield of only 1.2% for the polysaccharide SGP-LH ( Lin et al., 2007 ). In addition, the effect of extraction temperature on polysaccharide yield exhibits a pronounced nonlinear pattern. Moderate increases in temperature can enhance the kinetic energy of water molecules, promoting hydrogen bond disruption and cell wall matrix disintegration. However, when the temperature exceeds the thermal stability threshold of polysaccharides, glycosidic bond hydrolysis accelerates, resulting in reduced Mw and destruction of active structural domains ( Wang et al., 2025 ). Li et al. achieved a polysaccharide yield of 18.48% from S. grosvenorii using HWE at an extraction temperature of 75 °C ( Li, Zheng, et al., 2025 ). Therefore, in practical applications, appropriate extraction conditions should be selected based on the characteristics of target polysaccharides, seeking an optimal balance between extraction temperature and time to maximize yield while preserving structural integrity. Moreover, HWE for extracting SGPs has certain limitations, mainly reflected in its limited ability to disrupt dense cell wall structures, resulting in low extraction efficiency for polysaccharides tightly bound to lignin and cellulose. Therefore, future studies should further optimize HWE by integrating mathematical models such as response surface methodology or artificial neural networks to establish parameter prediction systems under multifactor coupling conditions, thereby achieving simultaneous improvement in extraction efficiency and polysaccharide quality.

#### Acid-alkaline extraction

Polysaccharides are often tightly associated with impurities such as proteins, lignin, and minerals through hydrogen bonds, ionic bonds, or hydrophobic interactions, forming stable complex structures that are difficult to disrupt by HWE, thereby limiting the yield of target polysaccharides ( San Clemente & Jamet, 2022 ). Acid extraction (AE) or alkaline extraction (ALE) can alter the system pH by introducing acidic or basic media, thereby cleaving the linkages between SGPs and impurities, releasing encapsulated or bound polysaccharide fractions, and significantly enhancing extraction efficiency. Jiang et al. obtained polysaccharide fractions SGP-H, SGP-A, and SGP-B using HWE (240 min, 70 °C, 1:30), AE (240 min, 60 °C, 1,30), and ALE (240 min, 70 °C, 1,30), with yields of 1.97%, 3.25%, and 3.13%, respectively ( Jiang et al., 2026 ). It can be observed that polysaccharide yields obtained via acid-alkali extraction are significantly higher than those from HWE, demonstrating the clear advantage of acid-alkali treatment in disrupting polysaccharide-impurity complexes. Interestingly, the yield of SGP-A is higher than that of SGP-B, which may be attributed to the fact that under acidic conditions, hydrogen ions can more effectively protonate glycosidic bonds and carboxyl groups in polysaccharide molecules, weakening ionic interactions with impurities such as proteins, while promoting partial hydrolysis of cell wall components like hemicellulose, thereby releasing more bound polysaccharides. In addition, acidic conditions may induce swelling and depolymerization of pectic substances, further enhancing polysaccharide accessibility ( Iñiguez-Moreno et al., 2024 ). However, the intensity of acid-alkali conditions must be strictly controlled to avoid excessive degradation. Excessively low pH values or high reaction temperatures may induce severe glycosidic bond cleavage, generating large amounts of low-Mw oligosaccharides or even monosaccharides, which not only reduce polysaccharide yield but may also disrupt the native chain conformation and functional domains ( Kang & Chang, 2024 ). In addition, strong acid or alkali treatments may also affect the stability and processing compatibility of SGPs within food systems. On the other hand, the large amounts of wastewater and salt by-products generated during acid-alkali extraction can increase post-treatment costs and environmental burdens; therefore, the development of green and recyclable extraction systems is particularly important for the industrial food applications of SGPs. Future studies should further integrate green solvent systems, response surface optimization, and online pH regulation technologies to improve extraction efficiency while simultaneously considering structural preservation, functional stability, and sustainable processing requirements.

#### Ultrasound-assisted extraction

UAE utilizes cavitation effects, mechanical vibrations, and thermal effects generated during the propagation of ultrasound in a liquid medium to achieve efficient disruption of S. grosvenorii cell walls and enhanced dissolution of polysaccharides ( Li et al., 2023 ). As an emerging extraction technique, UAE demonstrates significant technical advantages in SGPs research, achieving high extraction efficiency within a short time while effectively reducing energy consumption and solvent usage. Zhu et al. extracted a polysaccharide fraction (SGP-P) from S. grosvenorii using UAE with an extraction time of 45 min, temperature of 55 °C, and a solid-to-liquid ratio of 1:45 g/mL, and the obtained polysaccharide exhibited good antioxidant activity ( Zhu et al., 2020 ). Compared with conventional HWE, UAE can significantly shorten extraction time while maintaining or even enhancing extraction efficiency. It is noteworthy that the selection of ultrasonic parameters has a significant impact on polysaccharide yield and quality. When ultrasonic power is too low, cavitation is insufficient, resulting in incomplete cell wall disruption and limited polysaccharide release. Conversely, excessive power or prolonged extraction time may cause mechanical and thermal degradation of polysaccharide chains, leading to broadened Mw distribution or destruction of bioactive structures ( Tang et al., 2023 ). Therefore, Li et al. optimized the UAE of SGPs using response surface methodology, employing a Box-Behnken design (BBD) to systematically investigate the interactive effects of ultrasonic power, extraction time, and temperature on polysaccharide yield, and identified the optimal conditions as 300 W ultrasonic power, 30 min extraction time, and 60 °C extraction temperature, under which the yield was maximized ( Li, Zheng, et al., 2025 ). In addition, the temperature of the UAE is typically maintained at a relatively low level (generally below 70 °C), which reduces the risk of degradation of thermosensitive polysaccharide components and helps preserve their natural biological activities. However, the large-scale application of the UAE still faces several challenges. Excessive ultrasonic power or prolonged treatment time may lead to overaccumulation of cavitation effects, triggering free radical chain reactions and resulting in oxidative degradation and loss of polysaccharide activity ( Wang, Xiong, & Huang, 2023 ). Moreover, the energy consumption cost of ultrasonic equipment remains disadvantageous compared with HWE, and the uniformity of the ultrasonic field in large-scale continuous production still requires improvement. Nevertheless, due to its green and efficient characteristics, the UAE has become an important direction for technological advancement in SGPs extraction, and future research should focus on systematic analysis of structure-activity relationships to achieve controllable optimization of the extraction process.

#### Enzyme-assisted extraction

EAE, as an innovative technique, offers a key advantage in utilizing the high specificity of enzymes and mild reaction conditions to selectively degrade cell wall components of S. grosvenorii , thereby significantly improving extraction efficiency while preserving polysaccharide structural integrity ( Bains et al., 2023 ; Gao et al., 2022 ). The extraction temperature for enzyme-assisted extraction of SGPs is typically maintained between 40 °C and 50 °C, which ensures enzymatic activity while preventing thermal degradation of polysaccharide structures. Under conditions of 240 min extraction time and 40 °C, Lin et al. obtained the polysaccharide SGP-LE using EAE, with a yield of 2.3% ( Lin et al., 2007 ). Compared with HWE, EAE operates at temperatures 40–60 °C lower, effectively suppressing Maillard and caramelization side reactions, resulting in polysaccharides with lower reducing sugar content, which is particularly important for their hypoglycemic activity ( Li et al., 2024 ). Furthermore, compared with acid-alkali extraction, EAE avoids random cleavage of glycosidic bonds caused by strong acids or bases, resulting in a more uniform Mw distribution and better preservation of characteristic structural domains such as uronic acid) content and specific glycosidic linkages. Jiang et al. reported that the UA content of polysaccharide SGP-E obtained from S. grosvenorii via EAE reached 23.61%, significantly higher than that of SGP-A (17.91%) obtained by AE, directly reflecting the unique advantage of EAE in preserving acidic polysaccharide structural features ( Jiang et al., 2026 ). However, the limitations of EAE mainly lie in the high cost of enzyme preparations and the requirement for precise control of pH and temperature during enzymatic hydrolysis, which increases process complexity and production cost. In addition, variations in cell wall composition among S. grosvenorii from different sources make it difficult for a single enzyme system to achieve complete degradation, rendering the selection and optimization of compound enzyme systems critical for improving extraction efficiency. At present, the synergistic application of cellulase, pectinase, and hemicellulose has shown promising results, but systematic studies on enzymatic hydrolysis kinetics and polysaccharide release mechanisms remain insufficient. Future studies should further integrate enzyme engineering, online process control, and green processing concepts to establish a more precise enzymatic extraction system for SGPs that is suitable for industrial food production.

#### Ultrasound-assisted aqueous two-phase extraction

Ultrasound-assisted aqueous two-phase extraction (UA-ATPE) is a novel extraction-separation method that integrates an ultrasonic physical field with an aqueous two-phase system, combining efficient extraction with preliminary purification ( Tan et al., 2022 ). The core advantage of this method lies in the synergistic enhancement between ultrasonic cavitation effects and the partitioning mechanism of the aqueous two-phase system ( Liu et al., 2023 ). It is noteworthy that the composition of the aqueous two-phase system plays a decisive role in polysaccharide partitioning behavior, with the type and concentration of phase-forming salts, the nature of the organic phase, and the phase ratio jointly regulating selective distribution between the two phases. title: Biomolecular coacervation-mediated materials: Phase states, phase transitions, and biomedical applications
abstract: Biomolecular coacervation is increasingly recognized as a phase-evolution process, including liquid-liquid phase separation (LLPS), resulting in metastable liquid-like states, and phase transitions that give rise to gel-like states or solid-like states. These coacervate phase states exhibit distinct structural, dynamic and mechanical characteristics, making biomolecular coacervation regulation a powerful design strategy to engineer biomaterials for a broad range of biomedical applications. # Biomolecular coacervation-mediated materials: Phase states, phase transitions, and biomedical applications

## Abstract
Biomolecular coacervation is increasingly recognized as a phase-evolution process, including liquid-liquid phase separation (LLPS), resulting in metastable liquid-like states, and phase transitions that give rise to gel-like states or solid-like states. These coacervate phase states exhibit distinct structural, dynamic and mechanical characteristics, making biomolecular coacervation regulation a powerful design strategy to engineer biomaterials for a broad range of biomedical applications. In this review, we first summarize the classification of LLPS and the typical molecular driving forces. We then discuss the phase evolution of coacervates, with particular emphasis on LLPS, liquid-to-gel and liquid-to-solid transitions, the characteristics of liquid-like, gel-like and solid-like states, and the intrinsic molecular and environmental factors that regulate these processes. Finally, we examine how distinct phase-state properties govern the biomedical functions of coacervation-mediated materials, with representative applications in drug delivery, bioreactors, bioinspired adhesion and tissue engineering scaffolds. Hopefully, this review could provide a unified framework for understanding coacervation-mediated materials as programmable biomolecular coacervate systems and for guiding their rational design in biomedical applications.

## Keywords
Biomolecular coacervation; Liquid-liquid phase separation; Phase transitions; Biomedical applications

## Introduction

Biomolecular coacervation regulation has emerged as a versatile strategy for engineering biomaterials with low interfacial tension, adaptive viscoelasticity, compartmentalization capability or programmable stimuli-responsive behaviors, which are highly attractive for a broad range of biomedical applications, including drug delivery, bioreactors, bioinspired adhesion and tissue engineering [ [1] , [2] , [3] , [4] ]. These unique material properties of coacervates are fundamentally rooted in their dynamic phase behaviors, whose conceptual understanding has evolved from early colloid chemistry to contemporary studies of biomolecular condensates in living systems. Fig. 1 presents a timeline of key breakthroughs in coacervate phase evolution and phase state, and the development of theoretical models underlying phase behavior. The concept of coacervation originated in colloid chemistry, where Bungenberg de Jong and Kruyt defined coacervates in 1929 as liquids that have partially lost free mobility while retaining intrinsic fluidity [ 5 ]. In 2009, the discovery of liquid-liquid phase separation (LLPS) of P granules in C. elegans sparked widespread interest in intracellular coacervation, known as biomolecular condensation in cell biology [ 6 ]. With the extensive research on intracellular coacervate systems, biomolecular coacervation is increasingly recognized as a phase-evolution process, including LLPS, resulting in metastable liquid-like states, and phase transitions—liquid-to-gel and liquid-to-solid—that give rise to gel-like states or solid-like states [ [7] , [8] , [9] , [10] , [11] , [12] ]. Similar phase-evolution pathways are also widely observed in extracellular systems, such as mussel byssus [ [13] , [14] , [15] ], sandcastle worm cement [ [16] , [17] , [18] ], elastin fibers [ [19] , [20] , [21] , [22] ] and spider silk [ [23] , [24] , [25] ], where biomolecular precursors first condense into fluid coacervate phases and subsequently undergo phase transitions into gel-like or solid-like states [ 1 , 23 , 26 , 27 ], highlighting biomolecular coacervation regulation as a powerful design strategy to engineer biomaterials for different functional requirements. Inspired by biological coacervate systems, researchers have developed biomaterials based on engineered recombinant proteins/polypeptides, chemically synthesized peptides/polypeptides, and chemically modified natural proteins for a wide range of biomedical applications [ 1 , 28 , 29 ]. Thus, there is a need to systematically organize current knowledge on biomolecular coacervate phase evolution and to elucidate how distinct phase state characteristics govern their biomedical functions. Fig. 1 Timeline of key breakthroughs in phase evolution and phase state, and the development of theoretical models.

In this review, we first summarize the classification of LLPS and the typical molecular driving forces. Next, we discuss coacervate phase evolution, including LLPS and phase transitions, the characteristics of liquid-like, gel-like and solid-like states, and regulation strategies for biomolecular coacervation. Finally, we discuss how these phase state characteristics inform the design and function of coacervation-mediated materials for biomedical applications, including drug delivery platforms, bioreactors, bioinspired adhesion and tissue engineering scaffolds. Scheme 1 provides an overview of the organizational framework of this review. The key terminology used in this review is summarized in Table 1 . Scheme 1 Biomolecular coacervation-mediated materials: phase states, phase transitions, and biomedical applications. Biomolecular coacervation initially forms liquid-like coacervates through LLPS, which may subsequently undergo liquid-to-gel or liquid-to-solid phase transitions to generate gel-like or solid-like states. These representative phase states provide distinct material characteristics that can be exploited for different biomedical applications, including drug delivery platforms, bioreactors, bioinspired adhesion, and tissue engineering scaffolds. ## Classification of LLPS and molecular driving forces

### Classification of LLPS

LLPS can be broadly classified into three types: segregative, associative (complex coacervation), and simple coacervation ( Fig. 2 ) [ 3 ]. In segregative phase separation, mutual incompatibility or repulsion between different soluble species drives their partition into distinct phases, with each phase enriched in one component. Associative phase separation, commonly referred to as complex coacervation, arises from attractive interactions between chemically distinct macromolecules, most notably oppositely charged polyelectrolytes. Its thermodynamic driving force mainly originates from the entropy gain associated with counterion release, making the process highly sensitive to ionic strength, ion identity, pH, and charge stoichiometry. Simple coacervation, by contrast, involves the self-concentration of a single molecular species. This process is frequently observed in proteins with disordered regions, driven by multiple weak forces, such as hydrophobic effects, aromatic stacking and hydrogen bonding. ### Molecular driving forces of LLPS

LLPS is governed by the synergy and competition of multiple weak interactions, representing a delicate balance between entropic and enthalpic contributions ( Fig. 2 B). Electrostatic interactions are the primary driving force for complex coacervation and are highly responsive to pH and ionic strength. For example, pH-induced deprotonation of lysine residues in mussel foot protein Mfp-5 reduces intramolecular electrostatic repulsion and promotes liquid-to-gel transitions for underwater bonding [ 40 , 41 ]. Hydrogen bonding, particularly dynamic networks involving Dopa residues, enhances coacervate stability under high-salt or extreme pH conditions [ 42 ]. Synthetic peptides have been engineered with Tyr residues that are enzymatically converted to Dopa to strengthen coacervate stability [ 40 , 43 ]. Hydrophobic interactions, driven by the entropy gain from releasing ordered water molecules [ 44 ], mediate both functional assembly (e.g., tropoelastin) and pathological aggregation (e.g., FUS and TDP-43), wherein hydrophobic patch enrichment in the dense phase promotes nucleation and amyloid fibril formation [ 11 , 45 ]. In addition, cation-π interactions, particularly Arg-Tyr interactions [ [46] , [47] , [48] , [49] ], together with π-π stacking between aromatic amino acids [ 50 , 51 ], further enhance intermolecular cohesion and coacervate stability.

## Coacervate phase evolution and phase states

Biomolecular coacervation is a non-equilibrium kinetic process, which can continue to evolve, thereby exhibiting distinct phase states ( Fig. 3 A). In this section, representative examples are mainly derived from intracellular protein coacervates, particularly those formed by intrinsically disordered proteins (IDPs), as these systems provide well-established experimental models that link LLPS with subsequent phase transitions within a unified mechanistic framework. It is worth noting that some ECM proteins (e.g., collagen, elastin) and secreted adhesive systems (e.g., mussel foot proteins, sandcastle worm cement) can undergo a similar evolution process; however, due to limited characterization of phase behavior, molecular dynamics, and intermediate states [ 1 ], there are not discussed in detail in this session. Here, we systematically outline a widely observed coacervate phase evolution, with a particular focus on coacervate phase characteristics. Fig. 3 Biomolecular coacervate phase evolution. (A) Biomolecular coacervation is a non-equilibrium phase-evolution process driven by multiple weak intermolecular interactions and regulated by intrinsic composition and environmental factors. (B) Typical coacervate phase evolution pathways: from LLPS to liquid-to-gel or liquid-to-solid phase transitions.

### Coacervate phase evolution: LLPS and phase transitions

The phase evolution typically begins with LLPS-driven formation of a metastable liquid-like, which may subsequently evolve along two distinct pathways into either a gel-like state or a solid-like state ( Fig. 3 B) [ [7] , [8] , [9] , 52 , 53 ].

LLPS . Under specific environmental conditions (e.g., pH, temperature, ionic strength), a homogeneous solution spontaneously separates into two or more liquid-phase regions with different molecular concentrations, driven by the multiple weak non-covalent interactions (e.g., electrostatic forces, hydrogen bonding, hydrophobic interactions) [ 54 ]. From the principle of energy minimization, LLPS of biomolecules is generally achieved via two processes: the enthalpic contribution from intermolecular interactions and the entropic driving force arising from the rearrangement of ions and water molecules. The former reduces the system enthalpy via the formation of noncovalent interactions; the latter significantly increases the system entropy due to the release and increased freedom of solvent molecules after phase separation. Together, these enthalpic and entropic contributions lower the total Gibbs free energy of the system, leading to the spontaneous formation of microdroplets enriched with biomolecules [ 55 ]. It should be noted that if the effective attractive interactions between molecules are too weak to overcome the loss of mixing entropy, phase separation will not occur. The initially formed enriched phase typically manifests as dispersed, micrometer-scale spherical droplets containing highly concentrated biomolecules, yet remaining in a metastable state [ 56 ].

The microdroplet system formed via LLPS possesses high interfacial energy and spontaneously undergoes coarsening via two primary pathways to reduce the total free energy of the system: 1) Ostwald ripening. Driven by the Gibbs-Thomson effect, smaller droplets have higher solubility owing to their greater surface curvature. Molecules from smaller droplets dissolve into the continuous phase and diffuse to deposit onto the surface of larger droplets, leading to “the larger grow at the expense of the smaller” [ 55 ]. 2) Coalescence. Droplets collide via Brownian motion. Upon contact, their interfaces fuse, merging into a single larger droplet [ 57 ]. Both processes increase the average droplet size while reducing their number. Environmental perturbations (e.g., shear, centrifugation) or changes in solution conditions (e.g., salt concentration, pH, temperature, macromolecular crowding) can significantly affect coarsening kinetics [ [58] , [59] , [60] ]. Upon reaching a certain size, microdroplets may undergo sedimentation, leading to the macroscopically separated continuous dense and dilute phases. These microscopic droplets, irrespective of whether they subsequently undergo macroscopic phase separation to form a continuous dense phase, are uniformly referred to as “liquid-like coacervates” in this context, emphasizing their initial LLPS-mediated states with liquid characteristics.

Phase transitions. Over time or under changes in environmental conditions, the condensed liquid phase undergoes changes in phase state, primarily following two pathways: 1) Liquid-to-gel transition. Liquid-like coacervates undergo a phase-state transition into a kinetically arrested gel-like state, typically characterized by the formation of a percolated network, also described as gelation in some cases [ 61 ]. The amorphous, gel-like characteristics of postsynaptic density arise from such a percolated network [ 62 ]. Many IDPs (e.g., FUS [ 63 ], hnRNPA2 [ 64 ]) with low-complexity domains (LCDs) exhibit a reversible liquid-to-gel transition in vitro, which is tuned by the sticker-spacer architecture (e.g., valence and patterning of interaction motifs) [ [65] , [66] , [67] ]. Engineered biomaterials exploit the same architectural principles—combining associative stickers (e.g., aromatic, charged residues) with solvated spacers—to achieve programmable liquid-to-gel transitions [ 68 , 69 ]. 2) Liquid-to-solid transition. Liquid-like coacervates undergo a phase-state transition into a thermodynamic end-state or a kinetically arrested solid-like state depending on the specific coacervate system, typically characterized by the formation of amyloid or amyloid-like fibrils enriched in β-sheet, also described as aging in some cases [ 11 ]. The process is commonly observed in pathological proteins associated with neurodegenerative diseases, many of which are intrinsically disordered (e.g., α-synuclein [ 70 ], TDP-43 [ 71 ], hnRNPA1 [ 72 , 73 ]). Analogous transitions could be engineered by fusing the LCDs of neurodegenerative disease-associated proteins with functional modules and introducing external triggers (e.g., temperature) to program the transition kinetics [ 74 ]. During this progression, LLPS-derived microdroplets could function as critical “pre-aggregates”: on one hand, they drastically increase the local concentration of proteins within the coacervate, promoting sustained intermolecular contact; on the other hand, the droplet interface provides a unique surface environment that can significantly lower the nucleation barrier, thereby accelerating the nucleation and elongation of amyloid fibrils [ 73 , 75 ].

In summary, the coacervate phase evolution primarily yields three distinct coacervate phase states: liquid-like, gel-like, and solid-like. These phase states should be viewed as representative characteristic states along the coacervate phase evolution rather than rigidly separated categories, and individual coacervate systems may exhibit features of multiple phase states simultaneously [ [75] , [76] , [77] ]. A thorough understanding of the distinct characteristics of these phase states, together with precise control over coacervate phase evolution, is essential for engineering functional coacervation-mediated materials with programmable properties.

### Coacervate phase states: liquid-like, gel-like and solid-like

Here, we will seek to summarize the characteristics of the liquid-like, gel-like and solid-like states. Notably, these designations are used to describe coacervates that resemble liquids, gels, or solids, respectively, in certain material properties, under specific experimental conditions and observation timescales, rather than implying a particular structural organization or thermodynamic identity [ 78 , 79 ]. Fig. 4 provides schematic relative comparisons of these states along a temporal evolution pathway, thereby highlighting differences in interaction networks, molecular dynamics, and mechanical properties. To assign one or more appropriate phase-state designations to a coacervate, multiple complementary measurements—such as molecular dynamics, mechanical properties, structural characterizations—should be considered rather than relying on any single experimental result. Moreover, given the diversity of coacervate systems and the complexity of coacervation conditions, the summarized phase state characteristics may not encompass all the coacervate behaviors. Quantitative characterization of coacervate phase states varies considerably across different material systems, making it difficult to establish unified thresholds that distinguish liquid-, gel-, and solid-like states. Accordingly, these characteristics should be interpreted through relative comparisons within the same material system and under comparable experimental conditions. To provide experimental references, quantitative data for different phase states from several representative coacervate systems are compiled in Table 2 . Fig. 4 Schematic relative comparisons of liquid-like, gel-like, and solid-like states along a temporal evolution pathway. Liquid-like coacervates are dominated by transient interaction networks and exhibit high molecular mobility, as evidenced by rapid fluorescence recovery after photobleaching (FRAP), together with loss-dominant viscoelastic behavior (G″ > G′) over the entire frequency range. Gel-like coacervates are characterized by a system-spanning (percolated) physical network formed by longer-lived intermolecular interactions. They exhibit reduced but retained molecular mobility, reflected by slow and incomplete FRAP recovery, and frequency-dependent mechanical responses, with G″ > G′ at low frequencies but G′ > G″ at high frequencies. Solid-like coacervates are stabilized by persistent interaction networks, resulting in negligible molecular mobility with little or no FRAP recovery and G′ ≫ G″ over the entire frequency range.
