Liquid-like states are described as dense liquid phases formed via LLPS, in which biomolecules interact via weak, transient connections, thereby exhibiting high molecular dynamics [ 7 , 8 , 83 , 84 ]. Several characteristics are summarized here: 1) Highly internal dynamics. Components within liquid-like coacervates exhibit rapid diffusion and exchange, commonly quantified by fluorescence recovery after photobleaching (FRAP), with recovery times within tens of seconds. For example, approximately 80% fluorescence recovery was observed within ∼70 s for hnRNPA1 droplets [ 72 ], and diffusion coefficients of 1-4 μm 2 /s were reported for FUS(LC) liquid coacervates [ 75 ]. 2) Low interfacial tension. The interfacial tension between a liquid-like coacervate and its surrounding dilute phase is relatively low, with a typical reported range of 1-1000 μN/m [ 85 , 86 ]. As a result, droplets adopt spherical shapes with compartmentalization capability (a consequence of interfacial energy minimization) and rapidly fuse within seconds upon contact. Low interfacial tension also facilitates wetting and spreading on diverse surfaces. 3) Viscosity. The viscosity of liquid-like coacervates spans a wide range depending on multiple factors (e.g., molecular composition, chain length, environmental conditions). For liquid-like coacervates based on synthetic polyelectrolytes, viscosity can span approximately 0.1-1000 Pa s [ 85 , 87 , 88 ], while biomolecular coacervates show comparable diversity. With 25 base pairs (bp) of DNA linkers, the zero-shear viscosity of 25-bp chromatin coacervates in liquid state was approximately 40 times that of 30-bp chromatin coacervates [ 89 ]. The viscosity of wild-type liquid-phase FUS(LC) coacervates was 0.4 Pa s, whereas that of the liquid-phase mutant FUS(LC) coacervates ranged from 13 to 40 Pa s [ 75 ].

Collectively, these characteristics define the engineering value of the liquid-like state. For example, high molecular mobility facilitates molecular transport, while low interfacial tension and viscosity enable efficient wetting and conformal contact with complex biological surfaces.

Gel-like states represent states formed by liquid-to-gel transitions, in which biomolecules give rise to a system-spanning (percolated) network, thereby placing the biomolecules in a kinetically constrained state, whereas a certain degree of molecular rearrangement and dynamics is retained [ 61 , 62 , 90 , 91 ]. Several characteristics are summarized here: 1) Constrained molecular dynamics. Biomolecular mobility is severely constrained by the percolated molecular network of gel-like coacervates. This behavior is typically manifested by slow and incomplete FRAP, along with a pronounced reduction in diffusion coefficients. For example, reconstructed PSD coacervates in a gel-like state exhibited markedly reduced fluorescence recovery (<20% within 10 min) relative to their liquid-like counterparts (∼100% recovery within 300 s) [ 62 ]. Likewise, Murakami et al. [ 75 ] showed that FUS(LC) coacervates underwent a drastic reduction in diffusion coefficients from ∼1 to 4 μm 2 /s (liquid-like) to ≪ 1 μm 2 /s (gel-like), reflecting a transition from rapid molecular exchange to kinetically trapped dynamics. 2) Elasticity-dominated viscoelasticity. Liu et al. [ 92 ] demonstrated that enzymatic cross-linking within DEAE-Dex/Ty-Su-Dex coacervate shifted their viscoelasticity behavior from viscosity-dominated (G″ > G′, liquid-like) to elasticity-dominated (G′ > G″, gel-like), accompanied by a 14-fold increase in viscosity to 1.4 Pa s and a drastic reduction in the diffusion coefficient from 0.046 to 0.0033 μm 2 s −1 , indicating a more elastic but less dynamic network.

In summary, gel-like coacervates occupy an intermediate state typically characterized by a percolated network that restricts molecular mobility while imparting elasticity-dominated viscoelasticity, which enable engineered coacervate biomaterials to balance mechanical support with dynamic adaptability.

Solid-like states are described as assemblies formed through liquid-to-solid transitions in which biomolecules interact via persistent connections, leading to severely reduced or lost molecular mobility [ 8 , 12 , 93 ]. Several characteristics are discussed here: 1) Highly ordered or densely packed architectures. The structural basis of solid-like coacervates commonly lies in the formation of amyloid fibrils or amyloid-like protofibrillar assemblies [ 45 , 94 , 95 ]. Importantly, the distinction between “amyloid” and “amyloid-like” reflects a continuum of structural order and thermodynamic stability rather than a strict binary classification. In practice, their assignment should be based on the convergence of complementary structural and biochemical evidence rather than any single measurement or universal quantitative threshold, with the interpretation remaining context-dependent. In mature amyloid fibrils, β-strands align perpendicular to the fibril axis to form cross-β sheet architectures stabilized by extensive and repetitive intermolecular hydrogen-bond networks [ 96 ]. LLPS-derived condensed microenvironments facilitate this process by increasing local concentration and lowering nucleation barriers [ 45 , 97 ]. However, liquid-to-solid transitions do not always culminate in the formation of structurally well-ordered, mature amyloid fibrils [ [98] , [99] , [100] ]. When monomers form only small, soluble, and freely diffusing oligomers, secondary nucleation is suppressed, resulting instead in shorter, more curved, and structurally disordered protofibrils [ 45 ]. Structural studies of LCD-derived segments revealed kinked β-sheets that stack into protofibrillar networks stabilized by interactions between polar atoms and aromatic side chains, distinct from the steric zippers of classical amyloid fibrils [ 101 ]. These differences in structural organization give rise to distinct energetic stability and reversibility. Highly ordered cross-β fibrils generally occupy deeper energy minima and therefore exhibit greater structural stability with limited reversibility, whereas less ordered protofibrillar assemblies are typically kinetically stabilized and may remain partially reversible under appropriate physicochemical conditions. Nevertheless, both mature amyloid fibrils and protofibrils are enriched in β-sheet structures, facilitating the formation of persistent intermolecular networks [ 102 , 103 ]. Moreover, experimental measurements and molecular dynamics simulations reveal that the elastic modulus of these β-sheet-rich structures—including mature fibrils and protofibrils—ranges from 10 7 Pa to 10 10 Pa [ 102 , 104 , 105 ]. 2) Severely reduced or lost molecular dynamics. Kang et al. [ 106 ] showed that aging catalytic coacervates underwent a progressive liquid-to-solid transition accompanied by a dramatic loss of internal mobility: freshly formed coacervates (h0) were highly dynamic, as manifested by a FRAP recovery half-time of 0.5 s, an apparent diffusion coefficient of 1.04 μm 2 /s, and an immobile fraction of only 28.8%, whereas aged coacervates (h8) showed no observable fluorescence recovery, a diffusion coefficient approaching 0 μm 2 /s and an immobile fraction of 97.4%, indicating a dynamically arrested solid-like state. title: Recent Advances in Pathogenesis, Diagnosis and Integrated Traditional Chinese Medicine Therapy for Plasma Cell Mastitis
abstract: Plasma cell mastitis (PCM) is a predominant form of non-lactational mastitis with an increasing incidence worldwide. The condition is characterized by a complex pathogenesis, difficulties in differential diagnosis, and a high rate of recurrence, thereby presenting significant challenges in clinical management. Conventional Western medicine is limited by high postoperative recurrence, difficulty in distinguishing PCM from breast cancer, and unsatisfactory long-term efficacy of single anti-inflammatory or hormone therapy. Against these clinical bottlenecks, Traditional Chinese medicine (TCM) shows unique advantages and accumulated extensive clinical experience for the treatment of PCM. This review systematically delineates the epidemiological characteristics and key pathophysiological mechanisms, including activation of the IL-6/STAT3 signaling pathway, immune cell dysregulation, autoimmune responses, distinctive plasma cell infiltration, and diagnostic methodologies such as imaging techniques, histopathological examination as the diagnostic gold standard, and emerging biomarkers. In addition, the theoretical foundations, contemporary pharmacological mechanisms, and clinical applications of comprehensive TCM therapy for PCM are summarized. Evidence indicates that TCM interventions, guided by syndrome differentiation and targeting liver qi stagnation, phlegm-stasis congealing, and heat-toxin accumulation, exert therapeutic effects by modulating inflammatory signaling pathways, correcting immune dysfunction, and restoring the mammary gland microecological balance. Clinical trials have demonstrated that combining TCM with surgical procedures or western medical treatments significantly improves clinical outcomes, reduces inflammatory mediator levels, and lowers recurrence rates. However, there remains a need for standardization in TCM syndrome differentiation, therapeutic evaluation criteria, and high-quality randomized controlled trials. In summary, integrated TCM therapy constitutes a safe and effective approach for managing PCM, and further rigorous research is warranted to enhance its clinical application and facilitate international recognition of TCM in PCM treatment.

## Abstract
Plasma cell mastitis (PCM) is a predominant form of non-lactational mastitis with an increasing incidence worldwide. The condition is characterized by a complex pathogenesis, difficulties in differential diagnosis, and a high rate of recurrence, thereby presenting significant challenges in clinical management. Conventional Western medicine is limited by high postoperative recurrence, difficulty in distinguishing PCM from breast cancer, and unsatisfactory long-term efficacy of single anti-inflammatory or hormone therapy. Against these clinical bottlenecks, Traditional Chinese medicine (TCM) shows unique advantages and accumulated extensive clinical experience for the treatment of PCM. This review systematically delineates the epidemiological characteristics and key pathophysiological mechanisms, including activation of the IL-6/STAT3 signaling pathway, immune cell dysregulation, autoimmune responses, distinctive plasma cell infiltration, and diagnostic methodologies such as imaging techniques, histopathological examination as the diagnostic gold standard, and emerging biomarkers. In addition, the theoretical foundations, contemporary pharmacological mechanisms, and clinical applications of comprehensive TCM therapy for PCM are summarized. Evidence indicates that TCM interventions, guided by syndrome differentiation and targeting liver qi stagnation, phlegm-stasis congealing, and heat-toxin accumulation, exert therapeutic effects by modulating inflammatory signaling pathways, correcting immune dysfunction, and restoring the mammary gland microecological balance. Clinical trials have demonstrated that combining TCM with surgical procedures or western medical treatments significantly improves clinical outcomes, reduces inflammatory mediator levels, and lowers recurrence rates. However, there remains a need for standardization in TCM syndrome differentiation, therapeutic evaluation criteria, and high-quality randomized controlled trials. In summary, integrated TCM therapy constitutes a safe and effective approach for managing PCM, and further rigorous research is warranted to enhance its clinical application and facilitate international recognition of TCM in PCM treatment.

plasma cell mastitis; traditional Chinese medicine; immune pathogenesis; IL-6/STAT3 signaling pathway; integrated therapy

## Introduction

The investigative history of plasma cell mastitis (PCM) dates back to the early twentieth century. However, a comprehensive understanding of its etiology and pathogenesis has evolved gradually over an extended period. Earlier research posited that PCM represents a form of mammary ductal ectasia characterized by ductal dilation accompanied by plasma cell infiltration. 1 In the 1980s, the advent of immunohistochemical methodologies enabled researchers to detect elevated expression levels of inflammatory mediators such as interleukin-6 (IL-6) and signal transducer and activator of transcription 3 (STAT3) within the breast tissue of patients with PCM, implicating immune mechanisms in its pathophysiology. 2 Since the onset of the twenty-first century, advancements in molecular biology and omics technologies have further propelled PCM research, exemplified by the identification of novel transcripts through nanopore sequencing 3 and the investigation of alterations in breast microecology via metabolomic analyses. 4

Therapeutic approaches for PCM have evolved from surgical interventions to more integrative treatment modalities. Initial surgical management primarily involves lesion excision, which is associated with a high recurrence rate. 5 Post-2010, the integration of innovative surgical techniques—such as lesion-based duct resection (LBDR) and nipple correction—with pharmacological therapies, including biological agents and traditional Chinese medicine (TCM), has markedly decreased recurrence rates. 5 , 6 Furthermore, advancements in diagnostic imaging technologies, including superb microvascular imaging (SMI) and magnetic resonance imaging (MRI), have enhanced the precision of differential diagnosis between PCM and breast carcinoma. 7 , 8

Conventional Western medicine encounters prominent bottlenecks in PCM management. As PCM is categorized as a non-bacterial inflammatory disorder, empirical antibiotic treatment achieves limited efficacy and easily triggers bacterial drug resistance. 9 Although immunosuppressants and biological agents can control acute inflammatory responses, they bring obvious adverse reactions, high economic costs, and frequent disease relapse after drug withdrawal. 10 Radical surgical resection can relieve severe lesions yet tends to cause irreversible breast contour deformation and severe psychological distress for patients. 11 PCM features a protracted clinical course and recurrent episodes, often leading to permanent breast disfigurement, anxiety, depression and other mental disorders, which severely impair patients’ physical and mental health and quality of life. 11 There is an urgent clinical demand for a safe and refined therapeutic strategy that achieves disease control while preserving breast morphology.

Within this comprehensive treatment framework, TCM has emerged as a significant component supported by extensive clinical experience and demonstrable therapeutic efficacy. Against the above-mentioned clinical predicaments of Western monotherapy, this review firstly systematically sorts out the epidemiological features, pathological mechanisms and multi-dimensional diagnostic systems of PCM. Afterwards, it elaborates the theoretical connotation, pharmacological mechanism and practical application of TCM comprehensive therapy for PCM. Finally, the limitations of current TCM research and prospective research directions are summarized to provide theoretical reference for standardized integrated Chinese and Western medicine treatment of PCM (see Figure 1 ). ## Epidemiology

PCM, the predominant subtype of non-lactational mastitis (NPM), has exhibited a marked increase in global incidence. However, the absence of standardized diagnostic criteria and comprehensive large-scale epidemiological investigations has resulted in variability in the reported data. The literature indicates that PCM constitutes approximately 1.4% to 5.6% of benign breast diseases, with a notable increase in reported cases in Asian countries, including China and Japan. 12 , 13 A retrospective analysis involving 1,260 pathologically confirmed PCM patients in Chongqing, China, revealed a median patient age of 31 years; 92.8% had a history of childbirth, 67.6% had breastfed for six months or longer, and 44.9% developed the condition within three years postpartum. 12 The study further identified that over 60% of cases occurred in the 30–39-year age group, implicating reproductive and lactational history as significant risk factors. Additionally, socioeconomic determinants, such as psychological stress, reported in 20.5% of patients, and lifestyle modifications may indirectly influence PCM pathogenesis by modulating immune function. 12

Although global prevalence data remain limited, several investigations have suggested that environmental influences, shifts in reproductive behaviors, and advancements in diagnostic methodologies contribute to the rising incidence of PCM. For instance, activation of the IL-6/STAT3 signaling pathway is prevalent among patients with PCM, with the extent of pathway activation correlating with clinical manifestations such as nipple inversion. 2 This association not only elucidates potential pathogenic mechanisms but also underscores the role of inflammation-related pathways as a biological basis for increasing the incidence of PCM. 2 Moreover, the overall escalation in NPM cases, encompassing PCM and granulomatous lobular mastitis, accentuates the clinical significance of PCM as the principal NPM subtype. 13 Future studies should prioritize multicenter, large-sample epidemiological studies to delineate the global distribution and temporal trends of PCM.

The epidemiological characteristics of PCM vary considerably across populations, particularly age, sex, reproductive history, and clinical presentation. Predominantly affecting non-lactating women of reproductive age, PCM exhibits a median onset age of 31 years, with the highest incidence observed in individuals aged 30–39 years. 12 The aforementioned study of 1,260 patients demonstrated that 92.8% had experienced childbirth, 67.6% had breastfed for over six months, and 44.9% developed PCM within three years postpartum, suggesting that ductal injury during childbirth and lactation may be a critical etiological factor. 12 Clinically, PCM lesions predominantly localize to the central areola (78.9%), present as breast masses in 92.5% of cases (median size 6.8 cm), and exhibit a low bacterial culture positivity rate of 17.2%, reinforcing the nonbacterial inflammatory nature of the disease. 12

Regarding sex differences, PCM is infrequent in males; however, reported cases often involve comorbidities such as obesity (body mass index [BMI] ≥ 30 kg/m 2 ) and nipple inversion. 14 , 15 For example, a 55-year-old male patient presented with a left subareolar mass classified as BI-RADS 4C/5 on imaging and was pathologically confirmed to have PCM characterized by plasma cell infiltration. 14 This case highlights the necessity of differential diagnosis to exclude breast carcinoma in male PCM and suggests that obesity may contribute to disease pathogenesis via aberrant estrogen metabolism and hypoxia-induced inflammatory processes. 15 Ethnic variations in PCM distribution remain inadequately characterized, with existing studies predominantly focusing on Asian cohorts. Thus, cross-ethnic investigations are warranted to elucidate potential genetic and environmental determinants.

Variations in clinical severity and recurrence risk further reflect the population heterogeneity. Notably, patients exhibiting nipple inversion demonstrated a significantly elevated risk of PCM recurrence compared to those without this feature. Innovative nipple correction techniques, such as single suture or half-pocket suture methods, have been shown to reduce the recurrence risk by 63.7%, 6 indicating that nipple morphology may serve as a prognostic indicator and should be a focal point in clinical management. 16

The multifactorial risk profile of PCM includes nipple inversion, recent breast trauma, and parity as independent risk factors. A case-control study involving 82 patients with PCM and matched controls identified these variables as significant contributors to disease development. 17 , 18 Nipple inversion may facilitate inflammation through ductal obstruction, secretion retention, and bacterial colonization despite low culture positivity, whereas recent trauma may compromise ductal integrity and trigger immune responses. 17 , 18 Additional potential risk factors include obesity (BMI ≥ 25 kg/m 2 ), which may potentiate immune activation via adipose-derived inflammatory mediators, such as IL-6, and prolonged lactation, which can induce ductal dilation and secretion stasis. 12

Preventive strategies should prioritize early interventions in high-risk populations. For individuals with nipple inversion, corrective procedures during puberty or before pregnancy are recommended to mitigate ductal obstruction risk. 6 The efficacy of novel nipple correction techniques in reducing PCM recurrence underscores the importance of timely intervention. 6 Furthermore, lifestyle modifications aimed at minimizing breast trauma, maintaining hygiene, and alleviating psychological stress, reported in 20.5% of patients, may contribute to morbidity reduction. 12 Enhanced breast examination protocols and health education targeting postpartum women, particularly within three years of delivery, are essential for early symptom recognition, including mass formation and nipple discharge. 12 Prospective interventional studies are necessary to validate these preventive measures and develop biomarker-based risk prediction models incorporating indicators such as IL-6 and intercellular adhesion molecule-1 (ICAM-1) to facilitate precision prevention. 2 , 19 , 20

## Pathophysiological Mechanisms

### Immunopathological Mechanism

The immunopathological mechanisms underlying PCM are intricate and involve a coordinated interplay between the innate and adaptive immune responses. Central to this process is the activation of the IL-6/STAT3 signaling pathway and dysregulation of the complement system. Empirical evidence indicates significant upregulation of IL-6 expression in the breast tissue of PCM patients, which correlates positively with phosphorylated STAT3 (p-STAT3) levels. 2 IL-6, a pivotal pro-inflammatory cytokine, not only facilitates the differentiation and survival of plasma cells but also promotes immune cell infiltration through STAT3 pathway activation, thereby establishing a chronic inflammatory microenvironment. 10 , 19 Concurrently, complement system activation, characterized by elevated expression of C3, C5, and their respective receptors, plays a critical role in PCM-associated inflammation. Notably, the membrane attack complex (C5b-9) predominantly localizes to the membranes of mammary ductal epithelial cells, where it exacerbates inflammation by inducing epithelial cell injury and apoptosis. 21

An additional hallmark of PCM immunopathology is dysregulation of immune cell populations. Studies have demonstrated an increased prevalence of M1 macrophages and T helper 17 (Th17) cells within PCM breast tissue, along with a reduction in M2 macrophages and regulatory T (Treg) cells, collectively fostering a proinflammatory milieu. 10 For instance, IL-17 secreted by Th17 cells activates the nuclear factor kappa-light-chain-enhancer of activated B cell (NF-κB) pathway, thereby enhancing the secretion of inflammatory mediators such as IL-6 and tumor necrosis factor-alpha (TNF-α), which further intensifies the inflammatory response. 10 Moreover, the epithelial-mesenchymal transition (EMT) is instrumental in the fibrotic progression of PCM. The IL-6/JAK/STAT3 axis promotes the transdifferentiation of ductal epithelial cells into mesenchymal phenotypes by upregulating EMT-associated transcription factors, including Snail and TWIST, culminating in fibrosis and structural disruption of the breast tissue. 22 Additionally, exosomes serve as vectors for intercellular communication by transporting chemokines such as CXCL12, which facilitates M1 macrophage polarization and the propagation of inflammation, thereby establishing a self-perpetuating inflammatory cycle. 22

Elucidation of these immunopathological pathways offers promising therapeutic targets for PCM management. Pharmacological agents such as IL-6 inhibitors (eg, tocilizumab) or STAT3 inhibitors may mitigate clinical manifestations by interrupting key inflammatory signaling cascades, whereas complement inhibitors (eg, C5a receptor antagonists) have the potential to reduce epithelial cell damage. 2 , 21 Future research should focus on delineating the interactions among immune cell subsets and spatiotemporal dynamics of signaling pathways to inform the development of more precise immunomodulatory interventions.

### Characteristics of Plasma Cell Infiltration in Breast Tissue

Plasma cell infiltration is a key pathological characteristic of PCM, and its distribution pattern, phenotypic profile, and functional attributes are closely linked to disease progression. In PCM, plasma cells are predominantly localized around dilated mammary ducts, exhibiting either diffuse or focal infiltration, often accompanied by inflammatory cells, such as lymphocytes and macrophages. 2 , 12 Immunohistochemical analyses have demonstrated that plasma cells in PCM express high levels of CD138, a recognized plasma cell marker, and are associated with activation of the IL-6/STAT3 signaling pathway, with 93.3% of cells testing positive for IL-6. 2 , 23 For instance, in a murine model of PCM, administration of IL-6 induced infiltration of CD138-positive plasma cells within breast tissue, whereas treatment with the JAK inhibitor AG-490 significantly diminished plasma cell numbers, 23 indicating that the IL-6/STAT3 pathway serves as a critical regulator of plasma cell infiltration.

Furthermore, the phenotypic characteristics of plasma cells are correlated with the clinical manifestations of PCM. Notably, IL-6 expression is significantly elevated in PCM patients presenting with inverted nipples compared to those without inversion, concomitant with more pronounced plasma cell infiltration. 2 This finding suggests that nipple morphology may influence plasma cell infiltration by modulating the levels of inflammatory cytokines. Additionally, plasma cells in PCM may secrete autoantibodies, such as anti-ductal epithelial antibodies, which potentially contribute to autoimmune processes. 10 For example, mammary inflammation associated with Sjögren’s syndrome exhibits a plasma cell infiltration pattern analogous to that observed in PCM, characterized by the absence of IgG4-positive plasma cells, implying a shared immunopathological mechanism between these conditions. 24

The functional implications of plasma cell infiltration in PCM warrant further investigation. Current evidence indicates that inflammatory cytokines secreted by plasma cells, including IL-6 and TNF-α, exacerbate ductal epithelial damage and fibrosis, whereas antibodies produced by these cells may participate in immune-mediated clearance of ductal secretions. 2 , 22 Future research employing single-cell sequencing technologies to analyze the clonal diversity and functional status of plasma cells in PCM is essential to elucidate their precise roles in disease pathogenesis and progression.

### Autoimmunity

The autoimmune mechanisms underlying PCM have garnered increasing scholarly interest, with current research supporting the classification of PCM as an autoimmune disorder. First, autoantibodies, including anti-ductal epithelial antibodies, have been identified in the breast tissue of PCM patients. Additionally, an imbalance in immune cell populations, notably an elevated Th17/Treg ratio, aligns with the immunological profiles characteristic of autoimmune diseases. 10 For instance, interleukin-17 (IL-17) secreted by Th17 cells in PCM-affected breast tissues can activate the NF-κB signaling pathway, thereby promoting the secretion of pro-inflammatory mediators. Concurrently, functional impairments in regulatory T (Treg) cells may contribute to the disruption of immune tolerance. 10 Second, activation of the complement system, as evidenced by increased levels of components C3 and C5, may facilitate autoimmune responses through immune complex formation. Elevated concentrations of C3a and C5a have been observed in the breast tissue of patients with PCM, where they mediate inflammatory cell infiltration and epithelial damage via receptor-mediated mechanisms.

The autoimmune hypothesis was further substantiated by clinical correlations observed in PCM. For example, patients presenting with inverted nipples tend to exhibit higher titers of autoantibodies and more pronounced inflammatory responses, 2 suggesting that ductal obstruction may trigger immune activation by exposing autoantigens such as proteins present in ductal secretions. Moreover, the frequent comorbidity of PCM with other autoimmune conditions, including Sjögren’s syndrome, reinforces its autoimmune etiology. 24 Notably, mammary inflammation in individuals with Sjögren’s syndrome is characterized by lymphocytic and plasmacytic infiltration, mirroring the histopathological features observed in PCM. 24

Although preliminary evidence supports the involvement of autoimmune mechanisms in PCM pathogenesis, the precise processes governing autoantigen identification and breakdown of immune tolerance remain to be elucidated. Future research should focus on the identification of PCM-associated autoantigens through proteomic analyses and immunoprecipitation techniques, as well as on elucidating the mechanisms underlying immunomodulatory therapies such as glucocorticoids and immunosuppressants. 25 For example, glucocorticoids may attenuate inflammatory factor release by inhibiting the NF-κB pathway, whereas biological agents, including IL-6 inhibitors, could offer more targeted modulation of autoimmune responses 25 (see Figure 2 ). ### Diagnosis

Although most clinical and mechanistic studies concerning PCM therapeutic targets are currently conducted in Asian populations, the core molecular targets identified in these investigations, including the IL-6 signaling pathway and mammary gland microecological dysregulation, exhibit universal pathophysiological significance and global applicability. Such findings effectively bridge regional clinical observations and international basic research on PCM pathogenesis and diagnosis.

Imaging modalities constitute a critical component in the diagnosis of PCM, with ultrasound, mammography, and MRI each offering distinct advantages. The combined utilization of these techniques markedly enhances the diagnostic accuracy. Ultrasonography is the preferred imaging method for PCM, typically revealing a poorly defined hypoechoic mass within the areolar region, accompanied by ductal dilatation and abscess formation. 7 , 26 In a cohort study involving 111 PCM patients, ultrasound demonstrated a diagnostic accuracy of 82.0% and mammography of 74.8%, and the combined application of both modalities increased the accuracy to 91.9%. 26 Mammographic findings commonly include hyperdense shadows in the areola with ductal dilatation or calcifications; however, the specificity of mammography remains limited. 26

MRI plays a pivotal role in differentiating PCM from breast carcinoma. Characteristic MRI features of PCM include regionally distributed non-mass enhancement, heterogeneous internal enhancement, delayed eccentric diffusion, and associated signs such as nipple inversion, skin thickening, and sinus tract formation. 8 , 27 For instance, comparative MRI analyses of PCM and ductal carcinoma in situ (DCIS) revealed that PCM exhibits significantly higher rates of regional distribution, internal heterogeneous enhancement, and delayed-phase eccentric diffusion, whereas DCIS more frequently presents with segmental distribution and centripetal diffusion patterns. 27 Furthermore, diffusion-weighted imaging (DWI) sequences demonstrate high signal intensity centrally within PCM lesions, with apparent diffusion coefficient (ADC) values exceeding those observed in breast cancer, thereby providing a basis for differential diagnosis. 8 , 27

Emerging ultrasound techniques such as SMI further augment the diagnostic precision of PCM. SMI effectively delineates microvascular architecture within lesions, with resistive index (RI) and pulsatility index (PI) values in PCM being significantly lower than those in malignant lesions. The integration of SMI with conventional ultrasound increases the diagnostic accuracy from 75.59% to 83.16%. 7 Future research should focus on multicenter studies to establish standardized imaging diagnostic criteria for PCM and investigate the potential of artificial intelligence-assisted diagnostic models. 28

Histopathological examination remains the definitive diagnostic standard for PCM, which is characterized by ductal ectasia, plasma cell-predominant inflammatory infiltration, and periductal fibrosis. The pathological manifestations of PCM can be categorized into four stages: ductal dilatation, inflammation, abscess formation, and fistula development. 1 During the inflammatory phase, abundant plasma cells and lymphocytes surround the ducts and are accompanied by neutrophils and macrophages. 12 Immunohistochemical analyses have revealed high expression of CD138 in plasma cells, with positive rates of IL-6 and phosphorylated p-STAT3 at 93.3% and 70%, respectively, serving as adjunctive diagnostic markers. 2

Fine-needle aspiration cytology (FNAC) is valuable in diagnosing PCM, particularly in distinguishing it from breast malignancies. For example, in an 85-year-old female presenting with a left breast mass, FNAC identified plasma cell infiltration, which was subsequently confirmed as PCM via postoperative pathology, thereby preventing unnecessary radical mastectomy. 29 FNAC typically reveals numerous plasma cells, lymphocytes, and ductal epithelial cells without malignant cytological features. 21 Additionally, core needle biopsy (CNB) provides larger tissue samples, enhancing the diagnostic accuracy, especially in cases with inconclusive FNAC results. 14

Histopathological assessment also facilitates evaluation of the severity and prognosis of PCM. Patients exhibiting abscess formation tend to have a reduced risk of recurrence, whereas those with nipple inversion display more pronounced inflammatory infiltration. 6 , 30 Future efforts should aim to develop a pathological grading system for PCM, integrate clinical features for prognostic prediction, and explore molecular pathological markers such as IL-6 and complement component C5b-9. 2 , 21

The identification of novel biomarkers offers promising avenues for the early and differential diagnosis of PCM. Among these, IL-6, ICAM-1, complement components, and exosomes have demonstrated significant potential. Serum IL-6 levels, a key inflammatory mediator in PCM, are markedly elevated compared to acute mastitis patients and healthy controls, correlating with nipple inversion. 2 One study reported a median serum IL-6 concentration of 15.2 pg/mL in PCM patients versus 3.1 pg/mL in healthy individuals, with a diagnostic cutoff of 8.5 pg/mL yielding a sensitivity of 82.1% and specificity of 78.3%. 2

ICAM-1 expression is significantly upregulated in the mammary ductal epithelium and endothelial cells of PCM relative to that in normal breast tissue. 19 ICAM-1 contributes to PCM pathogenesis by mediating inflammatory cell adhesion and migration, and its expression levels are positively correlated with inflammation severity. 19 Moreover, complement components C3 and C5 and their active fragments (C3a and C5a) are elevated in the serum and breast tissue of PCM patients, with exosomal levels of C3a and C5a significantly exceeding those in healthy controls. 21 For instance, the median C5a concentration in breast tissue-derived exosomes was 12.3 ng/mL in PCM patients compared to 2.7 ng/mL in healthy subjects, suggesting its utility as a non-invasive diagnostic biomarker. 21

Transcriptomic and metabolomic analyses have identified potential biomarkers of PCM. Utilizing nanopore sequencing technology, researchers detected 39,408 novel transcripts in PCM tissues, with significant upregulation of immune-related genes such as IL-6 and CXCL12. 3 Metabolomic studies have revealed aberrations in glycerophospholipid and arachidonic acid metabolism within PCM breast tissue, potentially linked to inflammatory processes. 4 To validate the diagnostic utility of these biomarkers and assess their roles in treatment monitoring and prognostication, large-scale multicenter investigations are warranted 1 (see Figure 3 ). conclusions: PCM is an intractable non-lactational breast inflammatory disease featured with immune disorder-centered pathogenesis, difficult differential diagnosis and high recurrence rate, which seriously damages patients’ physical and mental health. This review systematically summarizes the research advances in the epidemiology, immune pathogenesis, diagnostic techniques and comprehensive treatment of PCM. Abnormal activation of the IL-6/STAT3 pathway, immune imbalance, autoimmune disturbance and plasma cell infiltration are critical drivers of chronic breast inflammation and tissue injury. The combination of imaging examination, pathological biopsy and novel molecular biomarkers can greatly improve the diagnostic accuracy of PCM. Monotherapy with pure Western medicine has prominent defects for PCM treatment. Empirical antibiotic therapy shows poor efficacy and easily triggers drug resistance, while immunosuppressants and biological agents bring obvious adverse reactions. Traditional Chinese Medicine (TCM) mainly treats PCM by soothing liver-qi stagnation, resolving phlegm and blood stasis, and clearing heat and detoxification via anti-inflammation, immune regulation and breast microecology reconstruction. Integrated TCM and Western medicine therapy can rapidly relieve clinical symptoms, suppress inflammatory response and reduce disease recurrence, so as to remedy the deficiencies of conventional Western medical treatment. Nevertheless, current TCM-related research has obvious limitations. Most clinical trials are single-center studies with small sample sizes without rigorous double-blind design, leading to low level of clinical evidence. Moreover, unified TCM syndrome differentiation criteria and quantitative efficacy evaluation systems for PCM have not yet been formulated. Future research shall carry out high-quality multicenter, large-sample, double-blind randomized controlled trials to verify the efficacy and safety of TCM. Further exploration on the immune regulatory mechanism of TCM and development of innovative Chinese medicinal preparations will facilitate the modernization of integrated Chinese and Western medicine therapy. In conclusion, integrated Chinese and Western medicine serves as a safe and effective therapeutic strategy for refractory PCM, which is worthy of extensive clinical promotion and in-depth research.

In parallel, functional studies demonstrated that hypoxia transcriptionally induces UPK1A-AS1 in HCC, where it promotes sorafenib resistance by suppressing apoptosis. Silencing UPK1A-AS1 restored apoptotic and enhanced sorafenib efficacy both in vitro and in vivo. Collectively, our findings suggest that UPK1A-AS1 is a hypoxia‐inducible oncogenic lncRNA that plays dual roles in cancer, with cancer type‐dependent associations with progression and immune modulation across malignancies and mechanistically mediating hypoxia‐associated drug resistance in HCC.

## Abstract

## Keywords
hepatocellular carcinoma; hypoxia; long noncoding RNA; pan-cancer analysis; sorafenib resistance; UPK1A-AS1

## 1. Introduction

Cancer remains one of the leading causes of morbidity and mortality worldwide and imposes a substantial public health burden. For numerous cancer types, particularly at the advanced stages, survival outcomes are still unsatisfactory. Global cancer statistics indicate that the incidence and mortality of many malignancies remain high despite advances in prevention, early detection, and systemic therapies [ 1 ]. These challenges highlight the urgent need to clarify the molecular mechanisms underlying tumor initiation and progression and to identify reliable biomarkers and therapeutic targets to improve cancer management.

Long noncoding RNAs (lncRNAs), defined as transcripts longer than 200 nucleotides without significant protein‐coding potential, have emerged as key regulators of gene expression and cellular behavior [ 2 , 3 ]. These molecules participate in chromatin remodeling, transcriptional regulation, RNA processing, and posttranscriptional control through mechanisms such as scaffolding, guiding, or decoying regulatory proteins [ 2 ]. Dysregulated lncRNAs have been shown to modulate multiple hallmarks of cancer, influencing cell proliferation, apoptosis, migration, genomic stability, and metabolic reprogramming [ 3 – 5 ]. Moreover, some lncRNAs can encode micropeptides that actively contribute to oncogenic signaling, further underscoring the functional diversity of this transcript class [ 4 ]. Given their cancer‐ and tissue‐specific expression patterns, lncRNAs have gained increasing attention as promising diagnostic and prognostic biomarkers, as well as potential therapeutic targets [ 5 ].

Among these cancer‐associated lncRNAs, UPK1A antisense RNA 1 ( UPK1A-AS1 ) has recently emerged as a functionally versatile transcript implicated in malignancies. Our previous work demonstrated that UPK1A-AS1 is significantly upregulated in hepatocellular carcinoma (HCC) and that its high expression correlates with a poor patient prognosis. Mechanistic studies revealed that UPK1A-AS1 promotes cancer cell proliferation by interacting with EZH2 and facilitating histone‐mediated repression of tumor‐suppressive genes [ 6 ]. Additionally, in pancreatic cancer, UPK1A-AS1 is induced by cancer‐associated fibroblast‐derived IL‐8 through NF‐κB signaling and confers platinum resistance by enhancing DNA double‐strand break repair via the Ku70/Ku80‐dependent nonhomologous end‐joining pathway [ 7 ]. In contrast, in esophageal squamous cell carcinoma (ESCC), UPK1A-AS1 is downregulated and functions as a tumor suppressor, inhibiting cell proliferation, migration, and invasion by sponging miR-1248 [ 8 ]. Similar context‐dependent functional patterns have been reported for other cancer‐associated lncRNAs. SNHG10 has been implicated in the regulation of proliferation, apoptosis, drug resistance, metabolic reprogramming, and immune evasion, but its expression patterns and biological effects vary substantially across tumor types [ 9 ]. Likewise, SOCS2-AS1 functions as a tumor suppressor in HCC, colorectal cancer, and endometrial cancer while exhibiting oncogenic properties in papillary thyroid cancer, glioma (GBMLGG), and prostate cancer [ 10 ]. Collectively, these findings suggest that the biological effects of cancer‐associated lncRNAs are strongly shaped by tissue‐specific molecular and microenvironmental contexts. Accordingly, UPK1A-AS1 may act as an oncogene in some tumor types while serving as a tumor suppressor in others. This functional heterogeneity highlights the necessity of a comprehensive pan‐cancer investigation to clarify the biological roles and regulatory mechanisms of UPK1A-AS1 across malignancies.

Considering its divergent and tumor type‐specific functions, the overall biological and clinical relevance of UPK1A-AS1 across human cancers has yet to be systematically defined. Integrative studies combining multidatabase transcriptomic profiling with prognostic and immune microenvironment analyses offer a valuable framework for investigating the roles of cancer‐associated molecules [ 11 ]. Adopting this strategy, we performed a comprehensive pan‐cancer analysis to delineate the expression patterns of UPK1A-AS1 in normal tissues and multiple tumor types and to clarify its associations with clinicopathological features, patient prognosis, and genomic alterations. We further investigated the relationship between UPK1A-AS1 expression and the tumor immune microenvironment, including immune and stromal cell infiltration, immunogenic features, and responses to immune checkpoint blockade across cancers. In addition, we combined in vitro and in vivo HCC models to investigate the functional role of UPK1A-AS1 in tumor progression and hypoxia‐associated sorafenib resistance. Together, these integrated bioinformatics and experimental analyses provide a systematic view of the biological and clinical importance of UPK1A-AS1 and support its potential as a prognostic biomarker and therapeutic target in cancer.

## 2. Materials and Methods

### 2.1. UPK1A-AS1 Gene Expression Analysis

The expression pattern of UPK1A-AS1 across normal and tumor tissues was analyzed via RNA‐sequencing data from the Genotype‐Tissue Expression Project (GTEx) [ 12 ] and The Cancer Genome Atlas (TCGA) databases, which were obtained from the UCSC Xena platform ( https://xenabrowser.net/datapages ). Integrated pan‐cancer analyses combining TCGA and GTEx datasets were performed via Sangerbox ( http://sangerbox.com/ ) to evaluate the expression landscape of UPK1A-AS1 across diverse cancer types. Furthermore, the cancer immunology data engine (CIDE) database ( https://cide.ccr.cancer.gov ) was utilized to explore the cell type‐specific expression profile of UPK1A-AS1 within the tumor microenvironment via single‐cell transcriptomic data.

### 2.2. Genetic Alteration Analysis

Genetic alterations in UPK1A-AS1 across various cancer types were analyzed via the cBioPortal for cancer genomics (cBioPortal) ( https://www.cbioportal.org ), which integrates multidimensional genomic data from TCGA Pan‐Cancer Atlas studies. The frequency and distribution of alteration types, including mutations, copy‐number variations (CNVs), and amplifications, were summarized across TCGA tumor cohorts to provide an overview of UPK1A-AS1 alteration patterns. Additionally, the somatic mutation profiles of the high‐ and low‐ UPK1A-AS1 expression groups (top 50% vs. bottom 50%) were compared via Sangerbox, which stratifies TCGA samples by gene expression and generates group‐specific mutation landscapes visualized as waterfall plots.

### 2.3. Functional Enrichment Analysis

To investigate the biological functions and signaling pathways associated with UPK1A-AS1 , enrichment analyses were performed on both genomic and transcriptomic data. Genes showing significant co‐mutation with UPK1A-AS1 across multiple cancer types were retrieved from the cBioPortal, where co‐mutation significance was assessed using one‐sided Fisher’s exact tests with Benjamini–Hochberg FDR correction, and the top 500 genes with the strongest correlation ( p ‐value < 0.05, ranked by the log2 ratio) were selected for subsequent pathway enrichment analysis (Table S1 ). Differentially expressed genes (DEGs) between the high‐ and low‐ UPK1A-AS1 expression groups in TCGA cohort were identified via the edgeR [ 13 ] package with the Benjamini–Hochberg method applied for multiple testing correction (adjusted p < 0.05 and |log 2 FC| > 1, Table S2 ). These gene sets were subjected to Kyoto Encyclopedia of Genes and Genomes (KEGG) [ 14 ] and Gene Ontology (GO) [ 15 ] enrichment analyses to determine the functional categories and molecular pathways potentially regulated by UPK1A-AS1 . All analyses and visualizations were conducted via R software (Version 4.3.3) [ 16 ] with the clusterProfiler [ 17 ], org.Hs.eg.db [ 18 ], GOplot [ 19 ], and ggplot2 [ 20 ] packages under default parameters.

### 2.4. Immune Infiltration and Immune‐Related Gene Analysis

Comprehensive immune infiltration profiling was performed across multiple cancer types via Sangerbox, which integrates transcriptomic and immune‐related data derived from TCGA cohorts. The tumor immune estimation resource (TIMER) [ 21 ] embedded within Sangerbox was used to quantify the associations between UPK1A-AS1 expression and immune infiltration levels and to evaluate correlations with immune checkpoint‐related genes, chemokines, and chemokine receptors. To further estimate the relative abundance of immune and stromal components within tumor tissues, Estimation of STromal and Immune cells in MAlignant Tumours using Expression data (ESTIMATE) [ 22 ] was implemented in R. Radar plots summarizing the immune infiltration characteristics were generated via the fmsb [ 23 ] package in R to provide integrated visualization of the immune landscape associated with UPK1A-AS1 expression.

### 2.5. Survival and Prognostic Analysis

The prognostic value of UPK1A-AS1 was evaluated across cancer types on the basis of patient survival data. In TCGA cohort, patients were stratified into high‐ and low‐expression groups according to the top 50% and bottom 50% of UPK1A-AS1 expression levels, and overall survival (OS), progression‐free survival (PFS), disease‐free survival (DFS), and disease‐specific survival (DSS) were analyzed via Sangerbox. Additional survival data derived from the CIDE database were used to examine the prognostic relevance of UPK1A-AS1 expression in immunotherapy‐treated cohorts. The predictive performance related to the immune checkpoint blockade response was further validated via the ROC Plotter ( https://rocplot.com/immune ).

### 2.6. Cell Culture

The HCC cell lines Huh7 (RRID: CVCL_0336) and MHCC‐97H (RRID: CVCL_4972) were obtained from the Cell Bank of Type Culture Collection (CBTCC, Chinese Academy of Sciences, Shanghai, China). These two cell lines were selected because they represent distinct metastatic potentials (Huh7 is less invasive, while MHCC‐97H is highly invasive) and are widely used models for HCC research. The use of these authenticated cell lines with valid RRIDs ensures the reproducibility and reliability of our findings. Cells were cultured in Dulbecco’s Modified Eagle’s Medium (DMEM, Gibco) supplemented with 10% fetal bovine serum (FBS, Gibco) and maintained at 37°C in a humidified incubator containing 5% CO 2 . For hypoxia treatment, cells were incubated for 24 h under a gas mixture containing 1% O 2 , 5% CO 2 , and 94% N 2 . Cells maintained under normoxic conditions were used as controls.

### 2.7. RNA Interference

The siRNAs specifically targeting UPK1A-AS1 and the corresponding negative controls were obtained from RiboBio. Briefly, 50 nM of each siRNA was transfected into cells via Lipofectamine RNAiMAX (Invitrogen) according to the manufacturer’s protocol. The sequences of the siRNAs used are as follows: si‐AS1‐1, 5′‐GGAGATGCTTGGTCCATCT‐3′; si‐AS1‐2, 5′‐CCTTGACAGTGCTGTTATT‐3′.

### 2.8. Lentiviral Construction and Transduction

The hU6‐shUPK1A‐AS1‐CMV lentiviral vectors used to knock down UPK1A-AS1 expression were designed and constructed by Genechem Company Ltd. To generate clones with stable UPK1A-AS1 knockdown, MHCC‐97H cells were infected at a multiplicity of infection of 30 with hU6‐shUPK1A‐AS1‐CMV lentiviral vectors or control vectors. The stable UPK1A-AS1 ‐downregulated clones were selected after 2 weeks of treatment with puromycin, and the expression of UPK1A-AS1 was determined.

### 2.9. RNA Extraction and qRT‐PCR

Total RNA was isolated via the TRIzol reagent (Invitrogen) following the manufacturer’s recommendations. qRT‐PCR was performed using a SYBR Green PCR kit (Takara Biotechnology). β‐Actin genes were used as internal controls. The specificity of the amplification products was confirmed by the melting curve analysis. Triplicate samples were analyzed in three independent experiments. The sequences of primers used were as follows: UPK1A-AS1 , F: 5′‐AGAGCGGTGGGTTAGGAA‐3′, and R: 5′‐GGGCAGATGGACCAAGCA‐3′. β-Actin , F: 5′‐TCAAGATCATTGCTCCTCCTGA‐3′, R: 5′‐CTCGTCATACTCCTGCTTGCTG‐3′. U6 , F: 5′‐CTCGCTTCGGCAGCACA‐3′, R: 5′‐AACGCTTCACGAATTTGCGT‐3′.

### 2.10. Immunohistochemistry (IHC) Assay

Paraffin‐embedded tumor tissue sections (5 μm thick) were labeled with primary antibodies, and immunoreactivity was detected with an envision system (Dako, Carpinteria). Briefly, formalin‐fixed, paraffin‐embedded tissue sections were deparaffinized, rehydrated, and subjected to heat‐induced epitope retrieval in citrate buffer (pH 6.0) via a pressure cooker. After blocking endogenous peroxidase activity and nonspecific binding, the sections were incubated with primary antibody (Mouse Monoclonal anti‐Ki‐67, Abcam, Cat Number ab279653; Cleaved Caspase‐3 (Asp175) Antibody, CST, Cat Number 9661; Rabbit Monoclonal anti‐HIF‐1α, CST, Cat Number 36169) overnight at 4°C. Following washes, detection was carried out via a horseradish peroxidase (HRP)‐labeled polymer detection system and 3,3′‐diaminobenzidine (DAB) chromogen. The slides were mounted per mount after dehydration.

### 2.11. Flow Cytometry Assay

Apoptotic cells were evaluated with an annexin‐V fluorescein isothiocyanate and propidium iodide apoptosis detection kit (Invitrogen) following the manufacturer’s protocol. The stained cells were then analyzed with a FACScan flow cytometer.

### 2.12. Animal Study

All procedures for the animal study were approved by the Animal Use and Care Committee of Nanfang Hospital, Southern Medical University (Guangzhou, China). Four‐week‐old male nude mice were subcutaneously injected with 1 × 10 7 MHCC‐97H cells and subjected to the indicated treatments. Mice were randomly assigned to each group ( n = 6 per group) using a random number table on day 13 after MHCC‐97H cell injection when the tumor volume reached 100–150 mm 3 . Drug administration was initiated immediately after randomization, and mice received daily oral sorafenib (30 mg/kg/day) or equal volume PBS until sacrifice. The tumor size was measured daily via an electronic caliper, and the tumor volume was calculated as (length × width 2 ) / 2. The tumor‐bearing mice were sacrificed for further analysis 19 days after the injection of MHCC‐97H cells. All tumor measurements and analyses were performed with investigators blinded to the group allocation.

### 2.13. Statistical Methods

Statistical analyses were performed using GraphPad Prism 8.0, R 4.3.3, and public online platforms. For two‐group comparisons, Student’s t ‐test or the Wilcoxon rank‐sum test was used as appropriate. UPK1A-AS1 expression levels in paired HCC and adjacent nontumor tissues were compared using a paired Student’s t ‐test. Comparisons among multiple groups were performed using one‐way ANOVA, followed by Tukey’s post‐hoc test. Details of correlation analyses are provided in the corresponding figure legends. Survival curves were generated by the Kaplan–Meier method and compared by the log‐rank test; forest plots were based on univariate Cox regression with Wald tests. Mutation frequency differences were evaluated by Fisher’s exact test. All statistical tests were two‐sided, and a p ‐value of less than 0.05 was considered statistically significant.

## 3. Results

### 3.1. Tissue‐ and Cell Type‐Specific Expression Profiles of UPK1A-AS1 in Human Cancers

Given that gene expression patterns can profoundly influence tumor behavior and cellular function, we next investigated the expression characteristics of UPK1A-AS1 across normal tissues and various cancer types. Analysis of the GTEx data revealed that UPK1A-AS1 exhibited variable expression levels across a wide range of normal human tissues. Relatively high expression was observed in the skin, vagina, testis, and bladder (Figure 1 A). We therefore used TCGA database to examine the expression landscape of UPK1A-AS1 across various cancer types. The results indicated that UPK1A-AS1 was expressed at higher levels in multiple malignancies, including esophageal carcinoma (ESCA), lung adenocarcinoma (LUAD), ovarian cancer (OV), pancreatic ductal adenocarcinoma (PAAD), breast cancer (BRCA), lung squamous cell carcinoma (LUSC), sarcoma (SARC), uterine corpus endometrial carcinoma (UCEC), liver HCC (LIHC), acute myeloid leukemia (LAML), mesothelioma (MESO), cholangiocarcinoma (CHOL), uterine carcinosarcoma (UCS), uveal melanoma (UVM), bladder carcinoma (BLCA), testicular germ cell tumor (TGCT), and skin cutaneous melanoma (SKCM) (Figure 1 B). Further integrative analysis via Sangerbox, which is based on combined TCGA and GTEx datasets, revealed differential expression patterns of UPK1A-AS1 across various cancer types. In the paired tumor and adjacent normal samples from TCGA cohort (Figure 1 C), UPK1A-AS1 expression was significantly downregulated in glioblastoma multiforme (GBM), GBMLGG, lower‐grade GBMLGG (LGG), BRCA, kidney renal papillary cell carcinoma (KIRP), pan‐kidney cohort (KIPAN), prostate adenocarcinoma (PRAD), kidney renal clear cell carcinoma (KIRC), and kidney chromophobe (KICH). In contrast, it was upregulated in colon and rectal adenocarcinoma (COADREAD), LUSC, LIHC, and CHOL. In the unpaired analysis combining TCGA and GTEx datasets (Figure 1 D), UPK1A-AS1 expression was significantly downregulated in GBM, GBMLGG, LGG, BRCA, LUAD, ESCA, stomach and ESCA (STES), KIRP, KIPAN, colon adenocarcinoma (COAD), PRAD, KIRC, Wilms tumor (WT), thyroid carcinoma (THCA), TGCT, and KICH. Conversely, it was upregulated in stomach adenocarcinoma (STAD), LIHC, SKCM, OV, PAAD, UCS, LAML, adrenocortical carcinoma (ACC), and CHOL. Collectively, these findings suggest that this lncRNA may serve as a potential regulatory molecule involved in tumorigenesis and cancer progression across diverse malignancies.

To further investigate the expression pattern of UPK1A-AS1 among different cell types within the tumor microenvironment, we analyzed its distribution via the CIDE database. The results indicated that UPK1A-AS1 was predominantly expressed in tumor cells. In addition, higher expression levels were observed across several T‐cell subpopulations, including effector CD8 + T cells, central memory CD8 + T cells, exhausted CD8 + T cells, and regulatory T cells, whereas its expression in naïve T cells was very low or barely detectable on the basis of transcriptomic data (Figure 1 E and Figure S1A ). The enrichment of UPK1A-AS1 in tumor cells suggests a potential tumor‐promoting role, while its specific expression pattern among multiple T‐cell subsets implies that this lncRNA may also contribute to the regulation of the tumor immune microenvironment and T‐cell functional states.

### 3.2. Clinical Correlations and Prognostic Value of UPK1A-AS1 Across Cancers

To explore the potential impact of UPK1A-AS1 on the prognosis of multiple cancer types, we performed a systematic analysis via Sangerbox. The results revealed that the expression level of UPK1A-AS1 was significantly associated with various clinicopathological features across multiple malignancies, suggesting its potential involvement in tumor initiation and progression. With respect to tumor invasion depth ( T stage), UPK1A-AS1 exhibited differential expression in COAD, COADREAD, KIRP, and LIHC (Figure 2 A), indicating a possible link between this gene and local invasive behavior. In terms of lymph node metastasis ( N stage), differential expression of UPK1A-AS1 was observed in COAD, COADREAD, KIPAN, THCA, and KICH (Figure 2 B), further implying that UPK1A-AS1 plays a role in regulating local metastatic processes. Notably, for distant metastasis ( M stage), significant differences in expression were detected only in COADREAD (Figure S2A ), suggesting a specific role in the distant metastasis of colorectal cancer. From the perspective of overall tumor stage, UPK1A-AS1 expression was correlated with disease progression in COAD, COADREAD, UCEC, head and neck squamous cell carcinoma (HNSC), LIHC, THCA, rectum adenocarcinoma (READ), and TGCT (Figure 2 C). In addition, a significant association with the tumor differentiation grade was observed only in LIHC (Figure S2B ), indicating that UPK1A-AS1 may serve as a potential indicator for malignancy assessment in HCC. Moreover, its expression differed according to sex in LGG, BRCA, SARC, KIRP, LIHC, and ACC (Figure S2C ).

We next assessed the prognostic value of UPK1A-AS1 across cancers via Sangerbox survival analyses. Elevated UPK1A-AS1 expression was significantly associated with poorer OS in multiple cancer types, including KIPAN (HR = 1.12, p = 5.9e − 9), KIRC (HR = 1.10, p = 3.3e − 5), ACC (HR = 1.21, p = 4.4e − 4), KIRP (HR = 1.13, p = 3.6e − 3), and MESO (HR = 1.14, p = 8.5e − 3) (Figure 3 A). Similarly, high UPK1A-AS1 expression correlated with shorter PFS in KIPAN (HR = 1.13, p = 1.1e − 9), KIRC (HR = 1.12, p = 1.1e − 6), ACC (HR = 1.23, p = 2.8e − 6), STAD (HR = 1.09, p = 8.7e − 4), STES (HR = 1.06, p = 3.2e − 3), KIRP (HR = 1.11, p = 6.7e − 3), and pheochromocytoma and paraganglioma (PCPG, HR = 1.16, p = 0.03) patients (Figure 3 C). Kaplan–Meier curves revealed that elevated UPK1A-AS1 expression was significantly associated with reduced OS in ACC, KIPAN, KIRC, KIRP, MESO, STAD, and LIHC patients (Figure 3 B). Similarly, high UPK1A-AS1 expression correlated with shorter PFS in ACC, KIPAN, KIRP, LIHC, LUSC, LGG, STAD, and STES (Figure 3 D). These results consistently indicate that UPK1A-AS1 functions as a potential adverse prognostic factor across diverse human cancers.

### 3.3. Genomic Alterations and Functional Implications of UPK1A-AS1 Across Human Cancers

In cancer genomics, somatic mutations are among the key drivers of tumorigenesis. These mutations include point mutations, insertions or deletions, and large‐scale structural variations such as CNVs, which can lead to oncogene activation or tumor suppressor gene inactivation [ 24 ]. Using the cBioPortal, we examined the mutation frequency of UPK1A-AS1 across various cancers. Copy‐number amplification was the predominant alteration type and was observed at relatively high frequencies in multiple tumor types, with the highest amplification rate detected in UCS (19.3%). Other cancers with relatively high amplification frequencies included OV (8.22%), LUSC (5.34%), esophageal adenocarcinoma (3.85%), SARC (4.31%), UCEC (3.21%), cervical squamous cell carcinoma (3.37%), PAAD (3.26%), LUAD (3.00%), and BLCA (2.43%) (Figure 4 A).

To further evaluate the clinical impact of these alterations, we compared OS and PFS between patients with and without UPK1A-AS1 alterations. Kaplan–Meier survival analysis and log‐rank tests revealed that patients without alterations presented significantly better OS, PFS, DFS, and DSS than those with alterations did, indicating that UPK1A-AS1 genomic alterations may be associated with unfavorable clinical outcomes (Figure 4 B and Figure S3A ,B).

We subsequently used Sangerbox to explore the relationship between UPK1A-AS1 expression and specific genomic features in LIHC and STAD. High UPK1A-AS1 expression was associated with increased frequencies of somatic mutations in DOCK2 (7.5%), KEAP1 (6.9%), SETD2 (5.7%), DNAH10 (5.2%), COL12A1 (4.6%), and ZDBF2 (4.0%) in LIHC and in ABCC9 (15.4%), SIGLEC1 (9.9%), PLXNC1 (9.9%), KRT72 (7.7%), ROBO4 (7.7%), and SLC17A6 (7.7%) in STAD (Figure 4 C).

We next retrieved genes co‐mutated with UPK1A-AS1 across pan‐cancer samples via the cBioPortal and performed KEGG pathway enrichment analysis. The results revealed several prominent pathways, including the metabolism of xenobiotics by cytochrome P450, the B‐cell receptor signaling pathway, renal cell carcinoma, platinum drug resistance, and Epstein–Barr virus infection (Figure 4 D). Moreover, GO enrichment analysis further revealed significant enrichment in drug metabolism‐related processes and positive regulation of lymphocyte, leukocyte, and T‐cell apoptotic processes, as well as additional enrichment in transcriptional regulatory pathways, arachidonic acid metabolism, and lipoprotein‐associated metabolic processes (Figure 4 E). Collectively, these results suggest that the expression and mutation of UPK1A-AS1 may influence key biological processes, including transcriptional regulation, tumor immunity, chemoresistance, and metabolic reprogramming, thereby contributing to cancer initiation and progression. The genomic characteristics of UPK1A-AS1 may thus hold potential predictive value in the diagnosis and therapy of cancer.

Collectively, the strong associations between UPK1A-AS1 expression, genomic aberrations, and unfavorable patient prognosis indicate that this lncRNA may act as an oncogenic regulator involved in tumor progression and could represent a novel prognostic biomarker and therapeutic candidate across diverse cancer types.

### 3.4. UPK1A-AS1 is Linked to Immune Infiltration and Immune Signaling Heterogeneity Across Cancers

To investigate the potential impact of UPK1A-AS1 on the tumor immune microenvironment, we conducted a pan‐cancer analysis using ESTIMATE, which generates immune, stromal, and ESTIMATE scores to evaluate the level of immune and stromal cell infiltration in tumor tissues. UPK1A-AS1 expression was negatively correlated with one or more of these scores in multiple cancer types, including HNSC, BRCA, BLCA, ACC, UCS, UCEC, THCA, TGCT, SKCM, SARC, and LUSC (Figure 5 A). Notably, BRCA, BLCA, ACC, and UCEC were negatively correlated with all three scores, suggesting that UPK1A-AS1 may be associated with a “cold” tumor immune microenvironment. In contrast, PRAD exhibited positive correlations, suggesting a potential association between UPK1A-AS1 and enhanced immune infiltration in this cancer type.

We further examined the association between UPK1A-AS1 expression and immune‐cell infiltration levels via the TIMER algorithm implemented in Sangerbox. Consistently, UPK1A-AS1 expression was positively correlated with the infiltration of multiple immune‐cell types in COAD, COADREAD, LIHC, and PRAD, whereas a negative correlation was observed in BLCA (Figure 5 B). Interestingly, the correlation between UPK1A-AS1 and CD4 + T‐cell infiltration was relatively high in COAD ( r = 0.29), COADREAD ( r = 0.27), and LIHC ( r = 0.31), suggesting a potential association of UPK1A-AS1 with CD4 + T‐cell infiltration within the tumor microenvironment. Collectively, these findings suggest that the UPK1A-AS1 expression is closely associated with immune‐cell infiltration across multiple tumor types.

To further explore whether UPK1A-AS1 might influence the tumor immune microenvironment by regulating chemokine signaling networks, we analyzed its correlation with various chemokines and their receptors across cancers. The results revealed widespread and significant associations between UPK1A-AS1 and multiple C─C‐ and C─X─C‐motif chemokines and receptors. Negative correlations were predominant in ACC, BLCA, THCA, LUSC, KIRC, STAD, and STES, whereas positive correlations were observed in UVM, LIHC, PRAD, COAD, COADREAD, and LUAD (Figure 5 C). These results suggest that UPK1A-AS1 expression is associated with chemokine signaling in a cancer type‐dependent manner, implying a potential link to distinct tumor immune microenvironmental features.

To further elucidate the functional differences associated with UPK1A-AS1 , GO and KEGG enrichment analyses were performed on the basis of the log 2 ‐fold‐change values of DEGs between the high‐ and low‐expression groups. Consistent with the immune correlation results, the downregulated pathways in the BLCA and UCEC cohorts were related primarily to immune activation and leukocyte function, including positive regulation of cell adhesion, positive regulation of cytokine production, antigen binding, activation of the immune response, lymphocyte‐mediated immunity, positive regulation of leukocyte activation, the immune response‐regulating signaling pathway, and leukocyte‐mediated immunity. In contrast, in PRAD, high UPK1A-AS1 expression was associated with the upregulation of multiple immune‐related processes, such as antigen binding, the immune response‐regulating signaling pathway, the activation of the immune response, lymphocyte‐mediated immunity, phagocytosis, complement activation, and leukocyte‐mediated immunity (Figure 5 D). Collectively, these results indicate that UPK1A-AS1 plays a multifaceted role in shaping the tumor immune landscape, reflecting its potential involvement in both immune regulation and tumor progression across diverse cancer types.

### 3.5. UPK1A-AS1 Expression is Correlated With Immunogenic Features and Immunotherapy Response Across Cancers

Tumor mutational burden (TMB) and microsatellite instability (MSI) are key indicators of genomic instability and mutation frequency, both of which influence the formation of neoantigens (NEO) and the efficacy of immune checkpoint blockade [ 25 ]. To investigate the relationship between UPK1A-AS1 and tumor immunogenicity, correlations between UPK1A-AS1 expression and TMB, MSI, and NEO were analyzed across multiple cancer types via Sangerbox. In CHOL, UPK1A-AS1 expression was negatively correlated, and high UPK1A-AS1 expression may harbor lower mutational and NEO loads, thereby reducing immune recognition. A similar pattern of negative correlation with both TMB and MSI was observed in STAD and STES, further supporting the potential association between UPK1A-AS1 upregulation and reduced genomic alteration. In contrast, UPK1A-AS1 expression was positively correlated with both TMB and MSI in KICH (Figure 6 A), suggesting a cancer type‐specific association with increased genomic instability and immunogenic features.

Conventional treatments such as topical retinoids, benzoyl peroxide, antibiotics, oral isotretinoin, and hormonal therapies are often associated with limited efficacy, slow response, irritation, photosensitivity, and poor tolerability, prompting the search for non-antibiotic strategies that preserve the microbiome. This review evaluates metal oxide nanoparticles as multifunctional agents with acne-targeted, anti-inflammatory, antioxidant, and photocatalytic activities suitable for the follicular microenvironment. The emphasis is placed on zinc oxide, titanium dioxide, copper oxide, iron oxide, magnesium oxide, cerium oxide, aluminium oxide and manganese oxide nanoparticles. The review further examines synthesis methods (physical, wet-chemical, and green plant/microbial synthesis), formulation platforms (hydrogels/nanogels, electrospun fibers, lipid carriers, microneedles, and near-infrared (NIR)-responsive nanomotors), as well as safety and regulatory aspects. Available evidence suggests that primary particle size (typically 20–70 nm), hydrodynamic aggregation (200–700 nm for follicular depots), zeta potential (−10 to −30 mV), and surface coatings ( e.g. , hyaluronic acid, polysaccharides, and polyethylene glycol (PEG)) significantly influence dermal fate. Metal oxide nanoparticles represent promising adjuvants and potential alternatives for the treatment of mild-to-moderate acne vulgaris and maintenance therapy, provided they are synthesized using standardized protocols, formulated through microbiome-friendly approaches, toxicologically evaluated using harmonized assessment frameworks, and validated through rigorous, adequately powered clinical trials.

# Metal oxide nanoparticles for acne vulgaris: mechanisms, synthesis, formulation, and translational prospects

## Abstract
Acne vulgaris is a chronic inflammatory condition of the pilosebaceous unit resulting from follicular hyperkeratinization, increased sebum production, overgrowth of Cutibacterium acnes , and immune activation, with subsequent activation of Toll-like receptor signalling and increased expression of IL-1β, IL-8, and matrix metalloproteinases, leading to scarring and hyperpigmentation. Conventional treatments such as topical retinoids, benzoyl peroxide, antibiotics, oral isotretinoin, and hormonal therapies are often associated with limited efficacy, slow response, irritation, photosensitivity, and poor tolerability, prompting the search for non-antibiotic strategies that preserve the microbiome. This review evaluates metal oxide nanoparticles as multifunctional agents with acne-targeted, anti-inflammatory, antioxidant, and photocatalytic activities suitable for the follicular microenvironment. The emphasis is placed on zinc oxide, titanium dioxide, copper oxide, iron oxide, magnesium oxide, cerium oxide, aluminium oxide and manganese oxide nanoparticles. The review further examines synthesis methods (physical, wet-chemical, and green plant/microbial synthesis), formulation platforms (hydrogels/nanogels, electrospun fibers, lipid carriers, microneedles, and near-infrared (NIR)-responsive nanomotors), as well as safety and regulatory aspects. Available evidence suggests that primary particle size (typically 20–70 nm), hydrodynamic aggregation (200–700 nm for follicular depots), zeta potential (−10 to −30 mV), and surface coatings ( e.g. , hyaluronic acid, polysaccharides, and polyethylene glycol (PEG)) significantly influence dermal fate.
