# Incidence of Pathogens and Evaluation of their Antibacterial Sensitivity among Iraqi cases with Inflammatory Acne

## Abstract
### Materials:

This study ran from April to October 2024. Samples of the study were taken from inflammatory papular and pustular acne lesions from 50 dermatology patients (22 males and 28 females) aged between 18 and 26 years.

### Results:

Staph aureus was the most prevalent bacteria with (29) 43.28% and Staph epidermidis the least common with (3) 4.47%. Sometimes patients had both P. acne and Staphylococcal aureus (12 samples, 17.91%). Both species showed high sensitivity to levofloxacin in the top of the list and the strongest resistance to ampicillin on the other side.

## Keywords
Antibiotic susceptibility; bacteriological study; inflammatory acne

## Introduction

Acne vulgaris (AV) is a multifactorial chronic inflammatory skin disorder; it is the most common skin disease that affects the pilosebaceous follicles; it accounts 85% of adolescent and young adults (1E). It appears with clinical polymorphic lesions, which consist of non-inflammatory (open and close comedones) and inflammatory lesions (papules, pustules, and nodules). In untreated cases, scarring appears (1 IR). The pathogenesis of AV includes four major factors; they are seborrhea, hyperproliferation of the infundibulum, abnormality of the flora, and inflammation.[ 1 2 ] Although AV is not an infectious disease, previous studies reported that several microorganisms are implicated in the pathogenesis of the disease. P. acne, Staph. aureus, Malassezia furfur, and Micrococcus spp are reported.[ 3 ]

Propionibacterium acnes ( P. acnes ) is a microbe of considerable significance within the scientific community and is a type of bacteria that is Gram-positive, meaning it retains a purple stain in the Gram staining technique. It is also non-spore-forming, indicating that it does not produce specialised structures for survival in unfavourable conditions. Furthermore, it is an anaerobic bacillus, which means it thrives in environments with low or no oxygen.[ 4 ] These bacteria primarily reside in the sebaceous region, which refers to the areas of the body that contain sebaceous glands, such as the skin. Predominantly localised within sebaceous regions of the skin, P. acnes is well established in its role in instigating inflammatory lesions in acne vulgaris. It displays lipase activity, catalysing the conversion of triglycerides into free fatty acids.[ 5 6 7 ] The presence of free fatty acids promotes the aggregation and establishment of P. acnes bacteria, leading to an inflammatory response. This response is further potentiated through complement activation mediated by anti-Propionibacterium antibodies.[ 8 ]

The administration of antibiotics in the treatment of AV effectively hinders the proliferation of P. acnes bacteria and/or their synthesis of pro-inflammatory substances. Historically, P. acnes exhibited susceptibility to various antimicrobial agents, including clindamycin, erythromycin, and tetracyclins, until the late 1970s.[ 6 ]

Antibiotic modalities, encompassing both topical and systemic routes, have been integral to AV management for decades. However, reports of P. acnes strains demonstrating resistance to several antibiotic classes, notably aminoglycosides, mupirocin, and metronidazole, underscore evolving challenges in treatment paradigms.[ 7 ]

## Material and Methods

This study was conducted during the period from April to October 2023. It was approved by the ethical committee in the medical college/university of Misan. Samples were collected from 50 patients (22 males and 28 females) attending to the dermatology and venereology department in Al-sader teaching hospital, Misan. Inclusion criteria: Any young adult aged between 18 and 25 years complaining for inflammatory AV without any associated other dermatological problems such as seborrhiec dermatitis, rosacea, and drug-induced acne. Pregnant women, breastfeeding, patients with polycystic ovary syndrome or hyperandrogenism, and those who receive systemic or topical antibiotics for one last month were excluded from the study. Samples of the study were taken from inflammatory popular and pustular acne lesions. Patients were diagnosed with AV by history taking and physical examination.

### Bacteriological study

Sterile needles, disposable sterile cotton swabs, and transport media were used for this purpose. The site of the lesion was first wiped with 70% alcohol and then with 0.5% iodine; the contents of the pustules were collected after being ruptured with a sterile needle. Samples were immediately transported to the microbiology laboratory by using cotton swabs with Amies transport media (Merk, Darmstadt, Germany).[ 9 ]

All samples were cultured on blood agar media (two plates for each sample) and subjected to both aerobic and anaerobic growth. For aerobic growth, samples were incubated at 37°C overnight for primary isolation, while for anaerobic growth, specimens reach the lab. The process occurred in less than an hour in the transport tube, where it was incubated for 5 days at 20–25 centigrade degree under anaerobic conditions (mechanical exclusion of oxygen: anaerobic incubator), which was performed by using AnaeroGen; Oxoid Ltd, Basingstoke, UK (2); after that, the growth was examined.

Pure individual colonies from both aerobic and anaerobic growth were identified by morphological and standard biochemical tests (Api20) (BioMerieux).[ 7 ]

### Antibiotic susceptibility

Antibiotic susceptibility was performed by the disc diffusion method; commercially available discs for (Ampicillin, Erythromycin, Ciprofloxacin, Tetracycline, Clindamycin, Azithromycin, Rifampicin, Levofloxacin, Doxycycline, Trimethoprim/Sulfamethoxazole, Amoxicillin/Clavulanic acid) antibiotics were used (antibiotic discs; Oxoid, Basingstoke, UK) according to the CLSI 2022 guidelines. The standardised Kirby-Bauer disc diffusion method was performed on Mueller-Hinton agar (Himedia). Inoculates were adjusted to a 0.5 MacFarland standard from an aerobic and anaerobic pure culture on blood agar. Mueller-Hinton agar plates were inoculated and incubated at 37°C for 24 h aerobic and for 5 to 7 days anaerobically.

### Statistical analysis

Statistical analysis in the present study was performed by using SPSS program, and the results were expressed as a percentage (%).

## Results

In the current study, the patients’ demographics and the main bacterial causes were detected. As shown in Table 1 , the age of most patients ranged between 17 and 28 years old with 56% female and 44% male.

Results of cultures show the primary culture and the bacterial shape under the microscope, as shown in Figure 1 .

Results of the catalase test are shown in Figure 2 ; the test reveals that the isolates were catalase positive. Api 20 was performed for all isolates for the purpose of identification, and the results are as shown in Figure 3 and Figure 4 .

Next, the bacterial distribution of subjects is described in Table 2 . From a total of 50 patients, 40 samples had positive growth culture. Three bacterial species were identified with interesting results; the most common bacteria was aerobic Staphylococcal aureus with (29) 43.28% and the least common bacteria was Staphylococcal epidermidis with (3) 4.47%, while anaerobic Cutibacterium acnes was (23) 35.32%; three of them mixed with Staphylococcal epidermidis and 12 (17.91%) with Staphylococcal aureus.

Figure 1 : The left picture displays the bacterial shape under the microscope, and the right picture shows case produce for positive samples.

The results of disc diffusion test for the antibiotic susceptibility are shown in Table 3 ; the Cutibacterium acnes sensitivity in descending order was levofloxacin, ciprofloxacin, tetracycline, clindamycin, rifampicin, and doxycycline. On the other hand, the Cutibacterium acnes showed resistance to two antibiotics, Amoxicillin and Amoxicillin/Clavulanic Acid, with both of them having (18/23) 78.26%. Azithromycin, Trimethoprim/Sulfamethoxazole, and Erythromycin showed closed results or comparable results between Antibiotic Sensitivity and Resistant.

Then, the same techniques were used for Staph. Aureus. The diffusion disc approach was used to test the antibiotic sensitivity for the samples. As shown in Table 4 , the Staph. Aureus was susceptible to Levofloxacin, Ciprofloxacin, Rifampicin, Tetracycline, and Trimethoprim/Sulfamethoxazole, with 100% and 75%, respectively. On the other hand, the Staph. Aureus showed resistance to four antibiotics, Ampicillin, Amoxicillin/Clavulanic Acid, Erythromycin, and Azithromycin, with 100%, 93.1%, 82.75%, and 79.31%, respectively.

Then, the same techniques were used for Staphylococcal epidermidis; the diffusion disc approach was used to test the antibiotic sensitivity for the samples. As shown in Table 5 , the Staphylococcal epidermidis was susceptible to Rifampicin, Levofloxacin, Amoxicillin/Clavulanic Acid, and Trimethoprim/Sulfamethoxazole with (3/3) 100%. On the other hand, the Staphylococcal epidermidis showed resistance to Ampicillin, Erythromycin, and doxycycline.

## Discussion

AV presents a multifaceted challenge, involving chronic inflammation in pilosebaceous units primarily found in seborrheic areas like the face, neck, chest, and upper back. The primary reason, Cutibacterium acne, has historically been targeted with antibiotics, both topical and systemic, to alleviate symptoms. However, the efficacy of this approach is increasingly hampered by the emergence of antibiotic-resistant strains.

Despite antibiotics like clindamycin, macrolides, and tetracyclines traditionally being effective against Cutibacterium acne, their overuse has led to a rise in resistant strains globally. This resistance not only compromises treatment outcomes but also heightens the risk of recurrent outbreaks. Moreover, recent studies have identified other microorganisms, such as Staphylococcus aureus and Staphylococcus epidermidis, which exhibit varying responses to antibiotics, further complicating treatment decisions.[ 10 11 12 ]

Previously, Cutibacterium acne was regarded the most causative anaerobic microbe in the pathogeneses of AV exacerbations; in the present study, from a total of 50 AV patients, other organisms had been identified, like staphylococcal aures, (29) Cutibbacterium acne (23), and staphylococcal epidermidis (3), with great differences to antibiotic response, and this reflected on the successfulness of therapy. Therefore, before prescribing any oral antibiotics for acne, history of topical and systemic antibiotic usage must be taken.

The most affected age group prone to have AV was 17–28 years, with predominantly female gender in the present study, and this is consistent with other previous studies.[ 9 ]

In respect to the types of bacterial species, in the present report, three types were found with different percentages, mainly staphylococcal aureus 29, then cutibacterium acne 23, and last staphylococcal epidermidis 3 mostly mixed with cutibacterium acne , in contrast to the study conducted by Iranians that showed P. acne 41%, then staphylococcal epidermidis 34%, and the least staphylococcal aureus 5% from samples collected from the face.

An Egyptian study showed the most common AV bacteria was mainly staphylococcal epidermidis (44%), followed by P. acne (35%) and then staph. Aereus (11%). Loena Sari et al . also report the most common aerobic bacteria in AV lesion was staphylococcal epidermidis (47.5%), then staph. aeruis (8.7%), while anaerobic bacteria was P. acne (21.2%), and the most common mixed growth was P. acne and staphylococcal epidermidis (13.7%). Variations in geographical regions may influence the bacteria implicated in AV, thus accounting for differences in bacterial distribution among acne cases. Current research has pointed to the idea that C. acnes and S. epidermidis have a symbiotic relationship. Both bacteria exist on the normal flora of the skin, and a disrupt in balance of these bacteria on the skin can result in acne or other bacterial infections.[ 13 ] Whether this is a root causality, just opportunistic and a side effect, or a more complex pathological duality between C. acnes and this particular Staphylococcus species is not known.[ 14 ] Antibiotics are commonly employed in treating acne, serving either as bactericidal agents or as anti-inflammatory agents. However, the widespread use of antibiotics has led to the emergence of resistant strains of Propionibacterium acnes (P. acnes) , a key bacterium involved in acne pathology.

An interesting paper from Iran in 2008 shows that P. acnes (Cutibacterium acne) , the most common microbe isolate taken from AV patients, was sensitive to Azithromycin (98.3%), Doxycycline (98.3%), and tetracycline (93.1%) and the least sensitive to cotrimazole (69%) and clindamycin (56.9%). About 31% of the P. acnes (Cutibacterium acne) was resistant at least to one antibiotic. In the present study regarding the P. acnes (Cutibacterium acne) , the sensitivity to the following drugs in ascending order was to Azithromycin (52.17%), Erythromycin (56.52%), Trimethoprim/Sulfamethoxazole (56.52%), Doxycycline (69.56%), clindamycin (73.915), and tetracycline (82.6%); this change in the sensitivity can explain by the revolution of antibiotics with time. However, on the other hand, our results showed that Levofloxacin and Ciprofloxacin were the most sensitive treatments in acne for both. Both of them were (96.55%) and P. acnes , 95.65% and 86.95%, respectively . [ 15 ]

According to an Egyptian study regarding the antibiotic susceptibility patterns of P. acnes ( Cutibacterium acne ) patients with AV, the results showed high sensitivity rates of levofloxacin (80%) than doxycycline (51.4%) and highly resistant to the following drugs in descending order: clindamycin (85.7%), erythromycin (82.9%), trimethoprim/sulfamethoxazole (80%), and tetracycline (62.9%).[ 16 17 ] In comparison with the present results, there is a similar finding but with a higher rate of sensitivity regarding levofloxacin (95.65%) and doxycycline (69.56%) and a lower rate of resistance regarding clindamycin (26%), erythromycin (43.47%), trimethoprim/sulfamethoxazole (43.47%), and tetracycline (17.39%).

The reason for the difference in the in vitro antibiotic susceptibility patterns of P. acnes among different countries is not clear, although it may be contributed to the different antibiotic prescribing habits and⁄or different ethnicities of the patients.[ 18 19 20 ]

Although the exact cause of P. acnes resistance to antibiotics is not fully understood, it can be related to the inability to obtain in vivo , in the sebaceous follicle of acne patients, a concentration of antibiotic greater than the minimum inhibitory concentration.[ 21 ] P. acnes resistant to antibiotics may be also related to poor treatment compliance, and easy access to therapeutic agents without medical supervision.

Prolonged use of antibiotics is also one of the factors that have contributed to the development of antibiotic resistance.[ 22 23 ]

However, further studies are recommended to assess the in vivo efficacy of this antibiotic in treatment of inflammatory acne to prove its validity and to exclude the possibility of emergence of cross-resistance among different types antibiotics.

## Conclusion

Overall, the susceptibility patterns of P. acnes in vitro varied among Iraqi individuals with AV in relation to routinely administered antibiotics (in our results, the antibiotic susceptibility/sensitivity to Cutibacterium acnes isolate was different/changed from previous studies, with high sensitivity to levofloxacllin, ciprofloxacillin, and tetracyclin and more resistance to ampicillin, amoxilin/clavulinic acid, and azithromycin), with high sensitivity of Cutibacterium acnes to more than one drug, levofloxacllin, ciprofloxacillin, and tetracyclin and high resistance to ampicillin and amoxilin/clavulinic acid and in between to azithromycin, erythromycin, and trim-sulfa. Regarding bacteria isolate in AV, the two most common are Staphylococcus aureus and Cutibacterium acnes and the least Staphylococcus epidermidis, which mostly existed in mixed growth with Cutibacterium acnes. Therefore, more research is needed to determine the effectiveness of these antibiotics in treating acne in real-life situations. We suggest that this study should be extended to include a broader sample of acne patients from various regions in Iraq to evaluate the clinical effectiveness of antibiotics that are susceptible to P. acnes in vitro , to give us the better strategy in the treatment protocol of AV to decrease the failure rate and bad complications of this disease. Last, we recommend to survey large study groups with different ages.

# Cultural Competency in Sustainable Dermatology: Climate Change, Environmental Impact, and Traditional Care

## Abstract
Climate change and environmental degradation profoundly affect skin health, necessitating sustainable dermatological practices. Integrating cultural competency enhances these efforts by respecting traditional care systems while promoting eco-conscious choices. Many Indian communities use plant-based, biodegradable, and locally sourced ingredients such as coconut oil, Shikakai, soapnut, hibiscus, and henna, aligning naturally with sustainability goals. Evaluating the life-cycle impact of dermatologic products, reducing plastic use, and incorporating cultural practices like sari or turban-based sun protection can advance equitable and green dermatology. Combining scientific evidence with traditional wisdom fosters inclusive, ethical, and environmentally responsible skin care for a resilient dermatological future.

## Keywords
Climate change; cultural competency; sustainable dermatology

## Introduction

Climate change significantly impacts overall and skin health. Ozone depletion predisposes to melanomas and keratinocyte carcinomas. Air pollution disrupts the skin microbiome, worsens inflammation, and can play a role in conditions such as photoaging, acne, atopic dermatitis, psoriasis, and pemphigus. Vulnerable and marginalised populations will bear the brunt of climate change.[ 1 ] Sustainable dermatology emphasises eco-friendly skin care and treatment practices, aiming to minimise environmental impact without compromising patient care.[ 2 ] Integrating cultural competency into these efforts ensures that care respects diverse beliefs, practices, and needs, enabling inclusive and environmentally responsible dermatological care.[ 3 ] This synergy enhances patient outcomes while fostering ethical and sustainable practices.[ 4 ]

Recognising cultural diversity is crucial to sustainable dermatology as traditional remedies and locally sourced ingredients often align with sustainability goals.[ 1 5 ] sustainability has environmental, social, and economic dimensions. Dermatologists must adapt eco-conscious practices to diverse socio-economic contexts, ensuring accessibility and affordability. By integrating cultural awareness into sustainability efforts, dermatologists can co-create environmentally responsible and culturally relevant solutions, promoting equity in care delivery.

The healthcare sector is a significant greenhouse gas emitter (4.4%).[ 6 ] Personal care products like soaps, aftershaves, shampoos, fragrances, sprays, and other agents used in skin or hair care routines also significantly impact the environment, making sustainability a key concern in dermatology. These products often contain synthetic chemicals, microplastics, and volatile organic compounds (VOCs), which can harm aquatic ecosystems, contribute to air pollution, and disrupt biodiversity.

A Life-Cycle Assessment (LCA), which analyses the environmental impact of all stages of a product from manufacture to disposal, should be considered for every dermatologist-recommended product. Excessive layers of packaging materials, including plastic land, are up in landfills. Patients may also be interested in their skin-care ingredients’ source and carbon footprint. However, several companies market ‘green’ ingredients and formulations, which are unconfirmed due to the absence of regulations.[ 5 ]

Low-carbon alternatives and lean care systems are integral to sustainable healthcare.[ 1 ] The environmental impact of skin care products is particularly important in rural communities in developing countries with limited waste management options. In India, several communities often address their skin-care needs with locally sourced traditional ingredients. The practices and ingredients are usually based on generational knowledge or ancient medicinal texts. Ayurvedic texts describe 1800 plants, and 8000 plants are mentioned in folklore literature for diverse uses.[ 7 ] Some ingredients’ lack of evidence and limited efficacy need to be weighed against cultural preferences and affordability. Some of these practices are reviewed below.

## Emollients

Plant-based oils such as coconut and sesame oil are commonly used for skin and hair care in India. The coconut ( Cocos nucifera L., family Arecaceae) is a multi-purpose tree in tropical and sub-tropical regions. The dried kernel, or copra, primarily used for oil extraction, contains 65–75% oil. Available as virgin or refined, coconut oil is an inexpensive, safe, and preferred emollient in several rural communities [ Figure 1a ].

## Abhyanga

Abhyanga is the traditional Ayurvedic practice of anointing herbal oils to maintain and promote health. Vegetable oils are used for traditional neonatal massages. These ancient practices promote relaxation without the use of multiple synthetic components.

## Lentils–saponins

Saponins, natural surfactants found in many plants, including lentils, have cleansing properties due to their ability to emulsify oils and dirt. For bathing, lentils can be ground into a fine powder, or the saponins can be extracted by soaking or boiling [ Figure 1b ]. These compounds can create a lathering effect when mixed with water. Lentil flours are commonly used to cleanse hair and skin in India. Oil is frequently applied before their use to avoid excessive dryness. Individual skin sensitivities may limit their use.

## Shikakai

Acacia concinna , or Shikakai, is a climbing shrub native to Asia, particularly in Central and South India. Traditionally used as a natural shampoo, its dried fruit pods are ground into a powder to create a gentle paste that cleanses and conditions the hair. It has foam-forming saponins and alpha-hydroxy acids for exfoliating alpha-hydroxy acids. Shikakai is widely used in India and the Far East as an eco-friendly, biodegradable alternative to synthetic shampoos.

## Soapnut

Sapindus, a genus in the Sapindaceae family, includes two main species, Sapindus mukorossi and Sapindus trifoliatus , native to tropical and sub-tropical Asia. The fruits, known as soapnuts or reetha, are widely used for hair cleansing in India [ Figure 1c ]. The main chemical components of soapnuts include saponins, sapindoside A and B, flavonoids like kaempferol and quercetin, and essential fatty acids. The traditional method involves soaking whole soapnuts in warm water, pressing the foamy liquid, and applying it to the hair. The dried powder is also used, often mixed with other natural ingredients like Shikakai, fenugreek, and fragrant herbs.

## Hibiscus

Hibiscus rosa-sinensis, also known as hibiscus or shoe flower, is an evergreen shrub native to East Asia, renowned for its vibrant flowers in shades ranging from white to red. In Kerala, a state in southern India, hibiscus has long been used in traditional hair care rituals. The flowers and leaves are prized for their cleansing and conditioning effects on hair. The foaming mucilage from the flowers and leaves is often extracted by crushing them with water [ Figure 1d ]. It is also infused into coconut or sesame oil for hair care. When burned, the flowers and leaves produce a natural black dye, further highlighting the plant’s versatility.

## Flowers–fragrance

The fragrance industry contributes to air pollution and generates packaging waste. In South India, women traditionally adorn their hair with flowers. Jasmine ( Jasminum spp.) from the Oleaceae family is commonly worn as flower strings [ Figure 2a and b ]. The jasmine scent is cherished globally and also plays a significant role in the perfume industry, where its aroma is derived from a blend of phytochemicals and alcohol-based compounds.[ 4 ]

## Sun Protection

Sunscreens protect against UV radiation, yet active UV filters, particularly organic ones, pose environmental concerns by accumulating in marine ecosystems and negatively impacting aquatic biodiversity. We have observed reduced compliance for sunscreen use due to prohibitive costs in several patients. In some states in North India, women cover their heads with their sari (‘ghoonghat’), while men use turbans [ Figure 2c ] for cultural or religious reasons. Some women use long stoles [‘dupatta’, Figure 2d ] to protect their faces from the sun. While these methods may not be ideal or suitable for all, incorporating existing cultural practices may improve sun safety behaviours sustainably.

## Henna

Lawsonia inermis , commonly known as henna, is a flowering plant native to southern Asia, tropical and subtropical Africa, and northern Australia. Henna has been used centuries as a dye for skin, hair, nails, and textiles. Its cosmetic use dates back to ancient India, the Middle East, and Africa. Henna is widely used as a natural hair dye, creating a range of colours from auburn to deep burgundy and black [ Figure 2d ]. Henna’s colouring properties come from lawsone, a naphthaquinone dye that binds with proteins in hair.

## Conclusion

Looking back on traditional customs and utilising locally available practices offers a sustainable path forward in dermatology. Skin and hair care rituals symbolise beauty, identity, and self-expression from ancient cultures to modern times. Yet, their production and use often reflect a culture of vanity, accompanied by the unsustainable exploitation of Earth’s resources. The demand for ethical consumerism is surging in an era of increased awareness and education. Individuals are now prioritising products that embody sustainability and social responsibility, paving the way for a dermatological future that harmonises tradition, innovation, and environmental stewardship.

# From Bioactive Selenium Nanoparticles to Multifunctional Dermatological Platforms: Mechanism-Guided Design and Translational Challenges

## Abstract
Skin diseases are characterized by complex pathophysiology and substantial clinical heterogeneity. Their onset and progression involve multiple interconnected processes, including oxidative stress, chronic inflammation, disruption of the skin barrier, microbial dysbiosis, and impaired tissue repair, which often limit the ability of conventional therapies to achieve sustained disease control. Selenium nanoparticles (SeNPs) offer distinct advantages in dermatological treatment by combining the intrinsic biological activities of selenium, such as redox regulation and immunomodulation, with the engineering versatility of nanomaterials. However, therapeutic approaches that rely solely on the inherent bioactivity of SeNPs are increasingly insufficient to address the complexity of disease-associated microenvironments. Accordingly, the development of SeNPs into intelligent, multifunctional therapeutic platforms has emerged as an important direction in this field. Existing reviews have largely focused on the biological functions, preparation methods, or broad biomedical applications of SeNPs, whereas the engineering principles underlying their transition from intrinsically active nanomaterials to intelligent dermatological therapeutic platforms have not been systematically examined. This review therefore focuses on how the intrinsic functions of selenium can be translated, through materials and delivery engineering, into platform-level capabilities relevant to the treatment of skin diseases. By linking disease-specific pathological features and delivery barriers with corresponding design strategies, we propose a mechanism-guided framework for the rational development of SeNP-based dermatological nanomedicines.

## Keywords
selenium nanoparticles; dermatological nanomedicine; multifunctional nanoplatforms; skin barrier; mechanism-guided design

## Introduction

Skin diseases constitute a considerable global health burden, encompassing inflammatory dermatoses, hair disorders, UV-induced skin injury, chronic trauma, skin tumor and so on. 1–4 Despite their clinical and therapeutic heterogeneity, these conditions often converge on shared, interrelated pathological features—compromised epidermal barrier integrity, redox imbalance, aberrant immune signaling, microbial dysbiosis, vascular dysfunction, dysregulated extracellular matrix remodeling, and impaired tissue repair. 5 These processes are not independent: barrier disruption heightens exposure to environmental antigens and microbes, oxidative stress amplifies inflammatory cascades, and chronic inflammation further impedes barrier recovery and tissue regeneration. 6 Consequently, effective dermatological treatment requires targeted drug delivery to the appropriate skin compartment. 7 , 8 It also demands coordinated modulation of multiple pathological pathways rather than suppression of a single downstream target. 9 , 10

Current dermatological therapies face three shared constraints. First, the stratum corneum impedes penetration of small-molecule drugs, biologics, and nanocarriers, limiting effective drug exposure in the viable epidermis, dermis, hair follicles, or wound bed. 7 Second, inflammatory, infectious, ischemic, or tumor-associated lesions establish a dynamic microenvironment characterized by excessive reactive oxygen species, aberrant pH, hypoxia, and protease imbalance, 11 , 12 often accompanied by sustained immune cell infiltration and microbial biofilm formation. 13 Third, repeated or prolonged use of corticosteroids, systemic immunosuppressants, pigmentation-modulating agents, or antineoplastic drugs may be limited by local adverse effects and systemic toxicity; 14 antimicrobial resistance further hinders long-term antibiotic therapy, 15 and some treatments lack tissue selectivity or lead to disease recurrence upon withdrawal. 16 Simply escalating the dose fails to overcome these barriers. 8 Instead, drug delivery depth, local retention, release kinetics, and therapeutic function must be matched to the anatomical and pathological features of the target lesion. 9

Within the field of nanomedicine, various inorganic nanoparticle platforms have been explored for dermatological applications. Gold nanoparticles, valued for their ease of surface functionalization, have been employed in photothermal therapy and drug delivery; however, their metabolic inertness and poor biodegradability raise concerns regarding prolonged local or systemic retention. 17 Silver nanoparticles exhibit potent antimicrobial activity, yet their biological effects are closely tied to Ag⁺ release, which may induce oxidative damage to host cells and argyria—limitations that restrict their use in chronic skin diseases requiring repeated treatment. 18 Zinc oxide nanoparticles serve in UV protection and photocatalysis, but under certain irradiation and inflammatory conditions, their ROS-generating activity may exacerbate host cell damage, necessitating strict control of dose and exposure. 19 Copper nanoparticles hold promise for pro-angiogenic and antimicrobial applications, yet concerns persist regarding their oxidative stability, dose-dependent toxicity, and copper overload. 20 Against this backdrop, SeNPs offer the potential to combine the redox and immunomodulatory functions of selenium with the engineering versatility of nanomaterials. 21 , 22 This advantage, however, holds only when dose, surface state, and in vivo biotransformation are adequately controlled. 23 , 24

The therapeutic value of SeNPs, however, cannot be reduced to the sum of their intrinsic biological activities. 21 Unmodified SeNPs are prone to aggregation, exhibit inconsistent bioavailability, lack targeting to specific lesions or cell populations, and are ill-equipped to modulate complex pathological networks. 25 , 26 The field has thus shifted from treating SeNPs as standalone active agents toward the construction of SeNP-based smart platforms. 27 , 28

Existing reviews have systematically covered SeNP applications in dermatology, as well as the preparation, physicochemical properties, and broad therapeutic uses of nanoselenium. 21 , 29 What remains absent is a design-centered analytical framework that explains why monofunctional nanoselenium falls short in addressing complex skin diseases and clarifies how surface functionalization, barrier-bypassing delivery, microenvironment-responsive release, and multimodal integration overcome these limitations. 27 Accordingly, this review is organized around the evolution of SeNPs from discrete bioactive nanoparticles to multifunctional platforms for skin therapy. We critically examine the relationship between disease-specific therapeutic barriers and corresponding engineering strategies—including surface functionalization, transdermal delivery, microenvironment-responsive release, local retention matrices, and combination therapy—and discuss representative applications in inflammatory skin diseases, androgenetic alopecia, UV-induced skin damage, chronic and infectious wounds, and post-melanoma surgical management. Finally, we address current limitations in material definition, dose standardization, mechanistic validation, manufacturing reproducibility, and long-term safety. Through this analysis, we reframe the central question from “what biological effects does nanoselenium exert” to “how can selenium-based multifunctional platforms be rationally engineered,” aiming to provide a mechanism-oriented analytical framework for the design and clinical translation of selenium-based dermatological nanomedicines.

The overall conceptual framework of this review is shown in Figure 1 . Figure 1 Evolution of selenium nanoparticles from monofunctional agents to intelligent dermatological therapeutic platforms (This figure is drawn by biorender). Selenium nanoparticles (SeNPs) possess multiple intrinsic biological activities, including anti-inflammatory, antioxidant, antibacterial/antibiofilm, immunomodulatory, pro-healing, and antitumor effects. However, monofunctional SeNPs are often insufficient to address the complex and heterogeneous microenvironments of skin diseases. By means of platform engineering strategies, SeNPs can be further improved by surface modification, transdermal delivery system, stimulus-responsive release, and synergistic drug loading. These methods increase nanoparticle stability, skin penetration, target lesion delivery, controlled release, and therapeutic synergy. Multifunctional SeNP platforms show possible uses for dermatitis, UV-damaged skin, hair loss, infected wounds or chronic sores, melanoma care after surgery, indicating a move from basic active nanomaterials to smart skin treatments with SeNPs. The diagram illustrates the evolution of selenium nanoparticles (SeNPs) from monofunctional agents to advanced dermatological applications. On the left, monofunctional SeNPs exhibit properties such as anti-inflammatory, antioxidant, antibacterial/antibiofilm, immunomodulatory, pro-healing and antitumor effects. The central section details platform engineering strategies, including surface functionalization with PEG, HSA and Lentinan, transdermal delivery systems using microneedles, local retention matrix options like hydrogel, film and nanofiber matrices and synergistic loading with Shikonin, Tranexamic acid and Mupirocin. The right section shows dermatological applications: dermatitis (psoriasis, atopic dermatitis, allergic dermatitis), UV-induced skin damage androgenetic alopecia, infected/chronic wounds and melanoma. Diagram of SeNPs′ functions, engineering strategies and dermatological uses. Abbreviations : SeNPs, selenium nanoparticles; ROS, reactive oxygen species; PEG, polyethylene glycol; HSA, human serum albumin.

## Intrinsic Bioactivities of SeNPs as the Mechanistic Basis for Platform Design

### Redox and Inflammatory Regulation

Antioxidant and anti-inflammatory activities represent two of the most prominent biological properties of SeNPs, linked through the reciprocal regulation between redox homeostasis and inflammatory signaling. 6 SeNPs exhibit moderate antioxidant capacity in cell-free radical-scavenging assays such as DPPH and ABTS, 30 , 31 while simultaneously bolstering endogenous cellular antioxidant defense. 32 , 33 Evidence indicates that SeNPs activate Nrf2-related signaling, promoting the expression or activity of antioxidant enzymes including glutathione peroxidase, superoxide dismutase, and catalase. 34 Concurrently, SeNPs elevate intracellular glutathione levels, thereby attenuating ROS accumulation and lipid peroxidation, reducing malondialdehyde formation, and preserving mitochondrial function against oxidative damage. 35 , 36 Unlike agents that rely solely on stoichiometric radical scavenging, SeNPs engage the endogenous antioxidant system to sustain longer-lasting redox protection. 22

The anti-inflammatory effects of SeNPs are closely linked to their capacity to limit oxidative stress. Excessive ROS activates NF-κB, the NLRP3 inflammasome, and other redox-sensitive inflammatory pathways. By reducing ROS burden and modulating downstream signaling, SeNPs can decrease the production of TNF-α, IL-1β, IL-6, and iNOS-derived NO while, in some models, increasing IL-10. 33 , 37 Skin-relevant studies further show reduced inflammatory-cell infiltration and shifts in macrophage polarization in allergic dermatitis, infected wounds, and melanoma. 33 , 37–39 Thus, the antioxidant–anti-inflammatory axis of SeNPs is supported directly in dermatological models rather than only in systemic inflammatory settings. 33 , 34 , 37

### Antibacterial, Antibiofilm, and Immune-Regulatory Activity

The antibacterial, antibiofilm, and immunomodulatory properties of SeNPs collectively underpin their potential in infection management. 38 SeNPs have demonstrated growth-inhibitory activity against a range of Gram-positive and Gram-negative pathogens, including Staphylococcus aureus , Escherichia coli , Pseudomonas aeruginosa , and Klebsiella pneumoniae . 40 , 41 Their antibacterial efficacy is modulated by particle size, surface coating, aggregation state, selenium release kinetics, microbial species, and exposure concentration. 42 Proposed mechanisms involve disruption of bacterial membrane integrity and permeability, induction of intracellular oxidative stress, interference with protein function and key metabolic enzymes, culminating in energy metabolism collapse and cell damage. 40 Notably, whereas SeNPs often alleviate excessive ROS in host cells, they can provoke oxidative damage in microbial or tumor cells—a divergence that underscores the dose-, cell type-, and microenvironment-dependent nature of their redox effects. 43 , 44

Beyond planktonic growth inhibition, SeNPs interfere with biofilm formation and maintenance. Evidence shows they reduce initial microbial adhesion and extracellular polymeric substance accumulation, decrease biofilm biomass and viable cell counts, and may destabilize biofilm architecture by modulating quorum-sensing systems and downregulating genes associated with adhesion and biofilm maturation. 45 , 46 Given that mature biofilms exhibit low metabolic activity, restricted drug penetration, and heightened tolerance, combining SeNPs with antibiotics can enhance therapeutic outcomes. 47 , 48 This combination strategy likely works by simultaneously disrupting biofilm barriers and suppressing bacterial proliferation. 49 In certain studies, antibiotic-loaded or surface-functionalized SeNP systems have lowered the effective antibiotic concentration required and improved efficacy against resistant strains and mature biofilms. 47 SeNPs thus serve a dual role: as intrinsically active antimicrobial agents and as local delivery vehicles for antimicrobial drugs or anti-infective coatings on medical device surfaces. 48

Host immune modulation may also contribute to the anti-infective and antitumor effects of SeNPs. In an MRSA infection model, surface-engineered SeNPs acted as bactericidal and immunomodulatory agents, whereas gluconic acid-coated SeNPs promoted M2-to-M1 macrophage repolarization in melanoma. 38 , 39 These findings suggest that SeNP-mediated immune regulation is context dependent and is shaped by dose, surface chemistry, administration route, and the local immune microenvironment. 24 , 38 , 39

### Tissue Repair and Regenerative Activity

The capacity to promote tissue repair constitutes another key biological activity of SeNPs, engaging multiple interrelated processes—reparative cell recruitment, extracellular matrix (ECM) remodeling, and angiogenesis. 50 , 51 In vitro evidence indicates that SeNPs enhance the proliferation and migration of fibroblasts and other repair-associated cells, accelerate scratch closure, and facilitate fibroblast activation toward a repair phenotype. 52 The resulting increase in fibroblast numbers and migratory capacity supports granulation tissue formation, laying the cellular groundwork for subsequent ECM deposition and tissue remodeling. 53

SeNPs also modulate collagen synthesis, deposition, and organization. 54 , 55 In animal wound models, SeNP-incorporated composites have been shown to increase collagen deposition at wound sites, improve the organization of collagen fibers, and promote granulation tissue maturation. 35 Some studies have concurrently observed upregulated expression of matrix-remodeling factors such as TGF-β, suggesting that SeNPs may accelerate the transition from the proliferative to the remodeling phase by modulating fibroblast function and ECM turnover. 56 However, TGF-β signaling and collagen deposition are inherently phase-dependent; sustained or excessive activation may heighten the risk of aberrant fibrosis and scar formation. An increase in collagen content therefore cannot be equated straightforwardly with higher-quality tissue repair. 51

In addition, SeNPs promote VEGF/VEGFA-related angiogenic signaling and new blood vessel formation, thereby improving local oxygen and nutrient supply to support cell survival, matrix synthesis, and tissue regeneration. 57 Their antioxidant, anti-inflammatory, and antibacterial activities collectively improve the wound microenvironment, attenuating the disruptive effects of excessive ROS, persistent inflammation, and microbial burden on the repair process. 58 The pro-repair effects of SeNPs thus do not arise from a single proliferative mechanism but likely emerge from the coordinated modulation of inflammation resolution, fibroblast migration, angiogenesis, and ECM remodeling, driving multiple phases of wound healing.

### Antitumor Activity

Direct evidence relevant to cutaneous tumors is concentrated mainly in melanoma models. Polysaccharide-stabilized and drug-functionalized SeNPs inhibited A375 melanoma-cell proliferation by inducing mitochondrial dysfunction, apoptosis, and cell-cycle arrest. 43 , 44 , 59 These studies showed modulation of Bcl-2-family proteins and activation of caspase-dependent apoptosis, although the contribution of the selenium core could not always be separated from that of the surface ligand or co-loaded drug. 43 , 44

Mitochondrial dysfunction appears to be a central mechanism of SeNP-induced melanoma-cell death. SeNP uptake can increase intracellular ROS, depolarize the mitochondrial membrane, promote cytochrome c release, and activate the caspase-9/caspase-3 pathway. 43 , 59 This pro-oxidant behavior contrasts with the antioxidant effects observed in stressed non-malignant skin cells and probably reflects differences in basal redox state, dose, particle size, coating, and intracellular distribution. 23 , 43 , 60

SeNPs may also interfere with melanoma-cell cycle progression. Surface-modified formulations have produced S-phase arrest and reduced the expression of cyclin D1, cyclin E, and CDK2, although the phase and magnitude of arrest vary with particle formulation and exposure conditions. 44 , 59

Taken together, the melanoma literature supports a combination of redox disruption, mitochondrial injury, caspase-dependent apoptosis, cell-cycle arrest, and, more recently, macrophage reprogramming. 39 , 43 , 44 , 59 However, most studies remain preclinical and use polysaccharide-, protein-, or drug-modified particles. Future work should therefore distinguish the selenium-core effect from the effects of coatings and co-loaded agents, and should define tumor selectivity, effective dose windows, and local safety in vivo. 39 , 43 , 44

## SeNP-Based Platform Engineering Strategies for Dermatology

### Particle Stabilization and Bio-Interface Engineering

SeNPs possess a high specific surface area and correspondingly elevated surface energy, rendering unprotected particles susceptible to aggregation during synthesis, storage, formulation, and upon contact with electrolytes or biomacromolecules. 26 Aggregation may alter hydrodynamic size, sedimentation behavior, protein adsorption, cellular uptake, and effective selenium exposure. 25 Surface engineering thus serves not only to improve colloidal stability but also to establish biologically reproducible interfaces. 23

SeNPs can be stabilized through steric hindrance, electrostatic repulsion, or a combination of both. In dermatological studies, human serum albumin improved the colloidal stability and biocompatibility of SeNPs used for UVB-induced skin injury, whereas lentinan modification combined particle stabilization with anti-allergic and selenoprotein-related activity. 33 , 60 Chitosan-containing SeNP films provided a locally retained antimicrobial interface in infected wounds, and gluconic acid coating altered SeNP interactions with tumor-associated macrophages in melanoma. 39 , 61 These examples show that a coating is not merely a physical stabilizer; it may also change cellular uptake, tissue interactions, and the biological contribution of the final formulation.

Consequently, improved efficacy after surface modification cannot be attributed automatically to increased selenium bioavailability. Dermatological studies should compare bare SeNPs, the coating material alone, and the final coated formulation at matched elemental selenium doses, while also documenting whether the coating changes particle size, aggregation, release, or cell-specific interactions. 33 , 39 , 60–62

### Barrier Bypass and Skin Compartment-Targeted Delivery

The stratum corneum remains the principal anatomical barrier to topical delivery, and barrier disruption caused by disease does not guarantee stable, reproducible drug penetration. 7 Different dermatological conditions further require therapeutic components to reach distinct anatomical compartments—epidermal keratinocytes in psoriasis, the perifollicular microenvironment in androgenetic alopecia, the viable wound bed in chronic ulcers, and residual tumor tissue following melanoma excision. 63

Soluble, degradable, or hydrogel-based microneedles can physically bypass the stratum corneum and deposit nanoparticles or co-delivered agents into viable skin. 64 In SeNP-related dermatological studies, microneedles have been used to deliver a ROS-responsive SeHA platform in psoriasis, selenium nanozyme-containing extracellular vesicles to the perifollicular region in androgenetic alopecia, and Se-AR PROTAC nanoparticles for local androgen-receptor degradation. 9 , 63 , 65 Their performance depends on needle geometry, mechanical strength, insertion depth, payload distribution, dissolution or swelling kinetics, and the fraction of the loaded dose that is actually deposited in skin. 9 , 63–65

In a recent study on androgenetic alopecia, researchers loaded hypoxia-induced selenium nanozyme-containing extracellular vesicles into astragalus polysaccharide-modified microneedles. 63 This system was designed to bypass the skin surface barrier and ameliorate the perifollicular microenvironment while modulating oxidative stress, angiogenesis, and inflammation. Microneedles thus shift selenium-containing therapeutic components from passive surface exposure to targeted perifollicular or intradermal delivery. 66

Therapeutic benefit in an alopecia model does not by itself prove that intact SeNPs accumulate within hair follicles. The Se-HEVs-AMN study demonstrated microneedle-mediated efficacy but did not fully resolve the spatial distribution and chemical state of selenium after delivery. 63 Future studies should combine elemental quantification with particle-specific imaging or selenium speciation to determine where selenium is deposited, in what form, for how long, and whether compartment-targeted delivery outperforms a simpler topical formulation. 62 , 67 The design objective should therefore be delivery matched to lesion location rather than maximal penetration. 8

### Local Retention Matrices and Sustained Exposure Control

Topically applied nanoparticle suspensions can be removed by friction, movement, sweat, wound exudate, or dressing changes, resulting in uneven and poorly controlled local exposure. Direct SeNP studies have addressed this problem using dynamic hydrogels, bacterial-cellulose/gelatin matrices, protein-based nanofibers, and adhesive gelatin-based nanocomposites. 37 , 50 , 56 , 68 These matrices do more than hold particles in place: depending on their composition, they can maintain moisture, absorb exudate, provide tissue adhesion, protect the wound surface, and regulate SeNP release. 37 , 50 , 56 , 68

Hydrogels entrap SeNPs within a hydrated polymer network. Depending on the formulation, particle migration may be further curtailed by electrostatic interactions, hydrogen bonding, hydrophobic interactions, covalent linkage, or reversible dynamic bonds. 50 Release kinetics are shaped by mesh size, swelling degree, particle–polymer affinity, degradation, erosion, and the diffusion coefficients of each payload. 52 Adhesive hydrogels add another advantage: they resist detachment from moist or mobile tissue surfaces. In wound care, hydrogel matrices absorb exudate, maintain moisture, reduce friction, and serve as a physical barrier—benefits that aid repair regardless of whether SeNPs are present. 53 , 69 One example is a bacterial cellulose/gelatin hydrogel with in situ–synthesized SeNPs, which maintains a moist wound environment, provides a porous scaffold, and sustains SeNP release for antibacterial, antioxidant, and anti-inflammatory action. 50 A more recent design—a heparin-grafted carboxymethyl chitosan (CMCS-g-Hep)/oxidized hyaluronic acid hydrogel—co-delivers SeNPs alongside basic fibroblast growth factor (bFGF), supplying SeNP-driven antimicrobial and redox modulation while slowly releasing the labile growth factor. This formulation promoted fibroblast proliferation and migration in vitro and accelerated skin defect closure in mice. 70

Beyond hydrogels, films, patches, electrospun nanofibers, sponges, and in situ gelling systems have all been explored as retention formats. 71 Films and patches suit relatively flat lesions and can deliver a well-defined dose per unit area, but they may occlude too aggressively or fail to conform to irregular, exudative, hairy, or highly mobile surfaces. 56 Electrospun scaffolds offer high surface area and tunable porosity, though burst release becomes a concern when the payload concentrates on fiber surfaces. 72 In one melanoma-focused study, polycaprolactone/chitosan nanofibers co-loaded with SeNPs and paclitaxel showed good fluid uptake, favorable wetting, and multi-day sustained release—though anti-tumor data were confined to A375 cells in vitro.

The most informative retention studies are those that compare free SeNPs, the blank matrix, the SeNP-loaded matrix, and a relevant standard treatment at matched selenium doses. Local retention and tissue selenium should be measured directly rather than inferred from release in phosphate-buffered saline. 62 , 67 Current hydrogels and nanofibers demonstrate formulation feasibility and short-term efficacy, but direct measurements of skin pharmacokinetics, selenium speciation, repeated-dose safety, and performance in human skin remain uncommon. 37 , 50 , 56 , 68 , 70 A retention matrix should therefore be viewed as a means of shaping the duration and location of SeNP exposure, not as a passive carrier.

### Pharmacological Complementarity Through Multi-Component Integration

Skin diseases involve several interacting pathological processes. 2 When multiple drivers sustain a condition, a single therapeutic agent may prove insufficient. 3 The redox-modulatory, anti-inflammatory, antimicrobial, immunomodulatory, and pro-repair capacities of SeNPs can be paired with agents targeting other disease-relevant pathways, yielding multi-component therapeutic platforms. 73

A well-designed combination requires a clear division of labor between components. In infected wounds, SeNPs have been paired with doxycycline or mupirocin to combine local selenium-associated redox and antimicrobial activity with established antibiotic action. 47 , 48 In UVB-induced hyperpigmentation, PEGylated SeNPs were combined with tranexamic acid, whereas a selenium/ketoconazole hydrogel was designed for seborrheic dermatitis. 73 , 74 These platforms illustrate pharmacological complementarity, but they also show why single-agent, vehicle, and physical-mixture controls are required to determine whether integration provides an advantage over simple co-administration. 47 , 48 , 73 , 74

A chitosan patch co-loaded with SeNPs and doxycycline illustrates a representative combination for infected wounds. 48 The patch ensures local retention, doxycycline provides established antimicrobial activity, chitosan contributes film-forming properties and potential additional antimicrobial effects, and SeNPs may supplement redox modulation and antibacterial function. In a similar vein, a hyaluronic acid supramolecular hydrogel integrating selenium and ketoconazole nanoparticles was developed for seborrheic dermatitis, pairing antifungal pharmacology with a selenium-based topical platform. 74 These studies establish formulation feasibility, yet without single-agent, physical-mixture, and vehicle controls, the individual contributions of selenium, the conventional antimicrobial, and the carrier remain difficult to disentangle. 48

conclusions:
Taken together, the available evidence does not support a universal advantage of SeNPs in dermatological therapy, nor does it suggest that increasingly complex formulations are necessarily more effective. Rather, the value of selenium is context dependent. SeNPs are most likely to offer a meaningful advantage when their redox-regulatory, immunomodulatory, antimicrobial, or regenerative activities directly address a dominant feature of the target lesion, and when the delivery system provides appropriate local exposure without obscuring the contribution of selenium itself.

The studies reviewed here also indicate that different engineering modules should be selected according to the therapeutic barrier they are intended to overcome. Surface stabilization may be sufficient when aggregation and inconsistent bioavailability are the main limitations. Microneedles are better justified when follicular or dermal targets cannot be reached by passive topical delivery, whereas hydrogels and related matrices are particularly relevant to chronic, exudative, or infected lesions requiring prolonged local exposure. Responsive release and co-delivery should be introduced only when the triggering condition or complementary therapeutic mechanism has been clearly established. From this perspective, progress in the field should not be defined by the number of functions incorporated into a platform, but by whether each added component addresses a specific and experimentally verified need.

The evidence base remains uneven across dermatological indications. Wound healing and infection currently provide the broadest support for multifunctional SeNP platforms, although these systems also present the greatest difficulty in separating the effects of selenium from those of scaffolds, antibiotics, and other active components. Studies in androgenetic alopecia and UV-related skin damage provide promising proof of concept, but remain dependent on highly composite systems and short-term animal models. By comparison, platform-level evidence in psoriasis remains limited, and direct studies of elemental SeNPs in melanoma and other cutaneous tumors are still scarce.

The central question for future research is therefore not whether SeNPs possess broad biological activity, but whether selenium incorporation provides sufficient additional benefit to justify the resulting formulation complexity. This will require composition-matched selenium-free controls, comparisons with simpler SeNP formulations and current standard treatments, standardized reporting of elemental, delivered, and retained selenium doses, and direct characterization of selenium distribution, biotransformation, and clearance. Chronic efficacy, relapse after treatment withdrawal, repeated-dose safety, and manufacturing reproducibility must also be established. Only platforms that demonstrate a defined selenium-specific contribution, controlled tissue exposure, and a clinically relevant advantage over existing therapies should be advanced toward translational development. Addressing these issues will be essential for moving SeNP-based systems from promising preclinical formulations toward practical nanomedicines for dermatological therapy.
