# Using evidence-based models of human behaviour to reduce endocrine-disrupting chemicals exposure: recommendations for strengthening interventions

## Abstract
Endocrine-disrupting chemicals (EDCs) represent a threat for the ecosystem and human health. Exposure routes include modifiable exposures, such as choice of food or cosmetics but also daily habits such as airing the room. However, current attempts to reduce modifiable exposure often rely on knowledge provision and awareness-raising campaigns. This is the case even though human behaviour, decision making and habits change have been studied for a long time, and numerous psychological theories demonstrate that the transition from awareness of a health threat to actually change daily behaviour is not straightforward. This paper calls for interventions on EDCs exposure reduction to build on solid understanding of human behaviour and use of behaviour change techniques to achieve significant impact. We illustrate how this can be done by presenting the HYPIEND project, a multicomponent behavioural intervention designed to help pregnant women and prepubertal children (and their parents) to reduce their modifiable exposure to EDCs in these sensitive periods. HYPIEND relies on theoretical models such as the Health Action Process Approach (HAPA) model, motivational interviewing techniques, and broader support through partners (for pregnant women) and the school environment (for children) through a school-wide project built on the School Wide Positive Behavioural Interventions Supports.

## Keywords
Endocrine disruptors; Awareness raising; information deficit model; Health Action Process Approach (HAPA); School Wide Positive Behavioural Interventions and Supports (SWPBIS); Behaviour change techniques (BCTs); Lifestyle interventions

## Disclaimer

The views expressed in this article are those of the authors. Publication in Open Research Europe does not imply endorsement of the European Commission.

## Context

The Endocrine Society defines an endocrine disrupting chemical (EDC) as: “an exogenous chemical, or mixture of chemicals, that can interfere with any aspect of hormone action”. 1 , 2 Among EDCs, some naturally occurring compounds can be found 3 ; however, most of them are synthetic, human-made chemicals. According to estimates of the European Environment Agency, approximately 70% of around 100,000 chemicals on the EU market have been poorly assessed for their safe use. 4 A significant number of them have been found to disrupt the endocrine system. As of June 2025, 227 substances were identified as EDCs at the EU level ( List I ), and additional 104 substances are currently under evaluation ( List II ). Importantly, the Global Chemical Outlook II states that global trends, such as population dynamics, urbanisation, and economic growth, are rapidly increasing chemical use, particularly in emerging economies. 5 Recent studies all around the globe have demonstrated the presence of EDCs in the environment. 6 – 8

EDCs can have substantial impact on ecosystem and human health. 1 For instance, they can induce a wide array of reproductive and developmental disturbances in aquatic species, 9 , 10 as well as in birds and mammals. 9 Studies conducted in grassland and freshwater ecosystems have demonstrated that EDCs-induced disturbances can lead to reductions in both biomass and the capacity for ecosystem recovery. 10 Regarding human health, EDCs can interfere with endogenous hormone biosynthesis, metabolism, or action, disrupting homeostatic and developmental processes. 11 Epidemiological and experimental studies have linked EDCs exposure to impaired reproductive function, immune impairment, neurodevelopmental deficits, metabolic disorders, and hormone-dependent cancers. 12

Interventions and communication campaigns are developed to reduce EDCs exposure. However, many of them rely on knowledge provision, with the idea that awareness raising is sufficient to induce behaviour change. For example, in their chapter Policy implication and community interventions to reduce EDCs exposure , Montano and Guglielmino propose that “information campaigns could be organized for the general population or population particularly exposed to EDCs. An action of this dimension could change exposure levels by informing and raising awareness of how to avoid the possible and different contact with individual EDCs and defend health from the sneaky snare of EDCs”. 13 p.221 Decades of work in behavioural sciences have demonstrated how the process is complex 14 ; and provide insights on how people change their habits. This paper is a call to use this scientific knowledge to build interventions that maximise their chances to ultimately have substantial impact on ecosystem and human health. We begin by discussing routes of exposure to EDCs, especially behavioural ones, before reviewing models of behaviour change. We then present examples of successful and less successful studies and campaigns, analysed through the prism of psychological determinants and behaviour change techniques. The HYPIEND project is then presented for illustrative purpose as an example of an intervention aimed at reducing EDCs exposure based on behavioural sciences. Given the trial is currently in progress, no outcome data have been collected yet and no results are reported in this publication. The main aim of the paper is both conceptual and methodological: emphasising the need to go beyond education to induce behaviour change in relation to EDCs exposure and provide an example of a theory-informed intervention.

## Routes of exposure

Human biomonitoring studies repeatedly report wide presence of EDCs in human bodies across various regions in the world. 15 People are exposed to EDCs from multiple sources, including environmental pollution (air, 16 , 17 water 18 – 20 and soil 21 ), but also through consumer products, including food. 22 , 23 Early life is a vulnerable period, as exposure begins as early as the peri-conceptional and prenatal periods (through the placenta), 24 and postnatally, through breast milk and food. 25 Modifiable exposure is broadly understood as a behavioural or environmental factor that is measurable and modifiable by individuals, communities, or governments. 26 For example, bisphenols are added to plastics to improve physical, thermal and mechanical properties of the product. Even if the use of bisphenol A in food contact materials was banned in the EU, substitutes are commonly found in water bottles, food containers, and can leach into their contents. 27 , 28 An important dermal exposure to bisphenols is often attributed to thermal paper – receipts; and more recently, clothes made from synthetic textiles. 29 Phthalates are plasticizers added to plastics to increase flexibility and resistance to high temperatures and to achieve the same properties, to personal care products (to reduce cracking of nail polish, avoid stiffness in hairsprays or as fragrance retainers). 30 Per- and polyfluoroalkyl substances (PFAS) are persistent EDCs used in water and stain-free surfaces like non-stick cookware, water-repellent clothing, stain-resistant fabrics and carpets, fast-food wrapping paper; and for smoothing effect in cosmetics. 31 Compounds that affect the endocrine system are frequently present in pesticides, as well as in their residues found in conventionally farmed crops and animal-derived foods. Ultra-processed foods are particularly high in these compounds due to processing, packaging, and formulation. 3 Flame retardants also represent a significant source of EDCs exposure, and their use has increased in parallel with the rising production and consumption of synthetic textiles. 32

Studies have shown that not everybody has the same level of exposure and suggest it can contribute to explain disparities in health outcomes between racial/ethnic groups or according to the level of income notably. 33 , 34 For example, Llanos et al. showed that personal care product use varied between females and males, and by ethnicity. 35 Govarts et al. 15 reported that exposure differed strongly depending on socioeconomical status and geographical location.

## Reducing exposure through behaviour change

Addressing risk factors associated with EDCs requires multifactorial interventions. 36 One important approach is to reduce exposure through behaviour change. Individuals can make choices about the type of bottle they use to drink water, how frequently they ventilate their homes, or whether to use certain cosmetics, such as nail polish or perfume. Of course, people also depend on the types of products offered on the market. 37 , 38 Therefore, regulatory and industrial actions are essential to reduce EDCs exposure. However, when several options are available, it remains that individuals must be willing to choose EDCs-free products, and beyond willingness, they need to be able to maintain these changes in their consumer habits in the long term. Those notions of willingness and capacity refer to important determinants of behaviour, which have been studied for a long time in psychology.

## Evidence-based models of behaviour change

Since the 1950s, scientists have studied what predicts behaviour. Early work from behaviourists explains that the future likelihood of a behaviour depends on the consequences (positive or negative) that the person experiences when engaging in that behaviour. 39 Theories aiming to explain human behaviour later evolved to include not only external influences, but also internal ones, such as the perceived capability of performing a behaviour, 40 , 41 beliefs about the consequences of the behaviour, perceived approval by others and intention. 41 , 42 Other theories focused on the perceived health threat as a motivator for adopting health behaviours, 43 , 44 suggesting that someone will perform a health protective behaviour if they believe they are vulnerable to a threat, perceive the threat as severe, and that they are capable of adopting a protective behaviour. However, reviews and meta-analyses show that threat-related variables do not predict behaviour well. 45 – 49

Models later evolved to include explanations about the process from intention to do something to the actual realisation of the behaviour. 50 The importance of both motivational (preceding the decision to act) and volitional (following the decision) phases for behaviour change were demonstrated in a meta-analysis. 51

Other models focus on the importance of the context explaining that behaviour is shaped by multiple interconnected levels, ranging from the individual to the policy. 52 In the case of children’s behaviour, models have considered specific influences, notably the fact that the decision of the action is often not the responsibility of the child, instead they are often asked/required by the adults to do specific behaviours. 53

This review of various models illustrates that even in the very early models of behaviour, information has never been considered sufficient to change behaviour successfully. Figure 1 illustrates schematically the process from information to behaviour change, incorporating findings from several behaviour change models.

Nevertheless, despite being insufficient, information and knowledge can still be necessary. Greyson and Johnson 54 showed how information is included in many of the models of behaviour. According to their analysis, beliefs about the consequences of the behaviour are constructed, at least in part, based on received information, and information can raise awareness of the need for change. In particular, information and knowledge may be needed for issues that people are not yet knowledgeable about. On the topic of EDCs, surveys and qualitative studies among various groups (students, pregnant women, and adults from the general population) indeed show that people lack knowledge about what EDCs are and the associated risks. 55 – 59 Correlational studies on the level of knowledge about EDCs and health behaviour showed mixed results: some report no significant association, 60 , 61 while another study showed that this association varied depending on the substances. 62 Knowledge about parabens was associated with more avoidance of chemicals in personal care and household products, but this was not the case for lead: lead was the most widely recognized substance, but the least avoided. 62

## Lifestyle interventions to reduce EDCs exposure

Reviews show that policy interventions (using natural experiment study design to test substances bans effects), as well as interventions that provide low-chemical personal care products, 63 plastic-free foodware, organic food, or fresh food to the intervention group compared to canned food for the control group, 64 succeed in reducing the levels of chemicals measured among participants. However, controlled consumption studies attribute a passive role to participants and do not reflect real life conditions in which individuals have to make choices. This limitation is underlined in the review by Park et al ., 65 showing that only four studies among the ones reviewed let participants choose themselves alternative goods or food. In addition, among the 12 interventions reviewed, half lasted less than ten days, 65 failing to assess temporal dynamics of behaviour change. The review by Sieck et al . 64 further indicates that educational and lifestyle interventions have more uncertain effects on measured chemical levels than policy measures and studies in which participants’ consumption is controlled. Moreover, in the two reviews cited, 64 , 65 interventions are not analyzed in terms of theoretical framework of behaviour change. Thus, only a limited number of intervention studies have specifically tested, based on a theoretical background, how to promote long-term, voluntary change of habits in relation to reducing EDCs exposure.

Studies focusing on knowledge and risk-awareness illustrate that it is not sufficient for inducing behaviour change. A first example is the PREVED -Pregnancy, PreVention, Endocrine Disruptors- study is an example of a workshop-based intervention study designed to reduce EDCs exposure in pregnant women, with a focus on canned food consumption. 66 The intervention focused on knowledge and risk perception, and the study sample size was 230, participants being for the majority born in Metropolitan France, and in a no precarious situation. Results showed that it failed to significantly change behaviour as in both control and intervention group there were similar proportion of participants whose consumption of canned food and drinks decreased, increased and remained stable. However, risk perception scores increased significantly in the intervention group. A second example is a study using biomonitoring as a technique to motivate exposure reduction. 67 The participating women (N = 135), nearly-half of them self-identified as Black/African American, received a personalized report mentioning either their individual chemical exposure levels, or exposure levels aggregated at the study level. Results were mixed: out of 15 behaviours, only four evolved in a positive direction (fewer food prepared using nonstick cookware; fewer microwave popcorn, and fewer use of a problematic dental floss; and more frequently having added or removed an item from the home due to concern about chemicals), the frequency of ten behaviours did not change, and one protective behaviour (damp-wiping dust) decreased at follow-up. Whether the biomonitoring report was individual or aggregated did not influence the results.

A few studies including techniques besides information provision showed positive effects on behaviour. The first one showed that an education program for Korean pregnant women, informing them about the effects of toxicants and providing strategies to practice protective behaviours, was successful in inducing behaviour change among participants exposed to the intervention (N = 40, compared to 56 in the control group), effect size Cohen’s d = 0.83 [ 1 ]. 68 However, a significant limitation of this study is the short timeframe of the evaluation: the post-test occurred four weeks after the intervention ended. Given the time it takes to develop new habits (range between 18 to 254 days according to Lally et al. 69 ), studies with longer time frames are needed to properly evaluate implementation of changes in daily lives. The study by Park and Chung, which targeted a cognitive bias that leads to consider oneself as less at risk than the average others, showed success in increasing protective behaviours in a sample of 140 young women. 70 The intervention group was exposed to several behaviour change techniques (BCTs), including self-checking one’s habits of exposure, an information session, assessing barriers to reduce exposure, and signing a health contract. Protective behaviours against EDCs included daily life habits such as consuming instant food from convenience stores and using disposable cups for example. The comparison of the evolution in the control group compared to the experimental group show an effect size of d = 1.29 [ 2 ].Their positive result is thus not surprising, as the intervention targeted a variety of psychological determinants and was not limited to providing knowledge. However, its quasi-experimental design and the lack of biological samples analyses reduce the reliability of these findings.

The mix-methods pilot study by Tsui et al. 71 provides a proof of methodological principle regarding an intervention developed with the community on the use of phthalate-free hair care products among pregnant Women of Color (mostly Hispanic, Black Hispanic, and Black non-Hispanic). The intervention, based on the Environmental Health Literacy framework 72 contained educational video, but also practical tips to reduce exposure. Tools to check product ingredient and alternative, less-toxic products were suggested to participants. The effect of the intervention was assessed through progression in the stages of change, and with urine samples collection. Qualitative data suggest a progression in the stages (moving from “never heard of EDCs, nor EDCs in hair care products” prior the intervention to “having decided to reduce their use of hair care products containing phthalates” and “having limited use of such products” after the intervention) and a reduction of phthalate metabolite concentrations.

A review by Martin et al . 73 of lifestyle interventions to reduce EDCs exposure among men and women in their reproductive age conclude on three key elements: 1) tailored education about how to avoid EDCs with interactive educational materials including question/answer option, 2) support and monitoring by counselors or peer discussion group to provide feedback and encouragement, 3) understand individual sources of exposure (through diaries for example) to provide replacement options for items known to contain EDCs.

## Example of an awareness-raising campaign in Belgium

As part of the Belgian National Action Plan on Endocrine Disruptors (NAPED, 2022–2026), aiming to raise awareness in vulnerable population groups (pregnant women, women planning pregnancy, young children (0–3 years), and adolescents), public awareness campaigns are planned. These campaigns are coordinated by the Federal Public Service Health, in close collaboration with regional and community authorities. It serves as an example of a public health intervention designed to increase awareness and knowledge of endocrine disruptors.

In May 2024, the first campaign, targeting pregnant women, was launched. It combined the delivery of practical, accessible advice with simple, everyday recommendations tailored to reduce exposure in daily life with a targeted digital communication strategy. Dissemination was based on strong partnerships and leveraged digital channels such as Meta, YouTube, Pinterest, and optimised web content through search engine optimisation.

Healthcare professionals were engaged during the campaign through an informative email, which invited them to download a specially developed Q&A document on EDCs. They were also given the opportunity to order promotional materials, such as postcards and posters, via the Federal Public Service website. In total, over 80,000 postcards and 16,500 posters were ordered and distributed to more than 1,300 healthcare professionals and institutions. A second campaign is planned for November–December 2025. It will broaden outreach to include caregivers of young children (0–3 years) while reinforcing key messages aimed at pregnant women and their partners.

An external evaluation , conducted by a polling institute before and after the campaign among a representative sample of 1,000 Belgians, revealed a generally positive reception, with an average satisfaction score of 7.3/10 overall, rising to 8.0/10 among pregnant women. Knowledge about EDCs increased by 7 percentage points, and the campaign generated widespread interest among both professionals and the general public.

However, despite these encouraging results, self-reported behavioural changes were limited. While participants expressed greater awareness, behavioural changes remained gradual. This highlights a common challenge in health promotion: while a one-off information campaign can effectively raise awareness and improve knowledge, it is rarely sufficient to produce sustained behaviour change.

## The HYPIEND behaviour change interventions

In the HYPIEND project, two multicomponent interventions have been designed with the aim of accompanying pregnant women and parents of prepubertal children to reduce their daily life exposure to EDCs. The interventions consist of a digital tool and a set of workshops. Moreover, a school-wide educational program based on explicit teaching of healthy behaviors and positive reinforcement and a plastic-free canteen will be implemented in the participating schools.

A reduction in EDCs exposure is expected through targeting the following categories of behaviour: Indoor air quality (e.g., ventilation, avoiding products with fragrances, choice of cleaning products, cleaning dust); choice of food (e.g., avoiding ultraprocessed food, fast-food, canned food and drinks and food with preservatives; favour organic when possible); food preparation (wash fruits and vegetables before eating and peel when relevant); food contact materials (to store, cook and consume); personal care products (choice of products, limit use of products); choice of clothing, furniture, toys and electronics; child’s behaviour (wash the baby/child’s hands after playing and before eating; for the perinatal study: do not allow to chew certain things; for the prepubertal study: have the child use a stainless steel bottle to drink); gardening and Do It Yourself activities; smoking; and occupational exposure (for the perinatal study only). Major targeted compounds are pesticides, bisphenols, PFAS, phthalates, parabens, benzophenones, flame retardants, PAHs, heavy metals, and isoflavones (the latter, for the prepubertal study only).

Both interventions rely on the Health Action Process Approach (HAPA). 50 This model was chosen because it is more comprehensive than alternative frameworks and does not treat intention as the sole predictor of behaviour. It clearly distinguishes between the motivational and volitional phases, emphasising how intentions are translated into action It is known that around one out of two decisions that individuals take will not be acted upon. 74 In the study by Harley et al., 63 the main reason for participants’ lack of compliance with the furnished low-chemical personal care products alternatives to theirs regular products was forgetting. This result highlights the importance of the volitional phase of behaviour change. For this reason, the HYPIEND interventions not only inform participants about what EDCs are and their potential impact but also inform them about changes that can be made at the individual level and contain techniques such as planning to help people implement their intentions. Those techniques are taken from a 93-techniques list, the BCTs Taxonomy. 75 The use of this taxonomy was dictated by the need of having an extensive choice of techniques to broadly cover behaviour change mechanisms. In addition, using techniques from the taxonomy allows to report the intervention ingredients in a standardized way, improving replicability for future interventions. 75 The appropriate techniques were selected using the Theory and Technique Tool , a related tool helping to identify relevant techniques based on empirical evidence. Participants from the control group will receive a booklet (also distributed to the intervention group) containing information about what EDCs are, and recommendations to reduce exposure, without any additional BCT.

Through the digital tool, participants are able to work on different missions aimed at minimizing exposure to EDCs. By selecting these missions successively, they receive frequent recommendations, tips and motivational quotes that help them to accomplish the selected mission. Some of the BCTs included in the digital tool are: graded tasks, used to increase task self-efficacy (i.e., initiate the change); action planning and problem solving, used to help intenders become actors; and providing tools to conserve mental resources, to increase maintenance self-efficacy (i.e., once the change starts and needs to become a habit).

Another tool used in the HYPIEND interventions is motivational interviewing. 76 It is an interviewing strategy to help the person resolve ambivalence to change, and trigger motivation emerging from within, by letting the person themselves evoke the arguments instead of the counsellor providing them. In the workshops, the animator will provide a brief education about EDCs and spend most of the session using motivational interviewing techniques in group, to help participants build a strong motivation to change. Figure 2 illustrates how the digital tool and the workshops target the HAPA constructs, with examples of BCTs used for each construct. For the perinatal study, group size range between 2 and 8 participants, and maximum 25 parents for the prepubertal study.

Lifestyle interventions must consider the broader social–ecological context, including family dynamics. 77 For example, evidence shows that partner involvement in maternal health promotes healthier behaviours within households, 78 which is particularly relevant for reducing EDCs exposure, a process often requiring collective family action. 73 Yet, most interventions still focus solely on mothers. 79 Including partners in EDCs-related intervention studies is therefore essential for several reasons: it reflects the shared biological responsibility for reproductive health, it acknowledges the social and behavioural dynamics of households, and it allows interventions to target both partners to improve efficacy. Couple-based interventions are particularly well-suited for modifying shared behaviours, 77 such as food choices, product use, or environmental exposures at home, which are often difficult to change in isolation. For this reason, the HYPIEND intervention with pregnant women include the cohabiting partner, and the HYPIEND study on prepubertal children includes the whole family and the school through the School Wide Positive Behavioural Interventions and Supports (SWPBIS).

SWPBIS is a multi-tiered intervention designed to positively reinforce students’ expected behaviours at school. 53 It aims to create a positive and secure school climate by explicitly teaching and positively reinforcing expected behaviours. These are defined beforehand in observable terms and explicitly taught to students. SWPBIS insists on the sense of adopting a behaviour (“Why” is it important to adopt a specific behaviour at school) and it asks teachers to model the expected behaviour (“How” to perform this behaviour). It is implemented throughout the whole school by all adults supervising the children. The effects of SWPBIS have been documented in several systematic reviews. 80 – 82 Sugai and Horner’s 53 model of positive behaviour support has been revisited and adapted to the context of the HYPIEND project ( Figure 3 ).

Based on the needs and observations of school stakeholders, health-related behaviours will be identified and explicitly taught at the school level or within the classes involved in the project. The behaviours taught and promoted in schools for children are adapted to their autonomy level, and do not require any purchase (e.g. handwashing, ventilating rooms, washing fruit and vegetables, etc.). To support the adoption of these behaviours, strategies such as positive reinforcement and re-teaching sessions will be implemented. Reinforcement will be supported by the school-family partnership, the actions carried out at the whole-school level, and the planning and instructional phases. The positive reinforcement provided by the primary caregiver that we use in schools is likely to encourage the child to adopt and sustain the desired behaviours over time. Several theoretical frameworks can be drawn upon to explain this. According to the systematic review by Kwasnicka et al., 83 the maintenance of behaviours over time can be explained in particular either by changes in habits (behaviours which have become habitual and are supported by automatic responses to relevant cues) or by the social motivation provided by the social environment (a supportive environment and social support are important for the maintenance of behavioural change. People tend to maintain behaviour that is in line with relevant social changes). Finally, the work of Deci and Ryan 84 allows to formulate the hypothesis that social support (i.e. positive reinforcement from a significant adult in our case) facilitates the internalisation of motivation.

Taking actions to reduce EDCs exposure is not necessarily accessible in the same way to all socioeconomic groups. Some recommendations to avoid EDCs involve buying more costly alternatives (e.g. labelled products). However, in order to prevent generating a feeling of helplessness among participants with low-income, we emphasize solutions that can be adopted by everyone at no cost, such as ventilating the home, washing hands, use homemade all-purpose cleaners, or reducing the number of cosmetics products use. In order to avoid exacerbating inequities, it is important to consider the social determinants of health. 85 In the HYPIEND project, this means including the social factors such as the partner and the whole family, but also the environmental dimension through the school-level intervention. Notably, the Positive Behavioural Interventions and Supports (PBIS) program adapted in the HYPIEND project has a history of being used to improve learning and social outcomes for children in low-income families and neighbourhood. 86

The effectiveness of the HYPIEND interventions will be tested through a) a tricentric Randomized Controlled Trial (RCT) involving pregnant women and their infants up to 18 months of age in Spain, Belgium and Poland, and b) a bicentric RCT carried out at primary schools from Spain and Belgium for 28 months, targeted to prepubertal children and their parents. Through these RCTs we will evaluate the potential effectiveness of the multicomponent interventions to reduce the internal concentration of several EDCs families. We will further evaluate whether the anticipated reduction in exposure to EDCs can mitigate their potential adverse effects on growth, neurodevelopment, and pubertal maturation. title: Consensus Recommendations for Management of Darier Disease: A Practical Approach
abstract:
### Background

Darier disease (DD) is a rare, autosomal dominant genodermatosis caused by pathogenic variants in the ATP2A2 gene, encoding the sarco/endoplasmic reticulum calcium ATPase. DD is characterized by chronic, recurrent cutaneous lesions and variable extracutaneous manifestations, resulting in significant impairment of quality of life. Disease onset typically occurs after puberty, with environmental triggers and variable expressivity.

### Objectives

The aim of this study was to provide practical, evidence- and consensus-based recommendations for the management of patients with DD, particularly for healthcare professionals in non-expert centers, and to highlight emerging therapeutic avenues.

### Methods

Recommendations were formulated on the basis of a systematic review of the literature and expert consensus from the European Reference Network for Rare and Undiagnosed Skin Disorders (ERN-Skin). Evidence from case reports, case series, and mechanistic studies was considered to provide guidance on symptomatic and advanced targeted therapies.

### Results and Recommendations

The panel agreed on a total of 68 recommendations.

Diagnosis is primarily clinical, supported by family history, histopathology, cytodiagnosis, and, whenever possible, ATP2A2 genetic testing. Genetic counseling should be offered to patients and at-risk relatives.

First-line management entails trigger avoidance, skin care using topical antiseptics, emollients, and anti-inflammatory agents, alongside symptomatic control. Topical treatments include corticosteroids, retinoids, and calcineurin inhibitors; systemic therapies (oral retinoids, immunomodulators) are indicated for moderate-to-severe or refractory disease.

Physical treatments (ablative lasers, cryotherapy, photodynamic therapy) are reserved for localized treatment-resistant lesions.

Targeted therapies (JAK/IL-17/IL-23/IL-4–13/MEK inhibitors), and topical gene therapy, are under evaluation or development.

Multidisciplinary management is recommended (neuropsychiatric, ocular, dental, and obstetric).

Long-term outcomes remain limited, and durable remission is currently unattainable; treatments must be individualized.

### Conclusions

DD is a chronic, genetic disorder that significantly impairs quality of life. These practical recommendations provide a framework for diagnosis, management, and follow-up, and highlight the need for clinical trials, registries, and biomarker-driven research to advance therapeutic strategies and explore novel, mechanism-based treatments.

### Supplementary Information

The online version contains supplementary material available at https://doi.org/10.1007/s13555-026-01838-3 .

### Supplementary Information

The online version contains supplementary material available at https://doi.org/10.1007/s13555-026-01838-3 .

## Keywords
Darier disease; Epidermal differentiation disorder; Therapy; Diagnostic; Complication; Acantholytic disorder; Retinoids; Systemic anti-inflammatory therapies

## Key Summary Points

Darier disease (DD) is a genetic, chronic, and complex disorder with a high burden and significant impact on quality of life. Diagnosis relies on clinical features, family history, histopathology, and genetic testing. Genetic testing and counseling should be offered to all suspected patients and their relatives. Owing to its genetic etiology, permanent remission is currently not achievable. Treatments are symptomatic, aiming to control inflammation, reduce hyperkeratosis, and prevent secondary infections, thereby improving patient quality of life. Avoidance or minimization of environmental triggers is essential. Standard-of-care symptomatic therapy—including topical antiseptics, emollients, keratolytic and anti-inflammatory agents—should be implemented in all patients. Consider systemic therapy in patients with severe or refractory disease. Choice of agent should be individualized on the basis of clinical context (keratosis, infection, inflammation, lesion extent, comorbidities). Retinoids should be considered as first-line therapy. For other drugs, evidence is limited to case reports and series, and response may vary between patients. Individualized monitoring and adaptable treatment are essential. Clinical trials and multicenter registries are needed to evaluate efficacy, compare therapies, study combination strategies, and identify biomarkers or patient stratification criteria.

## Introduction

Darier disease (DD), also known as dyskeratosis follicularis, Darier–White disease, or ATP2A2 -nEDD (OMIM#124200; Orphanet ORPHA:218), is a genetic disorder characterized by both cutaneous and extracutaneous manifestations. The disease typically begins after puberty and follows a chronic course with recurrent exacerbations. DD has been reported worldwide, with a prevalence ranging from approximately 1:12,000 to 3.8:100,000 individuals [ 1 – 4 ].

The inheritance pattern is autosomal dominant with almost complete penetrance in adults but variable expressivity. DD results from monoallelic loss-of-function variants in the ATP2A2 gene, which encodes the sarco/endoplasmic reticulum calcium ATPase (SERCA2) protein. SERCA2, a calcium pump located in the endoplasmic reticulum, plays a pivotal role in maintaining calcium homeostasis in keratinocytes. The pathogenesis of DD is complex, involving the interplay between SERCA2 haploinsufficiency and various environmental factors [ 5 – 7 ].

The current therapeutic options are diverse but nonspecific and of limited efficacy, underscoring the need for improved strategies for patients, who often experience a substantial disease burden. In the era of molecular disease characterization and the emergence of targeted therapies, ongoing research efforts are increasingly directed toward developing and validating pathogenesis-based and corrective treatment approaches to improve patient outcomes [ 8 ]. Although several reviews have been published in recent years [ 8 – 11 ], the European Reference Network (ERN)-Skin ( https://ern-skin.eu/ ) and an international expert task force have recognized the need for practical recommendations to support healthcare professionals (HCP) in the diagnosis and management of DD. Here, we aim at synthetic recommendations for diagnostic and treatment for HCP from non-expert centers to assist in the management of DD.

## Methods

### Literature Research

The recommendations are based on a systematic review of the literature combined with expert consensus reached within the ERN-Skin network and its associated international task force. The process followed established ERN methodological standards for guideline development, including evaluation of available evidence, assessment of clinical relevance, and formulation of practical statements to guide real-world care.

The systematic literature research was performed using the PubMed, Embase, and Medline databases from 2002 to 2023. The following key words were used: “Darier Disease OR Darier-White Disease OR Keratosis Follicularis” and “clinical presentation OR case series OR diagnostic OR physiology OR mutation OR (phenotype AND (gene OR genotype)) OR treatment OR therapy OR therapeutic OR management”. Altogether 2293 publications were identified, of which 621 dealt with DD. Exclusion criteria were: preclinical studies, articles without abstracts, and articles in a language other than English, French, and German. A total of 558 publications were screened, of which 471 were included in the assessment (Supplementary Fig. 1). Additional relevant publications from 2023 until September 2025 on “Darier disease and therapy” were also integrated. Each publication was assessed by two reviewers.

### Expert Consensus: Development and Digital Implementation of the Delphi Method

To obtain expert consensus on the recommendations, the Delphi method [ 12 ] was applied within the members of expert centers of the ERN-Skin and the international task force. The Delphi method was implemented using a purpose-built digital platform designed to preserve its core principles of expert anonymity, iterative feedback, and controlled convergence. To support structured and asynchronous participation by an international panel of medical experts, the platform was custom-developed on a robust open-source framework (PHP DevShell 3.5, LGPL license).

The system architecture mirrors the methodological structure of the Delphi process and is organized into projects, successive rounds, and evaluated items. Experts were invited by email to rate items on a standardized 1–9 relevance scale and could provide optional qualitative comments, with the possibility to complete questionnaires over multiple sessions.

A dedicated back-office interface enabled coordinators to monitor participation, automatically aggregate responses, and generate descriptive statistics (medians, percentiles, and distribution graphs) to inform decisions between rounds. Expert responses were fully anonymized, nonresponders were excluded from subsequent rounds to maintain panel consistency, and all communications complied with General Data Protection Regulation (GDPR) requirements.

Overall, this digital implementation transformed a traditionally labor-intensive Delphi process into a scalable, reproducible, and methodologically rigorous workflow while preserving analytical precision and methodological integrity.

This article is based on previously conducted studies and does not contain any new studies with human participants or animals performed by any of the authors. Consent was obtained for publication of patient photographs.

## Results

On the basis of the literature review summarized below (detailed review available on request) and their expert opinion, the panel agreed on a total of 68 recommendations divided into seven groups (Fig. 1 ). These recommendations are intended to assist HCPs, particularly those working in nonexpert or general dermatology centers, in recognizing and appropriately managing patients with DD. Fig. 1 Summary of the Delphi process

### Clinical Manifestations

DD is characterized by multiple, symmetrically distributed, crusted, keratotic papules, primarily affecting seborrheic areas (Fig. 2 ). These may coalesce into large plaques which, especially in intertriginous areas, may become hypertrophic, fissured, eroded, and malodorous, often complicated by secondary infections and poor treatment response [ 13 – 16 ]. “Classical” lesions include mucocutaneous keratotic papules, palmar pits, wart-like acral papules, and nail abnormalities (Fig. 2 ). “Nonclassical” lesions, observed in about one-third of patients, include acral keratoderma, leukodermic macules, giant comedones, keloid-like vegetations, and acral hemorrhagic blisters [ 17 ]. These cutaneous manifestations may characterize rare and underrecognized clinical variants and may sometimes coexist in the same patient or family, contributing to the clinical heterogeneity of DD. The cutaneous extent of the disease is highly variable. In severe or untreated cases, the disease can rarely progress to erythroderma, scarring alopecia, leonine facies, and palmoplantar keratoderma [ 18 – 21 ]. Approximately 10% of patients exhibit localized, asymmetric forms, which include the segmental, unilateral, zosteriform patterns, reflecting type 1 or type 2 genetic mosaicism [ 16 , 22 – 35 ]. Extracutaneous manifestations of DD are summarized in Table 1 . DD runs a chronic and unpredictable course as flares can be triggered by a wide variety of factors such as heat, sweating, friction, UV exposure, stress, poor personal hygiene, hormonal fluctuations, major surgery, infections, vaccinations, and common medications such as lithium, oral contraceptives, calcium antagonists, azathioprine, and interferon [ 13 , 36 – 47 ]. Infections, both systemic (e.g., coronavirus disease 2019 (COVID-19) or human immunodeficiency virus (HIV)) and localized, are also recognized as exacerbating factors [ 40 , 48 – 52 ]. Mucocutaneous lesions are frequently susceptible to infections by pathogens such as Staphylococcus aureus , Candida albicans , herpes simple virus (HSV), human papillomavirus, varicella-zoster virus, and poxvirus [ 10 , 13 , 53 – 58 ]. Most frequently, these infections are self-limited and should be suspected in case of rapidly worsening or treatment-resistant lesions, especially when they become painful, present with vesiculopustules, confluent erosions, or whitish exudates or if systemic signs and symptoms arise, such as lymphadenopathy, fever, and malaise [ 13 , 59 , 60 ] (Fig. 2 ). Disseminated infections may occasionally progress to Kaposi’s varicelliform eruption, erythroderma, sepsis, or fatal multiorgan failure [ 13 , 19 , 59 – 68 ].

Recent evidence has strengthened the association between DD and keratinocyte carcinomas on mucocutaneous DD lesions, both squamous and basal cell types [ 1 ]. These findings align with previous case reports [ 42 , 62 , 69 – 71 ] and molecular studies suggesting that SERCA2 haploinsufficiency may contribute to oncogenesis in human keratinocytes [ 14 , 42 , 69 ]. Additional malignancies occasionally described in association with DD include adnexal tumours, Paget’s disease, melanoma, and pulmonary small-cell squamous carcinoma [ 42 , 72 , 73 ].

The differential diagnosis of DD is summarized in Table 2 . Table 2 Differential diagnosis of DD Differential diagnosis Features References Hailey–Hailey disease (HHD, ATP2C1 -nEDD) Represents the main differential diagnosis as it shares several clinical, histologic, and pathogenic similarities with DD. HHD presents with painful, malodorous, vegetating, bullous, or erosive lesions in intertriginous areas that can be exacerbated by many environmental factors. Nail abnormalities are present in more than 70% of cases with broad white bands, but red lines or nail fragility are absent. HHD usually manifests earlier in life, is less commonly associated with pruritus, and lacks other typical cutaneous and extracutaneous features of DD. Nonetheless, the disease is usually transient, arising more frequently in middle-aged or older Caucasian men, with no specific involvement of the nails, mucosae, and extracutaneous sites [ 198 , 199 ] Other inflammatory dermatoses: • Seborrheic dermatitis • Pemphigus vulgaris, foliaceus, and vegetans • Lichen planus • Psoriasis • Pityriasis rubra pilaris • Acne vulgaris • Acanthosis nigricans • Confluent and reticulated papillomatosis • Reticulate erythemato-mucinous syndrome • Prurigo pigmentosa • Galli–Galli/Dowling–Degos disease [ 10 , 200 , 201 ] Mosaic DD with segmental or linear manifestations • Lichen striatus • Linear lichen planus • Epidermal naevi [ 28 , 32 , 56 , 199 ] DD Darier disease, nEDD nonsyndromic epidermal differentiation disorder, HHD Hailey–Hailey disease

### Noninvasive Diagnostic Methods

New noninvasive imaging techniques are valuable tools in the early diagnosis of DD, in detecting recurrences, and in supporting differential diagnosis. Among these, dermoscopy is the most accessible and typically shows a central yellowish–brown area corresponding to a compact keratotic mass, surrounded by a whitish halo of acanthotic epidermis, often with a reddish background and dotted or linear vessels. Plaque-type lesions may display parallel pink–reddish furrows and characteristic “tire tread-like” or “cracked riverbed-like” patterns [ 74 , 75 ].

In vivo confocal microscopy further enhances diagnostic accuracy by visualizing corps ronds, grains, and suprabasal clefts in real time, correlating well with the histological hallmarks of abnormal keratinization, acantholysis, and dyskeratosis [ 74 ]. Similarly, line-field confocal optical coherence tomography (LC-OCT) provides high-resolution vertical and horizontal images, revealing an epidermis of variable thickness with localized hyper-reflective stratum corneum, irregular hyporeflective suprabasal spaces, and scattered bright round cells with a targetoid appearance, while the dermal–epidermal junction and dermis remain unremarkable. These features closely mirror the histopathological pattern of DD, including hyperparakeratosis, suprabasal acantholytic clefts, and dyskeratotic cells such as grains and corps ronds [ 76 ].

### Laboratory Diagnostics

#### Histopathology

Typical histopathological features include suprabasal clefts in the epithelium, accompanied by acantholysis and the presence of dyskeratotic cells known as “corps ronds” and “corps grains” (Fig. 3 a). “Corps ronds” are larger structures typically found in the granular layer and contain irregular eccentric, and sometimes pyknotic nuclei. The underlying papillary dermis is covered by a single layer of basal cells and is forming villi extending into these clefts. Subcellular compartmentalization of stromal interaction molecule 1 (STIM1) may distinguish DD from Hailey–Hailey disease (HHD) [ 77 ]. If a skin sample is not available, cytodiagnosis (i.e., Tzanck test) may be helpful in indicating the presence of dyskeratotic and acantholytic cells [ 78 , 79 ]. Fig. 3 Histopathology ( a ) and molecular mechanisms of Darier disease (DD), including therapeutic targets ( b ). #### Genetic Testing

As over 300 pathogenic ATP2A2 variants without mutagenic hotspots, including missense, nonsense, splice-site mutations, and small indels, are associated with DD and novel diverse pathogenic variants are constantly reported, DD genetic testing should include comprehensive sequencing to capture a broad spectrum of variants [ 11 , 42 , 80 – 86 ]. Sanger sequencing or next-generation sequencing of ATP2A2 are commonly used methods [ 87 – 90 ]. For patients without ATP2A2 pathogenic variants, deep intronic variants or variants affecting transcription or splicing and epigenetic alterations may remain undetected. The incidence of sporadic cases is reported as approximately 40–50%, with a high penetrance of greater than 95% [ 11 ].

Mosaic DD can be confirmed by Sanger or NGS sequencing of ATP2A2 or WES from lesional skin and blood DNA, especially when blood DNA shows no ATP2A2 variant [ 26 ]. Type 1 mosaic DD is caused by a post‐zygotic mutation that manifests as affected dermatomes along Blaschko’s lines surrounded by normal skin [ 22 , 31 , 34 , 91 , 92 ]. Type 2 mosaic results when an individual with a germline mutation develops a second-hit somatic mutation, resulting in more severe segmental lesions superimposed on a milder generalized DD [ 26 ].

Comprehensive sequencing poses value for diagnostic confirmation, genetic counseling, and for expanding understanding of genetic diversity and its impact on clinical phenotype. Moreover, it enhances the accuracy of diagnosis and enables personalized management of the disease (Table 3 ). ### Treatment of Cutaneous Manifestations of DD

The large number of therapeutic approaches reported in the literature reflects the complexity and challenges of managing the cutaneous manifestations of DD (Fig. 3 b). First-line management focuses on preventive and symptomatic measures, including the avoidance of triggering factors, and the regular use of topical antiseptics, emollients, and keratolytic and anti-inflammatory agents (Fig. 4 ). These measures aim to reduce secondary infection, reduce keratosis, control inflammation, and restore skin barrier function, thereby minimizing disease exacerbations. Systemic therapies are recommended for disseminated lesions that are not responsive to topical therapies. Physical and procedural treatments are reserved for localized, treatment-refractory lesions or as adjuncts to medical therapy. The proposed approach is not intended as a step therapy model, but rather as an individualized therapeutic strategy tailored to the predominant clinical manifestations and extent of lesions, consistent with the management principles applied across dermatologic diseases. Fig. 4 Algorithm for management of Darier disease (DD)

As DD has a genetic etiology, permanent remission cannot be achieved with currently available therapies.

#### Topical Therapies

See Supplementary Tables 1–5 [ 25 , 76 , 93 – 109 ].

### Antiseptic Therapy

Regular use of antiseptics containing octenidine or chlorhexidine can reduce microbial colonization on compromised skin and thereby lower the risk of secondary infections [ 10 , 110 ].

### Topical Antibiotic Treatment

Short-course treatment with topical fucidic acid 2% cream is effective for localized secondary bacterial infections, particularly those caused by Staphylococcus aureus and Streptococcus species [ 35 , 110 ]. A case report described a 49-year-old woman in whom daily application of topical metronidazole 1% gel to the affected areas resulted in complete resolution of malodor despite persistence of the underlying skin lesions [ 111 ]. Prolonged or repeated use of topical antibiotic therapy should be avoided to reduce the risk of antimicrobial resistance [ 112 ].

Topical retinoids demonstrate therapeutic benefits (Supplementary Table 1). Adapalene 0.1%, applied once daily for 2 months, leads to a significant reduction in lesions with good tolerability and no notable side effects [ 103 , 113 – 117 ]. Tretinoin cream (0.01%) and tazarotene (0.01–0.1%) gel have shown similar efficacy, particularly in short-contact applications, and showed no side effects [ 107 , 116 ]. Early local adverse effects may be reduced through photoprotection, avoidance of extreme temperatures, and regular use of emollients [ 118 ].

### Topical Corticosteroids

During acute inflammatory flares, moderately to highly potent topical corticosteroids are often required. Class II–III agents can be used temporarily, while class IV steroids are reserved for short-term use in acute exacerbations [ 10 , 104 , 119 ].

Calcineurin inhibitors have also proven effective (Supplementary Table 2). Tacrolimus 0.1% ointment, especially beneficial in patients with coexisting atopic dermatitis, is typically used twice daily initially, followed by maintenance therapy with tacrolimus 0.03% [ 105 ]. Pimecrolimus 1% cream offers comparable results and safety, with no significant adverse effects reported. Both agents are preferred for use in intertriginous areas owing to their favorable safety profile.

### Topical Vitamin D Analogs

Vitamin D analogs are well recognized for three main actions: keratinocyte hyperproliferation inhibition, epidermal differentiation regulation, and cutaneous inflammation inhibition [ 25 ]. Few case reports/series report either substantial or variable improvement of DD lesions [ 25 , 94 , 99 ] (Supplementary Table 3).

### 5-Fluorouracil (5-FU)

Special considerations should be taken into account when using 5-FU as topical treatment in patients with DD (Supplementary Table 4) [ 120 – 123 ]. conclusions: DD is a chronic, genetically determined disorder that profoundly impacts patients’ quality of life and currently lacks a curative therapy. DD carries a huge stigmatizing effect along with a high infection risk. Our practical recommendations aim to guide diagnosis, symptomatic management, and ongoing follow-up of affected individuals. We acknowledge the limitations and have striven to provide the most accurate statements possible. Many of the therapies discussed remain unapproved in numerous countries, reflecting a common challenge in rare disorder management. The ongoing risk of therapy denial by payers owing to insufficient evidence persists. Continued collection of real-world data, as well as publication of case reports and case series, will be essential to further refine and strengthen future recommendations. We emphasize the urgent need for robust clinical trials, disease registries, and biomarker-driven research to advance therapeutic strategies and foster the discovery of novel, mechanism-based treatments. title: Harnessing probiotics to combat nonylphenol toxicity: a multiomics approach of gut microbiome remodelling in Silurus meridionalis
abstract:
### Background

As a ubiquitous environmental endocrine disruptor, nonylphenol (NP) threatens aquatic organisms, driving the need for sustainable mitigation strategies. While probiotics represent promising eco-friendly supplements, their molecular mechanisms against NP toxicity remain unclear. In this study, S. meridionalis received 7-week of probiotic ( Bacillus subtilis and Lactobacillus acidophilus ) pretreatment followed by 15 days of NP exposure. Integrated metagenomics, transcriptomics, and metabolomics analyses, with Reverse transcription quantitative real-time PCR (RT‒qPCR) and Enzyme-linked immunosorbent assay (ELISA) validation, were performed to elucidate microbial, genetic and metabolic responses. Growth performance, including the specific growth rate (SGR) and weight gain rate (WGR), was concurrently assessed.

### Results

NP exposure significantly suppressed WGR and SGR, and induced gut microbiota dysbiosis alongside and lipid metabolism disorders in S. meridionalis . Probiotic pretreatment effectively reversed these toxic effects and restored the inhibited WGR and SGR. Multiomics integration revealed that the protective effects of probiotics were mediated by a coherent “microbe-host” co-metabolism network across 3 progressive layers: (1) Microbial Remodelling: in which beneficial taxa (e.g., Bacteroides eggerthii and Cetobacterium sp. ) were enriched, and the functional capacity for short-chain fatty acid (SCFA) synthesis and ethanolamine metabolism was enhanced; (2) Host Gene Regulation: in which key lipid metabolism genes ( ek1 , cept1 , ept1 , mogat2 , and abcg2a ) were upregulated, and lipase activity was restored; and (3) Metabolic Pathway Activation and Physiological Repair: in which the activity of the NP-suppressed Kennedy pathway was reactivated, thereby promoting phosphatidylethanolamine (PE) and phosphatidylcholine (PC) synthesis and ultimately restoring gut barrier function. These results were further were corroborated by RT‒qPCR and ELISA.

### Conclusion

This study systematically elucidated that probiotics alleviated NP toxicity by remodelling a “microbiota-host Kennedy pathway gene–metabolite (PE and PC)-growth performance” regulatory network. The key mechanism is the beneficial microbiota activating the host Kennedy pathway and restoring gut phospholipid homeostasis and barrier function. These findings provide a theoretical basis for developing targeted, lipid metabolism focused probiotic feed additives for use in sustainable aquaculture.

# Harnessing probiotics to combat nonylphenol toxicity: a multiomics approach of gut microbiome remodelling in Silurus meridionalis

Growth performance, including the specific growth rate (SGR) and weight gain rate (WGR), was concurrently assessed.

### Results

NP exposure significantly suppressed WGR and SGR, and induced gut microbiota dysbiosis alongside and lipid metabolism disorders in S. meridionalis . Probiotic pretreatment effectively reversed these toxic effects and restored the inhibited WGR and SGR. Multiomics integration revealed that the protective effects of probiotics were mediated by a coherent “microbe-host” co-metabolism network across 3 progressive layers: (1) Microbial Remodelling: in which beneficial taxa (e.g., Bacteroides eggerthii and Cetobacterium sp. ) were enriched, and the functional capacity for short-chain fatty acid (SCFA) synthesis and ethanolamine metabolism was enhanced; (2) Host Gene Regulation: in which key lipid metabolism genes ( ek1 , cept1 , ept1 , mogat2 , and abcg2a ) were upregulated, and lipase activity was restored; and (3) Metabolic Pathway Activation and Physiological Repair: in which the activity of the NP-suppressed Kennedy pathway was reactivated, thereby promoting phosphatidylethanolamine (PE) and phosphatidylcholine (PC) synthesis and ultimately restoring gut barrier function. These results were further were corroborated by RT‒qPCR and ELISA.

### Conclusion

This study systematically elucidated that probiotics alleviated NP toxicity by remodelling a “microbiota-host Kennedy pathway gene–metabolite (PE and PC)-growth performance” regulatory network. The key mechanism is the beneficial microbiota activating the host Kennedy pathway and restoring gut phospholipid homeostasis and barrier function. These findings provide a theoretical basis for developing targeted, lipid metabolism focused probiotic feed additives for use in sustainable aquaculture.

## Keywords
Growth performance; Silurus meridionalis; Bacillus subtilis; Lactobacillus acidophilus; Kennedy pathway; Lipid metabolism

## Introduction

NP, a widely used industrial compound in surfactants and lubricants [ 1 , 2 ], poses a significant environmental threat. Its hydrophobicity leads to its accumulation in organic-rich sediments, making it a persistent aquatic pollutant [ 3 , 4 ]. As a typical environmental endocrine disruptor, NP induces both acute and chronic toxicity in aquatic organisms. In fish, crustaceans, and molluscs, NP disrupts reproductive hormone synthesis, leading to gonadal abnormalities and imbalanced population sex ratios [ 5 , 6 ].NP also induced intestinal toxicity, damage the gut epithelium, compromise barrier integrity, and perturb microbiome homeostasis [ 7 ]. Its long alkyl chain resistance leads to persistent accumulation in gut tissues, exacerbating barrier dysfunction and microbial dysbiosis [ 8 ].

Within antibiotic-free aquaculture, probiotics have been redefined as strategic microbial modulators [ 9 , 10 ]. Their function now extends beyond growth promotion to include the enhancement of environmental adaptability through dynamic microbiota–host interactions [ 11 ]. Probiotics transiently colonize the gut mucosa, directly or indirectly affecting host health through the secretion of metabolites, competition for ecological niches, and modulation of the local microenvironment [ 12 ]. Evidence from various models supports their multifunctional roles. For example, Lactobacillus enhances gut barrier function by activating the hypoxia-inducible factor signalling pathway through lactic acid production [ 13 ]. In Oncorhynchus mykiss , dietary probiotics improve gut morphology and absorptive capacity [ 14 ]. Studies have also shown that B. subtilis (including its spore form) promotes beneficial lactic acid bacteria, whereas L. acidophilus affects the microbiota composition, improves the gut structure, and increases digestive enzyme activity [ 15 – 17 ]. Furthermore, in Oreochromis niloticus , supplementation with multistrain probiotics (e.g., B. subtilis or L. acidophilus ) alters the gut microbiota to increase nutrient absorption [ 18 ]. In Litopenaeus vannamei , a supplement containing B. subtilis and L. acidophilus strengthens the gut barrier, enhances the utilization of carbon by the gut microbiota, and increases beneficial probiotic populations [ 19 ]. Similarly, in Sus scrofa , the same combination strengthens the mucosal barrier by increasing the abundance of beneficial microbiota and short-chain fatty acids (SCFAs) [ 20 ]. These findings highlight the dual role of probiotics in improving nutrient utilization and enhancing resilience by maintaining a diverse and functional gut microbiota. Although the role of probiotics in promoting gut homeostasis is well documented, their ability to reduce environmental pollutant toxicity and the related molecular mechanisms is not yet fully known.

S. meridionalis , an economically important species of the family Siluridae, is valued for its high intake ability, strong disease resistance, rapid growth, and nutritional value, making it a vital source of high-quality protein [ 21 , 22 ]. Due to its benthic habit, S. meridionalis is consistently exposed to NP in sediments [ 23 ]. It is unclear whether this affects the gut balance and whether probiotics can counteract the toxicity, as well as the molecular processes involved. On the basis of the aforementioned background, this study employed S. meridionalis as a model organism. By utilizing a “probiotic-pretreatment followed by NP-exposure” experimental design, we sought not only to evaluate the mitigation of NP‑induced intestinal toxicity by a B. subtilis and L. acidophilus complex but also to mechanistically decipher its protective effects. To achieve this goal, an integrated multi‑omics approach was used: metagenomics was used to analyse microbial community and functional pathway changes, transcriptomics was used to examine host genes related to lipid metabolism and intestinal barrier function, and untargeted metabolomics was used to track global shifts in the gut metabolome. Finally, through correlating and integrating of these data, a “microbial function – host gene – metabolite –phenotype” regulatory network was constructed, thereby providing a system‑level perspective on how the probiotic formulation alleviates NP‑induced toxicity.

## Materials and methods

### Experimental feed and design

B. subtilis and L. acidophilus used in this study were purchased from Shandong Linyi Yi Antibiotic-Free Biotechnology Co., Ltd. (Shandong, China). with viable counts of 1.0 × 10¹¹ CFU/g and 1.0 × 10¹⁰ CFU/g, respectively. In accordance with the experimental protocol, a stock solution of NP was initially prepared in ethanol and subsequently diluted to achieve the desired working concentrations of 0.1 mg/L and 0.25 mg/L. The two NP concentrations were chosen on the basis of a previous study in juvenile African catfish ( Clarias gariepinus ), in which exposure to 0.1–0.3 mg/L NP for 15 days induced marked reproductive toxicity [ 24 ]. Accordingly, the lower concentration (0.1 mg/L) was set to the minimum effective dose identified in that study, while the higher concentration (0.25 mg/L) was chosen as an intermediate point within the same range. Simultaneously, equal quantities of the two probiotic types were combined to create compound probiotic powder preparations, adhering to a mass ratio of 1.00% relative to the basal feed. These preparations were then dissolved in phosphate-buffered saline (PBS; pH 7.4), and the buffer solution volume (mL) was maintained at a feed mass (g) ratio of 1:10 [ 25 ]. The probiotic compounds were uniformly sprayed onto the basal feed, thoroughly mixed, and air-dried under ventilated conditions. Fresh feed was prepared daily, portioned appropriately, and stored at − 20 °C until required for use. After acclimation to the rearing conditions, the experimental fish were randomly assigned to six groups (20 fish per group, with three replicates per group) as follows: Group C: fed with basal feed only; Group NP1: fed with basal feed for 7 weeks, followed by exposure to 0.1 mg/L NP for 15 days; Group NP2: fed with basal feed for 7 weeks, followed by exposure to 0.25 mg/L NP for 15 days; Group NP1 + PB: fed with compound probiotic-supplemented feed for 7 weeks, followed by exposure to 0.1 mg/L NP for 15 days; Group NP2 + PB: fed with compound probiotic-supplemented feed for 7 weeks, followed by exposure to 0.25 mg/L NP for 15 days; Group PB: fed with compound probiotic-supplemented feed for 7 weeks without NP exposure [ 26 , 27 ].

### Experimental fish

The healthy S. meridionalis juveniles (4 months post-hatching, sexually immature) used in this study were obtained from a local aquaculture farm in Huishui County, Guizhou, China. Prior to the experiment, the fish were acclimated to laboratory conditions for 2 weeks. After acclimation, their total length and body weight were measured (mean total length: 20.56 ± 1.37 cm; body weight: 53.65 ± 4.02 g, mean ± SD), and they were randomly allocated to the different treatment groups. Feeding was performed twice daily (8:00 and 17:30) until apparent satiation. During the experimental period, the water quality was strictly controlled: the water temperature was maintained at 25 ± 2 °C, the dissolved oxygen concentration was maintained kept above 7.0 mg/L, the pH was 7.0 ± 0.5, and the ammonia nitrogen concentration was maintained below 0.08 mg/L [ 28 – 30 ].

### Enzyme activity measurement and differentially expressed metabolite validation

The levels of ethanolamine kinase (EK1) and lipase were measured according to the protocols provided by Jiangsu Saiyan Biotechnology Technology Co., Ltd. (Jiangsu, China). EK1 and lipase levels were measured according to the protocols provided by Jiangsu Saiyan Biotechnology Technology Co., Ltd. (Jiangsu, China). To validate the differentially abundant metabolite results, the contents of phosphocholine (PC), phosphatidylethanolamine (PE), and total phospholipids (PL) were measured using commercial enzyme-linked immunosorbent assay (ELISA) kits from the same manufacturer. PC was quantified using a sandwich ELISA kit, which employed an anti-PC antibody for specific recognition, a horseradish peroxidase (HRP)-labelled detection antibody, and a TMB colorimetric reaction. PC concentrations were derived from a standard curve (0–480 pg/mL). PE was quantified using a competitive ELISA kit, where an anti-PE antibody coated on the microplate and an HRP-labelled PE antigen that competed with sample PE for antibody binding were used. PE concentrations were determined from a standard curve (15–240 pg/mL) on the basis of the absorbance at 450 nm, which was inversely correlated with the PE content. PL was quantified using an oxidase-based colorimetric kit: phospholipids were enzymatically hydrolyzed to choline and then oxidized to generate hydrogen peroxide, resulting in the formation of a blue dye at 600 nm, with the absorbance proportional to the PL content. All procedures were performed strictly in accordance with the manufacturer’s instructions.

### Metagenomic analysis

After a 24-hour fasting period, the gut contents were collected from each fish for metagenomic sequencing. Genomic DNA was extracted was extracted using a commercial extraction kit provided by Guizhou Saiyan Biotechnology Co., Ltd. (Guizhou, China). The integrity of the extracted DNA was assessed via 1% agarose gel electrophoresis, and only samples with a primary band length of ≥ 10 kb were retained to ensure high sequencing quality. After confirming DNA quantity and purity, sequencing was performed on the Illumina Nova Seq high-throughput platform. Independent libraries were constructed for each sample, employing a paired-end sequencing strategy (PE150bp). Raw sequencing reads were initially evaluated using FastQC (v0.12.1) to assess the base quality distribution, mean sequence quality, and nucleotide composition. Quality control was subsequently conducted using Cutadapt (v1.17) and fastp (v0.20.0) to remove low-quality reads (length < 50 bp, average quality score < 20, or reads containing ambiguous bases) [ 31 ]. High-quality clean reads were then assembled using MEGAHIT with the “meta-large” preset parameter. A “single-sample preassembly-merging of unmapped reads−reassembly” strategy was applied to achieve efficient large-scale metagenomic assembly and optimization, thereby generating high-quality contigs for subsequent taxonomic annotation and functional analysis. Nonredundant gene sets were constructed using MMseqs2. The predicted sequences were aligned against the GenBank nonredundant (NR) database using BLAST, and hits with E values ≤ 1e − 5 were retained for species annotation [ 32 ]. Functional annotation was then performed by comparing the predicted genes against the GO, KEGG, eggNOG, Pfam, SwissProt, CAZy, VFDB, CYPED, and additional reference databases [ 33 ]. For downstream differential analysis, metagenomic features (taxonomic and functional) were retained if present in more than 60% of the samples, and their abundances were normalized to reads per kilobase million (RPKM). Differential features between groups were identified using the Kruskal‒Wallis test, with p < 0.05 considered to indicate statistical significance.

### Transcriptomic analysis

Total RNA was extracted from the gut samples of S. meridionalis using a commercial kit (Guizhou Saiyan Biotechnology Co., Ltd., China). RNA quality was rigorously assessed: purity (OD 260/280 ratio of 1.8–2.0) and concentration were determined spectrophotometrically, and integrity was verified by 1% agarose gel electrophoresis and an Agilent 2100 Bioanalyzer (all samples an RNA integrity number (RIN) > 7.0). Sequencing libraries were constructed from qualified RNA and sequenced on an Illumina HiSeq X Ten platform to generate 150-bp paired-end reads. Raw reads were processed using fastp (v0.23.0) to remove adapters, poly-N sequences, and low-quality bases, yielding high-quality clean reads [ 34 ]. These reads were aligned to the S. meridionalis reference genome (GCA_014805685.1) using HISAT2 (v2.2.1). Transcript assembly and quantification were performed with StringTie (v1.3.0). For functional annotation, the predicted protein sequences were aligned against the NR, Swiss-Prot, and KOG databases using DIAMOND (v2.0.15) with a significance threshold of an E value < 1e − 5. The top-hit protein (highest alignment score) for each transcript was used to assign functional annotations. Gene expression levels were quantified as read counts and FPKM using featureCounts (v2.0.9) and Salmon (v1.10.0), respectively. Prior to differential expression analysis, genes with CPM (counts per million) > 1 in more than 50% of the samples were retained and log2-transformed. Differentially expressed genes (DEGs) were identified with DESeq2 (v1.46.0), applying a threshold of adjusted p-value < 0.05 and |log₂FC| > 1) [ 35 ]. GO and KEGG pathway enrichment analyses of the DEGs were conducted using clusterProfiler (v4.14.0), with the results visualized via ggplot2 (v3.5.1) [ 36 ].

### Validation of DEGs by reverse transcription quantitative real-time PCR (RT‒qPCR)

Five differentially expressed genes (DEGs) ( ek1 , gpd1l , gpd1b , pgs1 , and abcg2a ) were selected for validation using RT‒qPCR. The total RNA utilized for validation was identical to that used in the transcriptomic analysis and was reverse-transcribed into complementary DNA (cDNA). RT‒qPCR assays were conducted employing the SYBR Green method. The primer sequences are listed in Table 1 . The β-actin gene served as an internal reference, and relative gene expression levels were determined using the 2^ −ΔΔCt method. Each gene was analysed using three biological samples, with each sample assessed in triplicate technical replicates. The data are presented as mean ± standard deviation (SD). Statistical significance among groups was evaluated using one-way analysis of variance (ANOVA) with Tukey’s post‑hoc test [ 37 ].

### Metabolomic analysis

Gut samples stored at − 80 °C were used for metabolomic analysis. All the experimental instruments (such as steel beads and tweezers) were sterilized at high temperature or disinfected with ethanol prior to use to ensure experimental consistency and prevent cross-contamination. Approximately 50 mg of each sample was weighed and mixed with 1mL of prechilled extraction solvent (methanol: acetonitrile: water = 2:2:1, v/v/v) containing internal standards. Stainless steel beads were added, and the samples were mechanically disrupted at 65 Hz for 90 s using a tissue grinder. This process was followed by intermittent ultrasonic extraction for 10 min to enhance metabolite recovery. The homogenates were incubated at − 20 °C for 1 h to precipitate proteins and then centrifuged at 12,000 rpm for 15 min at 4 °C. A 50 µL aliquot of the supernatant was transferred into a 2 mL centrifuge tube and stored overnight at − 20 °C. The samples were centrifuged again under identical conditions to remove residual impurities, and 120 µL of the final supernatant was transferred into pretreated amber vials for subsequent analysis. Metabolomic profiling was performed using a Waters ACQUITY I-Class PLUS ultrahigh-performance liquid chromatography (UHPLC) system coupled with a Xevo G2-XS QTOF high-resolution mass spectrometer. The chromatographic separation conditions were as follows: 98% A (0–0.25 min), 2% A (10.0–13.0 min), and 98%A (13.1–14.1 min), where mobile phase A was water containing 0.1% formic acid, and phase B was an acetonitrile/methanol mixture. The raw mass spectrometry data were processed using Progenesis QI software for peak extraction, alignment, denoising, and quantification. Prior to analysis, metabolomic features with < 80% missing values and a CV < 30% were retained and log2-transformed. Differentially abundant metabolites were identified using OPLS-DA (VIP > 1) combined with the Student’s t-test ( p < 0.05). Metabolites were annotated through multiple databases, including HMDB, KEGG, and Lipid Maps, to identify their chemical classes and potential metabolic pathways. The, significantly altered metabolites were subsequently subjected to statistical and pathway enrichment analyses using Python-based bioinformatics toolkits (e.g., pandas, scipy, bioinfokit), enabling elucidation of biologically relevant changes at the metabolic pathway level.

### Statistical analysis

The research data were analysed using OriginPro 2026 and the Windows version of SPSS v27.0 software, and are expressed as the mean ± standard deviation (SD). The statistical assessment of differences was conducted by applying one-way analysis of variance (ANOVA). Statistical significance was defined as p < 0.05. The growth parameters, included WGR (%) = (final weight – initial weight)/initial weight × 100 and SGR (%/d) = (Ln final weight − Ln initial weight) × 100/day.

Utilizing the scripy.stats.spearmanr function in Python (version 3.10.9), we performed Spearman’s rank correlation analysis to evaluate all pairwise cross-omics interactions, including microbe‒gene, gene‒metabolite, and metabolite‒microbe relationships. To minimize spurious associations arising from the omics data, significant correlations were defined as |r| > 0.7 and raw p < 0.05, followed by Benjamini–Hochberg false discovery rate (FDR) correction applied to all pairwise tests (FDR < 0.05). A conditional filter was then applied for integration: a “microbe–gene–metabolite” triplet was retained only if all three pairwise correlations (microbe–gene, gene–metabolite, metabolite–microbe) simultaneously satisfied |r| > 0.7 and FDR < 0.05. This strict criterion ensured that only closed-loop association architectures with mutual reinforcement across all three omics layers were considered for downstream analysis. KEGG pathway enrichment analysis was performed on the genes and metabolites present in the identified triplets using the hypergeometric test, with an FDR < 0.05 as the significance threshold. All correlation heatmaps and network visualizations were generated using the Majorbio Cloud Platform ( https://www.majorbio.com/tools ). Pathway figures were generated employing Figdraw 2.0.

## Results

### Gut biochemical indicators and growth performance

Exposure to NP significantly inhibited the growth and enzymatic activity in S. meridionalis (Fig. 1 ), with the key enzymes, EK1 and lipase showing a decrease in activity compared with the control group ( p < 0.05). The NP1 and NP2 groups also experienced lower SGR and WGR ( p < 0.05). However, the introduction of probiotics significantly alleviated these effects, with the NP1+PB and NP2+PB groups showing increased growth and enzyme activity compared with the NP group ( p < 0.05), they did not fully reach control group levels. The PB group showed no significant differences compared with the control group ( p > 0.05).
