## General culture media requirements for muscle cell cultivation

### Basal media

Basal media are formulated to meet minimal nutritional needs, enabling prolonged cell survival and propagation in cultures 57 . One of the most widely used basal media is Dulbecco’s Modified Eagle Medium (DMEM), a modified form of Eagle’s Minimum Essential Medium (MEM), originally developed by Harry Eagle in the 1950s by optimizing the nutritional requirements of human cancer and mouse fibroblast cells 57 – 60 . Ham’s F10, F11, and F12 are also derived from Eagle’s medium 61 . Presently, DMEM has emerged a standard medium for cultivating diverse mammalians, including muscle cells. Its formula contains glucose, amino acids, vitamins, and inorganic salts, tailored to support specific cellular growth requirements 60 . The general DMEM requirements for myoblast propagation are outlined in the following sections.

### Glucose

Glucose is the primary source of energy for cellular growth and functions like proliferation, metabolism, and differentiation 62 . In glycolysis, a six-carbon glucose molecule is metabolized into two of each three-carbon pyruvate and ATP, which fuels most energy-requiring cellular process, including muscle contraction 62 . Glucose also provides carbon backbones for synthesis of macromolecule such as nucleotides, amino acids, and lipids 62 . Metabolically active adult muscle and muscle satellite cells grow optimally in DMEM supplemented with 1000–4500 g/L of glucose 63 , 64 .

### Amino acids

DMEM contains thirteen L-amino acids, including arginine, cysteine, glutamine, histidine, isoleucine, leucine, lysine, methionine, phenylalanine, threonine, tryptophan, tyrosine, and valine 58 , 59 . In particular, L-glutamine is provided in 10- to 100-fold excess (e.g., 2 mM for muscle cells) due to its pivotal role in cellular functions 57 , 65 . Skeletal muscle and brain are the primary sites of glutamine production. Owing to its large tissue mass, skeletal muscle produces the majority of circulating glutamine, which represents ~50-60% of the free amino acids within this tissue 66 , 67 . L-glutamine is readily converted to L-glutamate by mitochondrial glutaminase, serving as an amino group doner for biomolecule synthesis and ATP production via citric acid cycle 67 . L-glutamine also functions as a carbon source that cannot be substituted by glutamic acid or glucose 65 . Furthermore, it can serve as an alternative energy source in certain metabolically active cell types 66 or under glucose-reduced culture conditions, as demonstrated in studies using human fibroblastic cells 68 . Besides protein synthesis, amino acids contribute to biomolecule synthesis, antioxidation, cell signaling, and act as sources of energy, carbon, and nitrogen 65 .

### Inorganic salts

DMEM contains seven salts, including Sodium chloride (NaCl), Potassium Chloride, Sodium Phosphate monobasic, Sodium Bicarbonate (NaHCO 3 ), Calcium Chloride (CaCl₂), Ferric Nitrate, and either Magnesium Chloride or Magnesium Sulfate. NaCl and NaHCO 3 are present in higher concentrations 57 , 59 to mimic physiological conditions. In aqueous solutions, these salts dissociate into respective ions that functions as cofactors and mediators of enzymatic reactions, metabolism, cell signaling, cell adhesion, and muscle contraction 69 , 70 . Most cells grow well at a slightly alkaline pH (7.2–7.4) in a 5% CO 2 incubator, buffered by NaHCO 3 71 . Together with amino acids, inorganic ions regulate osmotic balance, cell volume, and transmembrane potential 69 , 71 , 72 .

### Vitamins

Vitamins are small organic molecules required in small amounts for intracellular process. They act as antioxidants 72 , enzyme co-factors, and prosthetic groups in metabolism 73 . Of the thirteen essential vitamins, DMEM includes six B-complex vitamins (thiamine, riboflavin, niacinamide, pantothenic acid, pyridoxine, folic acid) and two vitamin-like compounds (choline, inositol), indispensable for cell survival and growth 58 , 74 . B-complex vitamins regulate carbohydrate, amino acid, and lipid metabolism, and are involved in single-carbon transfer, and synthesis of heme, purine, and pyrimidines 73 . Vitamin-like compounds primarily support lipid transport and metabolism to maintain the structural integrity and signalling functions of phospholipid cell membrane 74 .

### Serum supplement for myoblast proliferation and differentiation

The use of serum supplements in cell culture media has evolved significantly since the mid-20th century. The earliest application of serum components for myoblast culture was reported by Albert Fischer in 1948, who demonstrated that basal media supplemented with 0.05% dialyzed chicken blood plasma could support the short-term propagation (4–14 days) of chicken embryo myoblasts 75 . Based on this work, in 1954 and 1955, Harry Eagle demonstrated the long-term propagation (4–8 weeks) of mouse myoblasts in media containing 0.5–2% dialyzed HS 59 , and additionally showed that fibroblasts and HeLa cells could be cultured in media containing 1% dialyzed HS and 5% dialyzed human serum 60 . A major advancement came in 1958, when Theodore T. Puck and colleagues demonstrated that supplementation of media with 15% FBS, together with careful regulation of pH and temperature, prevented mitotic inhibition in human skin fibroblast-like cells and Chinese hamster ovary epithelial cells 76 . This approach enabled cells to be maintained at high proliferation rates for 3–6 months without developing aneuploidy, establishing a reliable framework for sustained cell expansion while minimizing chromosomal abnormalities 76 . Since then, FBS has been a key component of cell culture system for over 60 years, supporting diverse research and pharmaceutical applications 13 . It offers a rich blend of essential nutrients for in vitro cellular attachment, expansion, maintenance, and long-term cryopreservation, and continues to serve as the standard supplement for most animal cell cultures to date 13 , 77 , 78 . Although alternatives such as newborn calf serum, calf serum, and donor bovine serum are available, FBS predominates due to its high fetuin content, which supports cell growth 79 , and its relatively low levels of immune components (e.g., Igs, complement factors), which minimize undesired immune responses that could otherwise compromise experimental integrity and the reliability of research or diagnostic outcomes 13 , 76 , 80 .

### Fetal bovine serum - collection, composition, and cellular functions

FBS is derived from blood plasma through a two-step process. Whole blood contains plasma along with cellular components such as erythrocytes, leukocytes, and thrombocytes. Plasma itself is composed of ~90% water, with the remaining fraction consisting of 6-8% proteins, carbohydrates, blood clotting factors, minerals, and hormones 81 . To derive FBS, blood is cooled and allowed to clot for separation into two distinct fractions, serum (FBS) and fibrin clot with blood cells. The serum fraction is collected by centrifugation for downstream applications 82 . FBS has a highly complex molecular composition, containing thousands of macro- and micronutrients, including proteins, amino acids, lipids, carbohydrates, growth factors (GFs), hormones, minerals, and other biomolecules originating from diverse cells and tissues (Table 1 ). Less than two decades ago, 79–91 proteins were identified in three commercial FBS lots using the nano LC-MS/MS analysis 83 . The total protein concentration of these FBS lots ranged between 0.032 and 0.042 g/L 83 . With recent advancements in LC-MS/MS analysis, about 200–400 proteins and thousands of small molecule metabolites were characterized 84 . Albumins (37.09%) and immunoglobulins (Igs) (35.42%) are the most abundant, followed by apolipoprotein A1 (8.31%), serotransferrin (3.49%), and hemopexin (1.54%), collectively accounting for 85.85% of bovine serum proteins 84 . Most serum proteins, except Igs, are synthesised and secreted by the liver. Serum albumins are versatile proteins, well recognized for their roles in transport, antioxidant defense, pH regulation, protection against lipid peroxidation, and the support of cell proliferation and survival 85 . Albumins can covalently or non-covalently bind various biomolecules and ligands, such as fatty acids, amino acids, peptides, hormones, fat-soluble vitamins, metal ions, steroids, and pharmaceutical drugs, facilitating their intra- and intercellular delivery. Its antioxidant activity is attributed to sulphur-containing amino acids such as cysteine and methionine, which scavenge free radicals and prevent ROS generation through metal chelation 85 . Globulins are the second most abundant serum proteins, categorized into α, β, and γ (Igs) based on their electrophoretic mobility. Like albumins, globulins regulate nutrient transport, enzymatic reactions, and immunity. Igs are distinct as they are secreted by immune cells in response to infections, playing a central role in immune defense 86 , 87 . GFs and hormones in FBS are vital for myogenesis as they regulate the family of muscle-specific genes and proteins 10 . Cell cultures lack these nutrients and therefore require supplements like FBS, which provides at least thirteen GFs and fifteen hormones (Table 1 ). These small molecules regulate cell growth, metabolism, repair, signalling, and immune functions 10 . Hormones are produced and release into circulation by endocrine glands, while GFs are produced locally by different cell types. Studies using muscle cell models showed three families of GFs and hormones such as IGFs, FGF, and transforming growth factor beta (TGF-β) to have major effects on myogenic differentiation 10 . They control differentiation by regulating expression of myogenic regulatory factor genes, particularly myogenin 10 . TGF-β and FGF are potent differentiation inhibitors, while IGF stands out for multifaceted effects 10 , 88 , 89 . Specifically, IGF subtypes, including IGF-I, IGF-II, and insulin, promote proliferation, differentiation, nutrient uptake (glucose, amino acids, nucleosides), and macromolecule synthesis (protein, nucleic acid) 10 , 79 , 89 , 90 . FBS also contains various extracellular matrix glycoproteins (collagen, fibronectin, fibrinogen, laminin, integrin) that contribute to cell structure organization, signalling, and adhesion (cell-cell/-matrix), supporting tissue morphogenesis, differentiation, and homogenesis 91 . Notably, integrin-laminin interactions regulate cell adhesion, migration, proliferation, differentiation, and phenotype stability 91 , 92 . Fibronectins are critical for cell migration, wound healing, and inflammatory responses, highlighting multifunctional roles of glycoproteins in cellular dynamics 91 . ### Horse serum

HS is another commonly used cell growth supplement that provides essential nutrients and GFs necessary for cell growth. Unlike FBS, literature on HS is limited, particularly regarding its molecular profile, collection process, donor selection criteria (e.g., age, diet, sex, physiology), and suitability for research applications. Based on available information, HS is derived from healthy adult horse blood, mainly collected via venipuncture 93 – 95 . Standard blood collection guidelines should minimize trauma, bleeding, and hematoma formation 93 , 95 . HS is then separated from clotted blood using methods similar to FBS production. Unlike FBS, HS was reported to have high homogeneity between lots and to contain low levels of polyamine oxidase, the enzyme responsible for polyamine degradation. Consequently, polyamines are metabolized more slowly and accumulate, which has been associated with mitogenic effects 96 . HS was initially preferred over FBS due to lower cost and broader availability 97 , and moreover, it eliminates the need for animal sacrifice. It is commonly used for cultivating equine cells, but it also supports the growth of other mammalian cells 11 , 98 , 99 . HS is highly valued for its ability to stimulate myogenic differentiation of myoblasts or myogenic precursor cells into myotubes 11 , 98 . In 1960s, Yaffe and colleagues showed newborn rat skeletal muscle cells could optimally proliferate for months and differentiate into multinucleated fibers when cultured in media with HS or FBS 11 , 56 . Later study compared serum type (HS, FBS) and concentration on rat skeletal muscle cells (L8, L84) 11 . L8 cells cultured in basal medium with 10% HS exhibited a shorter proliferation phase and higher cell fusion within 1–2 days after reaching confluency than cells grown in medium with 10% FBS, which showed a longer proliferation phase and relatively lower fusion 11 . L8 cells showed poor growth and differentiation in 2% HS, but addition of insulin (1 × 10 −4 g/L) significantly improved both. Furthermore, L84 cells exhibited a similar proliferation and differentiation profile regardless of the serum condition tested (10% FBS, 2% or 10% HS). This study further emphasized the significant impact of cell density on myogenesis. For example, switching from 10% FBS to 2% HS in L84 cultures seeded at higher density (1.2 × 10⁶ cells/plate) resulted in enhanced cell fusion than lower density (1.7 × 10⁵ cells/plate). These cells also showed increased creatine kinase (CK) activity and myosin expression, which are key myogenesis markers 11 . These findings laid the groundwork for optimizing and standardizing muscle cell culture conditions, particularly the widely adopted approach of stimulating myoblast proliferation with 10% FBS, followed by differentiation in 2% HS, as extensively validated using C2C12 myoblasts 9 , 51 . Another study demonstrated that 10% FBS led to a higher cell doubling rate in equine bronchial fibroblasts compared to HS, whereas HS more effectively promoted fibroblast differentiation into myofibroblasts 99 . These observations indicate that FBS enhances proliferation, likely due to its high mitogen content, whereas HS favours differentiation through high myogenic factor levels 10 . However, limited research highlights the need for further studies, ideally using high-throughput proteomics and metabolomics to achieve better understanding of serum effects on muscle cell behaviour.

### Limitations of FBS and HS use in cellular agriculture

Despite their widespread use, FBS and HS are largely criticized worldwide for applications in cell-based therapeutics and food production, due to ethical, safety, variability, environmental, economic, and regulatory concerns, as outlined below.

### Ethical concerns

FBS is obtained as a by-product of the meat industry from bovine fetal blood, collected via cardiac puncture in a closed system when a foetus is detected at slaughter 100 . EU regulations prohibit the transport and slaughter of cows during the final 10% of gestation 101 , 102 ; however pregnant animals continue to reach abattoirs due to undetected pregnancies, illness, reduced productivity, or economic constraints, as reported by the European Food Safety Authority (EFSA) Panel on Animal Health and Welfare (AHAW) in 2017 101 . In parallel, there is growing concern regarding the potential suffering inflicted on foetuses during this process. According to the World Organization for Animal Health (OIE) and the American Veterinary Medical Association (AVMA), fetal death occurs from anoxia within 10-20 mins in utero post-slaughter, while the complete process from inspection to blood collection generally exceeds 40 mins 101 . Although fetal neurological development is incomplete and the capacity for consciousness or pain perception is limited 103 , the use of approximately 2 million foetuses annually to produce ~800,000 L of FBS, a number that continues to grow, raises further questions regarding the number of pregnant cows slaughtered, ethical practices, transparency, and the overall sustainability of FBS production 12 , 13 , 78 . Ethical issues also extend to HS procurement, despite it not being a slaughter by-product. # The role of sphingolipids in major depressive disorder and associated cognitive impairment: interactions with monoaminergic signaling, neuroinflammation, and neurogenesis

## Abstract
Major depressive disorder (MDD) represents a leading cause of disability. Despite decades of research focused on monoaminergic dysregulation, the exact pathophysiological mechanisms underlying MDD remain incompletely understood. This gap in knowledge has contributed to suboptimal therapeutic outcomes, with approximately one-third of MDD patients showing resistance to conventional treatments. Recent advances in lipidomics support that sphingolipids—including ceramides, sphingomyelins, and their metabolites—could play important roles in depression pathophysiology. This review examines the role of sphingolipid dysregulation in MDD and associated cognitive impairment, with a particular focus on interactions with neurogenesis and apoptosis, monoaminergic signaling, neuroinflammation, mitochondrial dysfunction and oxidative stress, glutamatergic signaling, and synaptic plasticity. Several clinical studies demonstrate altered sphingolipid profiles in MDD patients, with elevated ceramide levels correlating with depression severity. Preclinical evidence supports potential causal relationships between sphingolipid alterations and depressive behaviors through effects on neurotransmission, neuroplasticity, neurogenesis, mitochondrial function, and inflammatory processes. Many established antidepressants influence sphingolipid metabolism through distinct mechanisms—acting directly as functional inhibitors of acid sphingomyelinase (ASM) or modulating this pathway indirectly. This mechanistic convergence positions sphingolipid dysregulation as a potential central mediating node across major pathophysiological pathways in MDD and as a common pathway through which key risk factors may converge, potentially explaining its biological heterogeneity. Sphingolipid metabolism also offers a potential mechanistic explanation for the frequently observed cognitive deficits in MDD. This review synthesizes current evidence regarding sphingolipid involvement in depression pathophysiology and outlines promising avenues for personalized medicine through biomarker development and sphingolipid-targeted therapeutics.

## Keywords
Biomarkers; Depression; Cell biology

## Introduction

Major depressive disorder (MDD) represents a leading cause of disability, affecting social functioning, work productivity, and quality of life [ 1 ]. MDD shows a 12-month prevalence of 6% and a lifetime risk of 15–18%, affecting approximately 280 million people worldwide [ 2 ] and women twice as frequently as men [ 1 ]. MDD—a specific diagnosis requiring depressed mood and/or anhedonia (i.e., markedly diminished ability to experience pleasure) plus additional DSM-5 criteria—differs from depression, a broader term encompassing transient sadness or subsyndromal presentations. Multiple risk factors contribute to MDD pathophysiology, including chronic psychosocial stressors, adverse childhood experiences, genetic vulnerability, personality traits, metabolic factors, chronic inflammatory conditions, hypothalamic-pituitary-adrenal (HPA) axis dysregulation, and socioeconomic factors [ 1 ].

Despite decades of research focusing on monoamine dysfunction, particularly serotonergic, noradrenergic and dopaminergic signaling, the exact pathophysiological mechanisms underlying MDD remain incompletely understood [ 3 , 4 ]. The monoamine hypothesis, dominant since the 1960s, has proven insufficient to fully explain MDD’s complexity, including clinical presentation variability, differential treatment responses, and the typical weeks-long therapeutic delay [ 5 ]. Contemporary frameworks embrace a biopsychosocial model integrating psychological, social, and biological factors, the latter encompassing monoaminergic dysregulation, neuroinflammation, altered neurogenesis and apoptosis, mitochondrial dysfunction, glutamatergic signaling dysregulation, and altered synaptic plasticity, recognized as potential key contributors to MDD pathophysiology [ 3 , 4 ].

Current pharmacological treatments for MDD remain suboptimal, with approximately one-third of patients showing treatment-resistant depression [ 6 , 7 ]. This suggests potential biological heterogeneity where different pathophysiological mechanisms may underlie episodes in different patients, or even different episodes in the same patient [ 8 , 9 ]. This heterogeneity likely explains variable treatment responses and highlights the critical need for a deeper understanding of depression pathophysiology to identify novel therapeutic targets and biomarkers for personalized treatment selection [ 10 ].

Recent advances in lipidomics have suggested sphingolipids as potentially crucial players in MDD pathophysiology [ 11 – 14 ]. Research linking sphingolipid metabolism to MDD has developed over approximately 20 years, starting with observations that tricyclic antidepressants modified sphingolipid metabolism [ 15 ], gaining momentum with Kornhuber, Gulbins et al.’s 2005 demonstration of elevated acid sphingomyelinase (ASM) activity in MDD [ 16 ], continuing with identification of functional inhibitors of ASM (FIASMAs)—a class of medications including many antidepressants that inhibit ASM through lysosomal accumulation—in 2008–2011 [ 17 – 19 ], and culminating in Gulbins et al.‘s 2013 study [ 11 ] establishing that the ASM-ceramide system mediates antidepressant effects in rodent models. This research further gained visibility during the COVID-19 pandemic when Hoertel et al. [ 20 – 22 ] found that FIASMA antidepressants were associated with substantially reduced risk of intubation or death in hospitalized COVID-19 patients. Subsequent work [ 23 – 29 ] provided preclinical and clinical evidence that these effects are mediated, at least in part, by antiviral and anti-inflammatory mechanisms through ASM/ceramide pathway modulation. Additional observational studies [ 30 – 33 ] and randomized trials [ 34 ] confirmed reduced risk of severe outcomes, particularly with fluoxetine and fluvoxamine at medium-to-high antidepressant doses, suggesting that sphingolipid-mediated mechanisms may represent a common biological thread across psychiatric and systemic inflammatory conditions—a pattern echoing the very origins of antidepressant pharmacology, as iproniazid, the first marketed antidepressant, derived from an anti-tuberculosis agent [ 4 , 35 ]. Several comprehensive reviews have since highlighted the growing evidence for sphingolipid and broader lipid alterations in MDD pathophysiology [ 12 , 14 , 36 , 37 ], and focused research on sphingolipids has grown substantially over the past decade.

Sphingolipids, including ceramides (Cer), sphingomyelins, and complex glycosphingolipids, serve as both structural components of cellular membranes and bioactive signaling molecules influencing numerous cellular processes relevant to brain pathophysiology [ 38 , 39 ]. Clinical studies have shown altered sphingolipid profiles in many MDD patients, particularly elevated ceramide levels [ 40 , 41 ], correlating with depression severity [ 42 , 43 ]. Many antidepressants influence sphingolipid metabolism through their FIASMA properties [ 11 , 19 , 36 ], suggesting a fundamental role in MDD pathophysiology. However, these alterations show substantial inter-individual variability, potentially reflecting distinct MDD subtypes, comorbidities, medication status, or genetic factors influencing sphingolipid metabolism. These observations have raised questions regarding variability in the specific ceramide species altered, brain region-specific effects, and whether these changes represent causal factors, state markers, or epiphenomena.

Cognitive impairment affects many MDD patients across attention, processing speed, executive function, and memory [ 44 – 47 ]. These deficits often persist even after mood symptom improvement and significantly impact functional recovery and quality of life [ 48 , 49 ]. Sphingolipid roles in hippocampal neurogenesis, synaptic plasticity, neurotransmission, and neuroinflammation [ 50 – 52 ] may thus provide important insights into the mechanisms underlying both mood symptoms and cognitive dysfunction in MDD.

This narrative review examines the role of sphingolipids in MDD and its associated cognitive deficits, with particular focus on their interactions with neurogenesis and apoptosis, monoaminergic signaling, neuroinflammation and oxidative stress, mitochondrial dysfunction, glutamatergic signaling, and synaptic plasticity. We synthesize evidence from preclinical and clinical studies to provide an integrated view of sphingolipid involvement in MDD pathophysiology and explore the potential therapeutic implications of targeting sphingolipid pathways.

## Sphingolipid metabolism

### Overview of sphingolipid structure and functions

Sphingolipids serve both structural and signaling functions in cells, particularly those in the central nervous system (CNS) [ 19 , 52 , 53 ]. The basic structure of sphingolipids consists of a sphingoid base, typically sphingosine, to which an amide-linked fatty acid of variable chain length and saturation is attached, forming ceramide [ 54 ]. Ceramide serves as the central hub of sphingolipid metabolism, from which more complex sphingolipids are derived through addition of various head groups such as phosphocholine (forming sphingomyelin) or carbohydrate moieties (forming glycosphingolipids, including cerebrosides, globosides, and gangliosides) [ 55 ].

Beyond their role as structural components of cellular membranes, sphingolipids function as bioactive molecules involved in numerous cellular processes relevant to brain pathophysiology [ 55 , 56 ]. Ceramide and its metabolite sphingosine-1-phosphate (S1P) have emerged as key signaling molecules with often opposing effects [ 57 ]. Ceramide generally promotes cell growth arrest, senescence, and apoptosis, whereas S1P stimulates cell proliferation, survival, and migration [ 55 , 58 ]. This “sphingolipid rheostat” represents a critical mechanism regulating cell survival under various physiological and pathological conditions [ 57 , 59 , 60 ].

In the CNS, sphingolipids play essential roles in neuronal development, myelination, synaptic function, and neurotransmission [ 52 , 61 ]. Gangliosides support axonal growth, synaptogenesis, and synaptic transmission [ 62 ], while sphingomyelin is essential for signal transduction and membrane organization [ 43 ].

### Sphingolipid synthesis and degradation pathways

The metabolism of sphingolipids involves complex, interconnected pathways of synthesis and degradation, as illustrated in Fig. 1 . Ceramide, the central hub of sphingolipid metabolism, is generated through three main pathways [ 12 , 52 , 54 , 56 , 57 , 59 , 60 , 63 – 71 ]: (i) the de novo synthesis pathway, (ii) the sphingomyelinase pathway (including ASM and neutral sphingomyelinases [NSM]), and (iii) the salvage/recycling pathway, with detailed enzymatic mechanisms provided in Supplementary Text 1 . Solid arrows denote direct biosynthetic or catabolic reactions; dashed arrows indicate reverse reactions, recycling pathways, or catabolic degradation returning ceramide from complex sphingolipids. De novo pathway : Ceramide biosynthesis proceeds through sequential conversion of serine and palmitoyl-CoA to 3-ketosphinganine (via serine palmitoyltransferase, SPT), then to sphinganine (via 3-ketosphinganine reductase, KSR), followed by formation of dihydroceramide (via ceramide synthases, CerS), and final desaturation to ceramide (via dihydroceramide desaturase, DES). Sphingomyelinase pathway : Sphingomyelin undergoes hydrolysis to generate ceramide through three principal routes: acid sphingomyelinase (ASM), neutral sphingomyelinase (NSM), and alkaline sphingomyelinase (Alk-SMase, encoded by ENPP7, primarily expressed in the intestinal mucosa). The reverse reaction, catalyzed by sphingomyelin synthase (SMS), converts ceramide back to sphingomyelin. Salvage/recycling pathway : Ceramide is hydrolyzed to sphingosine by ceramidase (CDase); the reverse re-acylation of sphingosine to ceramide is catalyzed by ceramide synthases (CerS). Sphingosine undergoes phosphorylation by sphingosine kinases (SphK1/2) to form sphingosine-1-phosphate (S1P), which mediates pro-survival signaling. ## Sphingolipid alterations in MDD

### Preclinical evidence

Preclinical studies using chronic stress paradigms have provided insights into the relationships between sphingolipid alterations and depressive-like behaviors. These paradigms reliably induce depressive-like behaviors in rodents and lead to increased ceramide accumulation in key brain regions [ 11 , 72 ]. Male rats [ 73 ] show differential sphingolipid profiles along the hippocampal longitudinal axis, suggesting distinct region-specific effects of stress on sphingolipid metabolism.

Prior studies [ 74 , 75 ] show that sphingolipid changes precede behavioral symptoms in mouse models, with increased ASM activity and ceramide accumulation occurring before depression-like behaviors emerge, suggesting these alterations are early pathogenic events.

Several pharmacological approaches targeting sphingolipid metabolism have demonstrated antidepressant-like effects in preclinical rodent models. Yang et al. [ 76 ] developed a direct ASM inhibitor that reduced brain ceramide levels, enhanced hippocampal neurogenesis, and ameliorated depression-like behaviors in rats. Gulbins et al. [ 11 ] showed that amitriptyline and fluoxetine reduced ASM activity and ceramide levels in the hippocampus, and improved depressive-like behaviors in mouse chronic stress paradigms. This effect was absent in ASM knock-out mice. Furthermore, mice overexpressing ASM, treated with ceramidase inhibitors or injected with Cer16:0 into the hippocampus, had lower neuronal proliferation, maturation and survival compared with controls, and showed depression-like behavior even without stress. Antidepressant-mediated ASM inhibition reversed these effects. Jaddoa et al. [ 77 ] showed that chronic paroxetine reduced sphingosine levels in the rat hippocampus and prefrontal cortex and ceramide levels in the hippocampus, with concomitant downregulation of both SMPD1 (ASM) and ASAH1 (acid ceramidase) mRNA, suggesting transcriptional modulation of multiple sphingolipid enzymes.

Behavioral and neurobiological effects of ceramide alterations may depend on brain region and species. For example, Cer16:0 infusions into the dorsal hippocampus induce depression-like behavior in male mice, whereas Cer16:0 infusions into the basolateral amygdala induce anxiety-like behavior, while Cer8:0 and Cer20:0 produce no such effects [ 78 ]. Furthermore, under chronic stress conditions, distinct ceramide profiles emerge in different hippocampal subregions: complex glycosphingolipids (hexosylceramide, sulfatide, lactosylceramide) accumulate in the dorsal hippocampus, while long-chain ceramides (Cer16:0–Cer20:0) increase and very long-chain ceramides (Cer22:0–Cer26:0) decrease in the ventral hippocampus [ 73 ]. Another study [ 79 ] demonstrated that Cer20:0 injection into the ventral hippocampus induced short-term anhedonia-like behavior in rats. This regional and species specificity may reflect distinct roles of brain circuits in depression pathophysiology. These findings suggest region- and species-specific mechanistic links between sphingolipid dysfunction and MDD pathophysiology.

While most preclinical studies focus on ASM, other sphingolipid enzymes may have distinct contributions. Genetic NSM reduction produces opposite behavioral effects in male versus female mice (severe depression-like phenotype in males; reduced depression-like behavior in females) [ 80 ], yet unlike ASM, NSM deficiency does not affect hippocampal neurogenesis [ 80 , 81 ]. Direct sphingomyelin synthase (SMS) inhibition rapidly reverses depression-like behavior within 3 days via autophagy induction [ 82 ], bypassing conventional antidepressant latency. These findings suggest distinct mechanistic roles across sphingolipid enzymes in MDD pathophysiology.

### Clinical evidence

Several clinical studies demonstrate altered sphingolipid metabolism in MDD patients. Peripheral blood analyses consistently show elevated levels of specific ceramide species compared to healthy controls [ 41 , 42 ]. Brunkhorst-Kanaan et al. [ 40 ] observed significantly increased plasma levels of multiple ceramide species (Cer16:0, Cer18:0, Cer20:0, Cer22:0, Cer24:0, Cer24:1) in MDD and bipolar disorder patients compared to healthy controls, particularly in male patients. Depressive symptom severity also correlated with ceramide levels. Schumacher et al. [ 75 ] also found positive correlations between plasma ceramide concentrations, examined as the sum of Cer16:0 to Cer24:0 species, and MDD severity, independent of sex, body mass index, and age. Dinoff et al. [ 83 ] showed that the species Cer16:0, Cer18:0 and SM18:1 were associated with depressive symptom severity in individuals with coronary artery disease. Finally, a systematic review [ 42 ] found strong associations between depressive symptom severity and higher plasma levels of Cer18:0 and Cer20:0. Collectively, these findings suggest potential specificity in sphingolipid alterations rather than global changes, and that ceramide levels may reflect intrinsic aspects of MDD pathophysiology rather than secondary effects of clinical characteristics, such as comorbidity.

A post-mortem study [ 84 ] of brain tissue of suicide victims with unipolar MDD versus controls demonstrated Gsα relocalization to lipid rafts in the cerebellum and prefrontal cortex, where it is less likely to couple to adenylyl cyclase. This suggests that antidepressants may upregulate Gsα signaling by disrupting membrane microenvironments.

A longitudinal study of adult MDD patients [ 85 ] found that high baseline serum secretory ASM (S-ASM) activity was associated with milder clinician-evaluated and self-rated depressive symptom severity and state anxiety severity at follow-up and stronger symptomatic improvement in patients receiving antidepressants, an effect driven primarily by females. However, S-ASM activity did not differ between current MDD, remitted MDD, and healthy controls, suggesting prognostic rather than diagnostic utility.

Several limitations must be acknowledged. First, most clinical studies measure peripheral blood sphingolipids—whether these reflect CNS metabolism remains uncertain given blood-brain barrier (BBB) selectivity and potentially independent regulation of peripheral versus central sphingolipid pools. Second, specific ceramide species implicated vary across studies, likely reflecting methodological differences (lipidomic platforms, sample processing), patient heterogeneity (depression subtypes, comorbidities, medication status), or biological variability. Third, while preclinical studies support causal relationships—pharmacological or genetic sphingolipid modulation affects depressive-like behaviors [ 11 , 76 , 77 , 79 ], with sphingolipid alterations preceding behavioral changes [ 74 , 75 , 86 ]—clinical studies provide primarily cross-sectional evidence. Prospective longitudinal studies tracking sphingolipid changes before, during, and after depressive episodes are needed to establish temporal precedence and determine whether sphingolipid alterations represent causal factors, trait markers, state markers, or consequences of other pathophysiological processes.

### Sex differences in sphingolipid profiles

The sphingolipid system may contribute to sex-differences in MDD vulnerability. Preclinical studies showed that genetically reduced NSM activity produces a severe depression-like phenotype in male mice [ 80 ], but reduced depression-like behavior in female mice [ 80 ], which was paralleled by enhanced functional connectivity in females on fMRI [ 87 ]. This sex-divergent pattern contrasts with the ASM pathway, where no comparable behavioral dichotomy has been reported, suggesting enzyme-specific roles in sex-dependent MDD pathophysiology.

These preclinical findings may have clinical relevance: Mocking et al. [ 88 ] found, in remitted MDD patients, that lower hexosylceramide (HexCer) 20:0 levels predicted higher recurrence risk specifically in females, while total ceramide measures had limited universal prognostic utility. Such sex differences may reflect hormonal regulation, as estrogen modulates ceramide synthesis through suppression of SPT and CerS in the steroidogenic pathway [ 89 ]. Given MDD’s 2:1 female predominance, these interactions warrant dedicated investigation. Fig. 2 Theoretical Framework of Sphingolipid Dysregulation in Major Depressive Disorder. Sphingolipid dysregulation (increased ceramide involving acid sphingomyelinase [ASM] activation; with reciprocal decrease in sphingosine-1-phosphate [S1P]) is depicted as a putative central mediating and amplifying node linking six major pathophysiological mechanisms associated with major depressive disorder (MDD). This integrative framework synthesizes evidence from the manuscript, mainly from preclinical studies; comprehensive validation in MDD patients is required. Thick double-headed arrows indicate putative bidirectional regulation in two domains: monoaminergic signaling (5-HT signaling ↔ ASM/ceramide: ceramide alters 5-HT₁ A receptor coupling and SERT function; conversely, monoaminergic activity and antidepressants with FIASMA properties modulate ASM/ceramide levels) and neuroinflammation (TNF-α ↔ ASM/ceramide: TNF-α activates ASM while ceramide induces NF-κB-mediated cytokine production including TNF-α, forming a positive feedback loop). Standard arrows indicate direct molecular effects with experimental support for the remaining four domains. Thin arrows toward MDD symptoms reflect that each mechanism’s relative contribution may vary across patients or across episodes in the same patient. The six mechanistic domains are: (1) Monoaminergic signaling — ceramide, notably generated via NSM-dependent sphingomyelin hydrolysis at the plasma membrane, alters lipid raft composition, impairing 5-HT₁ A receptor coupling/signaling and SERT function; (2) Neuroinflammation — ceramide activates NF-κB, increases pro-inflammatory cytokines (TNF-α, IL-1β, IL-6), ↑ ROS generation, and promotes microglial activation; (3) Neurogenesis and apoptosis — elevated ceramide reduces hippocampal dentate gyrus (DG) neurogenesis and promotes pro-apoptotic signaling, decreasing BDNF/TrkB pathway activity, while S1P promotes neuronal survival; the ↑ ceramide / ↓ S1P balance determines cell fate; (4) Mitochondrial function — ceramide inhibits ETC Complex I, generating ↑ mitochondrial ROS, ↓ ATP production, and inducing mitochondrial outer membrane permeabilization, leading to cellular bioenergetic crisis; (5) Glutamatergic signaling — ceramide (notably NSM-derived at synaptic membranes) dysregulates NMDAR trafficking, modulates AMPAR expression, and disrupts Ca²⁺ homeostasis; and (6) Synaptic plasticity — ceramide impairs dendritic spine remodeling, ↓ activity-dependent BDNF secretion, and alters vesicle recycling. ## Molecular mechanisms linking sphingolipid metabolism to MDD (Fig. 2 )

### Effects on neurogenesis and apoptosis

Neuronal turnover, reflecting the balance between neuronal death and neurogenesis, represents a key neuroplasticity mechanism for cognition [ 90 , 91 ]. Enhanced dentate granule cell proliferation improves cognitive performance, whereas impaired neurogenesis or increased neuronal apoptosis produces cognitive deficits and compromised hippocampal-dependent memory [ 90 , 92 ]. Sphingolipids affect this apoptotic/neurogenic equilibrium. Elevated ceramide induces oxidative stress, reactive oxygen species (ROS) formation, lipid peroxidation, and ultimately cell apoptosis [ 93 ], while S1P promotes survival and proliferation [ 57 , 58 ].

Gulbins et al. [ 11 ] showed that mice overexpressing ASM or heterozygous for acid ceramidase display impaired hippocampal neurogenesis, neuronal maturation and survival. Amitriptyline and fluoxetine, antidepressants acting as FIASMAs [ 18 ], restored these hippocampal deficits. This effect was absent in ASM-deficient mice, demonstrating ASM-specific mechanisms. Moreover, ASM inhibition mitigated histopathological and behavioral changes in a murine model of traumatic brain injury [ 94 ]. Unlike FIASMAs, which act via lysosomal accumulation, direct SMS inhibition produces rapid endoplasmic reticulum (ER) ceramide accumulation and autophagy activation, reversing stress-induced depressive-like behavior within 3 days in mice [ 82 ]. Conversely, genetic NSM deficiency did not affect neurogenesis, maturation, or survival in mice [ 80 , 81 ], suggesting ASM and SMS, but not NSM, regulate these processes.

The ceramide metabolite S1P regulates neurogenesis and neuronal excitability [ 95 ]. Mice lacking sphingosine kinase (SphK) isoenzymes exhibit severe neurogenesis impairment, with pronounced forebrain cell loss and enhanced neuroepithelial apoptosis in the telencephalon and diencephalon [ 96 ].

The relative contributions of the different sphingolipid pathways to neurogenesis remain to be characterized in MDD patients, as evidence derives exclusively from rodent models.

### Effects of sphingolipids on monoaminergic signaling

Sphingolipids modulate serotonin (5-HT) receptors and transporters in neuronal membranes [ 97 , 98 ]. The direction of modulation depends on experimental conditions: metabolic depletion in sphingolipid-deficient cell systems enhanced function [ 99 ], while pharmacological ceramide synthase inhibition impaired receptor function [ 100 ]. This suggests that sphingolipids are essential for normal serotonin 1 A receptor function, with reversible effects upon sphingolipid replenishment, demonstrating dynamic sphingolipid-receptor coupling in membrane lipid domains.

The sphingomyelinase pathway may also affect 5-HT 1 A receptor signaling. Sphingomyelinase treatment of Chinese Hamster Ovary cells expressing human serotonin 1 A receptors enhanced ligand binding affinity [ 101 ], suggesting that enzymatic sphingomyelin breakdown in membrane lipid domains directly influences receptor function by altering the membrane lipid environment.

Müller et al. [ 102 ] provided in vivo evidence that transgenic mice overexpressing ASM exhibited monoamine hypo-activity and depression-like behavior, linking ceramide dysregulation to monoaminergic dysfunction. ASM overexpression reduced basal dopamine levels in the nucleus accumbens and dorsal hippocampus, while potentiating dopaminergic responses to alcohol and enhancing serotonergic responses to appetitive food stimuli [ 103 ], suggesting complex, context-dependent monoaminergic dysregulation.

Ceramides may also directly influence the serotonin transporter (SERT) function, the primary Selective Serotonin Reuptake Inhibitor (SSRI) target. In vitro studies showed that short-chain ceramide Cer2:0 treatment decreased dopamine uptake while increasing serotonin uptake through the dopamine transporter rather than SERT [ 104 ]. Given structural similarities between monoamine transporters, similar mechanisms may apply to SERT, though this hypothesis requires formal testing.

Sphingolipids also modulate noradrenergic and dopaminergic systems, with the norepinephrine and dopamine transporters (NET, DAT) sensitive to membrane lipid changes within specialized lipid microdomains [ 97 , 104 ].

Ceramide treatment modulates dopamine transport and release. Riddle et al. [ 104 ] showed that short-chain exogenous ceramide reversibly decreased dopamine uptake in rat striatal synaptosomes. Conversely, Jeon et al. [ 105 ] reported that cell-permeable Cer6:0 increased dopamine uptake in PC12 cells in the presence of calcium ionophore, while Cer8:1-phosphate enhanced dopamine release. This suggests that sphingomyelinase-dependent ceramide generation regulates dopamine release and potentially dopamine-dependent behaviors such as anhedonia.

conclusions:
Evidence supporting sphingolipid involvement in MDD pathophysiology has grown substantially, with the ASM/ceramide system emerging as an important therapeutic target. Antidepressants from multiple pharmacological classes may influence sphingolipid metabolism through different mechanisms. Some act directly as FIASMAs—reducing membrane ceramide and inducing autophagy via ER ceramide accumulation in preclinical models—while others may do so indirectly, via anti-inflammatory effects that reduce TNF-α–driven ASM activation, or through autophagy induction by pathways that may intersect with sphingolipid signaling. This mechanistic convergence is consistent with sphingolipid dysregulation functioning as a potential mediating node across major pathophysiological pathways in MDD—monoaminergic signaling, neuroinflammation, neurogenesis and apoptosis, mitochondrial function, glutamatergic signaling, and synaptic plasticity—and as a common pathway through which risk factors—including stress, genetic vulnerability, and metabolic dysfunction—may contribute to depression pathophysiology. Importantly, the relative contribution of each mechanism may vary across patients and across episodes in the same patient, which may help explain MDD’s biological heterogeneity. This positions the sphingolipid system as a potential integrative mechanism linking previously disparate findings in MDD research, though this hypothesis requires further investigation.

Multiple lines of evidence support potential causal involvement of sphingolipids in MDD. Clinical studies consistently demonstrate altered ceramide profiles in depression [ 40 , 41 ], though a systematic review [ 42 ] noted heterogeneity suggesting subgroup variations. Animal studies demonstrate temporal precedence, with sphingolipid changes preceding depressive behaviors [ 74 , 75 , 86 ] and dose-response relationships [ 75 ], though human longitudinal confirmation is needed. Biological plausibility is further supported by experimental evidence: pharmacological or genetic manipulation of sphingolipid metabolism affects depressive behaviors in animals [ 11 , 76 , 77 , 79 ], while antidepressants modulate sphingolipid profiles [ 19 , 134 ]. Collectively, this evidence suggests that sphingolipid dysregulation may contribute meaningfully to MDD pathogenesis through complex, multifaceted mechanisms, offering diverse therapeutic opportunities.

Despite accumulating evidence, several important limitations and gaps must be acknowledged. First, the specific ceramide species implicated vary across studies, likely reflecting patient heterogeneity, methodological differences, or distinct MDD subtypes. In addition, most clinical studies examine peripheral blood sphingolipids, and whether peripheral measurements reflect brain sphingolipid metabolism remains unclear. Notably, Schumacher et al. [ 86 ] showed in mice that stress-induced, NSM2-dependent ceramide-enriched exosomes in blood plasma directly inhibit hippocampal phospholipase D, inducing depressive-like behavior—suggesting peripheral ceramide may functionally influence the CNS rather than merely reflect it, though human replication is needed. Second, questions persist regarding whether sphingolipid alterations represent causal factors or state markers reflecting current disease activity. While cross-sectional studies show elevated ceramides during depressive episodes, a prospective longitudinal study of remitted MDD patients found that sphingolipid predictors of recurrence were species- and sex-specific—notably HexCer20:0 in females—while total ceramide measures showed limited universal prognostic utility [ 88 ]. This emphasizes the need for species-specific and sex-stratified sphingolipid analyses. Third, longitudinal studies tracking sphingolipid changes across depressive episodes remain limited, and regional specificity of sphingolipid alterations in human brain remains largely unexplored, with preclinical region- and species-specific findings yet to be confirmed in human tissue [ 73 , 80 ]. Fourth, interactions between sphingolipid dysregulation and other pathophysiological mechanisms—including immune signaling, HPA axis dysfunction, and metabolic factors—require systematic investigation. Moreover, MDD can co-occur with anxiety disorders, metabolic syndrome, and neurodegenerative diseases such as Alzheimer’s disease—conditions themselves associated with altered sphingolipid metabolism [ 56 ]. This high comorbidity rate complicates efforts to identify sphingolipid signatures specific to MDD versus those reflecting shared pathophysiological mechanisms across disorders. Disentangling disorder-specific from shared sphingolipid alterations and their interactions will require carefully designed studies comparing MDD patients with and without comorbidities, as well as cross-diagnostic comparisons. Fifth, approximately half of MDD patients do not respond to their first antidepressant trial, possibly reflecting biological subtypes where sphingolipid dysregulation is not the primary driver, individual variability, genetic polymorphisms affecting sphingolipid metabolism or antidepressant pharmacokinetics, or sphingolipid-independent pathophysiological mechanisms. This biological heterogeneity highlights the critical need for biomarkers enabling patient stratification and personalized treatment selection. Finally, whether sphingolipid alterations represent trait markers predisposing to vulnerability, state markers reflecting current disease activity, or secondary consequences of other pathophysiological processes remains to be fully determined through carefully designed prospective research.

The relationship between sphingolipid dysregulation and cognitive impairment in MDD requires particular attention, as cognitive symptoms often persist despite mood improvement and significantly impact functional recovery. Plasma ceramides have been associated with faster cognitive decline and increased dementia risk in older adults [ 161 ], suggesting that targeting sphingolipid pathways might address both emotional and cognitive aspects of MDD. Supporting this possibility, long-term SSRI treatment—many SSRIs being FIASMAs—was associated with delayed progression from MCI to Alzheimer’s disease by approximately 3 years in one retrospective study of patients with depression history [ 133 ], suggesting a potential sphingolipid-mediated mechanism, though prospective replication is needed.

The therapeutic latency observed with current antidepressants aligns with the time required for sphingolipid redistribution and autophagy induction. Novel approaches such as direct ASM inhibitors, exemplified by Substance 21b [ 76 ]—which inhibits ASM, induces hippocampal neurogenesis, and normalizes depression-like behaviors in rats—offer the possibility of more rapid-acting interventions, bypassing the accumulation time required by FIASMAs, though clinical safety and efficacy require thorough evaluation. Developing brain-penetrant, selective modulators of specific sphingolipid enzymes could provide more precise therapeutic tools with fewer side effects and potentially faster onset of action than current FIASMAs.

Several challenges require careful consideration in translating sphingolipid research to clinical practice. The long-term effects of systemic sphingolipid modulation remain poorly understood given the essential roles of sphingolipids in multiple organ systems, and preservation of beneficial sphingolipid signaling must be ensured. The complexity of interconnected sphingolipid enzymes and metabolites presents both therapeutic opportunities and risks of unintended consequences to be carefully addressed before clinical implementation.

Research priorities span the full translational spectrum. At the basic science level, priorities include elucidating mechanisms linking specific ceramide species and sex differences to depressive behaviors, and developing and validating selective genetic and pharmacological tools targeting specific ceramide synthase isoforms. At the translational level, priorities include longitudinal and parallel peripheral-CNS measurements to distinguish state from trait markers, large-scale validation of ceramide ratios and ASM activity as prognostic biomarkers, and standardization of sphingolipid assays and establishment of population reference ranges—currently lacking and a source of substantial inter-laboratory variability—as prerequisites for clinical implementation. At the clinical level, biomarker-stratified trials are needed to (i) test whether ceramide profiles or ASM activity predict differential treatment response, (ii) guide personalized interventions—including in treatment-resistant populations—and (iii) explore whether sphingolipid-targeted approaches can be combined with conventional treatments to address both mood and cognitive symptoms.

Continued investigation of sphingolipid pathways—from basic mechanisms to clinical translation—holds genuine promise for developing more effective, biologically-informed, and personalized treatments for patients with MDD.
